title: Wes Streeting’s unintelligible jargon shows how well he’s bedded in at the MoD | John Crace | The Guardian
description: For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets – though he did admit he isn’t ‘keen on fighting a war’
Author: John Crace
Headline: For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets – though he did admit he isn’t ‘keen on fighting a war’
Content: Wes Streeting, who was giving evidence before the defence select committee, looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD.Photograph: House of Lords/PAView image in fullscreenWes Streeting, who was giving evidence before the defence select committee, looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD.Photograph: House of Lords/PAThe politics sketchUK newsWes Streeting’s unintelligible jargon shows how well he’s bedded in at the MoDJohn CraceFor the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets – though he did admit he isn’t ‘keen on fighting a war’Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.18 EDTShareWhen Andy Burnham announced his first cabinet in July, few would have hadWes Streetingmarked down as a likely defence secretary. Not even Wes. And no one is more bullish about Wes’s life chances than Wes. It just didn’t seem a natural fit. Defence secretaries tend to be more the unsmiling types who operate in the shadows. Politicians like John Healey, with the pallor of someone who has spent too long in underground bunkers with military chief of staffs. People who slide in and out of rooms without making a fuss.Wes has always been someone who likes to be noticed. Enjoys the theatre of Westminster. The first to arrive at a party and the last to leave. A natural gossip. “Psst – you’ll never guess what Zelenskyy just said to Trump.”But in the past few months, Wes has had something of a personality change. At the recent Labour party conference, he kept his appearances distinctly low key. No longer the life and soul of Liverpool, out till 2am before getting up to do the media round just four hours later. It can’t be long before we see him driving a tank somewhere near the Russian border. Wes is gonna be Wes.He also has the distinct advantage of not beingPenny Mordaunt, the former Tory minister who has done more to terrify a nation than any living defence secretary. A few weeks ago, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians in which Michael Gove was cast as the prime minister and Penny as defence secretary. The set up was that Russia had torpedoed a ship off Scotland, with the politicians and the military placed in a mock-up Cobra meeting and left to come up with responses as the situation developed.View image in fullscreenAppearing on Sky’s The War Game, Penny Mordaunt – pictured here practising in anticipation of the annual World Conker Championships – was hell-bent on escalating the reality show’s fictional conflict.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThis could have been the moment to restore faith in our democratic institutions. To admire the insight and clarity with which our leaders handle a crisis. To see how they repay the trust and power which we bestow on them. In which case, you should think again. What actually emerged is that politicians are no brighter than the rest of us. They just have egos which make them believe they are the right people in the right place at the right time. And that we are lucky to have them.To put it bluntly, The War Game was a total shitshow. Just one bad decision after another. For the first two episodes, The Govester was like a rabbit in the headlights. Completely clueless as the UK came under increasing levels of attack. The best he could offer was to repeat back the last thing that was said to him and bark “ASAP!”Penny, though, was a total menace to herself and the country from the word go. If this is really how defence secretaries behave, we should all be out digging bunkers in open land and stocking up on tinned food. Not that it would do much good. From the outset, Penny was hell-bent on escalating the conflict despite being told Britain’s military defences were totally threadbare and that the UK was only a middle-ranking global power. She couldn’t wait to use up the UK’s arsenal of weapons, and by the end two nuclear warheads were 20 minutes away from annihilating two major cities. Bye bye Britain. Still, at least she would go down as our last ever defence secretary.So Streeting’s first appearance before the defence select committee was, first and foremost, a moment to give thanks he wasn’t Penny and that we are all – more or less – still here. And Wes looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD. He now talks mainly in letters – SDR, DIP and NAD – and jargon that is designed to be unintelligible to most mortals. Mostly, he wanted to get through the entire session by saying as little as possible and to send any stray reporters who had wandered into the committee room by mistake to sleep. He’d have liked to be more open, he said. But if he was, he’d have to kill us. For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets. If not exactly his happiest place, then still a happy one.View image in fullscreenStreeting’s appearances at the Labour party conference had been distinctly low keyPhotograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAWes began by telling the committee that the UK and its Nato allies were facing their gravest threat since the cold war. Given that, you could understand why he wan’t particularly keen on telling us just how unprepared we were for some kind of an attack as our enemies might be listening. When Streeting had taken on the defence job he had spent most of the first week telling the media that he would – like his predecessor – resign if he thought the money being allocated was inadequate.Three months on and he was rather dancing on the head of a pin. He couldn’t say how, when or even if the commitment to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 would be met. We just had to keep the faith that somehow it would all work out OK. John Healey said it would all end up OK, and if John Healey said so then we ought to believe him. After all, it wasn’t just a question of spending more money – it was also about spending the money he did have better.It also turned out that some of our defence capacity was largely illusory. Both because it took six years for most military contracts to be delivered, by which time there was a fair chance the hardware would be obsolete, and because much of the increased spending had been backloaded until after the next election. Politicians never tire of passing on costs to future governments.The MoD’s permanent secretary, Jeremy Pocklington, spent at least five minutes trying to persuade the committee that backloading wasn’t really backloading even if it looked like backloading. For that kind of mind-numbing bullshit, Jezza has been awarded the Companion of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath. Still, Wes did say at one point that he “wasn’t keen on fighting a war”, which I suppose is a start. Gives him the edge over Penny at the very least.Explore more on these topicsUK newsThe politics sketchWes StreetingPenny MordauntcommentShareReuse this content

title: Could I make six figures from my couch? Influencers said yes – so I tried | Small business | The Guardian
description: I was seduced by content creators hawking easy side hustles. Like the language used in MLMs, it seemed too good to be true
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: I was seduced by content creators hawking easy side hustles. Like the language used in MLMs, it seemed too good to be true
Content: Illustration: Raúl Soria/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Raúl Soria/The GuardianSmall businessCould I make six figures from my couch? Influencers said yes – so I triedI was seduced by creators hawking passive income hustles. Like the language used in MLMs, it seemed too good to be trueVivian HoTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.40 EDTShareA very specific kind of content began taking over my social media feeds at the end of last year.I had just finished a short-term contract and returned, with some reluctance, to the financial masochism of freelancing. As I mourned the end of steady paychecks and paid days off – as well as finally having enough money for regular haircuts – I couldn’t tear my eyes away from the glow of the screen.Atypical videostarts with an ordinary-looking woman doing ordinary things: typing on a laptop, sipping coffee, perhaps doing some light cleaning. Bright, optimistic music blares in the background.Then text stretches across the frame: she has made thousands of extra dollars each month, working just a few hours a day from the comfort of her home.Sometimes the woman – and it’s almost always a woman – speaks directly into the camera. She was able to quit her job and spend more time with her family thanks to her side hustle! It allowed her to pay off debt, cover her mortgage and travel, all while setting her own hours! And with her tips and tutorials, you too can begin making money like her.How AI’s threat to entry-level jobs is turning gen Z into ‘Generation Entrepreneur’Read moreAcross the screen come promises like:“How to makepassive income online…”“How toearn dailywith your phone …”“Side hustles forwomen…”“Lazy girl side hustles that havemade me over $100K…”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe gospel of making money on the side, answering to no one but yourself and with no prior training or special skills, has gone global. As of October, Instagram alone had 8.5m posts tagged #sidehustle and 25.6m tagged #passiveincome, with content creators posting from kitchens in the midwest, beaches in New Zealand, country rambles in the UK and hammocks in Bali.“It’s the perfect hybrid of labor and leisure, where the money comes in as you are going about your day,” said Brooke Erin Duffy, a communications professor at Cornell University who studies the impact of social media on creative work and labor. “The term ‘passive income’ puts an especially seductive spin on this. You don’t have to do anything and you just reap all of the benefits.”These women were offering ways to make money that seemed doable: designing and selling stationery, earning commission on goods I already use, creating products with little to no overhead. The “passive” part would come in after a few hours of upfront work: you set up your hustle once, then sit pretty as the profits pour into your bank account.With my financial future looking a lot more uncertain, I decided to put some of their hustles to the test. I went in with cautious optimism: I wanted to know how realistic these schemes really were, and whether I could actually make money from any of them.What I found instead was what I believe to be the new face of multilevel marketing – and the future of scamming and getting scammed.It’s easy to understand the allure of side-hustle content.Plainly put, things are looking grim. In 2026, amid anaffordability crisis, a few extra hundred dollars a month can be life-changing. It can mean paying down debt, being able to take a sick day or ordering a pizza when you’re too tired to cook.But influencers rarely present side hustles as a response to global financial insecurity. They sell them as easy freedom, attainable without even getting out of bed. It’s easy to see why people buy in.“On TikTok, I see reels that go insanely viral of just girls of all ages, being like, ‘how can I make money from home?’” said Erin McGoff, a career advice content creator who has more than 7m followers across different platforms.I had a few rules for what I was and wasn’t willing to do. I didn’t want to put my face on any social media, and I didn’t want to use AI to create any products or videos.Making and selling digital templates – probably the hustle that resurfaced the most during my nightly doomscrolling – checked all these boxes. The idea is simple: use the graphic design platform Canva to create invitations, planners or ebooks, then sell them on marketplaces such as Etsy. And according to the influencers, the earning potential is enormous:“Use Canva topay off your debtin under 45 seconds …”“Canva is basicallya money printer…”“How Canva canpay your rent…”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueI like pretty stationery and enjoy putting together E-vites centered on ridiculous party themes, so I decided to try it out and go all in with a boozy bachelorette aesthetic, heavy with bright colors and graphics of alcoholic beverages. I named my storeGirlyGirlStationeryand focused on putting together invitation templates that looked like a Barbie fever dream after a night of drinking pink prosecco.But a professional graphic designer, I am not. I got overwhelmed quickly, second-guessing every design decision. I felt myself clenching my jaw trying to align my images and format my borders. In one instance, I had a listing up for several weeks before I realized that I had placed the goose illustration comically off center.To make things worse, a quick Etsy search turned up thousands of templates that looked better than mine, many clearly using the same Canva artwork and styling. Some shops had more than 2,200 templates for sale; it had taken me eight hours to make eight and another five to fix them after realizing I had used Canva Pro elements that buyers would have to pay to download.I made my first sale 12 days after I officially launched my Etsy store – an addictively giddy feeling that was undercut by the fact that I didn’t really make any profit.I had kept the prices of my products low to drive upfront sales, with each template going for $2. Not taking into consideration the one-time $19 fee I paid to set up the shop, but adding in the processing fee, the transaction fee and the listing fee of $0.20 per listing, I made about $1.25 on that one sale.In total for my first month on Etsy – about 23 and half hours of work – my net profit was negative 32 cents.I grew up in the type of middle-class Massachusetts suburb where multilevel marketing (MLM) schemes had a foothold.I remember listening to my mother complain each time she returned from what was supposed to be a casual social gathering but had turned out to be an acquaintance’s sales pitch for tupperware or cubic zirconia jewellery. After graduation, I watched from afar as a number of my former schoolmates began guilting their Facebook friends into buying “buttery soft leggings” and sisterhood-empowering mascara.So when I started watching side-hustle influencers, some of the language felt immediately familiar, particularly in the way they present something nonsensical in a sensical way, making the aspirational seem easily achievable.Take this Instagram video: “Instead of watching Netflix tonight, take 30 minutes, open Canva andcreate a digital productthat you can sell 1,000 times a month for $17. That’s $17,000 each month.”Yeah, OK – the math checks out. And I do watch a lot of Netflix. But wait, will I actually sell this product 1,000 times a month?Most audaciously, some had found another way to monetize the hustle itself.If at first you don’t succeed, buy my masterclass,pdf, ebook or training program, they told their followers. Many of those products traced back to the same small ecosystem, with influencers spawning new micro-influencers who repeat the same scripts.“There are thousands of accounts that are like ‘make money with Katie’, ‘make money with Marie’, ‘make money with Stephanie’, and they all are selling $7 courses,” said McGoff, the career advice content creator. “It’s a digital marketing or digital products course, but what the course does is it upsells you to a more expensive course and then that course just incentivizes people to sell the course.”These courses immediately sent up a red flag for me. And yet, I reasoned, these women weren’t just trying to get me to buy questionable courses, nor were they dangling the prospect of private jets or luxury beach vacations before me. These weren’t get-rich-quick schemes, but a chance tomake some extra cashwithout putting on a bra orchanging out of my sweatpants. They boasted flexible hours that work around nap times and school pickups for mothers and homemakers who already feel exhausted. The upfront costs were minimal: all you needed was an internet connection.double quotation markIt’s a deceptive offer, that somehow you can just do this and that it can work for everybodyStacie BosleyI contacted Stacie Bosley, an economics professor at Hamline University who specializes in the MLM industry. She confirmed that, at face value, these side hustles did not meet the definition of an MLM.In an MLM scheme, Bosley said, “you’re contractually buying the right to sell a company’s products but you’re also getting compensated for recruiting people and that compensation is not really tied to legitimate sales.” She continued: “It’s just sort of dressing around a pyramid scheme in that it’s really not about retail sales, but about recruitment.”These side hustles don’t have one big bad overlord at the top of the pyramid. Each is supposed to be an independent venture: you make a product and sell it. Yet influencers promote them with the cultish zeal of Mary Kay saleswomen. With digital templates, that enthusiasm defies basic economics: if everyone follows their advice and starts selling Canva templates on Etsy, the market becomes flooded, making it harder for anyone to stand out.“It’s a deceptive offer, that somehow you can just do this and that it can work for everybody without any acknowledgment of demand,” Bosley said.***I decided to branch out.Next up was affiliate marketing, another popular hustle that met my personal rules. This one has you promoting a brand’s products through a personalized link that earn you commission whenever someone makes a purchase through it. It’s like a referral code, except you get paid instead of getting a discount.The side hustlers kept telling me that Ididn’t needto have a huge follower countor social media presence to become an affiliate marketer, with companies such as ShopMy, LTK and Amazon Associates making it easy.But like the digital template scheme, it just didn’t make sense. Why would anyone bother to buy a product through me, with my hyperlink, if they didn’t know me?I didn’t want to use my personal social media accounts, but influencers had a workaround: create a new account dedicated to affiliate marketing. SeveralrecommendedPinterest, where you can post images linking directly to products, andDigiStore24as the affiliate network that provides links to products you can earn commissions on.Sadly, most of the products on DigiStore24 are the sort of garbage you would send to your spam folder: shady supplements, weird energy pendants and online courses on how to be a better lover. I decided to try my luck with a light therapy mask – the only product I do use on a frequent basis. I made three pins that all together got 79 impressions in their first six weeks – and no sales.After a few weeks of nothing, I decided to try another affiliate marketing site,FlexOffers.com– and I was almost immediately rejected. The email told me I should get back in touch with them should I “later have more traffic sources”.So I went directly to brands I knew. Sephora’s affiliate program directed me to Rakuten Advertising, where I applied to promote Wet ‘N Wild and Dr Brandt, this time using my actual Instagram account. Both applications were rejected the same day for failing the company’s social media network policy, with no explanation of what that meant.double quotation markWhat they’re selling, it’s the same as MLMs ... They’re selling a dreamMara EinsteinThat was when the logic of the side hustle economy began to come into focus.Influencers had insisted that anyone could do this: no following, business experience or digital expertise required. But almost every hustle I tried seemed to demand precisely those things. “Affiliate marketing is a real way to make money, but it is far from a get-rich-quick secret and it is definitely not passive,”saidMcGoff.What was much more reliable was the attention generated by talking about side hustles. Creators boosted engagement by asking viewers to comment words like “content” or “begin” to receive free prompts and tutorials, turning would-be entrepreneurs into hopeful followers. I watched one woman start a new Instagram account in May devoted entirely to side hustles. Six months later, she had more than 27,000 followers.The hustle, increasingly, seemed to be selling theideaof the hustle. It’s the influencer as a possibility: if you work hard enough and follow their instructions, you too can quit your office job, be your own boss and make six figures for just a few hours of work a day.The pyramid may look different, but by borrowing the tactics, psychology and promises of MLMs, it feels like a pyramid scheme all the same.“What they’re selling, it’s the same as MLMs,” said Mara Einstein, a media studies professor at Cuny Queens College and author of Hoodwinked: How Marketers Use the Same Tactics As Cults.“They’re selling a dream.”And yet, not everyone in this space is a scammer.On one end, there are grifters and creators who aren’t fully honest about their earnings and partnerships. Waleed Khan, a 24-year-old financial consultant in Calgary who isreviewingvarious side hustles, said he discovered that one personpromoting the “clipping” side hustle– when you make money by breaking down popular videos into clips and posting them on to YouTube shorts – was actually the founder behind the clipping website he was instructing viewers to use for the scheme.And on the other end, there are people who really do make these hustles work.After giving birth to her son, Tricia Orme, a 38-year-old mother of two in Washington state, started exploring print-on-demand. And she was “really bad at it” at first, Orme said. “My designs were terrible.”But as she kept going, she found a hole in the market. She needed a way to show customers what her designs would look like on clothing without having to photograph models wearing each product herself. So she began using AI to generate stock images of people in blank clothing, then placing her designs on to them.Thus, she became the @mockupmama. The digital products she sells are the stock images she created on AI, so that others pursuing a print-on-demand side hustle have ready-made mockups on which to display their products.‘It’s become a nepo baby sport’: how secondhand fashion got so expensiveRead moreAfter making $146,578.22 in Etsy sales over the course of three years, she has turned her focus toward mentorship and teaching how to sell and market digital products.“I am such a firm believer that if you have more than you need, build a longer table, not a higher fence,” she said. She has had about 300 people buy a $150-250 course from her and has about 155 active students who pay $19 a month to be in her private coaching group.She is, by all accounts, successful – and that shouldn’t be a surprise. Success stories will happen because once you take away the social media, these hustles are basically a combination of sales and marketing – trades as old as time itself. Digital products, be they print-on-demand T-shirts or silly stationery, is just art you make on a graphic design platform.But not everyone is an artist, or talented at sales or marketing. Orme, for example, had worked in corporate retail and had an understanding of the marketplace before beginning her venture.“It’s like dating apps,” Einstein said. “Almost everybody knows at least one or two people who met through a dating app. So you keep pointing to them like, ‘keep trying, you can do this too.’”“Part of their job is making it look easy,” said Duffy, the Cornell communications professor. But in reality, success in these spaces is a combination of “pluck, luck and the algorithm”, she said.Over six months, I tried to launch five different side hustles. I made just two sales and spent more than $200 on Etsy fees, a Canva subscription and eRank, a tool Orme recommended for identifying popular search terms and boosting sales.Khan, the Calgary content creator, also didn’t make much from digital templates. The only big profit he’s made so far is the C$600 he got for using AI to create websites for small businesses – and that only happened when he got off the internet and put in real world effort.“The claim was you can make $15,000 a month doing this,” he said. “I made these websites. I called 20 or 25 local businesses and calling didn’t work. Eventually I went in physically to these businesses, to 10 or 15, and only two of them said yes.”I had difficulty finding others struggling with their side-hustle journey, as this is not a space with a big audience for failure – but it’s very clear that Khan and I are not the only ones out there.And then there’s the question of what all these hustles are putting out into the world.Every day, new accounts pop up, promising new ways to make money: using AI to copy bestselling coloring books, or churning out slop videos for YouTube views. Etsy, once a haven for handmade crafts and original work, is now awash with generic templates and AI-generated goods.I thought I had escaped the MLM trap: no boxes of garbage to store, no friends to guilt into buying it. But the garbage is still there. We’ve just moved it out of our homes and garages and on to the internet.

title: Check the waistband – and beware sneaky jargon: the expert guide to buying clothes that last | Ethical and green living | The Guardian
description: Should you look for French seams or overlocking? Is dry-clean only a red flag? And how do you spot quality when shopping online? We asked the pros
Author: Hannah Rochell
Headline: Should you look for French seams or overlocking? Is dry-clean only a red flag? And how do you spot quality when shopping online? We asked the pros
Content: Shop smart: a few simple checks can help you spot better-made clothes before you buy.Photograph: Punyupa/GettyView image in fullscreenShop smart: a few simple checks can help you spot better-made clothes before you buy.Photograph: Punyupa/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterEthical and green livingExplainerCheck the waistband – and beware sneaky jargon: the expert guide to buying clothes that lastShould you look for French seams or overlocking? Is dry-clean only a red flag? And how do you spot quality when shopping online? We asked the prosHow to make your leather last a lifetimeHannah RochellTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTake a look at the outfit you’re wearing now: how many times have you worn each item? And how long have you had them? Just over 10 years ago, Eco-Age founder Livia Firth and journalist Lucy Siegle launched the 30 wears challenge to encourage people to buy clothes they would wear at least 30 times.The 30 wears challenge is a great concept. As a journalist interested in sustainable fashion, I’ve enjoyed applying this rule for years and found the goal can often be surpassed, but with one proviso: clothing must be chosen carefully. The goal is only realistic if garments are of good enough quality to stand up to repeated wear. So, how do you know if your clothes really are well made? Does it mean you have to spend a fortune on them? Do you need to know the difference between a French seam and an overlock seam? And how can we judge clothing quality before buying if we are,like 37% of Britons, getting most of our clothes online? I spoke to experts to find out.How to buy clothes that lastCheck the inside of the garmentView image in fullscreenInside out: checking the seams can reveal how well a garment is put together.Photograph: satura86/GettyAsk anyone who knows about clothes how to check for quality, and they will always talk about seams. “A seam’s primary purpose is to give a piece of clothing shape, and crucially structural integrity,” says Leigh Morris, a sustainability and product development consultant. “A bad seam, either poorly constructed or poorly placed, is the difference between a piece of clothing that looks good, feels great, and lasts, or one that feels awkward, looks questionable, and starts to come apart way before its time.”But it’s not necessarily about whether a garment has a premium French seam (which neatly hides raw edges) or a more affordable overlock one (a quicker technique that sews over the raw edges with loops of thread). Both types have their place so long as they are done to a high standard. “It’s very much about whether or not the seams are loose and you can just tug slightly at them to see if they separate easily,” saysAndrea Cheong, a fashion educator and author ofWhy Don’t I Have Anything to Wear?“If the inside is as good as the outside, it’s a good indication we’re on the right track. Examine high-friction areas [that are prone to] splitting, like the crotch on trousers.”View image in fullscreenFeel for it: look beyond the surface for signs of good garment construction.Photograph: koldunova/Getty“In good garment construction, certain inner details are reinforced and properly concealed,” says Vianna Chan, a textile technologist and content creator for the blogStyled by Science. “A quality garment reinforces areas that bear the brunt of daily movement, such as pocket corners and zips. Gently pull both sides of a seam. If you see dense stitches that hold firm, rather than individual threads stretching apart and letting the light through, that is a good sign. Fast fashion skips many of these steps because labour and materials are expensive.”She explains that fast-fashion waistbands, which are often a folded-over fabric sewn on to exposed elastic, are something to look out for, adding that well-made full waistbands, which usually consist of a band reinforced with sturdy interfacing to prevent rolling and conceal raw edges, help spread tension across the waist. “Sewing in a full waistband takes more time [ie labour costs], and requires more fabric and thread. Because these details are not visible from the garment’s outside, they are the easiest place to take shortcuts,” Chan says. So don’t worry if you know nothing about sewing – just get used to turning your potential new clothes inside-out and giving them a gentle tug.Look out for dry-clean-only labelsView image in fullscreenRead before you buy: care labels can offer clues about how practical a garment will be to own.Photograph: Towfiqu Ahamed/GettyWe sometimes think dry-clean-only labels are a sign of good quality clothing, but they can mean the opposite, because the simple act of washing might make the garment fall apart. Morris warns this is especially true for pieces that you would have in heavy rotation in your wardrobe, such as tops and jumpers. “Brands can often default to using ‘do not wash, dry clean only’ labels if the fabric used was primarily selected for look or effect and not for wear, or if rigorous testing was not undertaken in the development and selection process.”These labels place more responsibility for care on the wearer and give the brand more scope to argue that the garment was damaged by incorrect care, rather than badly made.Of course, there are some items that should be dry cleaned. “Tailoring is a prime example due to the complexity of construction and components used,” continues Morris. It’s also worth considering how much you’ll wear the item in question, not least because constant dry cleaning is a pain, expensive, and not great for the environment. “Is it a special garment? Is it tailoring? Is it occasionwear?” adds Cheong. “Also, where did you buy it? Because if you bought it from [a high-street store], it’s unlikely to be such a fine premium material that you do need to get it dry cleaned.”Check what your clothes areactuallymade ofView image in fullscreenMaterial matters: always check the fibre composition of clothing – don’t rely on broad brand claims.Photograph: Marija Bazarova/GettyBeware of material deception, where marketing language can make a garment sound as though it’s made from something it isn’t. Natural fibres such as wool and linen can be more sustainable than some synthetics, and they can feel more premium and are often more breathable and comfortable to wear. That can mean – in my experience at least – you’re likely to wear them more often.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChan suggests that if a brand uses labels such as “silk like”, it may be trying to mimic the look and feel of silk while using a synthetic fibre such as polyester. “Other sneaky examples are: ‘wool like’, ‘linen feel’, ‘premium blend’, ‘natural feel’. None of these speaks to the actual fibre composition and is instead meant to mislead the customer into thinking they are getting something of higher quality. Always read the label as your source of truth.”Watch how the clothes moveView image in fullscreenScreen test: a brand’s social media videos can help you judge how clothes move before buying online.Photograph: Tang Ming Tung/GettyIf, like me, you don’t live near a big city, or even a town with any fashion stores, you probably do most of your clothes shopping online. So how do you virtually turn clothes inside-out? “I think watching clothes and movement is really useful,” says Cheong. “How baggy is the lining? Does the skirt move properly? Does it bunch around the hips and the waist or the shoulders when the model’s moving?” If a brand doesn’t have videos on its website, try looking at its Instagram account. If available, read product reviews and always check the returns policy so you can send back anything that doesn’t pass your home inside-out test.It’s also a good idea to consider the cost per wear of an item before you buy it. This is calculated by dividing the cost by the number of times you expect to wear it: for example, a £30 T-shirt worn the suggested 30 times would cost £1 per wear. The longer your clothes last, the more you are likely to wear them, so even an expensive £200 cashmere sweater would cost just under £1.70 per wear if you wore it once a month for 10 years (I have one such sweater).Buy less and from labels you trustView image in fullscreenBehind the scenes: seeing how garments are made can give shoppers more insight into a brand’s production processes.Photograph: Ekaterina Goncharova/GettyI haven’t shopped on the high street for nearly eight years; instead, I choose to buy from smaller, independent brands and those that produce in limited batches. These types of brands often have a wealth of information about their supply chains, to the point where they boast about the wonderful factories and artisans who make the clothing. In fact, you may even see pictures and videos of the production processes on their websites and social media feeds: a great indicator of quality. Many will add reassurance that their skilled workers are being paid fairly. They may also be using natural fibres with certifications such as the Global Organic Textile Standard, or cotton sourced through schemes such as the Better Cotton Initiative. All this may mean you pay a little more. But in my experience, buying less and wearing more evens out the cost in the long run.If you’re unsure how the clothes you want to buy are made, drop the brand an email or social media message to ask. I have done this many times; it not only weeds out brands that don’t cut the mustard – in turn saving me money – but also builds my trust in those I’ll buy from in the future, albeit less frequently than in my fast fashion days.For more:From beeswax to baby wipes: how to make your leather last a lifetimeHow to look after your knitwear: expert tips to stop shrinking, bobbling and mothsCheck the men’s rail – and embrace imperfection: a stylist’s guide to shopping secondhandHannah Rochell is a journalist who specialises in writing about – and experiencing – a slower, more sustainable lifestyle, which she documents on her SubstackSlowette. This involves everything from switching toeco-friendly cleaning productsand advocating fordehumidifiersinstead of tumble dryers, to shopping exclusively at responsible fashion brands and learning to sewExplore more on these topicsEthical and green livingThe FilterRecyclingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPAView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPAOpinionBrexitBrexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them onRafael BehrRussian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matterTue 13 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTShareRussian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimeaon the European Union.According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”.The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and thatUkraineis not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence.That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union.When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as“ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda”. That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson.There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives.In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it.Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause.This is the context in which Andy Burnham’srecent assertionthat Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit.That isnot a controversial claimto anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional.No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power.Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities.Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaigngot a helping hand from Moscow. The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies.The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anywayare compatible.Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely.Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders.The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel.The hope, entirely vain, is todepress pump pricesand assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November.On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus ofrhetorical venomfor Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia isan Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin.The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture.Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips.It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that heshould be allowed to decidewho governs Venezuela and who sells its oil.That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it.And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”.Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionVladimir PutinEuropean UnionEuropeBoris JohnsonForeign policyUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors? | Piracy at sea | The Guardian
description: The long read: At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?
Author: Michael Scott Moore
Headline: The long read: At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Steffan Roth/Roberto Schmidt/Getty/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Steffan Roth/Roberto Schmidt/Getty/Guardian DesignThe long readPiracy at seaI was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?Michael Scott MooreTue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTShareI knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled toSomaliato report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage.I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant.Tahlil was a skinny, almost cheerful man who spoke little English and swept the junk-littered yard of his unfinished prison house with a grandmotherly calm. When he came into my room, he would give me his snaggletoothed smile and teach me a few Somali words (for “sun”, “cloud” and so on). He carried rifles but never threatened to shoot me. Tahlil did not seem particularly tough – he would cook and wash dishes alongside lower-ranking guards – but he commanded respect. I thought of him as a low-ranking guard leader in the vast school of clan pirates in central Somalia, who ranged from foot soldiers to a handful of top bosses, warlords who travelled with armed escorts. Tahlil said the men who had captured me were the “bad group”, while he and his guards were the good group. He promised to keep me safe in “his” house until the real pirates negotiated the ransom. I heard this kind of thing all the time in Somalia.The “bad group” of rougher and fiercer guards was led by a squat man with rotten teeth named Ahmed Diriye. I had understood Tahlil and Diriye as team leaders of the “good” and the “bad” – so it surprised me when, one day, I saw both men squeeze into the front seat of a crowded SUV to visit some random part of the Somali bush, laughing and joking in the seat like old friends. It would be years before I understood how wrong my impression of Tahlil had been.During my years in captivity, I was usually kept alone. I was beaten on multiple occasions. I saw a friend of mine being tortured. I was frightened most of the time. I was also livid – at my captors, and at myself, for getting kidnapped.For two separate periods I had access to a short-wave radio, and I could listen to whatever programming came into range. One day, on the BBC World Service, I heard a story about Abraham Lincoln. He supposedly gave a speech during the US civil war in which he referred to southerners as fellow human beings who were simply in error. A Yankee woman criticised his meekness and wondered if southerners were not mortal enemies of the union, who ought to be destroyed. “Why, madam,” Lincoln replied, “do I not destroy my enemies when I make them my friends?”I resisted this story at first. I wasn’t interested in edifying tales of secular saints. I lived through most of my days in a state of quiet fury.In September 2014, after 977 days as a hostage, I finally walked free. Two months later, back home in Berlin, I received a Facebook message. It began: “hello michael i am ur friend mohamed”. The author was Tahlil.Had it come from any other pirate, I would have dumped this message in the digital garbage can. But I was curious what Tahlil could want. He wrote: “I am happy u r out of bondage” and wished me a “happy and joyous life”. The message raised my temper. He was trying to ingratiate himself with me, to dissociate himself from the “real” pirate gang, and pretend we were all OK. After 32 months of horror he still thought I would believe his fairytale about “good” and “bad” pirates in Somalia.View image in fullscreenA Somali pirate near a hijacked Taiwanese vessel in 2012.Photograph: Farah Abdi Warsameh/API did not lash out. I wanted information. During the sporadic, long-running conversation that followed, I asked Tahlil to shore up my memories and correct my sometimes blurred impressions of the most squalid phase of my life. He gave names. He sent pictures. He answered questions, not always honestly. He helped me research a book about the ordeal, The Desert and the Sea, which took two years to write.Of course, Tahlil did want something. He must have known that asking for cash wouldn’t work, since my family, friends, benefactors and various magazines I’d worked for had together sent $1.8m in ransom money to Somalia to have me released. But in the spring of 2015, he asked to come to the US. “I live in constant fear,” he wrote, “and I have no one to help me … I am left with only two options: to flee the country illegally or to continue living this way.”At the time, the FBI had an open investigation into my kidnapping, and I had informed them about my ongoing online conversation with Tahlil. I was not about to help him immigrate. But it did sound as if he might cooperate with the government. So if I were to help Tahlil come to the US, it would be to help the FBI arrest him upon arrival. For a journalist it’s no small thing to participate in an operation with the feds, but when the pirates took me hostage, they converted me from a journalist to a kidnapping victim, and I felt that the ethical line had already blurred.I was conscious that Tahlil was not the most important man to throw in jail. On the other hand, piracy is organised crime, and I hoped that a smaller boss, under pressure of evidence, might cough up dirt on his higher-ups. I wanted the right people to be punished. But I knew it was a gamble, in both practical and moral terms.The FBI set up an operation to lure Tahlil to New York, where he would be arrested. “If you have second thoughts about all this,” one agent told me in the fluorescent-lit Manhattan field office one afternoon, “just let us know.” He meant that once Tahlil was arrested, any question of punishment or forgiveness would be out of my hands. The FBI would have a case to prosecute, and my one-time jailer would be subject not to my sense of right or wrong, but to US law.In the summer of 2018, the FBI made covert arrangements for Tahlil and flew him to New York City, where he expected to stay in a hotel for two weeks. There was no promise of payment, but I helped lure him with a fake story about the hotel and “final factchecking” on the book. He, in turn, acted vague about his purposes in America. He seemed to vacillate between hope and despair. He would regularly check in to see if his visa and plane ticket were ready. Sometimes he would say he wondered whether he might get arrested. But he never seemed too interested in seeing me. I think we lied to each other for weeks.On 10 August 2018, when he landed at JFK airport, the FBI arrested Tahlil. The agents said he seemed genuinely surprised. I hoped he would accept a plea and help the Bureau arrest one of the top pirate bosses, such as Mohamed Garfanji. Garfanji was aninfamous figurein the state of Galmudug who had tortured my friend Rolly Tambara, an elderly hostage from Seychelles, by dangling him from a tree by his ankles and beating him with a bamboo cane. Garfanji also threatened to sell me to the terrorist group al-Shabaab. I have not forgiven him.By November, three months after his arrest, Tahlil had still not cooperated, and I was having profound second thoughts. If the full weight of the US government came down on the shoulders of a seemingly gentle and low-ranking boss like him – and no one else’s – the whole operation would seem pointless and cruel. In late 2018, the New York Times publisheda short article about the case. “I’m not as happy as you might imagine that he’s in jail”, I told the journalist.In the comments beneath the article, readers wondered whether I had “Stockholm syndrome”. Some people could not understand how a former hostage could wish anything short of savage vengeance on his captors. He must be hypnotised; he must be traumatised; he must be out of his mind.But forgiving your captors is not the same thing as “Stockholm syndrome”. Not even close.In my first few months as a hostage, my companion in captivity was Rolly Tambara, a 69-year-old fisher with tattoos on his forearms and a dry but unwavering sarcasm. He spoke English in a French-inflected island pidgin. He knew how to be a hostage, having been at it three months longer than me. At this point in my captivity I was still charged with a hair-trigger rage, and he would try to calm me down. Whenever our guards acted in an arbitrary or cruel manner, he mumbled, ironically: “We are the devil, Michael. And they are like God.”He was right. The first thing a criminal needs to clarify once he has you under his violent control is that he is right, and you, by definition, are wrong. As hostages, we lived in a world turned on its head, and the consequences of rejecting its hierarchy could be lethal. “Within a matter of hours, the hostage is treated like an infant and has a kind of regression to infantile emotions,” the influential psychiatrist Frank Ochberg hassaid. “They can’t eat, they can’t talk, they can’t use a toilet, they can’t move without permission. To do it risks death and they accept the feeling that ‘this is the giver of life just like my mother was’.”View image in fullscreenKristin Enmark is taken to hospital after the Norrmalmstorg Square bank robbery in Stockholm, 1973.Photograph: Classic Picture Library/AlamyOchberg was talking about Stockholm syndrome. The term has its origins in a six-day hostage standoff that followed a failed bank robbery in Sweden in 1973. The robber, Jan-Erik Olsson, took several employees hostage at a bank in Stockholm, using a knife and a submachine gun. He demanded freedom for an incarcerated friend, a great deal of money and a Ford Mustang for a getaway car. One captive was a 23-year-old stenographer named Kristin Enmark, who seemed to empathise with him from the start. The Swedish authorities met most of Olsson’s demands within a day. By this point, Olsson had been joined by a friend; when he asked if they could drive away with two hostages – to reduce the chances of the cops shooting him dead – the answer was no. Enmark, during a phone call from inside the bank to Swedish prime minister, Olof Palme, said that she and another woman genuinelywantedto leave with Olsson and his friend in the Mustang. “We are more afraid of the policemen than these two boys,” shetolda journalist in another phone call from the bank.Enmark seemed angrier with her own government than with her kidnappers. This posture mystified both Swedish authorities and the general public. But a psychiatrist named Nils Bejerot – who had worked as a negotiator for the Swedish government – told journalists that all the hostages suffered from a syndrome that led victims to stick up for their abusers. He called it “the Norrmalmstorg syndrome” after the bank’s location on Norrmalmstorg Square. To the rest of the world it became “Stockholm syndrome”.It wasn’t until the following year that the term took hold in the US and beyond. Patty Hearst, the 19-year-old granddaughter of the newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst, was taken from her Berkeley apartment by a far-left gang called the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA). Two months later, Hearst appeared on a bank surveillance video as “Tania”, threatening customers during an afternoon heist in San Francisco. “Up, up, up against the wall, motherfuckers!” she hollered. People wondered if the privileged daughter of a rich American publishing family had lost her mind. Was she brainwashed? Acting under duress? Had she started to workforthe SLA? (She had.) Did she have Stockholm syndrome?After Hearst’s arrest in September 1975, a famous defence lawyer named F Lee Bailey took up her case. He wielded the term “Stockholm syndrome” to keep her out of jail. It didn’t work in the courtroom, but she went free after 22 months because of a commutation by President Carter. Bailey’s headline-making arguments in the Hearst case are the main reason that people all over the world know the phrase “Stockholm syndrome”. But it’s never been listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, because evidence for it has never been clear enough for a formal definition.Whether or not the term is valid, there is no dispute that the pressures on a hostage’s mind are real. Humans can have any number of reactions to absolute rule – rebellion, peacemaking, sympathy, obedience, rage – and no single response is “wrong” in a short-term crisis. Hostages who fall in love with their persecutors, convert to another religion, or identify with a gunman’s delusional notion of the world all give up their sense of self out of self-preservation. The mental strain has to resolve itself somehow.What helped deliver me from my overwhelming sense of murderous anger, after more than two years in Somalia, was something I heard on the shortwave radio. It was a homily by Pope Francis about forgiveness. I was suffering not just from feelings of outrage, but also from a self-lacerating guilt about my own mistakes, which had led me to this miserable existence. I lived with a recurring urge to grab one of the Kalashnikovs and shoot either the pirates or myself. “How many of us perhaps deserve condemnation!” said the pope, adding that a person’s sins were like the stars at night. “We look at the sky, so many stars, but when the sun comes in the morning with so much light, the stars are no longer seen.”This homily woke up a dormant Catholicism within me – not the whole system of belief, but a living river of feeling. I did not have road-to-Damascus conversion, and I wasn’t about to sit down with the pirates for an earnest chat about guilt and reconciliation. But after thinking about the pope’s homily for a few days I noticed how bitterness and anger were acts of will, like suffering itself, and how a slight step backwards, an unhooking of the mind, could let in a flood of mercy and light. I did it in silence. But I found that this mental shift made it easier to smile at the guards in the morning when they delivered a Thermos of oversweet tea and unlatched the steel shutters on my window. Whatever else I was condemned to suffer, I came to see that rage and self-pity were not mandatory aspects of the sentence.When people ask if that isn’t just a “version of Stockholm syndrome”, I argue it was the opposite: to forgive a persecutor helpsmaintainyour sense of self. It isn’t the same as adopting a false view of the world, or identifying with enemy interests. It’s a cool-headed resolution that dissolves the need for vengeance.In retrospect, Enmark understood how strange her state of mind must have seemed to others. When the bank robber came up with the bright idea of shooting another hostage through the leg – promising not to hit any bone – Enmark tried to convince the hostage that it might turn out fine. (“But Sven, it’s only in the leg,” she said.) In an interview many years later, she pointed out that she was in a situation where “all your values, the morals you have, change in some way”. But in a matter of days she had found a working survival mechanism. It’s worth noting that in spite of the criminal’s lunatic threats, no one died in this standoff. Enmark found the right tone to handle an erratic, narcissistic gunman for almost a week.When it was over, the gunman couldn’t believehewas the captive, sentenced to a decade in jail. “It was the hostages’ fault,” he later complained. “They did everything I told them to do. If they hadn’t, I might not be here now. Why didn’t any of them attack me? They made it hard to kill.”In February 2019, six months after they had picked up Tahlil at JFK, the FBI arrested a Somali-American citizen named Abdi Yusuf Hassan in the frozen parking lot of a Starbucks in Minneapolis. In Somalia, he held a formal title, minister of interior of the state of Galmudug, where I was kidnapped and held. Hassan had lived between the US and Somalia for years.The FBI believed Hassan had made off with about $250,000 of the ransom money that had been paid to release me. After that, he had retreated to Minnesota, which left the pirate bosses in Somalia to argue about the remaining cash. (Five ranking bosses died in a shootout over the ransom after I was gone.) I pieced this story together in vague outline when I wrote The Desert and the Sea, but after Hassan’s arrest in Minneapolis, and particularly after the trial of Tahlil and Hassan, I started to see there were whole dimensions of my case that I knew nothing about.View image in fullscreenAbdi Yusuf Hassan.Photograph: Sherburne County Jail/APBoth men were charged with conspiracy to kidnap an American, “terrorism” (in the sense that I was threatened with death in Somalia) and related firearms offences. Neither accepted a plea deal. They each faced 30 years or more, against a mountain of damning evidence.I had rebuilt my life in Berlin and California, and I was anxious to get the trial over with. It should have run for two weeks in the spring of 2020, but Covid and other unexpected troubles delayed things until February 2023. By the time it finally came around, I was sick of hearing cliches about pirates as “protectors of the Somali coast”, and I wanted to see some semblance of official justice.In court, Tahlil looked well-fed and wore a Covid mask. Hassan had grey in his hair. My job on the witness stand was to tell the story of my captivity as I remembered it, from start to finish. The defence objected a handful of times, first at my constant use of the word “seems” or “I had the impression …” and then, sharply, at a comment I mumbled into the microphone: “A lot of this is impressionistic.” All I meant was that it was difficult to know absolute facts in Somalia while I navigated that world as a hostage, without my glasses. But the judge agreed that I should stick to facts, rather than trying to interpret them for the jury.It was cathartic to tangle with defence teams on the witness stand. A lawyer for Tahlil, Steve Lynch, spent part of his cross-examination asking me about guards at Tahlil’s house. “The dozen or so men who were in the house,” he said, “some of these men did not appear to have military training; is that right?”“It was always hard to tell about military training with the guards,” I said, trying not to use Lynch’s own word “appear”.“But some of them seemed to be, you know, people who were fishers – right?” he suggested. I felt a bolt of outrage, because the pirates I met were overwhelminglynotfishers trying to protect their livelihoods. That was propaganda, repeated by well-meaning journalists in the west from the moment pirates had made headlines in 2005. In the 1990s and early 2000s it had an element of truth, but by the time they were hijacking oil tankers and cargo ships, pirate gangs no longer consisted primarily of poor fishers defending the Somali coast from illegal fishing vessels. They were clan soldiers with Kalashnikov training – poor men who needed jobs, certainly, but still members of brutal organised criminal networks.I leaned into the microphone and said, low and clear, so no one in the courtroom would miss it: “Absolutely not.”“Let me ask you this,” he said. “Did some of the people who were there … did they seem to be relatively simple people?”“They were clan soldiers,” I said.Not what the defence wanted to hear. Other witnesses echoed this point during the two-week trial: most pirates were clan soldiers, not simple fishers. The witnesses were Somali spies, informants from the ranks of local Galmudug police or the pirate network itself. One key witness told the court that Tahlil was more sophisticated than the cheerful guard leader he had played around me. In fact he was a captain in the Somali army, the witness said, and he ranked as a mid-level boss in the pirate network.After the trial, as I read the 2,000-page court transcript, Tahlil came into focus. He’d spent a surprising amount of time on the hijacked tuna vessel, out of my sight. The ship, called the Naham 3, was a long-line tuna vessel run by owners in Taiwan and Oman. It had been hijacked in open water near Seychelles, more than 700 miles from Somalia. (Territorial waters for any nation reach 12 miles out.) The ship was 50 meters long and had a vast maze of fish freezers in the hull, which, according to witness testimony, Tahlil had converted to an armoury. “Tahlil was responsible for collecting all those weapons at the end of the guards’ shifts and locking them overnight in the ship’s freezer,” said one US prosecutor, Gillian Grossman, in her summation, “which the pirates used as a sort of makeshift gun locker. Tahlil controlled access to those weapons. He was the only one with the key.”Remarkable. This mass of information shifted my impression of him. I no longer thought of my skinny, mild-mannered Facebook informant as a minor boss. If he stashed weapons in the freezer hold, he was involved in the Naham 3 case, too. I doubt he had hijacked the ship, just as he hadn’t physically kidnapped me – but as an armourer he was responsible for all the pirates’ weapons, and in that sense he was also partly responsible for the long captivity of the 28 fishers held hostage on the ship. Twenty-six of them were finallyreleased in 2016, having spent nearly five years as hostages. Two died in captivity.It also turned out that Tahlil and Hassan were friends, although I had never seen them together. The feds had a binder full of Facebook correspondence and phone calls between them. The defendants called each other “brother” and “my friend”. But Tahlil seemed to acknowledge his own lower rank by using “minister” and “my respected leader”.My urge to forgive Tahlil eroded like a salt statue in the rain. Not that anger or vengeance rushed back; but I was less interested in showing grace. The released fishing crew members that I spoke to had little interest in forgiveness. One Filipino, Arnel Balbero, wrote to me that he hoped “all of the pirates are put in jail … Because of them there’s a lot of dreams in life broken.”As for Hassan, it came out in court that he owned a home in Galkayo just down the road from one of my prison houses. According to a pair of Somali witnesses, it was a hideout and a meeting point for some of the highest-ranking pirates I encountered. Alongside his work as the long-distance interior minister for the state of Galmudug, in his capacity as a local landlord Hassan found a way to profit from my presence in the neighbourhood by renting a house to my kidnappers.I expected to hear some kind of plausible counter-narrative in court about Tahlil and Hassan. It never came. Both men argued that they had infiltrated the pirate gang with some hope of giving me comfort or helping me escape. If that were true, why had they not aided the FBI, never mind the prosecution team? Why did Hassan own a house in Galkayo that was full of ranking pirates? And how did Tahlil come to work as an armourer, responsible for every Kalashnikov I saw, every grenade launcher, every machine gun?The Somali witnesses said Tahlil had reached out to me on Facebook because the top pirate bosses had paid a final, insulting compensation of $8,000 for his armoury services. He had felt stiffed. So he messaged me in 2014 and began to help me with my book, dreaming about a new life in the US. That made sense. I still felt a measure of pity for him that I didn’t feel for Hassan. I had learned some illuminating facts from Tahlil and convinced him to board a plane. After I absorbed the evidence against him, the Tahlil in my mind had become a less hapless, more calculating man, but I didn’t think he deserved a minimum sentence of 30 years.View image in fullscreenMichael Scott Moore in September 2026.Photograph: Steffen Roth/The GuardianGetting these punishments “right”, whatever that meant, felt important for the same reason that forgiveness on the floor of a filthy prison house had felt liberating. It was a form of agency. I had lost my desire for revenge, but not for justice. But, by this point, justice was out of my hands.People talk blithely about closure, as if a criminal case in a bland federal courtroom can bring peace to the victim of a violent crime. I don’t think it can. You have to find peace on your own. The US Department of Justice did a tremendous job in prosecuting my captors, but psychological comfort wasn’t part of the deal.On the day of his sentencing, in late 2024, I read out a terse letter for Tahlil in court. I asked Judge Allyne Ross to hand him less than 30 years if she could. “I know what it is to be held against my will,” I said. “I also learned mercy in Somalia as a means of survival … This is not the same as forgetting what happened.”Tahlil gave a speech insisting on his innocence, insisting (still) that he had wanted “to help Michael”. Ross listened to everything. At last she handed out two 30-year sentences. Tahlil’s would have been lower if a minimum of 30 on one firearms charge were not strict law in New York state. For Hassan, given the weight of evidence, the 30-year sentence was “appropriately severe”, she said, “in contrast to Tahlil’s”.Another of my captors, Bashko, had been arrested in 2021, this time by FBI agents and local police in Djibouti, a nation north-west of Somalia. He was sent to the US, where he faced similar charges in New York – involving conspiracy to kidnap, terrorism and firearms – but pleaded guilty for a lighter sentence.I first became aware of Bashko as a lean and clever young gunman on the Naham 3 who wrapped his head in flamboyant turbans to keep the sun off. He was good-humoured and smart, a ground-level guard from start to finish. For two years, he guarded me almost every day with his Kalashnikov, sitting cross-legged on the floor of a given prison house. We used to hold long, sometimes entertaining conversations in fractured English and Somali during our sweltering prison-house afternoons. Our worldviews rarely lined up – he justified my captivity with the most violent, infidel-phobic verses of the Qur’an – but we had lively arguments.If the poverty trap applied to any pirate I met, I believe, it applied to him. He did not fit the desperate-fisher profile, but he’d signed on as a foot-soldier because he was poor and had few other options. Bashko faced a sentence ranging from zero, or time served, to 25 years, and I saw no reason for him to spend a third of his life in jail. So I wrote a letter to the judge, emphasising his low rank.“His willingness to talk and joke also made my captivity easier,” I wrote. “He ordered samosas for me as a snack. He mediated between me and more aggressive guards, and he sometimes arranged for me to sleep without chains. Once, in a fit of temper, I flushed the keys to those chains down the toilet, which I think caused him a little trouble.”Bashko was sentenced in the fall of 2023. The judge gave a long assessment of the case. “There is a word for the inhumanity of Mr Moore’s kidnappers, all of them, leaders and followers,” said Judge Paul Engelmayer. “The word is ‘evil’. We don’t use that word often in courthouses, and we don’t use it often in criminal sentencing. It is reserved for the worst of the worst crimes. It fits here.”He went on to say that my letter was not the final word. “A court can never subcontract its determination of the just sentence to a victim, whether the victim seeks vengeance or mercy.” But the letter perhaps had some effect. Engelmayer slashed Bashko’s maximum sentence from 25 years to 12 and a half.I couldn’t be at the hearing in New York, but I was told that Bashko was agitated in the courtroom – and that he wanted to give me a “postcard”. His lawyers would be sending it to me, I learned. I was away at the time, and for a couple of weeks I imagined Bashko’s message would be a screed about how I had ruined his life.When I returned home, I found a thick envelope, not a postcard. I opened it with some trepidation. It was a handcrafted greetings card with no language at all, no English or Somali, just a sliding pop-up contraption made of pink and white paper, which, when you opened it, unfolded into an eloquent flower.After his trial, Bashko was moved to Leavenworth federal correctional institution in Kansas, and I tried to visit him while writing this essay. The bureaucratic system was sluggish and unresponsive, but we did manage to speak on the phone.Bashko’s voice was deeper than before, and his English was now strong. He thanked me for writing to Engelmayer. “I know you were helping me, for real, Michael. I want to say I’m sorry … Bashir from 10 years ago? He’s different, for real. Before, I knew nothing. You remember?”“I remember.”“God bless you. Everything is good now,” he said.It was strange, but he sounded excited, even happy.“I can’t hate the jail. I know what I did before,” he said. “I did bullshit.”The business of kidnapping: inside the secret world of hostage negotiationRead moreI raised my eyebrows. In Somalia he had been full of doctrinaire, self-righteous religious beliefs. It sounded as if, in prison, he had arrived at some deeper revelation. “I told the judge: ‘I’m guilty.’ I say: ‘If you give me 30 years, I don’t care. If you give me 15,’ that’s what I told him. I said: ‘Judge, I did wrong. I’m sorry.’”He had no chance of remaining in the US after his prison term. He wasn’t angling for anything in return. He was serious.“Thank you, Bashko. You sound like a new man.”“Your family, everything is good, right?” he said.“My family is good right now, thank you.”“I hope you can forgive me, please.”I hesitated. I’d grown so used tonothearing confessions for this period in my life that I had no idea what to say. A forgiveness that had been completely personal, inward – a form of self-liberation – turned shy in the face of a spoken request. But the piece of mail he had sent was still on my sideboard; in fact I could see it from where I sat with my phone.“Well, yeah,” I said at last. I cleared my throat. “Yes, Bashko.”“Thank you, Michael Scott Moore.”It cost me nothing to grant. I thought about Lincoln and his vaporised enemies. For the first time, I felt something had shifted out in the world – something beyond my own life had transformed because of this halting, doubting, uncertain trajectory of forgiveness I had been writing about for years – and it was more powerful, in its effects, than any project of vengeance.Support for this article was provided by a grant from thePulitzer Center.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
Content: ‘We’re creating alien beings … and the reality is we only have a couple of years to adapt to that’ … computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, Ontario.
