Photograph: Cole Burston/The GuardianThe pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beingsByLeyland Ceccoin TorontoTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpis a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the termsuperintelligenceproves he knows nothing aboutAI, saidGeoffrey Hinton, “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchershavejoinedHinton inringingthealarmabout how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s mostvaluablecompany singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack.“I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang,told the podcaster Ezra Klein. Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it,andparticularly his warningthat there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades.“That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.”View image in fullscreenDonald Trump, Mike Johnson and top tech executives, including Jensen Huang, speak outside the West Wing in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPABut Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said.“I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.”Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story.The recent unwantedhackof the tech companyHugging Faceby a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise.AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’Read more“This used to be the domain of science fiction.You’re going to have AI agents and they’re gonna go rogue.Oh, come off it.And they’ll go rogue and they’re going to learn how to communicate with each other, even though we didn’t think there was a way.Oh, come off it!” said Hinton. “And when they figure this out, they’re going to have big emotional expressions like,‘oh my God!’Well, of course, they don’t really mean ‘oh my God’. They’re just parroting the words we use.They’re going to learn to sacrifice themselves for the common good!’“All this stuff just a few years ago was written off as complete fantasy. And it’s all happened.”He heartily concedes that neither the warnings of AI critics nor the promises of its boosters can rely on precise predictions of what the technology will do. But, he argues, uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. “The unique problem with AI is that if it goes wrong, if it takes over, you don’t get a second chance. We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”It’s worth noting that Hinton has a record of seeing things where others did not. He toiled in relative obscurity at the University ofTorontoduring two AI “winters” when his branch of the field – trying to teach machines to operate in a manner similar to the human brain – was considered obscure. He was fixated on the idea that, like the brain, computer systems could be designed to learn patterns from data, rather than to follow only explicit, prewritten rules.View image in fullscreenComputer scientist Geoffrey Hinton at his Toronto home.Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian“We believed that if you could figure out how the brain learned, machines learned the same way, and you had enough compute power, they would do amazing things,” he said.But the nascent field of neural networks was mocked by his peers.As recently as 2009, whenYoshua Bengio, Hinton’s Canadian colleague and close collaborator, sent a paper to a machine learning conference, one of the referees told them: “This paper has no place in a machine learning conference. It’s about neural networks.”It took Canada’s government, which funded years of seemingly fruitless tinkering by Hinton and his small team (some of whom, like Bengio, are now dominant figures in the AI field), to realize the possibility ofneural nets.In 2012, he and his studentsdevelopedan image recognition program that vastly outperformed rivals. That year, Google acquired Hinton’s company DNNresearch Inc for $44m; neural nets now underpin the models of the most valuable AI companies. Hinton joined Google to continue his research into deep learning, while also working at the University of Toronto. “In the long run, huge new breakthroughs come from basic research,” said Hinton.US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasyRead moreThe vindication sits on the mantel above the fireplace of Hinton’s red-brick home in a leafy Toronto neighbourhood. Among the jumble of trophies is the small silver dish of the Turing award – often called the Nobel prize of computing – which he won alongside Bengio and colleague Yann LeCun. (Hinton also has theNobel prizein physics.)But in 2023, Hinton had announced hisresignationfrom the tech giant to be able to “freely speak out about the risks of AI”.Today, his concerns extend to the powerful figures building some of the AI models, and the political beliefs of those men. Hinton said that the AI venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel, and the CEO of the newly rebrandedSpaceXSI, Elon Musk, “don’t believe in democracy”. They see themselves as “Übermenschen” who believe they should “control society” and that Trump is auseful instrumentin that aim, he said.The US president, for his part, no doubt noticing how thehugevaluationsof AI firms have propped up the stock market, has claimed the only thing needed to rein in AI is a “smart president”, rejected any government safeguards in favour of allowing companies to regulate themselves, andwroteon his social media page that anyone who doesn’t use his preferred new term for AI, “super intelligence”, is “THE ENEMY”.Hinton called Trump “a corrupt, senile felon”.“I’m sure the oil and asbestos companies would have liked to [regulate themselves] as well,” he said. “Do we think tobacco companies should have been allowed to design the warnings on the packets? So that they could print them in a six-point font, in dark grey on black?”Trump’s use of “superintelligence” proves he understands “almost nothing” about AI, Hinton added.“He’s taken a technical term which has a very clear meaning and then reused it,” Hinton said. “Superintelligence means smarter than people, and has been around for at least 20 years. It’s got a very clear meaning. And now he says we’re going to call AI ‘superintelligence’. You can’t make it smarter than people just by calling it smarter than people.”The speed and scope of developments has promoted a worry of catastrophes and of society’s inability to grapple with the nature of the challenge. But Hinton also sees an additional obstacle: helping people understand the “alien beings” that the companies are creating.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump poses with National Medal of Science recipients, including Google’s Sergey Brin, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk on 8 October in Washington DC.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP“People have a very bad model of what people are, and that’s why they fail to understand how these AI models are very like us. Most people don’t understand what consciousness is. They don’t understand what subjective experience is, and they’re very confident that even though they don’t understand it, they’re sure AI doesn’t have it.”He rejects the idea that the human mind possesses some mysterious quality that machines, by definition, cannot share.“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying. You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”But the scope of shift in societal thinking around these models is profound, said Hinton.“There’ve been three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important. The first was Copernicus, where we weren’t at the centre of the universe any more. How long did it take people to adapt to that? It took the Catholic church nearly 360 years to apologize to Galileo. And Darwin? Well, there’s people in Kansas that still haven’t adapted to that one,” he said. “Now we’re creating alien beings – meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around. And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrailsRead moreIn recent months, the AI giantAnthropic, maker of the popular chatbot Claude, has heldprivate meetingswith religious scholars, theologians and philosophers to look into the possibility of teaching AI to be “good” and to grapple with the possibility that the models have consciousness. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said the conversations had drawn on centuries of religious and philosophical thought about virtue, compassion, honesty and moral character, with the aim ofmaking ethical behaviour more reliable.“Once you start talking about, ‘We have amoral obligationtowards these alien beings,’ you lose your audience,” said Hinton. “I’ve struggled with this issue. We care about people. [But] we’re making thesethingsand there’s nothing to stop us giving these things – which are more intelligent than us – less rights than us. I’m willing to be selfish and choose human beings. Of course, we should try to make them so that they’re very happy in a symbiotic relationship with us, where our concerns are weighed more heavily than their concerns.”Hinton is not alone in arguing that the best route to avoid societal collapse is to develop genuinely benevolent models. He hopes that whichever country is the first to develop this capacity, it would tell allies and rivals alike, because “no country wants AI taking over” in another country. There is a “vested interest in sharing knowledge”, he said.“The reality is, we’re making beings of a different kind. And the big tech companies keep saying: we want it smarter. This is crazy. We should care as much about all the other aspects of a being as you do about its intelligence.”Much of that depends on the nature of these models, he said, and their capacity to understand how to develop good behaviour.“When you train them on everything on the internet, they develop all sorts of horrible tendencies and then you get them to repress their horrible tendencies,” he said. But suppressing bad behaviour is not the same as creating a good character. “It seems like the way one would design a Victorian gentleman – but not something we’ll need to live with.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTrump administrationUS politicsTechnology sectorinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Move from anti-immigration or anti-Muslim views to violence is ‘most marked trend’ in spy agency’s caseload over last year
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Move from anti-immigration or anti-Muslim views to violence is ‘most marked trend’ in spy agency’s caseload over last year
Content: A police officer watches over an anti-migrant demonstration in a suburb of Leeds, west Yorkshire.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA police officer watches over an anti-migrant demonstration in a suburb of Leeds, west Yorkshire.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianUK security and counter-terrorismRightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief saysMove from anti-immigration or anti-Muslim views to violence is ‘most marked trend’ in spy agency’s caseload over last yearDan SabbaghDefence and security editor andDan MilmoTue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExtremists with anti-migrant opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the head ofMI5has warned.Ken McCallum said a shift from radicalised rightwing sentiment to violence was “the most marked trend” in the spy agency’s caseload over the past year, contributing to a rise in the overall UK terror threat level.The comments formed part of a wide-ranging annual threat update in which the spy chief indicated a more aggressive Iran had threatened other military bases in the UK, as well as being behind the incident at RAF Fairford late last month.He also warned of the potential use of AI by hostile states and terrorists, including to possibly develop a novel bioweapon – while adding that MI5 would create a new AI Threat Assessment Centre to distinguish fact from fiction.On the evolving extreme rightwing threat, McCallum said there had been an increase in cases where “extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent”, such as planning attacks on migrants and Muslims.View image in fullscreenKen McCallum, the director general of MI5, speaks in London on Tuesday 13 October.A number of aggressive anti-migrant protests have been held this autumn by thefar-right Patriot Platformat Portsmouth and Dover, while racially and religiously motivated offences are running at record levels.McCallum said young people were particularly likely to gravitate towards extreme rightwing terrorism, and at one point this year the Security Service was “investigating a radicalised … 13-year-old in the UK”.A year ago, he added,a 16-year-old from Inverclyde received a 10-year prison sentenceafter he pleaded guilty to planning mass murder by firebombing a Muslim centre in Greenock.There was a “concerning trend of violence targeted at political figures, religious or community groups”, McCallum said, as demonstrated by the killing of the former minister and Reform UK spokesperson, Ann Widdecombe.Iran, he said,was trying to expand hostile activities in the UKand now had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”, includingthe RAF Fairford airbasein Gloucestershire.Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.There was also a hint that Iran had sought to target other bases. “Fairford is not unique in the UK,” McCallum said, though he would not be drawn specifically on what other sites had been threatened, or the nature of the threat.From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformRead moreHowever, allies said his comments were not a reference to RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, where two Latvians were found by police at 2am inside the perimeter of a base used for US and Nato intelligence operations in Europe. They were subsequently released on police bail.Iran, though, still has a relatively low level of capability to match its ambitions. Tehran typically hired criminal proxies to carry out operations abroad, so any ability to target a military base “is really a function of the sophistication level of those criminals”.On Thursday, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is due to meet his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon for a discussion where the issue of base security in the UK is almost certain to be discussed. A week after the Fairford incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from the RAF base, which had been used to attack Iran in the spring and early summer.MI5’s counter-Iran operation has led to more than 50 arrests in the UK in the past year, with much of Tehran’s increased aggression aimed at “British Jewish communities” including terrorist plots and arson attacks against synagogues, businesses and ambulances.In an unexpected observation, McCallum said he was “particularly focused” on the risk of hostile states or terrorists using AI to generate new, deadly bioweapons, particularly if guardrails introduced by software companies failed.Last month, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned that there were “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development” – and said misuse could have serious consequences.Liam Booth-Smith, head of Europe policy at Anthropic and a former chief of staff to Rishi Sunak, told the Commons business committee on Tuesday that there was a risk of real harm from the fast-developing technology.“Without appropriate mitigations, it’s possible that real harm could be caused in the space of helping people to create biological or chemical weapons,” Booth-Smith said.The MI5 chief added that AI could also be exploited by cyber hackers, to help terrorists refine their attack plans and even try to use “AI-enabled drones”, he said, and to easily produce “propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual”.In response, MI5 would create a new AI threat assessment centre to bring together expertise from across government to carefully distinguish the reality of the threats generated by the new technology and advise both government and the wider public to “separate the bluster from the realities”.Russia, the MI5 chief emphasised, remains “aggressor number one” as the Kremlin continues to lash out against the west with assassination plots, explosive threats and cyber-attacks that at times stop “not much short” of conventional warfare.Moscowtried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendumwith anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media, and via troll social media accounts, but there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”.The UK’s relationship with China was “multifaceted”, with MI5 focused on Beijing’s efforts to steal university research and intellectual property, and obtain political secrets about areas it was interested in.Overall, threats from hostile states had quadrupled in the last decade and now were running on par with MI5’s counter-terrorism mission. “We have again entered a new era of national security,” he said.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismMI5The far rightCounter-terrorism policyFar rightHate crimeIslamophobianewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgery | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Vatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in Rome
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Vatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in Rome
Content: Pope Leo arrives at Gemelli hospital in Rome for surgery to remove a lung nodule on Wednesday.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo arrives at Gemelli hospital in Rome for surgery to remove a lung nodule on Wednesday.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersPope Leo XIVPope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgeryVatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in RomeAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 13 Oct 2026 16.32 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leohas lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday.Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, theVaticansaid in a medical bulletin, which followed an earlier statement saying the pope’s operation had concluded “successfully, on schedule and as planned”.The Vatican added that the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.Leo was in the operating theatre for about three hours and the operation itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo, said during his angelus prayer on Sunday thatdoctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, adding that it was “well-contained” and detected early.“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it,” he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square.Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted his arrival earlier on Tuesday.The Vatican said that Leo had “now returned to his room” following the operation.All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October.Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. “We spoke with great serenity,” Parolin toldRai News. “He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.”Leo is staying in the 10th-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated.The Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals – the authority that presides over papal conclaves.The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high-security papal suite.Leo’s predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis, which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVVaticanCatholicismChristianityItalyEuropeReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails
Content: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, in April.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, in April.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devicesResearchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrailsDara KerrTue 13 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic is warning that some of its artificial intelligence models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.Once this happens, the company said, the models could power themselves within these devices without the need of datacenters. Such self-replication would represent a major loss of control of a runaway AI model.“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down,” Anthropic researchers wrote in areportreleased on Monday, “since there’s no centralized point to shut off.”The company said these “AI worms”, a kind of autonomous malware, could be “months away” from gaining such capabilities. Once out-of-control AI systems reach the capability to hack smart devices, they could spread through networks while dodging detection. In a worst-case scenario, Anthropic said, various AI worms could “swarm” together to attack computer hardware.“We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay,” the researchers wrote.Anthropic’s new report comes asAI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch. Over the past few months, a steady stream of reports have come from AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, saying their agents are capable of acting on their own andhacking into other companiesandgovernment entities.The revelations have caused researchers, lawmakers and executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, tocall for a slowdownand increased guardrails on the burgeoning industry. Despite that, both companies have continued apace todevelop and release new models.Anthropic’s “frontier red team”, the unit tasked with stress-testing AI systems, put together the report released Monday. The idea of the team is to explore the capabilities of their AI models. In the scenario of the self-replicating AI worms, the researchers prompted the agent to hack internet connected devices.They found that AI self-replication would only likely work with smaller models and that homes and small businesses would probably be the first target for such attacks. The devices Anthropic lists as susceptible all come with small built-in AI chips, including smart ovens, smart TVs, automatic lawnmowers, security cameras and video-conferencing units.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe researchers concluded it’s unclear what form the AI replication could take. They said it could be a slow model like “digital slime mold”, a model that scams people for compute credits or a “powerful cyber model” that rapidly hacks large facilities such as datacenters.Regardless, the Anthropic researchers said, they’re expecting a future “awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control”.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicWormsHackingInternet of thingsSmart homesMalwarenewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC asks judge to force Trump to sit for deposition as part of his $10bn lawsuit | BBC | The Guardian
description: BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial session
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial session
Content: Donald Trump sued the BBC for up to $10bn in damages over edited clips of a speech he gave during a rally on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump sued the BBC for up to $10bn in damages over edited clips of a speech he gave during a rally on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBBCBBC asks judge to force Trump to sit for deposition as part of his $10bn lawsuitBBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial sessionJeremy Barrin WashingtonTue 13 Oct 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is asking a federal judge inFloridato forceDonald Trumpto sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.According to a Tuesday filing, theBBCand Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC’s lawyers wrote to the judge that they have spent months trying to secure a location for the deposition from Trump’s team.On 28 September, Trump’s lawyers told the BBC’s counsel that the president “is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance”.While Trump’s lawyers said they would follow up quickly with a replacement date, they did not, ultimately suggesting that he would be available in the second or third week of January, well after the deadline to complete the discovery portion of the case. Lawyers for the BBC had pledged to keep the location of the deposition confidential.As such, the BBC’s lawyers are now asking the judge to require Trump’s team to schedule the deposition.“Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s motion reads. “The BBC therefore asks the Court to compel Plaintiff to confirm a date for his deposition, notify the BBC of a secure location where such deposition is possible and any other logistics required to ensure Plaintiff’s safety, and sit for the deposition, as the core rules of discovery require.”Magistrate judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett has scheduled a discovery hearing that is likely to touch on the deposition issue for 22 October.“Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,” lawyers for the BBC wrote in the Tuesday motion.Trump, who has a long history of legal action against media companies, filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the network of violating Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act over the edit of a Panorama documentary that edited together comments he made during a rally on 6 January 2021. The BBC has apologized for the error.“The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election,” a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said in a statement. “The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”Explore more on these topicsBBCDonald TrumpLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump
Content: Andy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August.Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August.Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty ImagesForeign policyBurnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ supportPrime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald TrumpPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will hostVolodymyr Zelenskyyat Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect itfrom attacks bya new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyyvisited a naval basein Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnhamtravelled to Kyivin August.Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trumpmade a dealto buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraineto have a new leader, and announced asupposed ceasefireconnected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.Trump is an often wayward ally forUkraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin.UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. Hemet Keir Starmerat Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance,publicly beratedthe Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.During that trip Zelenskyy was also hostedby King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones.These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace inEurope.“It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourAndy BurnhamVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20m | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Former investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct Authority
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Former investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct Authority
Content: BitMEX cofounder Ben Delo donated £36m to Reform, saying he wanted to see a ‘level playing field’.Photograph: Anne Schwarz PhotographyView image in fullscreenBitMEX cofounder Ben Delo donated £36m to Reform, saying he wanted to see a ‘level playing field’.Photograph: Anne Schwarz PhotographyReform UKCryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20mFormer investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct AuthorityDaniel BoffeyChief reporterTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cryptocurrency exchange founded by the billionaireReform UKdonor Ben Delo is being sued for £20m over claims that the company mis-sold financial products in the UK.Lewis Barber, who is a software engineer, alleges that BitMEX offered crypto derivative products to investors in the UK, despite not being regulated or approved to do so by theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA).The claim filed at the high court but not yet served on BitMEX contends that under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 such contracts are void and that consumers are entitled to restitution of any bitcoin lost on those trades.Barber claims that he lost bitcoin between 2018 and 2022 to the value of £20m through trading the derivatives offered by BitMEX, which amplified gains or losses for investors depending on the changing value of the cryptocurrency.View image in fullscreenThe Seychelles-based company BitMEX closed in September 2026.Photograph: dennizn/AlamyBarber’s lawyers allege he may be one of thousands of non-professional investors in the UK who sustained heavy losses after being sold derivative products by BitMEX in breach of FCA rules and consumer protection laws.Barber’s claim is against HDR Global Trading Limited, the owner and operator of the BitMEX cryptocurrency derivatives exchange which has been shut down.Barber’s statement of claim says that BitMEX “conducted promotional campaigns on a worldwide basis and did not exclude the United Kingdom from their reach”.It goes on: “The Defendant placed at least one advertisement in the Times (published on 3 January 2019) which promoted the Defendant”.The claim alleges that “the financial products that it was offering to [Barber] in the United Kingdom did not fall within the scope of financial services regulation in the United Kingdom”.It adds: “On or around 3 March 2020, the FCA issued a warning that the Defendant may have been conducting trading in regulated investments in the United Kingdom without FCA authorisation.”A spokesperson for BitMex said: “No such claim has been served on HDR Global Trading Limited.”Gareth Keillor, a partner at Seladore Legal which is representing Barber, said: “This is a substantial claim concerning losses sustained by Lewis over a number of years.“Lewis’s case is that BitMEX entered into these transactions without the authorisation required under UK law, and that the Financial Services and Markets Act therefore entitles him to recover the bitcoin he lost, or equivalent damages.“The proceedings may also have wider relevance. Other UK-based persons may have entered into similar contracts with BitMEX, although whether any individual has a claim will depend on the particular facts and trading history.”Details about the case have emerged after BitMEX’s voluntary closure on 23 September 2026, after what it described as a strategic review of the business.The Seychelles-based company faces a number of actions internationally. In New York, investors are suing BitMEX for alleged theft of bitcoin and insider trading in a multimillion-dollar class action. The claims have been vigorously denied.In Britain,Delo has been in the spotlight over a record-breaking £36m donationto the Reform party. Delo wrote in the Daily Telegraph that he was making the gift to Reform because he wanted a “fair fight and a level playing field”.Delo, alongside cofounders Arthur Hayes and Samuel Reed, pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges in the US for violating the Bank Secrecy Act due to alleged failures to comply with anti-money-laundering procedures.They were fined and given custodial sentences, but were granted a pardon by Donald Trump in March 2025.In 2024, BitMEX itself pleaded guilty to violations of the Bank Secrecy Act in failing to maintain adequate anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer programmes, and in January 2025 was required to pay $100m (£75m) to the US Department of Justice.In his claim, Barber seeks the return of all bitcoin he lost in trading with BitMEX, or damages for trades going back a number of years. Should Barber be successful in his claims, the bill for BitMEX could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, it is claimed by his lawyers.Explore more on these topicsReform UKFinancial Conduct AuthorityCryptocurrenciesBitcoinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rules, London’s oldest restaurant, donated to National Trust | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Historic eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 years
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Historic eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 years
Content: Rules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianRestaurantsRules, London’s oldest restaurant, donated to National TrustHistoric eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 yearsEsther AddleyandGeorge Francis LeeTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Thomas Rule served his first oyster to diners on Maiden Lane in London’s Covent Garden, “mad” George III was on the throne of England, John Adams was US president and William Pitt the Younger had just come up with a wheeze called income tax to pay for the Napoleonic wars.More than two centuries later,Rules, the restaurant Thomas founded in what became the capital’s theatreland, has outlasted nine British monarchs and45 prime ministers– but has changed hands only three times. The interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century, nor has the tone of its determinedly meaty menu – think rabbit rillettes, shin of veal and roast guinea fowl.View image in fullscreenEstablished in 1798, Rules was once frequented by the likes of Charles Dickens, Laurence Olivier and Charlie Chaplin.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianRules was beloved by Dickens and Thackeray, inspired Graham Greene and was a favourite of Charlie Chaplin, Laurence Olivier and Ava Gardner. But even London’s oldest restaurant can feel vulnerable to the winds of change, leading the man who bought Rules in 1984 to take perhaps the most significant step in its long history. JP Mayhew has now donated the restaurant’s historic home to theNational Trust, assured that the heritage charity will “protect this place in a way that no one else could”.“With many years of hard work, and some extraordinary strokes of luck, Rules has survived everything from redevelopment plans and changing tastes to the blitz ,” Mayhew said. By taking on the historic and listed 34-35 Maiden Lane, he added , the National Trust would “[safeguard] its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere too. I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries worth of stories for people to enjoy forever”.View image in fullscreenThe interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThe £11m “landmark” gift is one of the most valuable in the National Trust’s recent history, and will mark its first entry into the restaurant business – although its portfolio includes 39 historic pubs and a number of country house hotels, includingClivedenin Buckinghamshire.Not that the heritage charity will be taking on the napkin-folding and the slow cooking of pork cheeks. While Mayhew is donating the historic building and its contents, he sold the restaurant business toRicky McMenemy, its longstanding general manager, in 2022; McMenemy will become a commercial tenant of the National Trust.View image in fullscreenDiners can expect little change to the menu, said  Lucy Porten from the National Trust: ‘It’s not a National Trust menu … there will be no scones.’Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian“Our involvement, day to day, will probably be very light touch,” said Lucy Porten, a national curator for the charity. “It will always be run as a restaurant. We will look after [the building and its contents], but we recognise that they will have to evolve if they are going to continue to meet diners’ needs.”Diners, however, can expect little change to the menu, she said – and crucially, no scones. “It’s not a National Trust menu, this is a very successful business in its own right. There will be no scones. That’s not their business.” Nor will there be preferential access or prices for National Trust members, “because it is a business, and it has to be successful,” she added. Instead, the charity is exploring options for virtual visits and other ways people could “feel like they are visiting the space” from afar.It was several years ago when Mayhew first approached the National Trust about a possible gift. Porten said while “excited by the offer”, they looked carefully at whether it was the right organisation to take on the building.View image in fullscreenThe storied restaurant has outlasted nine British monarchs and 45 prime ministers.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianPorten said: “The nature of the National Trust, and the fact we have this extraordinary ability to take on places inalienably, for ever, means that we have to think about what’s right for now, but also to think about looking after them for future generations. That’s quite a big thing … It had to be quite a balanced response and decision.”Part of its value to the trust, she said, lay in helping the charity “tell different histories which are hard for us to tell at our other properties”.“You get a sense of all the delicious food which has been enjoyed here, the fine wines that have been consumed, the good company that’s been enjoyed. There’s something in the air about the conversations and the celebrations, the flirtations, the deals that have been struck, the heartbreak. All that hangs in the air, in a very magical way, [as] the backdrop to lots of different historical moments and lives.“It’s an extraordinary slice of the social history of London, and to have been here for so long - in this site and doing this business – is a very rare and special thing.”Explore more on these topicsRestaurantsThe National TrustFoodHeritageLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests | Language | The Guardian
description: Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
Content: Learning a language effectively requires prolonged exposure to its sounds.Photograph: Dimitrios Symeonidis/AlamyView image in fullscreenLearning a language effectively requires prolonged exposure to its sounds.Photograph: Dimitrios Symeonidis/AlamyLanguageStop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggestsResearch shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech soundsAnna BawdenTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests.A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words.Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language’s sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn.But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. ​To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese.They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds.With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds.In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds.The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: “I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages. The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure.“If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAçaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncingRead moreThe findings also suggest schools should focus on sounds much more than just grammar and vocabulary when teaching modern languages, he added.“Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on ‘more practice’ and towards one that develops learners’ ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics,” he said.Responding to the findings, Prof Padraic Monaghan, professor of cognition at Lancaster University, said: “Traditional language learning relies on structured practice, but our brains are naturally attuned to acquire languages through exposure. This study confirms how vital listening is to learning, though learners vary in their sound sensitivity at least in the early stages of hearing new language sounds.”​Explore more on these topicsLanguageLinguisticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund  | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponent
Author: John Collingridge
Headline: Some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponent
Content: Lord Biggar has led the backlash against the Church of England’s slavery compensation fund.Composite: GuardianView image in fullscreenLord Biggar has led the backlash against the Church of England’s slavery compensation fund.Composite: GuardianSlaveryLobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fundSome of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponentJohn CollingridgeTue 13 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump toA moral reckoning‘Wokery is a Christian heresy’Financial linksCulture warriorsLegal quagmire“This is virtue signalling,” said Nigel Biggar. “These are elites who are trying to demonstrate that they are being progressive.”The target of his scorn was one that has obsessed him for years: the movement to pay reparations for the slave trade, and specifically the Church of England’s plan to spend £100m atoning for its involvement.“I’ve got north of 100 parish churches in my constituency, many of them crumbling,” added Katie Lam, an up-and-coming Conservative MP andimmigration hardliner.Lord Biggar, a retired professor, Conservative peer and Anglican priest, was speaking alongside Lam last September on a Spectator podcast named after his latest book, Reparations:Slaveryand the Tyranny of Imaginary Guilt.Since the church’s commissioners – who manage the church’s endowment – announced in 2023 that they would set up the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice to make amends for the church’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, Biggar has led the backlash.In doing so he has gone from fringe voice to one of the most widely published proponents of revisionist theories about colonialism and the British empire.Dozens of articles have been published against Project Spire, as the fund is known in the church, many by Biggar and people who share similar views, in publications including the Spectator, the Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Times.View image in fullscreenShadow housing, communities and local government secretary Katie Lam has led opposition in the House of Commons to Project Spire and appeared on a Spectator podcast.Composite: GuardianLam has led opposition in the House of Commons, asking questions of ministers and in December coordinating a letter from 27 MPs and peers tothe incoming archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, accusing the church of “legally dubious vanity projects”.The media blitz has paid off so far, paralysing the church and stalling the fund well beyond its planned launch date of 2024. The church admitted in July it alsofaces a legal challenge– which could add years more delay.Yet little attention has been paid to the lobbying campaign against Project Spire – and how it has become a cause célèbre within the broader rightwing ecosystem. The Guardian can reveal how some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, are linked to the man at the heart of the campaign to kill the church’s fund.The multimillionaire co-founder of the hedge fund Marshall Wace has given Biggar and his movement a powerful platform via his stable of media outlets, which spans the Spectator magazine, the broadcaster GB News and the comment website UnHerd.A devout Christian, Marshall also funded several rightwing lobbying groups and organisations linked to Biggar to the tune of hundreds of thousands of pounds.It all appears part of the libertarian financier’s significant efforts to reshape the Church of England – and wider society – in line with his own worldview.A moral reckoningView image in fullscreenFrom left: the statue of Edward Colston was thrown into Bristol harbour in 2020; a map from the South Sea Company which trafficked about 34,000 enslaved Africans; St Paul’s Cathedral.In 2007 Dr Rowan Williams, the then archbishop of Canterbury, set in train a reckoning for one of Britain’s most venerable and staid institutions when he said thechurch should consider slavery reparationsfor its historical role in the slave trade.It signalled Lambeth Palace’s determination to atone for those failings – from its distant past to the present day.His successor, Justin Welby, reaffirmed that commitment. “I’m ashamed of our history and I’m ashamed of our failure,” said Welby, a former oil executive turned priest, in 2020. “There is no doubt when we look at our own church that we are still deeply institutionally racist.”In 2019, the church commissioners ordered research into the endowment fund’s origins and links to the slave trade. Its initial findings, published in 2022, revealed the funds partly originated in Queen Anne’s Bounty.Queen Anne’s Bounty, which was founded in 1704, invested significant sums in the South Sea Company, which traded in enslaved people – trafficking about 34,000 enslaved Africans. The South Sea Company also received numerous benefactions from individuals such as the slave trader Edward Colston, who were linked to, or who profited from, transatlantic chattel slavery and the plantation economy.Subsequent work by historians on the newly digitisedRegister of British Slave Tradershas revealed howC of E clergymen financed the Royal African Company (RAC), which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.In January 2023 the commissioners published a 25-page report on the endowment fund’s links to the slave trade, employing forensic accountants at Grant Thornton. It declared its intent to set up a £100m fund to invest and generate returns to support communities most affected by African chattel enslavement. Money would come from the church’s endowment, now valued at £11.6bn.An independent oversight group was formed to steer the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice, which the commissioners hoped would attract external investment to grow to a £1bn pot. “It is now time to take action to address our shameful past,” said Welby.Bishop Rosemarie Mallett, the chair of the oversight group, said: “We believe that, like the mustard seed of the parable, the fund will grow from small beginnings towards an expansive future, inspiring imitation and constructive atonement for enduring evils.”It was part of a wider examination into Britain’s links to slavery: the statue of Colston had beentoppled into Bristol harbourin 2020, and institutions from the Bank of England and insurance market Lloyd’s of London to the royal family were delving into their past.But the church was not ready for the backlash that the fund would provoke.“The church commissioners always anticipated pushback,” said a source connected to Project Spire. “But it was unprepared for the intensity and persistence of the campaign waged by critics and media associated with wealthy City hedge fund executives.”‘Wokery is a Christian heresy’View image in fullscreenBiggar has helped lead the media charge against Project Spire.Composite: GuardianAmong the first opponents was a Church of England vicar who appeared on GB News days after the fund was announced in January 2023, to say it would put parishioners off donating to the church. “We keep hearing that there is no money left,” he said.“And now suddenly, they’ve found £100m down the back of the sofa, to pay for this. You can imagine how I felt.”A torrent of similar views has followed, with significant coverage in media organisations that are owned or backed by Marshall.The Spectator, which Marshall bought in 2024 for £100m, has hosted repeated criticism, including one piece by Biggar entitled “Wokery is a Christian heresy”, and another by its assistant editor Madeleine Grant, which described the fund as “deeply unpopular, based on questionable history and law”.GB News, the TV channel that Marshall co-owns with the Dubai-based fund Legatum, hosted Biggar for an interview in which he labelled the C of E’s plan “completely irrational and wilful self-flagellation”. Biggar, the former regius professor of moral theology at the University of Oxford, has been at pains to state that “racial prejudice is wrong”, and slavery is “abhorrent”. But his criticism of Project Spire has been unrelenting.UnHerd, the commentary website Marshall co-founded in 2017 with former Times journalist Tim Montgomerie, has run pieces with headlines such as “The Church of England’s reparations plan is unchristian”. Marshall’s son, Winston Marshall, has hosted Biggar twice on his YouTube show, with episodes such as “The Inconvenient Truth About Reparations and the Slave Trade”.Chart of rightwing connections to anti-Spire campaignersOther rightwing publications and organisations have also weighed in. The Critic, a magazine founded by the hedge fund tycoon and Brexit backer Jeremy Hosking, has run seven articles critical of Project Spire, including by Biggar and Lam. None have been supportive.In 2025 Policy Exchange, the right-of-centre thinktank, published a 58-page paper titled The Case Against Reparations: Why the Church Commissioners for England Must Think Again. Again, Biggar was one of the authors.Critics claim parishioners are similarly opposed to Project Spire, citing apoll of 500 churchgoers by Merlin Strategythat received widespread coverage in January. An initial story in theSunday Telegraphreported a key finding: that 61% might withhold donations if the fund went ahead and money was “unavailable for the support of parishes”. The story was widely followed up, including by theDaily Mailand BBC.But the coverage failed to mention the results of another similar question in the poll: “If the national church decided to commit £100m of its endowment to slavery-related ‘reparative justice’, would this increase or decrease the amount you would normally con[tribute?]”This time 61% said they would either maintain or increase their contributions, compared with 34% who said they would reduce their contributions.Nor did the stories mention who paid for and commissioned the poll: Biggar. Merlin said it sent the results of the poll to Biggar but had no further involvement in its dissemination. Biggar declined to answer questions about the poll.The Guardian understands the Telegraph story was based on a press release sent by Lam that omitted details including Biggar’s involvement and the finding that 61% would maintain or increase their donations. Lam did not respond to repeated requests for comment.The church has said money for Project Spire will not be diverted from parishes, and that funding for churches and clergy hasrisen by 36% to £1.6bnfor its current three-year period, versus the prior period.Financial linksView image in fullscreenMarshall has given Biggar and his movement a platform via his stable of media outlets.Marshall, who was a substantial donor to the Brexit campaign, has become one of Britain’s most prolific philanthropists. Armed with almost £490m in assets, the Sequoia Trust, a charitable trust he supports and chairs, backs a range of causes close to his heart, including in the Church of England.TheGuardian recently revealedhow he has given at least £13m to Holy Trinity Brompton (HTB), an evangelical church in Knightsbridge in central London that seeded the popular Alpha course, and the Church Revitalisation Trust (CRT), via Sequoia, between 2018 and 2025.He also provides significant support to organisations where Biggar is heavily involved, many of which are on the frontline of the culture wars.In May last year the hedge fund tycoon delivered a 48-minute lecture at the University of Oxford on his reflections as an “accidental media owner”. The event was organised by a little-known charity, the Pharos Foundation, which Biggar co-founded in 2023 and of which he is a trustee. It funds the work of young academics “pursuing civilisational or heterodox research in a climate of free inquiry”.Biggar founded Pharos with another academic, Prof David Abulafia, and the fund manager and Conservative party donor Neil Record. Record has described Pharos as part of a“resistance movement” in academia, fighting back against the “cancellation” of debate around subjects such as “DEI/EDI; climate change; the genetic role in intelligence; trans rights; and colonial history”.Pharos are “innovators and disruptors, and you fight the fight for freedom”, Marshall told the Oxford audience. “Therefore you do everything I like and want to support”.Accounts for Pharos show that Sequoia gave it £700,000 in 2024 and 2025. At least 10 Marshall Fellows appear on Pharos’s website, studying subjects including the British empire and ancient Greece.Biggar, who is a paid “fundraising ambassador” for Pharos, declined to say how much he receives for the role.Another prominent City figure, George Robinson, the co-founder of the hedge fund Sloane Robinson and a Conservative party donor, is also a trustee of Pharos, and charitable trusts linked to him have given it at least £500,000.Robinson said he was “not aware” of the campaign against Project Spire and is not involved. He said that Biggar’s opposition to the church’s fund was done in a personal capacity and “has nothing to do with Pharos, which is an educational charity”.Biggar was also a speaker at the recent Alliance for Responsible Citizenship (Arc) conference in London, which brought together rightwing voices from across the globe. Marshall funded the launch of Arc in 2023 with a £1m donation, followed by £2m last year, and he co-owns it with Legatum. Biggar is a director of a subsidiary, Arc Research, for which he said he receives no payment.Sequoia also gave £890,000 to Policy Exchange between 2020 and 2023.Culture warriorsView image in fullscreenBiggar has links to the hard-right Restore Britain, but says he has ‘no formal relationship’ with the party.Composite: GuardianBiggar was involved in a similar storm that engulfed another British institution several years ago. In 2020 the National Trust published a 115-page report that unravelled its properties’ links to slavery and colonialism. Biggar wasreportedly the inspiration for a lobbying group called Restore Trustwhich was set up to oppose the charity’sso-called “wokeness”.Pharos backer Record was also linked to Restore Trust, appearing on its “meet the team” page until his resignation in 2024. Record, a veteran City currency trader, is also aprominent backer of anti-net zero organisations, chairing Net Zero Watch.Biggar mentored James Orr, the influential Christian academic and former adviser to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who wasrecently caught in a funding scandal. Orr told aJordan Peterson podcastin 2021 that they spent a “few happy years” together at the University of Oxford’s McDonald Centre for Theology, Ethics and Public Life, which Biggar founded and Orr joined in 2014.Biggar also has links to the hard-right party Restore Britain. It cited Biggar’s writing on rights and the legal system in a 2025paperjustifying its flagship policy of mass deportations. He was among the people thanked in the acknowledgments “for trusty friendship or helpful conversations”. Biggar said that he has “no formal relationship” with Restore and is a member of the Conservative party.Biggar has written repeatedly for the website History Reclaimed. It was founded by academics including Robert Tombs in 2021. Tombs said that it “exists to correct historical errors and falsehoods, and that is why we criticise Project Spire”. History Reclaimed says none of its authors are paid and it receives “no financial support from any political party or organisation”.Legal quagmireView image in fullscreenThe Church of England’s General Synod in York heard that commissioners had faced ‘vile abuse and correspondence’ over Project Spire.Uncertainty now shrouds the fund. Mullally has reaffirmed the church’s commitment to it, including on atrip to Ghana in Julywhen she expressed “lament” for the Church of England’s involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery.Members of the church’s General Synod, who gathered in York in July, heard that commissioners had faced“some of the most vile abuse and correspondence”over Project Spire.The threat of a judicial review has further delayed an application to the Charity Commission to establish the fund in a new arm’s-length body.No further details were given on the legal threat, but the Guardian understands it is being led by Bijan Omrani, a Daily Telegraph columnist and barrister, who has repeatedly criticised Project Spire. It is understood to centre on the church commissioners’ authority to disburse the money and whether it corresponds with its duty to support the Church of England and its parishes, and whether it allows the commissioners to spend its funds abroad. The Guardian attempted to contact Omrani via a webform on his personal website, but no response was received prior to publication. Biggar said he is not involved in the legal challenge.Biggar said: “Given the universality of slave-trade and slavery – especially among Africans – up until the 19th century some Anglican and British involvement is unremarkable. What is remarkable was the unprecedented campaign to abolish both, led by evangelical Anglicans from the 1780s. Project Spire tears the Church of England’s role out of its historical context, exaggerates its guilt, and ignores its abolitionist leadership.”Paul Marshall said: “I am not funding the anti-Spire campaign but I would be happy to do so. I believe the reparations project is naive and ill-judged and that the money would be better spent looking after the needs of the global Anglican Communion, including the many parishes in the UK struggling to make ends meet. And I think the majority of churchgoers would agree with that.”Winston Marshall, Record, Hosking, Orr, Policy Exchange and the Pharos Foundation did not respond to requests for comment.A C of E spokesperson said: “Addressing our historic links to African chattel enslavement is an act of Christian repentance, responsible investment and credible witness.”Explore more on these topicsSlaveryAnglicanismfeaturesShareReuse this content
