title: Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation? | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster
Content: Volodymyr Zelenskyy on a large screen. Experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.Photograph: Attila Husejnow/APView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy on a large screen. Experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.Photograph: Attila Husejnow/APUkraineExplainerDid Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass musterAisha DownTue 13 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the weekend, Ukraine carried out at least three airstrikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian search engine company Yandex. Reportssuggestat least two of these datacentres took significant damage, with Telegram footage appearing to show one on fire. Yandex acknowledged the strikes, and Russian media reported that several websites appeared affected by the downed datacentres.On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the strikes had dampenedRussia’s massive disinformationoperation,saying: “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.”It is a commendable hope, but experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.Did Ukraine’s strikes lead to a decline in Russian disinformation?Probably not. While a few graphs went viral on social mediasuggestingthere had been a big decline in activity from Yandex bots, those graphs are unrelated to Russian disinformation.“Our platforms are still monitoring Russian social networks across the world and there is no discernible change in their posting patterns,” said Amil Khan, the chief executive of Valent, a tech startup that tracks disinformation.Khan and his team track about 40 disinformation networks around the world, from the UK to Australia to Syria, and monitor what narratives they put out and how publics respond to them. They have seen no drop in the volume of posts from these networks, saying: “Yandex datacentres have no practical connection to social media bot farms.”So what exactly did happen?Yandex is a search engine which also hosts websites and bots. Data from Cloudflare, which monitors worldwide internet traffic, shows a marked decline in activity from bots associated with the Yandex network on 8 October and 11 October, corresponding to the dates of two of the strikes.The independent Russian news outlet Meduzareportsthat a number of websites in Russia are down: major banks, retailers, sports apps and Yandex’s services such as Yandex Go and Yandex Eats. It suggests the damage took out a large part of Yandex’s operation and could take months to fully repair.Some online commentators have mistaken the Cloudflare data to mean that the decline in bot activity has led to a major drop in disinformation on social media. But this is not what experts have noticed.What are these different kinds of bots?“The term ‘bot’ can mean many different things,” said Michał ‘Rysiek’ Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. “When Cloudflare data shows a precipitous drop in ‘bot’ traffic, that does not mean ‘automated social media troll accounts’, it means ‘software that makes automated web requests on a large scale.’” What Cloudflarepicked upwas a decline in activity from Yandex’s web crawlers. These are used by search engines to index websites and help users to find them, said Khan.State-sponsored disinformation networks – the kind of “bots” a lot of people misinterpreted this as – could still be affected by the strikes, said Woźniak. “But those effects are going to be much more indirect.”Those networks are far more distributed, and more resilient, said Ned Mendez, the head of research at Alliance4Europe. “Platforms will routinely flag traffic from datacentres as likely automated, so serious bot operations run more through distributed methods, such as residential connections and phone farms, that airstrikes can’t really knock out.”So how could Ukraine disrupt Russian disinformation in Europe?“We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” said Mendez. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.”Khan said the Ukrainians could consider taking action against companies such as the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin’sWagner-linked troll farmthat was engaged in influence operations until 2023. But another tactic could be to work with Europe to disrupt the supply chain and recruitment pipeline of private sector contractors used by the Kremlin.Another tactic could be to pressure big social media companies to moderate disinformation on their platforms. Khan’s team has successfully worked with Meta to tamp down on inflammatory content in Sudan.But, said Khan, the Trump administration would probably push back on this, hard. “I can see why blowing up datacentres is an easier option.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDatacentresEuropeexplainersShareReuse this content

title: The Cherry Orchard review – Kristin Scott Thomas makes a modern matriarch in trad, earthy Chekhov | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This Ranevskaya feels of our time but Conor McPherson’s plain-speaking adaptation, co-starring Stephen Mangan, doesn’t always hit you emotionally
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This Ranevskaya feels of our time but Conor McPherson’s plain-speaking adaptation, co-starring Stephen Mangan, doesn’t always hit you emotionally
Content: Faded grandeur … Kristin Scott Thomas (Ranevskaya), right, and cast of The Cherry Orchard at Harold Pinter theatre, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenFaded grandeur … Kristin Scott Thomas (Ranevskaya), right, and cast of The Cherry Orchard at Harold Pinter theatre, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewThe Cherry Orchard review – Kristin Scott Thomas makes a modern matriarch in trad, earthy ChekhovHarold Pinter theatre, LondonThis Ranevskaya feels of our time but Conor McPherson’s plain-speaking adaptation, co-starring Stephen Mangan, doesn’t always hit you emotionallyArifa AkbarTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been several starry Madame Ranevskayas in recent times. The prodigal Russian landowner, returning to her beloved estate and cherry orchard, was searingly played byNina Hoss in 2024and less memorably byHelen Hunt this summer. Now here is Kristin Scott Thomas, who brings a hard-edged modernity that you believe in. She feels of our time, despite the references to dachas and peasants, and could be an upper-middle-class Chelsea mother or minister’s wife, stewing in regret and an unfulfilled life.Ian Rickson’s elegantly directed production uses a plain-speaking new adaptation by Conor McPherson. The pair have previous form on Chekhov, from six years ago, when they brought a pitch-perfect version ofUncle Vanya to the West End. This too is handsome and engaging, the crumbling drawing room of Chloe Lamford’s set design bearing damp patches and a faded grandeur.View image in fullscreenAn interestingly powerless interpretation … Stephen Mangan (Lopakhin) in The Cherry Orchard.Photograph: Johan PerssonDespite Scott Thomas’s modernity, the production itself feels traditional. Chekhov called his final play a comedy, though it subsequently came to be described like his other dramas as tragicomic, and McPherson stays faithful to that original vision. There is much humour here, albeit with moments of wistfulness, and the script is adept at drawing out the dithering ridiculousness of this entitled aristocratic set. There is an earthy, sweary frankness too in how the characters speak.Scott Thomas looks the part as the matriarch, wearing an emotional armour. Her performance is full of subtle inflection, biting her nails with worry, switching on the smiles and warmth as required. When she speaks of the death of her young son, drowned in the estate’s lake, you see her guilt and sadness being quickly hidden away.View image in fullscreenWearing an emotional armour … Kristin Scott Thomas (Ranevskaya) in The Cherry Orchard.Photograph: Johan PerssonStephen Mangan plays Lopakhin, the serf’s son who is still in milky-eyed awe of Ranevskaya, and draws out the social standing of his character. He is aware of his low estimation in the eyes of this family despite his self-made merchant status. He casts nervy glances to Ranevskaya who imperiously ignores his presence on first entry, and always stays something of an overgrown and intimidated schoolboy in the face of this family. It’s an interestingly powerless interpretation, though only half convincing.The atmosphere of absurdity and pettiness works well, with endless witterings, funny moments and an atmosphere of languor. There is guitar playing too from clerk Yepikhodov (Shubham Saraf). Peter Wight brings pompous comedy as Ranevskaya’s brother, Gaev, and Ruby Bentall is strong as German governess, Sharlotta.Nina review – a riveting series of horribly invasive auditions for The SeagullRead moreThe cast, as an ensemble, work well together, each in their own world, yet casting glances over at the other. But some of the edges are softened, such as the fire of student and would-be revolutionary Trofimov (Jack Riddiford). You don’t feel much pathos for the set as a whole, and the drama never quite enters dark or tragic territory. The scene in which the family is faced with a begging peasant certainly confirms their cold entitlement and you register their sense of infringement as this stark outside reality enters their airbrushed world, but it doesn’t hit you emotionally.There are other affecting moments though, the biggest from the plot line around adopted daughter, Varya (Vinette Robinson), and her wait for Lopakhin to propose. Her yearning, by the end, is palpable, as is her disappointment when she bears the pain of her family’s fall, along with his ascension. And when the servant Firs (Karl Johnson) is left behind, like a forgotten piece of furniture, you feel the carelessness with which Ranevskaya regards those deemed to be below her. It justifies the end to come for this old world order.AtHarold Pinter theatre, London, until 9 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsTheatreAnton ChekhovKristin Scott ThomasStephen ManganIan RicksonWest EndConor McPhersonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Chicks review – exquisite harmonies and hard-won vindication in anniversary show | The Chicks | The Guardian
description: Two decades after country music blacklisted the band for their Iraq war protest, the trio celebrate their unapologetic album Taking the Long Way
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Two decades after country music blacklisted the band for their Iraq war protest, the trio celebrate their unapologetic album Taking the Long Way
Content: The Chicks perform at their Taking the Long Way 20th anniversary tour at the Fox Theatre in Detroit, Michigan, on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Thomas FalconeView image in fullscreenThe Chicks perform at their Taking the Long Way 20th anniversary tour at the Fox Theatre in Detroit, Michigan, on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Thomas FalconeThe ChicksReviewThe Chicks review – exquisite harmonies and hard-won vindication in anniversary showBeacon Theatre, New YorkTwo decades after country music blacklisted the band for their Iraq war protest, the trio celebrate their unapologetic album Taking the Long WayAdrian HortonTue 13 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast month, with almost no fanfare, the US formallycompleted its withdrawal of troopsfrom Iraq, after 23 years of violent quagmire. But it was the beginning of that conflict that loomed over New York’s Beacon Theatre on Monday night, wherethe Chicksplayed the second of three sold-out shows. In March 2003, eight days before the US invaded Iraq, the country supergroup’s lead singer, Natalie Maines, said on stage in London she was “ashamed” that then president George W Bush was from the trio’s home state of Texas, triggering a swift, self-righteous and scarily prescient backlash.More than one person at the Beacon wondered aloud where fellow fans were back then, when a single comment, circulated on AM radio and cable news, led to CD-burning protests and death threats. (High school, was a common answer.) I myself was nine, with a child’s stark view of morality and consequence. Our country was at war, I knew, in an impossibly faraway place, and my favorite band bore the cost of criticizing it. One day, I could catchblue-sky hitsincluding Travelin’ Soldier, Landslide and Cowboy Take Me Away on the radio on the way to school; the next, they were gone.George Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!Read moreThe incident, AKA “the blessing”, as Maines put it on Monday, was pointedly addressedon Monday night, at one of a handful of shows commemorating the 20th anniversary of Taking the Long Way,the Chicks’ scorched-earth, chart-smashing retort to what many now recall as early “cancellation” (though it is perhaps more accurately, and ominously, seen as a form of proto-social media, post-truth coordinated harassment). Though it looms large for a particular demographic – largely white and female, many queer – I almost didn’t recognize the moment when the band played that 2003 clip on stage as a prelude to their bitter barn-burnerNot Ready to Make Nice, because in it Maines is laughing, speaking off-handedly. People forget, it was never supposed to be that serious.If only. The band revisited several clips from Shut Up and Sing, Barbara Kopple’sessential 2006 documentaryon their fall and rise, throughout this statement of show; in one, a montage of cable news hosts and vox pop randos decry “Saddam’s angels” as “traitors” who disrespected the troops, spoke too loudly, broke country music’s rah-rah rules.“Well, imagine that … we thought that was the worst it could get,” Maines told the rapturous crowd on Monday, still laughing. “Now I would give George W Bush a big kiss. Because now we’re ashamed that the president of the United States is from the United States.” Time has not been kind to the country, unfortunately foreseen on the group’s seminal fourth studio album as hypocritical, vindictive and perhaps irrevocably divided. But it has been kind to the artists formerly known as the Dixie Chicks (theydroppedthe “Dixie” in 2020), whose exquisite, industry-standard harmonies and liberatory bluegrass-pop has aged like fine wine.The trio appeared enriched and polished by the two decades since Taking the Long Way’s release – which included a 14-year hiatus, a couple tours, one more album (2020’sGaslighter) and one bitterly fractured nation. The album, played in full during the show’s first act, now appears unnervingly prescient, at turns an elegy and a kiss-off to home towns perhaps permanently estranged. Maines – along with sisters Martie Maguire and Emily Strayer on fiddle and banjo, respectively (and, fitting for theirRick Rubin-aided pivot toward pop and rock, a full backing band) – kept the 14-track run-through as potent and trained as her never-better vocals, lucid as ever. It was just the songs, interspersed with documentary clips illustrating both the public and the private storms – the backlash but also young mothering, touring around IVF (So Hard), finding words for, say, a grandmother’s struggle with Alzheimer’s (Silent House).‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generationRead moreThe group used brief interludes to shout out collaborators including the Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith (who, I learned, played drums on Not Ready to Make Nice); Maines’s father, the renowned pedal steel guitar player Lloyd Maines; Semisonic’s Dan Wilson, who wanted to call the album Undivided and initially proposed an apology ballad (“We said, ‘fuck that,’” Maines recalled on stage). They also made nods to Mike Campbell, who lent his experience with Tom Petty to Lubbock or Leave It, the Chicks’s most straightforward rock tune, and the gospel steel guitarist Robert Randolph, whose closing track I Hope, with its outdated faith in disagreeing “lovingly”, is afforded some bite via background footage of civil rights protests then and now.But perhaps nothing proves a point like a blistering second act that tears through the hits, reminding that even scratching the surface of the group’s electric discography will get a full-throated and complete singalong. From karaoke staple Goodbye Earl into emancipation anthem Wide Open Spaces, a welcome bluegrass down moment in White Trash Wedding into a sublimely record-faithful version of Cowboy Take Me Away, the nine-song finale is more of a mutual catharsis than a concert. By the time the band reaches its torrid finale in Sin Wagon – the Chicks being perhaps one of few mainstream shows where a fiddle solo is met with raucous applause – the case is long past made. The incident may have made the Chicks a cautionary tale, but there’s vindication in the long run.Explore more on these topicsThe ChicksCountryNew YorkPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’re honoring a life well-lived’: embalmers describe their work (in great detail) | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Embalming is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death – but what exactly does it entail?
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Embalming is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death – but what exactly does it entail?
Content: Illustration: Photograph: Getty Images / Frame: Ibrahim RayintakathView image in fullscreenIllustration: Photograph: Getty Images / Frame: Ibrahim RayintakathMemento mori: a series about deathWell actually‘You’re honoring a life well-lived’: embalmers describe their work (in great detail)Embalming is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death – but what exactly does it entail?Madeleine AggelerTue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTShareMost people don’t like to think about what happens to people’s bodies after they die. Victoria Bilstein is an exception.“I’ve actually wanted to be an embalmer since I was 10 years old!” says the funeral director, embalmer and author based in the midwest. As a child, Bilstein had two leg surgeries that incorporated bones from two deceased donors. After that, she wondered about the people who had helped save her life and the families who had lost them.She saw this work as an opportunity to help grieving families. “I wanted to be able to do postmortem reconstruction on donors so their families had the option for a viewing,” she says. “It felt like such an amazing way to honor my donors.” In her six years in the industry, she estimates she’s worked on at least a thousand embalmings.Most people who are planning burials and viewings for loved ones choose to have them embalmed.What happens to your pets when you die?Read moreBut fewer and fewer American families are choosing burials. According to the National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA), theburial ratein 2025 was 31.6%, while the cremation rate was 63.4%. By 2045, the NFDA expects the cremation rate to reach 82.3%.Part of the reason is price. According to the life insurance company Unity Financial,the average costof a simple cremation is between $1,000 and $3,000, while the average cost of a full funeral service with embalming, visitation, a casket and a ceremony is between $10,000 and $15,000.Some clients fear that embalming is a “very cold and detached process”, says Bilstein. She does her best to disabuse them of this.“I view embalming as something that’s very dignified and respectful, and an act of caregiving,” she says. “As the embalmer, you get to wash someone’s hair for the final time, clean their nails. You have the opportunity to restore them to their original appearance and you’re always prioritizing honoring their dignity as human beings and honoring a life well lived.”What is embalming?Embalming is the process of sanitizing, preserving, and restoring a human body after death, Bilstein explains.It is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death, often with the goal of making the body suitable for “public viewing, long-distance transportation, or for medical or science purposes, such as anatomical research”, as per theFuneral Consumers Alliance.When is embalming required?“Many people think embalming is legally required for every funeral, or that it preserves a body permanently,” says Dr Camelia L Clarke, NFDA spokesperson and president at Paradise Memorial Funerary Corporation. “Neither is true.”Embalming temporarily slows natural changes, she explains, and its purpose is to “give a family time to gather and, if they wish, to see their loved one”.Embalming is not the only technique that can be used if families wish to view the deceased. Refrigeration is also an option, says Brad, a funeral service educator and creator of Fun Funeral Facts, who asked that his last name be withheld – this is less invasive and involves fewer chemicals, meaning it can be seen as a more environmentally friendly option.But because it preserves the body for longer, Bilstein explains that embalming is often required for public viewings, transporting a body across state lines, international flights, and viewings of remains that are considered infectious (such as those with Covid or influenza).What does embalming entail?PaperworkWhen a deceased person arrives at a funeral home, the first steps are bureaucratic, explains Clarke.“We confirm their identity, review the information we’ve received, and assess their condition,” she says. Funeral directors must also obtain authorization from the family before embalming.SanitizingThe deceased is then transferred to an embalming table, undressed and washed with disinfectant soap, says Brad. Clothing and jewelry is set aside and catalogued to be returned to the family.During cleaning, an embalmer covers the deceased appropriately. “Dignity and respect is our primary concern,” says Bilstein.Feature settingOnce a body has been embalmed, it becomes more difficult to move facial features, Bilstein says. So an embalmer does what is called feature setting beforehand – making sure the eyes and mouth are closed, and arranging the face and body so they look peaceful.The body is positioned as it would be in the casket, Brad says – legs straightened, and hands crossed over the abdomen. A block is usually placed under the head to keep the head and neck in place.Setting the face is more involved, explains Bilstein. To keep the eyes closed, embalmers may use glue or plastic eye caps – silicone discs with small spikes on their surface that hold the eyelid in place. The mouth is usually sutured closed with string or wire.If instructed by the family, the embalmer will shave any facial hair. “Embalmers also like to remove any downy hair on the face because it helps makeup sit more naturally later,” Bilstein says.Arterial embalmingThere are two primary components to the process, says Bilstein: arterial embalming and cavity embalming.A chemical solution is mixed in an embalming machine – a device that pumps chemicals through the body.Embalming fluid is generally made up of formaldehyde, water and a variety of other chemicals. The industry’s use of formaldehyde, a colorless, flammable gas known to becarcinogenicto humans, has long been controversial, but so far, no alternative has been found that is equallyeffectiveor affordable. To protect themselves, embalmerswearpersonal protective equipment (PPE) and work in rooms with multipleventilation systems.In arterial embalming, Brad says, an embalmer selects one of the deceased’s major arteries (usually the common carotid artery in the neck) to introduce the solution, and a vein (usually the internal jugular vein in the neck) to drain blood from the body. A tube connected to the embalming machine is inserted into the artery, and embalming solution is pumped through the body’s vascular system. This solution displaces blood, which is emptied through the selected vein.The process is finished once tissue is firm and evenly colored, Brad says.Cavity embalmingFor cavity embalming, a sharp, pen-shaped instrument called a trocar is inserted into the abdomen, pelvic and chest cavities, and attached to a device that sucks out fluids. Then the trocar is used to inject a highly concentrated form of embalming fluid into the same cavities. Holes from the trocar are plugged with a trocar button, made of plastic.Finishing touchesTo complete the process, all incisions are sutured closed, hair is washed and brushed, and the body is disinfected again with soap and water. The deceased is transferred from the embalming table, dressed in a hospital gown and covered with a sheet, Bilstein says. Embalmers often apply moisturizer to the decedent’s face and hands because the embalming process is so dehydrating, says Bilstein.Finally, the embalmer cleans and disinfects the area, and writes a report. All in all, the process usually takes about one and a half to three hours depending on the condition of the deceased, though complicated cases can last much longer.Can every body be embalmed?“Embalming has its limitations,” says Bilstein.She often compares the procedure to surgery. A standard case, without complications, is like a minor surgical procedure. A case involving major physical trauma is more like a major surgical procedure – the work is more invasive and involves more steps.‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with deathRead moreFor instance, Bilstein says, if facial bones need to be rebuilt, this may involve reconstructive work with glue, wood or plastic.Sometimes, damage makes arterial embalming and viewing impossible. “I had to have that tough conversation with a family,” Bilstein says. Bilstein sees much of her role as protecting families as they grieve, which means being realistic with them about what she can accomplish.But there have been instances where she’s seemingly made the impossible possible.“I’ve had cases where the family didn’t think a viewing would be possible, and I spent hours and hours on the case, and they were able to view and have an open casket,” she says. “Those are really rewarding cases, when you can give a family that opportunity to see their loved one.”

title: Frank and Percy review – bromance becomes romance for Ian McKellen and Roger Allam’s dog walkers | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ian McKellen and Roger Allam reprise their roles for the film version of Ben Weatherill’s play in a star-filled bittersweet comedy about finding love later in life
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Ian McKellen and Roger Allam reprise their roles for the film version of Ben Weatherill’s play in a star-filled bittersweet comedy about finding love later in life
Content: Unexpected … Ian McKellen as Percy and Roger Allam as Frank.Photograph: Jack Merriman/John Gore Studios/BK StudiosView image in fullscreenUnexpected … Ian McKellen as Percy and Roger Allam as Frank.Photograph: Jack Merriman/John Gore Studios/BK StudiosMoviesReviewFrank and Percy review – bromance becomes romance for Ian McKellen and Roger Allam’s dog walkersLondon film festival:McKellen and Allam reprise their roles for the film version of Ben Weatherill’s play in a star-filled bittersweet comedy about finding love later in lifePeter BradshawTue 13 Oct 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a tender sweetness to this silver-years romance of new experiences and new ideas – and also some sugary sentimentality, an autumnal woodwind score telling us how to feel, and a bit of sitcom-cartoony characterisation in the all-star gallery of supporting turns. Sometimes that works and sometimes it doesn’t. But the movie’s easy-going good nature wins out – and there’s a terrific contribution from Joanna Lumley, playing Belinda, an elegant woman poignantly suffering from early onset dementia. Screenwriter Martin Sherman adapts thetwo-hander stage-play by Ben Weatherillin which Roger Allam and Ian McKellen originally starred. They return here for the expanded movie version and Sean Mathias once again directs.Allam plays Frank, a retired history teacher whose wife died of cancer a few short years ago (Belinda is his sister-in-law) and who now likes to walk his dog Toffee on Hampstead Heath. McKellen is Percy, an academic sociologist and climate scientist who can be found there too, with his dog Bruno. Percy is rather acrimoniously separated from his now ex-partner, a waspish and querulously self-pitying figure gamely played byStephen Fry.In their differing ways, the men are lonely; Frank has nothing to do but mope around the garden centre, brooding over memories from his marriage, and volunteering at a charity shop where he has to stand, andDerek Jacobi, as a salaried employee, is allowed to sit. Percy goes in for age-gap dates from a niche website called Papa Search – some broad comedy cameos here for Ncuti Gatwa and Hugh Skinner – but he’s not satisfied. His friendship with Frank grows, his mischievous donnish sense of fun vibing unexpectedly with Frank’s stolid northern common sense. Then one day over a drink, Percy asks if it might be quite all right if he kissed Frank. Wonderingly, Frank agrees – and it is the start of something new; he says: “I felt like I did when I had a cataract removed.”This leads Frank to ponder if he is bisexual – but perhaps it is more that he is simply sexual, and sexual in a way that he never expected to be at this time of life, or any time of life, and could only have been with this individual person. We get some bittersweet comedy as Frank and Percy realise that their social life consists of funerals, and Percy has a startling Yorick moment looking at the churchyard’s headstones. “Oh my God! I’ve had him!”Naturally, the course of true love, or any sort of love, does not run smooth and at one stage Belinda, in a moment of lucidity, tells Frank: “How lucky you are to have a broken heart at 77!” True enough. It’s a love story as comforting as the cups of tea and slices of cake to which the characters are partial.Frank and Percy screened at theLondon film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsIan McKellenRoger AllamStephen FryTheatreLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain Clayface | Movies | The Guardian
description: He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?
Content: Hunky gory … Rhys Harries in full rock’n’roller mode.Photograph: Austin HargraveView image in fullscreenHunky gory … Rhys Harries in full rock’n’roller mode.Photograph: Austin HargraveMovies‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain ClayfaceHe cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?Ryan GilbeyTue 13 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violentDC Comicssupervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”double quotation markThe audition lasted three months. How did I stay sane? I didn'tHarries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but thenthese,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”View image in fullscreenLooksmaxxing … Naomi Acki and Rhys Davies in Clayface.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesHarries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross betweenDarkman, in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, andThe Substance, the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.View image in fullscreenIf the face fits … as Matt Hagen in Clayface.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesA perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horrorCrow, where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”View image in fullscreen‘He may ultimately be the star here’ … in Hunky Dory in 2011.Photograph: Aegis Film Fund/Kobal/ShutterstockThe son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedySlaughterhouse Rulez, where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunitSuspicion, opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mysteryWhite Lines, then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche inThe Return, a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such asThe Marvels,Joker: Folie à DeuxandSupergirl, Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which ispredicted to lose more than $100m, indicate that fatigue has set in.On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”It seems unlikely, in the wake ofthe costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Diggerand the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.Clayface is in cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDC ComicsHorror filmsSuperhero moviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Loves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretary | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in then, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in then, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKatie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationLoves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretaryArwa MahdawiThe Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in thenTue 13 Oct 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.23 EDTSharePoor Donald Trump. His (third) wife seemingly can’t bear to benearhim and his (fifth) press secretary recently abandoned him to be with a baby she had only recently met.“She decided she loved her children more than she loved Donald Trump,” the presidentlamentedin August when Karoline Leavitt decided to step down a few months after giving birth. “I’m very upset about this. She has to go home and spend time with her children. That does happen on occasion with some people – when they love their children.”Apparently, Leavitt loves her childrenandFox News, because, in a highly predictable turn of events, the 29-year-old has got agig there now. But don’t worry too much about the president: he’s found himself a new woman to attack the press and act as his mouthpiece. On Friday, Trump announced that he’dappointed Katie Zacharia, previously a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, as the new press secretary. Unlike some of Trump’s other lackeys, Zacharia has government experience: she was once a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Her most important qualification, however, is her fealty to King Trump. “She has an unblemished record of support,” Trump said in his announcement. “She is … a devoted fan and member of Maga!”While you’ve obviously got to worship the president to get a top comms role with him, there are a few other job requirements. Not least a willingness to embrace what former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway called “alternative facts”. Zacharia gets full marks in that department. Last year the press secretary, who once worked foran anti-abortion advocacy group, claimedon Xthat the abortion medication mifepristone “is connected to the manufacturer of the deadly gas Zyklon B, used in the World War II concentration camps”. While there is a tenuous corporate connection whichconspiracy theoristshave tried to play up, mifepristone was developed in the 1980s by a French company.The origins of mifepristone aren’t the only alternative facts Zacharia is fond of. She has echoed Trump’s big lie that the 2020 election was “stolen” and used herTruth Socialaccount to promote theQAnon conspiracy theory, which posits that Trump is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’s alsopromotedPizzagate, the baseless theory that Hillary Clinton and her 2016 campaign chief, John Podesta, were operating an underground child sex-trafficking ring from a Washington DC pizza shop.While Zacharia scores highly when it comes to devotion and unhinged theories, I suspect that she’s going to need to ramp up her public hatred of Joe Biden if she wants to stay on her boss’s good side. Biden is dealing with stage four cancer and mostly staying out of the public eye, but Trump still acts as if he’s running against the man. According to a recentReuters analysis, Trump has invoked Biden’s name about 900 times this year. And not in a pleasant way.Beni Rae Harmony, 24, who is Trump’snewassistant press secretary, seems to suffer from the same Biden Derangement Syndrome afflicting the president; indeed, it might be part of the reason she got the job. A Christmas 2021 photo of Harmony wearing a“Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirtwhile holding a rifle recently did the rounds online. The White House subsequentlydefended Harmony, calling her “a trusted voice for the Maga movement”.Beyond bashing Biden, another helpful quality for a Trump spokesperson is a fondness for insults. White House communications director, Steven Cheung, whom Trumpreportedlyrefers to as “my sumo wrestler” probably leads the pack there. He’s forged ashock-jock stylecomms strategy and endeavours to be as crass as possible. Cheung has told the former secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, to “shut his stupid mouth”, labelled senator Jon Ossoff “the biggest cuck loser in politics”, anddescribedthe former FBI head, James Comey, as “one of the dumbest motherfuckers in human history”. He’s alsofondof calling people “retards”, recently directing the slur atCNN host Erin Burnett.Cheung’s rhetoric would get a lot of ordinary people fired. But it has made him a fixture in Trumpworld: he’s been with the president in various capacities for adecade now. That’s rare for Trump, whocycles through staff. If Zacharia lasts even a year in her new role, meanwhile, I’ll be surprised. With a (very likely) disastrous midterm election approaching, she has her work cut out and will need all the alternative facts she can find. Zacharia has also admitted that she is probably not even the best person for the job. “President Trump does not need a spokesperson,” Zachariagushed on Xlast month. “He is his own best Press Secretary.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026Kellyanne ConwayRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson | The Guardian
description: Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs, says Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Author: Jane Martinson
Headline: Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs, says Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs MimsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs MimsOpinionPoliticsOne thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemyJane MartinsonFarage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costsTue 13 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTShareWhile the merits of aso-called Britannia shieldto protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system wereenthusiastically heraldedby the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with abanner headlinecalling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile,hailed the Toriesfor seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to anall-expenses paid tripto Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in the runup to the Makerfield byelection in June 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAThe search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since theJune byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may havedubbed Burnham’s first conference speech“the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.This coverage reminds Alastair Campbellof his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”,wrote thatthe country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of itscoverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people.According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. Hisshort-form videoson fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which hasbarred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front pagewith the headline“Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”.But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacityExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionConservativesAndy BurnhamNewspapersRupert MurdochKemi BadenochcommentShareReuse this content

title: Yes, Britain’s railways are a mess. But is anyone sober enough to care? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning, writes Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning, writes Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: We’re not on time, so break out the bubbly.Photograph: posed by models; Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyView image in fullscreenWe’re not on time, so break out the bubbly.Photograph: posed by models; Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyOpinionLife and styleYes, Britain’s railways are a mess. But is anyone sober enough to care?Zoe WilliamsProsecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morningTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTShareOn Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the land, so between the homophones and my lifelong inability to start listening to a train announcement until halfway through, I cannot tell you at what point this journey became a five-train, four-hour odyssey. All I know is what’s happening on every train, in every part of the country. The 7.48am is a calm and ordered cohort of people who think they know where they’re going and will be there soon. And from 9.04am onwards, everyone’s drunk, all the way to everywhere.Between Rugby and Birmingham New Street, there was an incredibly festive crowd going to the Horse of the Year show, squishing real fruit into cans of Pimm’s, because it was breakfast time, and also because it was funny. But what were the horses going to make of all this? Because they’re quite short on appreciation for ludic pranking, and famously easy to frighten.double quotation markStafford to Liverpool was a stag do, and it was brunch o’clock by nowBetween Birmingham New Street and Wolverhampton, there was a 40th birthday party with a load of mini-bottles of prosecco, and they were extremely charming and well signposted in some ways (for instance, how did I know it was a 40th? Because of the massive flashing deely-boppers saying “40”), but I still had so many questions. Why buy 15 tiny bottles, when you could get four regular bottles for a fraction of the price, and they would have exactly the same effect? What earthly state are you going to be in when you get there? Is there somewhere you could have a little snooze before your next appointment? Maybe things are different when you’re 40, but I dimly remember it, and it’s notthatdifferent.Between Wolverhampton and Stafford, it’s only 13 minutes, so I was mainly awed by how many people could even be bothered to open a can of Stella. Stafford to Liverpool was a stag do, and it was brunch o’clock by now, so running up and down the carriage, yelling “Ay ay ay” in a fake scouse accent, dressed in a Brazilian flag, all fell under the umbrella “having a normal one”.I abhor British exceptionalism, except on this one subject: exceptionally bad train network; exceptionally fun trains. Would recommend.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026On Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan.
