title: In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay? | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Preparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workers, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Preparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workers, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Louise Casey speaking at a care home in north London in July 2026Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenLouise Casey speaking at a care home in north London in July 2026Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAOpinionSocial careIn Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?Polly ToynbeePreparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workersTue 13 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTShareResidents with advanced dementia lined the day room, glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape, with that terrible human vacancy everyone most fears for their own end days.This was Millvina House in Anfield,Liverpool, which I visited withLouise Casey, who is heading the commission on social care in England, last week. Here is a snippet of what she saw: an angry man jolting into life, shooting out his arm at her and bellowing: “Out! Get out! Get out!” A young care assistant went to stroke his back and calm him down. It’s a hard job, and part of it is watching for warning signs of aggression, one of dementia’s dreadful symptoms. “People don’t want to know,” Casey said, “but if you are born, you will die. Chances are you will need care, and dementia is the biggest killer.”In her travels she has been appalled by the standards of social care she has found in some places, with so many people getting far too little help. The evening before this visit, she had been out with care workers attending to people at home. She said she had come away “profoundly, deeply shocked”. She had photographed an elderly man with diabetes, swollen legs and a stroke affecting his left side, who was unable to open a bottle of water. He had no relatives nearby. “He couldn’t afford more care, so he’d just cut their visits by half.” Then there was a woman with early dementia and an untreated, infected stoma bag, which she said had looked “so sore”.Casey’s shock at this “hidden misery” was matched by her admiration for care workers: “Only young girls, going into unknown homes, paid just £6.50 for a half-hour visit; it’s grim. But they are so patient.” She noted they were being paid about £4,000 a year less than if they had become healthcare assistants in the NHS. With better care, Casey thinks many more people should stay in their own homes – indeed, most would prefer to. “Even at four visits a day,” she said, it would be cheaper than residential homes such as Millvina House.Millvina is a good symbol for the tangle of problems facing Casey. It is rated “requires improvement”, struggling out of a troubled “inadequate” past and hoping the results of its latest inspection will be better. The nursing home used to be privately run but was put into special measures afterthe Care Quality Commission (CQC) reporteda lack of staff, shortage of medicines, unlawful restraint, dangerous neglect of residents with diabetes, incorrect doses of antibiotics and doubts on adequate feeding and hydration. After gaininginterim controlin July 2024, Liverpool city council officially took it overin September 2025, fearing its collapse would mean the loss of 60 much-needed beds – in the previous two years, 187 beds in Liverpoolhad already been lost. Its sister home, Brushwood, has also been insourced back to the council: here,the CQC founddirty baths and toilets, staff using disrespectful and dehumanising language, agency staff who didn’t know residents’ names and multiple safeguarding failures.Casey urges insourcing to council or voluntary services: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.” She wants to stop private-equity ownersprofiteering from care homesat one end, but at the other she sees services barely surviving unless better-off residents subsidise those on too-low state funding.Now council-owned, Millvina costs a lot more to run at a better standard, the council leader tells me. Local authority staff are better paid – something private providers, contracted to cut costs, have little incentive to match. That was the logic behind Margaret Thatcher’s privatisation of social care, but perversely the state ended up with a far higher bill. To force councils to privatise, central government paid for those entering a private residential home, but not if they used domiciliary care or council-owned care. The result was an explosion of people entering private residential care instead of staying in their own homes. The state’s bill for nursing homes and residential careshot upfrom £20m in 1979 to £459m in 1986. That misguided privatisation is likely to feature in Casey’s imminent report outlining the sector’s history. Expect a brutal description of its current state.Soon comes Casey’s first of several reports, this one on finance, which will lift the lid on where wealth resides. Overwhelmingly it is older people who have most wealth, a foundational fact underpinning whatever Casey’s final plans will be for a national care service. The people needing the care are better able to pay for it than working-age taxpayers. Expect that generational truth to shape her conclusions.Lest some misunderstood Andy Burnham’spromise of universal free care at the point of use, it is unlikely that better-off people will be significantly freed from their current residential payments, which amount to £14bn. That contribution can’t be magicked away into general taxation, though liabilities could be capped.Creating a fair system for elderly people may be easier than solving the inadequate state of care for working-age adults in need of support, which absorbs nearly half of councils’ care costs (Casey is writing separate reports about this). But political heat focuses on older people using family inheritances on care, a situation unresolved asnearly 30 years of forgottensocial care commissions, white papers and select committee inquiries gather dust.“Everything is on the table,” Casey says. Does that include Burnham’sown 2010 plan, in which everyone with capital would pay in a lump sum on retirement (or a lien on their home) and thereafter get free care? “Everything.” She and the government are examining a care plan by Steve Webb, a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister, forauto-enrolmentof 1p in the pound on income tax for over-40s, politically saleable as people can opt out.What of the clash with Burnham’s devolution plans? Some councils with similar profiles of deprivation, disability prevalence and median income provide up to twice the care of others, reportsthe King’s Fund. Voters want power devolved to councils – yet they hate an unfair postcode lottery between localities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLook at the conflicts Casey faces: public v privately run services, taxpayer funds v family payments, the NHS v council funding for different disabilities, and local v national standards.Her report will also collide with Toryinheritance tax promisesto the rich. The right to pass on property to family is at the heart of passionate feelings about people being obliged to sell homes (that they will no longer use) to pay for residential care. Should young working people, many unable to afford a home themselves, pay more taxes so others can pass theirs to their children?A third of first-time buyersrely on the help of family. The wealth gap is worsening, asthe Institute for Fiscal Studies reportsa “growing importance of inherited wealth” for some, while others will get next to nothing.Casey wants to set off an alarm on the miserable quality of care she finds, but her fiercest fight may be over inheritance and generational justice. How will she cut through these political knots? It’s easy to believe her when she replies: “I will do what’s right, however controversial. That’s it.”Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSocial careOpinionOlder peopleLocal governmentLiverpoolEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci | The Guardian
description: If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Author: Nathalie Tocci
Headline: If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Content: Marine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential electionPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential electionPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersOpinionThe far rightEurope’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everythingNathalie TocciIf far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tiltTue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTShareWhen it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country inEuropewe have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week,calling a snap electionfor next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his bighousing reform packagein parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.In addition to Spain,France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able toform a majorityin the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party waspunished at the pollsand the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, afterViktor Orbán was oustedin a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats,scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’srecent victoryin eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times.But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirmGiorgia Melonias Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Friedrich Merz in Berlin after  Burnham ‘opened the door to Britain rejoining the EU’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAAnd it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outsideItalyis that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade,publicly recognisethat Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone.Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnistExplore more on these topicsThe far rightOpinionEuropeSpainItalyFranceMarine Le PenGiorgia MelonicommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno | The Guardian
description: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Content: ‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AIMegan MorenoAmid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each otherTue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTShareWe have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagersaddicted to phones, alonelinessepidemicand thedangersof AI. The release ofThe Social Reckoningleads us to ask, “How badwerethose guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am Iif I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.But what if we are focusing on the wrong problem?The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself. It may be our growing unwillingness to curiously, thoughtfully and openly communicate about the role technology plays in our lives.As a pediatrician, this issue often manifests in my clinic. Parents arrive with worries about their teens’ screen time. The parent will demand that their child “fess up” and reveal how many hours they waste on their phone every day. The atmosphere is immediately charged. The teen becomes defensive. The parent is frustrated.I often suggest that we start somewhere else.I ask: “Can you share a little about what you do when you are using technology? What do you enjoy? Are there things about your technology use you are worried about and willing to discuss?”I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AIRead moreThe answers are not usually what people expect. One teen tells me about the friendships she maintained on social media after moving to a new town. Another shows me videos he created to promote his school’s upcoming play. One shares how digital design tools are changing the fashion industry, so she is trying to learn about them now. Another quietly admits that gaming has become so consuming that it feels stressful.As the conversation unfolds, something changes. The tension in the room eases. Parents relax. The teen patientmighteven smile a few times. We talk about strategies, relationships, stress and health.What began as an argument about a device becomes a bigger conversation about health, relationships and life itself.It often feels that our conversations about technology have become trapped in a false choice between two extreme camps. One camp is made up of the pro-tech enthusiasts, thought to embrace every new device or platform. The other camp is composed of preachers of digital abstinence.View image in fullscreen‘What obligations do technology companies have to children?’Photograph: Feature China/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesThe result is a polarized debate dominated by blame, shame and moral judgment. Instead of asking how technology affects our relationships, our sleep, our work, our wellbeing, we argue endlessly about whether technology is “good” or “bad”.I was reminded of this recently during a community event focused on digital media. The event included a youth panel with several brave adolescents, willing to speak to an audience of their teachers, community members and parents. I asked the adolescents a question: could you describe a positive conversation you had with a parent about technology?Every single panelist shook their head.“I’ve never had that,” one teenager said, uneasily eyeing her mom who was sitting in the front row. The other panelists agreed.It was a striking moment. Parents routinely talk their children through setbacks in sports, clubs, friendships and school. They listen, ask questions and offer support. Yet when it comes to technology, many conversations begin and end with warnings, criticism or fear.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is this?For years, parents have been barraged by alarming headlines about screen time and mental health. Many parents worry there is probably only one right way to approach technology, and they’re failing miserably. Parents are also navigating the necessity of using their own devices for work, home and communication.‘My son genuinely believed it was real’: Parents are letting little kids play with AI. Are they wrong?Read moreThe real anxious generation just might be parents.So how do we fix this? The solution begins with curiosity. Parents can ask what interests their children have online, and why those interests matter. Parents can ask their kids about what questions or worries they have about their tech use, and share some of their own concerns. If a parent missteps by scrolling cute cat videos and delaying dinner, they can acknowledge it and make it a teachable moment for themselves and their kids.Because children do not need adults who have all the answers.They need adults willing to ask questions.These conversations matter because they lower the temperature of the debate. Once we move beyond panic and polarization, we can begin asking better questions on the societal level. How should digital platforms be designed to ensure safety? What obligations do technology companies have to children? What policies would support healthier digital environments?If we want to preserve human connection in the age of social media and AI, the answer is not to simply spend less time with technology. It is spending more time talking openly with one another. The irony of the current moment is that as we worry endlessly about technology pulling us apart, it might be our inability to have conversations about technology that ultimately divides us.Megan Moreno, MD, MSEd, MPH, is a co-author of Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World, published by the American Academy of Pediatrics on 13 October.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChildrenDoctorsHealthComputingChildren's healthChildren's techcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambition | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards
Content: ‘The reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.’Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreen‘The reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.’Photograph: AFP/GettyOpinionBrexitThe Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambitionEditorialThe prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewardsTue 13 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareThe German philosopher GWF Hegel famouslyevokedthe owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision.Havingdeclaredthat it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnhamtoldthe House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour thered linesin Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off.A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnockassertedto an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin.View image in fullscreenGeorg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831).Photograph: Prisma Archivo/AlamyThat might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds withpollsindicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield.For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels iscontemplatingdeeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold.As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the ToryBrexityears, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat.It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantlyboostLabour’s percentage vote share. His overriding earlythemehas been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outlet | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: To win support for early releases, the government will have to show that community supervision works
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: To win support for early releases, the government will have to show that community supervision works
Content: ‘A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed.’Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed.’Photograph: Jeff Morgan/AlamyOpinionPrisons and probationThe Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outletEditorialTo win support for early releases, the government will have to show that community supervision worksTue 13 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTShareTheearly release of thousands of prisonerswas bound to be awkward for a new prime minister. Politically speaking, Andy Burnham’s decision to exclude those convicted of manslaughter and some other offences made sense. But with about 2,000 offenders being freed this month, the risk is that by cutting the numbers, he has added to overcrowding problems inside. With the prison and probation services under huge pressure, and a ballot on industrial action expected, there is an urgent need for moves from the government to strengthen both.Shielded from view as prisons are, and despite the efforts of campaigners and writers such asJimmy McGovernto draw attention to them, conditions have been allowed to deteriorate to a shocking extent. The latest annual report from the prisons watchdog drew a dismal picture oframpant drug use, organised crime and governors wasting time on form-filling. It warned that the Prison Service’s managers appear to favour crisis management over improvement.Criticisms of the probation serviceof England and Wales contained inthe latest reportby the Institute for Government’s (IfG) appear measured, by comparison. Probation’s problems are less attention-grabbing, and senior leaders are not singled out for blame. But analysis of the impact of sentencing reforms, combined with ongoing staff shortages and tagging failures, are cause for very serious concern all the same. This is a vital public service that was already facing serious difficulties before its caseload was massively enlarged.View image in fullscreenJimmy McGovern.Photograph: Ian West/PAProblems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the service. The IfG highlights the toll of “near-constant organisational change”. One result has been de-skilling, with staff increasingly reliant on risk-management protocols rather than judgment. The number of recalls to prison due to breached conditions, rather than new offences, undermines rehabilitation and worsens overcrowding. But an overstretched workforce seems unable to break this cycle. There is simply not enough time to build relationships.Thefailure to fit 45% of tags on timeis obviously unacceptable; ministers need to get a grip and explain what is happening. The IfG also recommends further sentencing reforms aimed at making the system clearer. Rightly, it points out that the growing gap between jail sentences imposed in court and time actually served risks undermining trust and angering victims. Similarly, licence periods should end at the point where supervision ceases. Currently, there is a pretence that more people are serving community sentences than is actually the case. This places the probation service in a false position.The pay dispute is the immediate challenge. As part of a settlement, ministers should pledge to rebuild capacity and fill vacancies. Looking further ahead, probation needs closer links to the local services that can help offenders to get back on their feet. The merger with the Prison Service has failed to deliver promised gains.Managing risks to the public must remain a priority. But Enver Solomon, who leads Nacro, the criminal justice charity, is right to argue for a more“person-centred” style of probation work. No one who knows anything about prisons thinks that they are fulfilling their rehabilitation remit. A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed. But as increased numbers of prisoners are diverted towards probation, the service needs resources to deliver what is asked of it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people | Conservative conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: Letters: Terry Peach responds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, while Penelope Turton writes on her promise to cut inheritance tax
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Terry Peach responds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, while Penelope Turton writes on her promise to cut inheritance tax
Content: Kemi Badenoch speaks at Conservative conference in Birmingham on 7 October 2026.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch speaks at Conservative conference in Birmingham on 7 October 2026.Photograph: GettyConservative conference 2026LettersThe Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich peopleTerry Peachresponds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, whilePenelope Turtonwrites on her promise to cut inheritance taxTue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareKemi Badenoch’s conference speech rehearsed the argument that Andy Burnham’s economic policies were warped by his “nostalgia” for the 1970s, unlike her own forward-looking programme for “a better tomorrow” (Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan, 7 October).She appears not to see that her preference for a lesser-regulated capitalist market economy, with lower public expenditure, taxes and national debt, coupled with “tough love” welfare policies, is itself harking back to arguments that have circulated for centuries.Admittedly, her position is not as extreme as the one espoused at the beginning of the 19th century by the leading political economist David Ricardo,who arguedthat Great Britain would be happy and prosperous if the “evil” of the national debt was extinguished completely, and the country embraced a system in which trade is left “perfectly free” and taxation reduced to a bare minimum.His own “tough love” proposal was to scrap the Poor Laws, as they encouraged overbreeding by the working class, thereby depressing market-determined wages.Terry PeachChesterKemi Badenochsays “people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort” and regards inheritance tax (IHT) as unfair double taxation on people who have already paid tax on their earnings. In fact, most IHT revenue is driven by inherited and asset-derived wealth, which expands through unearned capital appreciation and is untaxed during a person’s lifetime.Badenoch has elsewhere called IHTimmoral. The real moral injury is borne by all those low-paid, hard-working people who face a choice between heating or eating, and for whom acquiring sufficient wealth in a lifetime to leave money to their children is an unimaginable dream.Penelope TurtonLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Why most Manchester City fans stand by their club | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Letter: Andrew Burton suspects that had other teams delivered similar success, fans would have been just as forgiving of their owners
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Andrew Burton suspects that had other teams delivered similar success, fans would have been just as forgiving of their owners
Content: ‘At City, UAE ownership brought unprecedented success to a historic club.’Photograph: Dave Thompson/APView image in fullscreen‘At City, UAE ownership brought unprecedented success to a historic club.’Photograph: Dave Thompson/APManchester CityLettersWhy most Manchester City fans stand by their clubAndrew Burtonsuspects that had other teams delivered similar success, fans would have been just as forgiving of their ownersTue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareRe Sean Ingle’s article (How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime?, 5 October), I suspect that most City fans are no more supportive of the United Arab Emirates regime than those of Arsenal were of the Rwandan government during its sponsorship deal, or Newcastle’s of Saudi Arabia, or those of the11 clubswhose shirt sponsors were gambling companies in 2025-26. Fans are simply concerned with how their club is managed and success on the pitch.At City, UAE ownership brought unprecedented success to a historic club. The new regime delivered the most feted coach of our time, who revolutionised how the game in England was played. Highly successful City youth teams nurtured young talent that has gone on to grace numerous other squads in thePremier Leagueand beyond, including England players. City Women, reigning double winners, are the current force in English women’s football.The Premier League in the 21st century has invariably been bought. City were late to the party when rules were put in place which in effect blocked wealthy owners of clubs outside already established contenders investing enough to become competitive. I doubt that a majority of supporters of clubs such Newcastle, Villa or Forest are any more appreciative of the so-called “fair play” rules than City’s are. Had they delivered similar success, I suspect they would have been just as forgiving of their owners.Andrew BurtonBuxton, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Yes, the music is lovely, but cathedrals are crumbling | Anglicanism | The Guardian
description: Letter: They are some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings, yet they receive no secure state funding, writes Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: They are some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings, yet they receive no secure state funding, writes Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins
Content: Choral Eucharist at Canterbury Cathedral. ‘Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist,’ writes Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChoral Eucharist at Canterbury Cathedral. ‘Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist,’ writes Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAnglicanismLettersYes, the music is lovely, but cathedrals are crumblingThey are some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings, yet they receive no secure state funding, writesDr Coco Parkinson-HugginsTue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareJonathan Davies’ article (Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it, 7 October) speaks beautifully to the contribution of English choral music to our living cultural heritage, highlighting the importance of cathedral choirs in particular, in giving children access to “world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach”.What he misses however, is just how under threat these bastions of England’s religious, cultural and spiritual heritage actually are.Despite recent research from the Theos thinktanksuggesting 74% of adults in England have visited a cathedral over the last three years,80% of cathedrals in England are now in structural deficit. Several have recently reached crisis point, including those inPeterboroughandSt Davids. One in four cathedrals in England is now charging for entry, and even after significantly diversifying their income portfolios (including throughcontroversial silent discos), they continue to struggle.More than 90% of visitors surveyed by Theos (including 94% of non-religious visitors) thought of cathedrals as a hub for community life, and the same number see them as a symbol of local identity and a way to connect with history and tradition. Despite their significant social and cultural contributions to communities, and being some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings (two are Unesco world heritage sites and many are almost 1,000 years old), cathedrals receive no secure state funding and limited contributions from central church authorities. Unlike museums and galleries offering free admission, cathedrals are also not subject to the same VAT exemptions on repairs or maintenance.This has left many cathedrals crumbling, and their finances with them. Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist. If more is not done to protect them, that reality could be closer than we think.Dr Coco Parkinson-HugginsResearcher, TheosHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Yes, obesity is a problem – but a greater one is the food industry and its greed | Ultra-processed foods | The Guardian
description: Letters: Ultra-processed foods are displacing traditional diets, warns Prof Kent Buse. Plus letters from Hugo Harper, Dr Pawan Randev and Patricia Hampton
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Ultra-processed foods are displacing traditional diets, warns Prof Kent Buse. Plus letters from Hugo Harper, Dr Pawan Randev and Patricia Hampton
Content: ‘The generations below me have eaten ultra-processed diets from birth.’Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreen‘The generations below me have eaten ultra-processed diets from birth.’Photograph: Alamy/PAUltra-processed foodsLettersYes, obesity is a problem – but a greater one is the food industry and its greedUltra-processed foods are displacing traditional diets, warnsProfKent Buse. Plus letters fromHugo Harper,Dr Pawan RandevandPatricia HamptonTue 13 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareYour editorial on cancers in under-50s (8 October) rightly names food among the culprits. But the confrontation it calls for should be aimed less at obesity than at what produces it. Obesity is the intermediary; the exposure is a food system engineered for profit.The Lancet’s series on ultra-processed foodsshowed these products displacing traditional diets worldwide and driving chronic disease, and documented more than 200 interconnected lobby groups through which the industry organises its influence to block regulation.I was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 51, narrowly escaping these statistics; the generations below me have eaten ultra-processed diets from birth.Governments know what works: marketing restrictions, warning labels, fiscal measures, schools and hospitals free from ultra-processed food, and policymaking protected from industry interference.Yvette Cooper should treat the companies that shaped our diets in the same way that her predecessors eventually treated tobacco: not as partners to consult, but as an industry to regulate.Prof Kent BuseChair, policy and prevention committee, World Obesity FederationThe worrying rise in early-onset cancers underlines the urgency of government intervention on obesity. Our food system is broken when high-fat, -salt and -sugar options are consistently the most accessible and affordable.Advances in cancer research and weight-loss drugs will play a key role in managing diet-related illness, but treatment alone cannot solve a public health crisis. We must fix the food environment driving obesity in the first place. That requires changing the incentives for large food businesses that make and market the food we eat.The government’s proposed healthy food standard sets out the most ambitious action for reforming the food environment to date, but progress has stalled since its announcement. It has the potential to reduce national obesity rates by about one fifth in adults and a quarter in children. Nothing else on the table comes remotely close to that.The first step is establishing mandatory health reporting so that companies can no longer mark their own homework. Then we need clear targets for major food businesses to improve the health of what they actually sell. Ultimately, we cannot protect future generations from preventable diet-related disease until healthier food is the easiest and most affordable option. We cannot let our strategy be “wait for people to get sick and then put them on the drugs”.Hugo HarperDirector, NestaCancer has become thegreatest cause of death among people with type 2 diabetes in Englandand the problem of metabolic risk and cancer is one of the great threats to health. However, this isnot known by health professionals or the 4 million patientswith this condition.Cancer screening programmes work effectively with informed participation. GPs and their practices can use the annual diabetes check to highlight the cancer prevention. Screening programmes and primary care can work together to prevent cancer, if resources are targeted in the best way. TheWorld Cancer Research Fund reporthas added urgency – let’s use it effectively.Dr Pawan RandevFormer Cancer Research UK GPI read with interest Anna Bawden’s article (Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds, 6 October. It seems that “lifestyle choices” are largely responsible for this, but I wonder just how much of a choice is open to us nowadays. We can choose to drink less alcohol, not smoke, exercise more and eat more healthily, but our choice of healthy food is limited, as products become increasingly industrialised with the addition of chemical additives, and we have little or no control over environmental or agricultural pollutants. To all this we might add the stress of the increasing cost of living and difficulty in finding jobs.I believe it is perhaps not so much a question of poor lifestyle choices, but a lack of lifestyle choices.Patricia HamptonMilan, ItalyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Barrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester United  | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Pablo Barrios struck after 53 seconds and Leny Yoro was shown red as Atlético Madrid added to Manchester United’s woes with a 2-0 victory
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Pablo Barrios struck after 53 seconds and Leny Yoro was shown red as Atlético Madrid added to Manchester United’s woes with a 2-0 victory
Content: Pablo Barrios (No 8) celebrates after firing Atlético Madrid ahead inside the first minute.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAView image in fullscreenPablo Barrios (No 8) celebrates after firing Atlético Madrid ahead inside the first minute.Photograph: Juanjo Martin/EPAChampions LeagueBarrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester UnitedSid Loweat the Riyadh Air MetropolitanoTue 13 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick had seen it in his players, he said, but no one else can. Not so far in the Premier League, where they have sufferedtheir worst start in 40 years, and not here in Madrid, where Manchester United’s head coach insisted they would embrace the challenge. The reaction was coming, he promised; he had looked at them and was sure of it. Instead, they were a goal down after just 53 seconds and all that came was the old familiar sting, that early opener from Pablo Barrios and a second from Ademola Lookman condemning them to another defeat.So much for a reaction, a rebellion: in their place a kind of resignation, a sense that maybe this is just United’s reality: a game that began badly, did not get very much better, and finished even worse. True, the result could have been different, Bryan Mbeumo unable to convert two first-half chances while Bruno Fernandes struck the bar and put an opportunity wide, but that did not diminish the feeling that something is really wrong. It may even have deepened it.‘I expect more’: Lisandro Martínez hits out at Manchester United hierarchyRead moreEven the late, harsh red card for Leny Yoro which can be offered in mitigation did not change a simple fact: at the end of another insipid night, United lost. Unitedarelost, perhaps.“Sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there,” United’s manager said the night before, a message that perhaps hinted at something rotten beneath the surface, but on the opening goal no one was really there. They weren’t there on the left, where Lee Kang-in’s pass sent Álex Baena into a wide-open space; they weren’t there to close him down as he cut into the area; and they weren’t there on the right either, where Barrios was running through alone. Baena laid across and Barrios’s shot went off Ayden Heaven and into the net.Barrios held up six fingers, the number of the club captain, Koke, whose mother had died in the hours before kick-off. From the bench Koke’s shirt was raised. All around the Metropolitano, supporters roared. This was set, it seemed.Although another effort from Baena soon hit Lisandro Martínez, United did find a foothold and could have found a way back. Mbeumo had two clear chances in quick succession: the first, after nice footwork on the right, went wide; the second, following a neat exchange with Youri Tielemans, was stopped by Jan Oblak on the other side. From the corner, Carlos Baleba headed straight at the keeper.View image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes reacts after Manchester United concede a second goal, scored by Ademola Lookman.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAThat was short-lived, though, Atlético soon asserting themselves, moving the ball with a pace and conviction United couldn’t match. Barrios and Baena couldn’t be controlled, and the spaces they opened were vast. The pressure United applied tended to arrive late or not at all. On the touchline too the contrast was stark: Diego Simeone prowled, Carrick stood motionless in the corner of his technical area, chin in his hand. The Argentinian was booked for waving an imaginary card. Maybe United’s manager could try that. Something, anyway.By half-time, Atlético had enjoyed 66% of possession. They could also have had a greater lead. Álex Grimaldo rattled a superb free‑kick off the bar and just before the break Johnny Cardoso’s sweeping finish was ruled out when the video assistant referee revealed a Marcos Llorente handball in the buildup. The second half then began with a neatly floated ball from Barrios setting up Julián Álvarez to volley against a post. Again, the space, time and the ease with which the move played out was just too big.At the other end, Bruno Fernandes then had a wonderful opportunity to level it. Tielemans did superbly to find him, the ball sitting up and Oblak coming off his line to meet him – the kind of opportunity, in short, that is supposed to end only one way but that this time ended another.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited’s captain lifted the ball past the keeper and wide. Soon, Atlético were back again, Baena bending a shot wide, although Atlético appeared to have settled, the game drifting. That perhaps suited United: with Atlético’s threat no longer so present, the ball was theirs for the first time and the lead was still only one, opportunity there. Fernandes, increasingly involved, swung a shot against the bar.View image in fullscreenLeny Yoro trudges off after being shown a red card.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAWhich was when it finally, definitively and far too easily fell apart. Suddenly, on 74 minutes, Jonathan David was running through the middle on to a Morten Hjulmand ball. Yoro went with him, grappling as they ran, and the pair fell. Although Glenn Nyberg didn’t give a foul, allowing the move to play out with David scrambling the ball to Lookman, a voice in his ear called him to the screen to watch the challenge again. When he returned, he had a red in his hand.The decision felt harsh. It was also the end. Three minutes later, Atlético were running through United again. Grimaldo slotted a pass into David, inside the area and, although his shot was saved by Senne Lammens, Lookman was there to score. Heaven and Fernandes were removed; this was done, nothing left to fight for, not that they had fought much in the first place, the reaction postponed for some other day.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueAtlético MadridManchester Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: James and Russo lead rout of Greece as ruthless England set up Ukraine playoff | Women's World Cup 2027 qualifiers | The Guardian
description: Two goals from Lauren James and Alessia Russo helped England to a 5-0 win over Greece (8-1 on aggregate) that sets up a World Cup playoff against Ukraine
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Two goals from Lauren James and Alessia Russo helped England to a 5-0 win over Greece (8-1 on aggregate) that sets up a World Cup playoff against Ukraine
Content: Lauren James (left) is congratulated by fellow goalscorer Alessia Russo after netting her second and England’s fourth goal.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenLauren James (left) is congratulated by fellow goalscorer Alessia Russo after netting her second and England’s fourth goal.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAWomen's World Cup 2027 qualifiersJames and Russo lead rout of Greece as ruthless England set up Ukraine playoffPlayoff semi-final second leg: England 5-0 Greece (agg 8-1)Goalscorers: Russo 3 75, James 16 34, Stanway 30Suzanne Wrackat the King Power StadiumTue 13 Oct 2026 16.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA mercurial Lauren James scored two and provided an assist in a thrilling four-goal first 45 minutes against Greece, as England put themselves two games away from securing their place at the World Cup.James’s double was matched by Alessia Russo, who scored either side of the break, and her Arsenal ­teammate Georgia Stanway was also on the scoresheet, with the Lionesses setting up a playoff final against Ukraine in November and December. It was a clinical and slick statement from England, albeit against a team they should bypass with ease.Any Greek hopes of arriving in Leicester and launching a Trojan horse-style smash and grab, after a hugely impressive performance in their3-1 defeat by an ­unconvincing Lionessesteam in Crete, were quickly dashed.England v Greece: Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff, second leg – liveRead moreSarina Wiegman had said on the eve of the game that she wanted to see improvement in the final third. In the King Power Stadium, which had a club vibe to it before kick-off as dance remix after dance remix blared out, the Lionesses responded to their manager’s call, Russo producing the first goal from the first shot and first attack in the third minute.James was the architect, the ­Chelsea player driving forward and picking out the No 9, who shrugged clear of Eleni Markou’s challenge before firing a low shot in.View image in fullscreenAlessia Russo gets England up and running with a third-minute goal.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersIt was Russo’s fourth goal in four games for club and country, with the Arsenal forward having gone five Women’s Super League games without a goal before this run, and it was a sign of things to come from a team keen to shake off criticism of their lack of ruthlessness.James was in majestic form, her injury worries behind her this season, and England fans were treated to a glimpse of what they missed at the Euros in Switzerland in 2025, when a less than half-fit James struggled and looked frustrated as her body failed to meet her demands on it.James has said that the best is yet to come from her and Wiegman agreed. “I think so,” said the manager. “She was really enjoying herself, scored some great goals, but also picked up some great positions. I thought she looked really fresh and played well.”On the Chelsea forward’s use more centrally, having previously been preferred in a wider role, Wiegman said: “As a winger or inverted winger she does similar things. She can play any position up front, right or left, because she’s right- and left-footed. When she plays on the outside she also gets the opportunity to come inside, and I think she can do both things then, and that’s when she comes to life.”James delivered England’s ­second and fourth in Leicester, her two first-half goals sandwiching ­Stanway’s header into the far corner from ­Lauren Hemp’s chipped cross.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Stanway heads in England’s third goal as they swiftly put the result beyond doubt.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersFor her first, the 25-year-old ­cushioned Maya Le Tissier’s pass before sending a rising drive goalwards with her left foot. Her second was far simpler, the unmarked forward turning in Hemp’s ball from close range.Job well and truly done, James was withdrawn at half-time in favour of Beth Mead, Wiegman’s jewel safely nestled back in a velvet pouch after shining so brightly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWiegman leapt on the opportunity presented by the 7-1 aggregate scoreline to rotate ­further at the hour mark, with Niamh Charles, Jess Park and Freya Godfrey given a chance to demonstrate why they should be on the plane to Brazil should England overcome Ukraine.Whether the changes took the sting out of the game or England just eased back on the intensity given the margin did not really matter because the home team remained in complete control of the ball. Their more than 50-place superiority in the Fifa world rankings was far more ­evident in Leicester than it had been in Heraklion.Russo was the beneficiary of ­England’s patience as the clock ticked down, collecting Keira Walsh’s angled pass before she raced clear, stepped around Styliani­Katergiannaki in the Greece goal and rolled the ball into the empty net.“I think today we played a lot better,” said Wiegman. “We totally dominated the game … As soon as we got in behind and we scored that goal that helped and I think after that we were really, really good in the final third.”Ultimately, despite the performance put on there isvery little to be learnedfrom a game against a team so far below England’s level. Any slip-up would only ever have been of England’s own making, as the poor defending for Greece’s goal in Crete demonstrated. However, perhaps that sluggishness could be ­attributed to a rustiness after a four-month break from international football.Ukraine are up next, the homeless team preparing to face the European champions after a 4-1 aggregate defeat of Slovakia.England met Ukraine in their World Cup qualifying group earlier in the year and secured a 9-1 margin across the two matches, so it would take the most almighty of collapses for the Lionesses to fail to book their place in Brazil now.Quick GuideRoundup: Scotland and Wales advance to playoff finalsShowMelissa Andreatta claims herScotlandside “stuck to our principles” in the 3-2 win overCzechiawhich booked a place in round two of the Women’s World Cup play-off against Sweden.Leading 2-0 from the first leg of the round one play-off but losing Caroline Weir to an injury in the warm-up at St Mirren’s Marbill Coaches Stadium, Scotland found themselves a goal down in the third minute when the Czechis full-back Denisa Vesela sent a shot from 30 yards soaring over a helpless Sandy MacIver. That lead lasted only two minutes before Lauren Davidson clipped in an equaliser from 12 yards but the visitors steeled themselves again and in the 32nd minute Klara Cahynova headed in a corner from Michaela Khyrova.However, Kathleen McGovern levelled early in the second half following a botched clearance by the Czechia defender Lucie Bendova and in the 72nd minute, when Barbora Votikova, the visiting goalkeeper, spilled a cross from the substitute Erin Cuthbert, Christy Grimshaw was on hand to lift the ball over the line and the home side ran out deserved winners.The Scots will take on Sweden, who beat Lithuania 10-0 on the night and 15-0 on aggregate, in a two-legged tie with the matches taking place between 26 November and 5 December, with Scotland at home first.Andreatta told BBC Scotland: “What it showed is what Scotland’s all about.“We stuck to our principles, ground out a result and that puts us in a good place for what’s ahead. I think these two games being so tough and testing us in all different ways, gives us the confidence to go again against Sweden."Walestook a step towards qualifying for the Women’s World Cup for the first time after a 3-0 win overAlbaniaat Parc y Scarlets. Rhian Wilkinson’s side, who won the reverse fixture 1-0 in Shkoder last week following Ezmiralda Franja’s own goal, also set a new national record after extending their unbeaten run to 10 matches.Any nerves on the night were eased when Mayzee Davies headed home in the 34th minute, while Elise Hughes and Hannah Cain struck after half-time to seal a comprehensive 4-0 aggregate triumph. Wales will next take on Norway in their playoff final in December for the right to head to Brazil next year. Norway sit 13th in the world rankings, 18 spots higher than Wales.Kess Elmore marked her firstNorthernIrelandstart with a goal but could not prevent them from falling to a 3-1 loss toPortugal, completing a 7-1 aggregate defeat in their playoff.TheRepublic ofIrelandputKazakhstanto the sword again, claiming a 12-0 aggregate win to move closer to qualifying. An 8-0 victory in last week’s first leg in Astana meant the Republic were all but home and hosed.Jessie Stapleton bagged the Republic’s final goal in the Kazakh capital and the Leicester defender opened the scoring just before half-time, while Katie McCabe struck just after the interval. The substitute Lucy Quinn and Denise O’Sullivan were also on target as the Republic cruised into the play-off final, where they will take on Poland across two legs in December.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Explore more on these topicsWomen's World Cup 2027 qualifiersEngland women's football teamWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Timber’s touch of class and supersub Saka secure Arsenal win against Lille | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Eberechi Eze was also on target as Arsenal scored three goals in seven second-half minutes in a 3-0 win against Lille in the Champions League
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Eberechi Eze was also on target as Arsenal scored three goals in seven second-half minutes in a 3-0 win against Lille in the Champions League
Content: Jurriën Timber clips Arsenal into a second-half lead against Lille.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenJurriën Timber clips Arsenal into a second-half lead against Lille.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoChampions LeagueTimber’s touch of class and supersub Saka secure Arsenal win against LilleEd Aaronsat the Emirates StadiumTue 13 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwelve wins in a row and counting. On a night when Arsenal remembered Ken Friar – the club’s life president who was instrumental in their move from Highbury to the Emirates in 2006 – it was fitting that Mikel Arteta’s side should rack up yet anotherChampions Leaguemilestone at their home that has become a fortress.Such has Arsenal’s dominance been here in recent seasons that when Bukayo Saka slotted home their third against a dogged Lille side, it was the 36th goal they have scored at the Emirates in the league or group stage since returning to Europe’s top table under Arteta three years ago. In those 12 wins, they have remarkably conceded only three times.Barrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester UnitedRead moreArsenal have also now racked up 14 successive league-stage victories in this competition – three short of Bayern Munich’s record – even if Arteta’s side were made to work for this one and had to wait until the 64th minute to find the breakthrough. That came from the unlikely source of Jurriën Timber after Arsenal’s second-string attack – and Viktor Gyökeres in particular – had looked laboured. But while Arteta may be concerned that it needed the introduction of Saka from the bench along with Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz to put this game to bed as Eberechi Eze added a second before Saka rounded off the scoring with a third in the space of seven minutes, they never looked in any danger of losing their proud record as Olivier Giroud received a standing ovation on his return to north London.“I’m sure he is very happy to see how the boys played. But not only that, because I know how proud he felt about what we built,” said Arteta of Friar. “It’s a really sad day for everyone who loves football. The legacy that Ken is going to leave for this club is going to be for ever.”Arsenal had earlier paid tribute to Friar, who worked his way up from the box office to club secretary before becoming managing director in the 1980s, when his death at the age of 92 was confirmed. The players wore black armbands as a mark of respect. Friar would have been especially proud of their formidable record here under Arteta in this competition that stretches back to the 2023-24 season, when they returned to the tournament after an absence of six years. It is little wonder that Arteta was so reluctant for redevelopment plans to go ahead given the disruption any temporary move away to Wembley or elsewhere would have caused.Despite the absence of Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi after they were both injured during the warm-down after the victory over Leeds on Saturday, the Arsenal manager was still able to make five changes. Lille’s manager, Davide Ancelotti, who worked under his father, Carlo, at Everton and Real Madrid among others before being appointed during the summer in only his second senior role, resisted the temptation to start with 40-year-old Giroud against his former club.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka slots home Arsenal’s third goal from close range.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersRestored to his favoured right flank after excelling on the left against Leeds, it had not been saying much that Noni Madueke had once again been Arsenal’s most dangerous outlet in a first half in which they struggled to create much against a deep-lying defence.Bruno Guimarães and then Mikel Merino spurned decent chances, while Ayase Ueda had the ball in David Raya’s net after Nabil Bentaleb’s shot deflected off Timber and hit Hákon Haraldsson on the way through, with the video assistant referee confirming the Japan striker was marginally offside.But Arsenal lacked creativity without Ødegaard and Gyökeres showing plenty of hustle and bustle yet making little real impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt summed Arsenal’s first half up when he could not get out of the way after Eze forced Berke Ozer into his first proper save and was promptly flagged offside. Ozer then had to scramble the ball away from the feet of the Sweden striker after spilling a shot from Guimarães on the stroke of half-time.The referee, Felix Zwayer, waved away appeals at the start of the second half when Guimarães went down in the area under pressure from Alexsandro but the Arsenal midfielder seemed to be looking for the contact. A wayward effort that almost made it into the upper tier from Madueke was the signal for Arteta to summon Ødegaard, Saka and Havertz to get ready.Before they had time to be introduced, Arsenal finally found the breakthrough when Madueke picked out Timber to apply a deft finish with his right foot after a brilliant first touch. Saka made an immediate impact by setting up Eze to dispatch the second with his left foot – possibly with the help of a deflection – less than three minutes later, before adding a third after combining with Havertz and Ødegaard. Lille must have wondered what had hit them.As well as the chance to pay their respects to Giroud, the Arsenal fans were treated to a late cameo from the dazzling Max Dowman to round off another very satisfying evening that has become the norm.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueArsenalLillematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Louis Rees-Zammit demands end to artificial Prem pitches after leg burns at Saracens | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: The Bristol winger Louis Rees-Zammit wrote on social media: ‘Someone do something about it!’ and their coach, Pat Lam, left three players out because of the pitch
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: The Bristol winger Louis Rees-Zammit wrote on social media: ‘Someone do something about it!’ and their coach, Pat Lam, left three players out because of the pitch
Content: Louis Rees-Zammit runs past Noah Caluori of Saracens in Bristol’s defeat on the artificial pitch on 10 October.Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenLouis Rees-Zammit runs past Noah Caluori of Saracens in Bristol’s defeat on the artificial pitch on 10 October.Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsPrem RugbyLouis Rees-Zammit demands end to artificial Prem pitches after leg burns at SaracensBristol wing: ‘Someone do something about it!’Pat Lam left three players out because of the pitchGerard MeagherTue 13 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouis Rees-Zammit has called for an end to artificial pitches in the Prem after posting a graphic image of the wounds he sustained during Bristol’s defeat at Saracens’ StoneX Stadium on Saturday.The Wales wing revealed the extent of the friction burns caused to his right leg after running out for the Bears on Saracens’ artificial pitch with the caption: “Can we please stop playing on these AstroTurf pitches!! Someone do something about it!!”Saracens sack player who sparked Stokes captaincy crisis after latest incidentRead moreSaracens were the first Prem club to install an artificial pitch, in 2013, before Newcastle andGloucesterfollowed in 2014 and 2021. Worcester also used one before going into liquidation. After Saturday’s defeat, the Bristol director of rugby, Pat Lam, took aim at the surface and revealed he had omitted Pedro Rubiolo, AJ MacGinty and Steven Luatua from his side for fear of injury.“They came off big injuries last year and so it wasn’t worth putting them on that pitch,” Lam said. “If we were playing the game at home or if it was a semi-final, they would have played.” A number of players have spoken out about artificial pitches in the past including the former England internationals Joe Marler and Jack Nowell, who has been omitted from Exeter lineups to avoid the risk of injury. In 2021, World Rugby allowed players to wear leggings and base layers to reduce the risk of burns.View image in fullscreenLouis Rees-Zammit’s post shows the injuries to his leg after the Saracens match.Photograph: lrzammit/InstagramThe argument for artificial pitches is that they allow greater use even in extreme weather conditions. The Saracens and England hooker Jamie George, who is preparing for his side’s Champions Cup fixture at Connacht on Saturday, which will be played on an artificial pitch, said: “I think everyone reacts differently to these kinds of pitches. Everyone’s entitled to their opinion in terms of what they think about the pitches. I know the StoneX pitch meets all the rules and regulations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We make sure that we train on artificial surfaces on the week leading up to playing there at the weekend. Whether there is an advantage in that, whether that means our bodies get more used to it, you’d have to speak to a sports scientist, but I know that is an area of focus for us.”Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyRugby unionSaracensBristolNewcastleGloucesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Football regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester City | Football politics | The Guardian
description: David Kogan said he would resign if he faced political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: David Kogan said he would resign if he faced political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Content: Concern had been raised that the proximity of Manchester City’s ownership to the Abu Dhabi state could trigger a political intervention by the UK government.Photograph: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConcern had been raised that the proximity of Manchester City’s ownership to the Abu Dhabi state could trigger a political intervention by the UK government.Photograph: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu/Getty ImagesFootball politicsFootball regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester CityKogan says he has faced ‘absolutely no political pressure’Regulator wants deal on redistribution through leaguesPaul MacInnesTue 13 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chair of the Independent ­Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, has said he will resign if he faces any political pressure on how to respond to Manchester Citybeing found guiltyof breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, insisting “my independence is absolute”.Kogan could remove City’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) should the damning verdict of an independent commission be upheld at the end of an ongoing appeal process. ­Concern had been raised, however, that the proximity of City’s ­ownership to Abu Dhabi’s rulers could trigger a political intervention by the UK ­government and an immediate test of the new regulator’s powers.Burnham’s meeting with City’s al-Mubarak and other contact with club disclosedRead moreThose concerns have been rebuffed by Kogan. “Our independence is absolute and my independence personally is absolute,” he said. “I [have] made it very clear … any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. And, just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic.”Kogan was speaking on Tuesday at the launch of the long-awaited State of the Game report, a document that lays out the financial challenges facing the English football pyramid. The City case has cast a huge shadow as the regulator prepares to introduce a new licensing regime for clubs later this season. “We have powers within the legislation that allow us to review not only owners and directors and senior executives, but also whether those owners are fit and proper ­people to run clubs going forward,” said Kogan, describing the process by which the regulator might intervene.“That process is reliant on us ­having very detailed knowledge and information, which requires a ­certain amount of investigation. Then we would take judgments based on the legal advice that we then receive.”Should a club owner ultimately be found to have failed a “fitness” test related to “integrity, honesty and financial soundness”, the regulator could force the club to be sold. “We deal with issues of this type much more frequently than you might realise because we are constantly looking at clubs,” Kogan said, stating if any decision by the regulator became the subject of legal action then clubs would be asked to foot the bill through a funding levy.View image in fullscreenDavid Kogan reiterated that the regulator had powers to determine whether owners such as Manchester City’s were ‘fit and proper’.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAThe acceleration of revenues among the Premier League’s biggest clubs is one of the key findings in the State of the Game report. The highest earning top-flight club currently earns 605 times the revenue of the lowest earning National League club. At the same time, spending has increased at all levels of the game, with 94% of the 116 clubs under the regulator’s regime posting a financial loss in 2025-26. In one particularly eye-catching statistic, the report found 11 Football League clubs recorded costs that exceeded their income even once player wages had been stripped out.Kogan argued that a number of external factors that fall outside the regulator’s purview are affecting the game, including the expansion of the club calendar, the regulation of ­players’ agents and the recent rise in interest rates. However, he argued that one key measure – the agreement of a redistribution deal between the Premier League and EFL – could unlock change immediately.While Kogan accepts the Premier League’s argument regarding the need for parachute payments due to “colossal” drops in revenue caused by relegation, he believes they have had a “distortive effect that’s grown over the years”. Kogan said that if a deal was done that reduced parachute payments but increased the amount going to all clubs then “that will go some way towards looking at the ­distorted effect”. Once that money was distributed, he said, “you’re going to see a softening effect going through down the 116 clubs”.View image in fullscreenManchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour, and chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, are under scrutiny.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThe Premier League welcomed the publication of the report, arguing: “It recognises what English football has built – the world’s most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth.”The league argued that a recent offer of financial redistribution to the EFL – understood to amount to £320m per season – “meets the ­objectives the IFR has set out in its report” and said it “remains ­committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and ­balances the interests of all clubs”.The EFL said the report’s findings “reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid” and it remained “committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game”.Meanwhile, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, Lisa Nandy, said the stark figures covered in the report had “blown the doors off the game”. She urged football authorities to “consider these findings for the good of the game, for the fans, and for the communities of which they are so often the bedrock”.Explore more on these topicsFootball politicsFinancesManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: racist chanting mars Swansea’s win at Millwall | Championship | The Guardian
description: Swansea scored a last-minute winner to stay top of the Championship but game at Millwall held up by racist chanting
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Swansea scored a last-minute winner to stay top of the Championship but game at Millwall held up by racist chanting
