Content: Ronald (left) celebrates scoring a late winner for Swansea in their game at Millwall, which was suspended for almost seven minutes due to racist chanting.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenRonald (left) celebrates scoring a late winner for Swansea in their game at Millwall, which was suspended for almost seven minutes due to racist chanting.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAChampionshipChampionship roundup: racist chanting mars Swansea’s win at MillwallRonald’s last-minute winner keeps Welsh side on topMiddlesbrough edge Stoke in thriller; Watford gloomPress AssociationTue 13 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSubstitute Ronald scored a last-minute winner to keepSwanseatop of theChampionshipafter their match atMillwallwas held up for almost seven minutes due to a complaint about racist chanting at the Den.The referee, Edward Duckworth, halted the match in the 65th minute and walked to the dugouts to speak with Lions manager, Alex Neil, Swans counterpart Vítor Matos and fourth official Ruebyn Ricardo.Joy for Eckert as 10-man Southampton edge out Portsmouth in feisty derbyRead moreA security guard was also on the scene, with the referee seeming to point to an area in the stands behind the Swansea dugout. When play eventually resumed it was announced in the stadium that there had been a report of racist chanting, adding that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.But the unsavoury incident could not take the gloss off a dramatic last-gasp 1-0 victory for the table-toppers.The Brazilian defender Neto Borges bagged a dramatic injury-time winner after earlier scoring an own goal as high-flyersMiddlesbroughsecured a thrilling 3-2 victory over battlingStoke.The 30-year-old netted his first league goal for 18 months as Boro stay second in the table after stretching their current unbeaten run to five games.Callum Brittain had fired the visitors ahead three minutes into the second half before Junior Tchamadeu’s shot deflected in off Borges for an unfortunate own goal soon afterwards.The England Under-21 hitman Will Lankshear restored the visitors’ lead with his eighth league goal in 10 games after Stoke keeper Viktor Johansson inexplicably spilled Brighton loanee Amario Cozier-Duberry’s left-foot strike from the edge of the area. It took the striker to the top of the Championship scoring charts.Substitute Robert Bozenik looked to have earned the home side a point, slotting home after Boro skipper Luke Ayling’s poor clearance with five minutes left, but Borges scored from close range in the first of four minutes of stoppage time.View image in fullscreenNeto Borges fires in Middlesbrough’s winner.Photograph: Nigel French/PAWatford’s woeful season took another turn for the worse as they conceded four first-half goals in a 5-1 defeat atCardiffto drop into the relegation zone.Rising Republic of Ireland star Jack Moylan scored twice in the first half, winning and converting an 11th-minute penalty and then picking his spot to beat Federico Ravaglia in a one-on one in the 35th.Hornets skipper Mattie Pollock had brought down Moylan for the penalty and then headed into his own net from a corner in the 41st minute before Ollie Tanner added the fourth in the fifth minute of first-half added time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBirminghamunderlined their growing promotion credentials with a commanding 4-0 victory over 10-manPrestonat St Andrew’s. Two goals from August Priske and one each for Liam Millar and Demarai Gray gave Chris Davies’ men a third win in four games – and their first at home. Preston, who played most of the second half with 10 men, remain rooted to the bottom of the table.Ivan Mesik scored a dramatic last-gasp leveller forCharltonto clinch a 2-2 draw atBurnley, extending the hosts’ 360-day wait for a home league win. Largie Ramazani’s 57th-minute goal putBurnleyinto a 2-1 lead at Turf Moor, but substitute Mesik denied equalised with virtually the last kick of an absorbing contest.West Bromstaged a dramatic late revival to beatWrexham2-1 at Stok Cae Ras. Kieffer Moore’s stunning second-half strike gaveWrexhamhope that they could claim back-to-back home wins for the first time since February. But West Brom scored twice in five minutes through Isaac Price and Aune Heggebo to stop the rot after derby defeats to Wolves and Birmingham.Wolvessuffered their first home league defeat of the season asBoltonwon 3-1 at Molineux. Atsuki Ito gave Steven Schumacher’s visitors a deserved 28th-minute lead and although Jean-Ricner Bellegarde equalised five minutes after the break, substitute Sam Dalby and Josh Sheehan struck in the last 20 minutes to seal victory.A magnificent goalkeeping display from Balazs Toth inspiredBlackburnto a 1-0 victory overBristol Cityat Ashton Gate. Toth was simply unbeatable on the night, making a string of outstanding saves, particularly in the first half. Oladapo Afolayan rifled home the only goal in the 38th minute.PosTeamPGDPts1Swansea109232Middlesbrough106213Birmingham106174West Brom102175West Ham911166Stoke101167Blackburn102158QPR93149Wolverhampton921410Millwall1001411Bristol City10-21412Charlton10-31413Southampton9101314Bolton10-31315Sheff Utd911216Wrexham10-41117Lincoln City9-41118Cardiff1011019Norwich9-2920Portsmouth8-2821Burnley10-4822Watford10-11823Derby9-7624Preston North End10-124Explore more on these topicsChampionshipMillwallSwansea CityMiddlesbroughStoke CityWatfordCardiff CityShareReuse this content

title: Matt Richardson vows to cooperate with investigation into alleged misconduct | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Matt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation into allegations of serious misconduct after he was withdrawn from this week’s World Track Cycling Championships in Shanghai
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Matt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation into allegations of serious misconduct after he was withdrawn from this week’s World Track Cycling Championships in Shanghai
Content: Matt Richardson was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes before he was withdrawn from the World Track Cycling Championships.Photograph: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatt Richardson was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes before he was withdrawn from the World Track Cycling Championships.Photograph: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesCyclingMatt Richardson vows to cooperate with investigation into alleged misconductRichardson ‘disappointed’ to miss world championships‘I understand the seriousness of what has been raised’Sean IngleTue 13 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation intoallegations of serious misconductafter he was withdrawn from this week’s Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.In an Instagram post on Tuesday, Richardson said that he understood the seriousness of the allegations, which the Times reported were related to his behaviour to other riders, and promised that he would act with contrition to anyone he had offended.Seixas makes Giro di Lombardia history after riders stage safety protestRead more“I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI TrackCyclingWorld Championships,” said Richardson, who switched allegiance from Australia to Britain after the Paris 2024 Olympics.“British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will cooperate fully with its processes. I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected. Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete.”The 27-year-old, who was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes in China, with chances in the team and individual sprints and the keirin, admitted he was disappointed to have to pull out.“I am deeply disappointed to miss the World Championships, and I wish the Great Britain team and every rider competing the very best,” he added. “I ask that my family’s privacy is respected at this time.”In a statement, UK Sport said it supported the seriousness with which British Cycling was treating the allegation but stressed that Richardson must be given a fair hearing. “We support the seriousness with which British Cycling is treating this matter and it is essential that proper and fair process is followed,” it said.“The highest standards of integrity and athlete welfare are non-negotiable when it comes to UK Sport’s commitment to winning well.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patrice Motsepe’s Caf presidency under pressure after Afcon U-turn as Eto’o waits in wings | Football politics | The Guardian
description: Patrice Motsepe’s leadership of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) is under growing pressure, with officials from across the continent warning they have lost trust in the president
Author: Romain Molina
Headline: Patrice Motsepe’s leadership of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) is under growing pressure, with officials from across the continent warning they have lost trust in the president
Content: Patrice Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are trying to gain Gianni Infantino’s approval should Motsepe step down early.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APView image in fullscreenPatrice Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are trying to gain Gianni Infantino’s approval should Motsepe step down early.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APFootball politicsPatrice Motsepe’s Caf presidency under pressure after Afcon U-turn as Eto’o waits in wingsRivals lining up to position as potential replacementsAfcon tournament expected to return to biennial cycleEd AaronsandRomain MolinaTue 13 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrice Motsepe’s leadership of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) is under growing pressure, with officials from across the continent warning they have lost trust in the president and rivals including Samuel Eto’o positioning themselves potentially to replace him.A return to a biennial Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) cycle is expected to be confirmed at Caf’s executive committee meeting in Abidjan next month after Motsepe surprisingly announced the U-turn last week – 10 months after the decision was taken tohold it every four years. That move is said to have wide support within Africa, but several sources have said there has been a weakening of trust in Caf’s leadership, with some questioning Motsepe’s management.Most national association presidents are said to have been unaware Motsepe intended to announce the proposed change to Afcon’s frequency until the issue was raised at a strategic conference in Cape Verde last week. Motsepe confirmed he was not intending to stand for re-election for a third time when his term expires in 2029 and pledged Africa’s “unconditional support” for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president in March on the “unanimous” behalf of all 54 of Caf’s member associations.It is understood Infantino remains extremely popular in Africa even though there are 10 to 15 member associations who would consider voting against him, asrevealed in August. Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are believed to be attempting to gain Infantino’s approval should the South African billionaire be persuaded to step down early.View image in fullscreenFormer Barcelona forward Samuel Eto’o is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee.Photograph: Steve Luciano/APThey include Eto’o, the former Barcelona and Inter striker, who is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee, Ahmed Yahya of Mauritania, Côte d’Ivoire’s Yacine Idriss Diallo, and Souleiman Waberi, a Fifa council member from Djibouti who has been chargedwith embezzlement and money laundering. He has denied the allegations. Other candidates may emerge from southern Africa.Sources indicate that Infantino could hold the key to whether Motsepe continues. The other option would be to challenge Motsepe through Caf’s statutory mechanisms, which say an extraordinary general assembly can be convened after a written request from at least two-thirds of the members of the executive committee.Infantino is thought to have fallen out with Motsepe after Motsepe allowed the Somali referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the United States for the 2026 World Cup, to take charge of Uefa’s Super Cup final in August amid growing tensions with European football’s governing body. However, sources have indicated their relationship has improved in recent weeks as Infantino has sought to solidify his support in Africa.Motsepe promised annual distributions of about $700,000 (£528,000) from Caf to each association at the conference in Cape Verde – an increase of $500,000 – and is understood to have increased payments to executive committee members for attending meetings from $150 to $350, and to have introduced for them an annual bonus payment of about $8,000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat is despite growing concerns over Caf’s finances, with a broadcast deal signed with IMG due to expire after the 2027 Afcon. Asreported by the Guardianin February, there are major doubts about whether that tournament will go ahead owing to questions over the readiness of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda to host in June and July. Some sources are predicting that tournament could be pushed back to Christmas and the new year, which would cause major disruption to the European club season.Caf is believed to have broadcast offers for future tournaments from IMG and an unnamed firm, although it is not known how the package will be structured and whether the proposed return to a two-year cycle could affect its commercial value. A Caf spokesperson said the process remained ongoing and that no rights had been awarded.Explore more on these topicsFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: F1 returns to Africa for first time since 1993 with 10-year Rwanda deal from ‘early 2030s’ | Formula One | The Guardian
description: Formula One has answered Lewis Hamilton’s call to have a race in Africa after the sport’s bosses announced Rwanda will join the calendar
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Formula One has answered Lewis Hamilton’s call to have a race in Africa after the sport’s bosses announced Rwanda will join the calendar
Content: A rendered image of the planned new purpose-built track in Bugesera, 25 miles south of Kigali in Rwanda.Illustration: Formula 1/PAView image in fullscreenA rendered image of the planned new purpose-built track in Bugesera, 25 miles south of Kigali in Rwanda.Illustration: Formula 1/PAFormula OneF1 returns to Africa for first time since 1993 with 10-year Rwanda deal from ‘early 2030s’African Grand Prix will take place at new track near KigaliStefano Domenicali: ‘Today is a landmark moment for F1’Giles RichardsTue 13 Oct 2026 08.16 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar, ­having ­concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a ­purpose-built ­circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It will mark the first time F1 has raced in Africa since 1993.The meeting, to be known as the African Grand Prix, will be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 40km south of the capital, Kigali, and constitutes a successful conclusion to the sport’s long-held ambition to return to the African continent, which Lewis ­Hamilton has championed.Christian Horner: ‘Not all teams act that way. You don’t see the same brutality as when I left’Read moreF1 last raced in Africa at Kyalami in South Africa in 1993 and the seven-time world champion Hamilton has been outspoken in his belief that it should return, working behind the scenes to facilitate it.“For the past six or seven years I’ve been fighting in the background to get a grand prix, sitting with stakeholders and asking the question: ‘Why are we not in Africa? There’s one on every other continent, why not Africa?’” he said this year.View image in fullscreenGilles Villeneuve holds the victory silver cup as his Ferrari teammate Jody Scheckter of South Africa douses them both with champagne to celebrate their one-two victory at the 1979 South African Grand Prix.Photograph: APThe Rwanda track will be designed by WurzDesign, run by the former driver Alexander Wurz, but no ­specific date has been set for the first race, with F1 only stating the “early 2030s”. That timescale allows for it to be built and then authorised to full FIA – the governing body – Grade 1 status, with a rendition of the circuit indicating an intent for it to flow across the natural contours of the landscape.South Africa – which hosted its race in East London, now known as KuGompo City, from 1962-66 before it moved to Kyalami in 1967 – was also in the running to host a race amid abooming fanbasein the country. F1, however, went with the proposal from Rwanda and its long-term commitment. The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda development board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth, including hosting events, ­conferences and entertainment.The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.In 2024 Rwanda hosted the FIA prize-giving gala, at which the country’s president, Paul Kagame, announced the intention to bid for a grand prix.The country has, ­however, attracted accusations of ­sportswashing, notably with Amnesty International forcefully criticising the Rwanda tourist board’s sponsorship of Aston Villa, saying: “The country is prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRwanda’s president, Paul Kagame, speaks at the press conference to announce the deal to stage a Formula One grand prix.Photograph: Jean Bizimana/ReutersKagame welcomed the return of F1, believing it would prove inspirational across the continent. “Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa,” he said. “Many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.”The F1 chief executive, Stefano Domenicali, insisted the agreement represented a broader long-term commitment between F1 and Rwanda.“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” he said. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent. This is about much more than hosting a grand prix. Together, we can create lasting economic and social benefits through tourism, investment, skills development and local business growth, ensuring the positive impact of this event is felt for generations.”South Africa, meanwhile, still ­harbours hope of bringing a grand prix back to the country, with its sports minister, Gayton McKenzie, reacting to reports Rwanda would be given the nod last week by posting on X: “Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a ­continent of 55 countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030.”Explore more on these topicsFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There was a chance to stop him’: Parents react with fury to paedophile nursery worker revelations | Child protection | The Guardian
description: More than 50 families call for investigation into how Vincent Chan was allowed to return to job after inquiry by nursery
Author: Sirin Kale
Headline: More than 50 families call for investigation into how Vincent Chan was allowed to return to job after inquiry by nursery
Content: Vincent Chan was reported to his employer by a concerned parent in 2021 but was cleared to return to work.Photograph: Metropolitan Police/PAView image in fullscreenVincent Chan was reported to his employer by a concerned parent in 2021 but was cleared to return to work.Photograph: Metropolitan Police/PAChild protection‘There was a chance to stop him’: Parents react with fury to paedophile nursery worker revelationsMore than 50 families call for investigation into how Vincent Chan was allowed to return to job after inquiry by nurserySirin KaleInvestigations correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 14.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe parents of the victims of paedophile nursery worker Vincent Chan have reacted with fury to the news that he was cleared to return to work after “significant concerns” wereraised by the parent of a young girl.As first revealedin the Guardian, Chan was reported to his employer, the nursery chain Bright Horizons, by a concerned parent in 2021.After being investigated by Bright Horizons, with the knowledge of Camden council, Chan was cleared to return to work at the nursery on the Finchley Road in north-westLondon. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself abusing three-year-old girls in his care.“I feel a level of anger that I can barely put into words,” said one mother. Images of her daughter were found on Chan’s personal devices after his arrest.She added: “In 2021, around the time serious concerns had been raised about Vincent Chan, he was made my daughter’s key worker. We trusted him with her most intimate care, believing she was safe.“Knowing there was a chance to stop him before he had such extensive access to her is unbearable. I am heartbroken, but above all furious at Bright Horizons for failing to protect our children.”The families have called for an immediate “independent examination” of how the 2021 complaint was handled.In a statement issued by the law firm Leigh Day, which is representing 50 families affected by Chan’s abuse, they called for a “full and independent account of what happened, who knew what, when they knew it and why these decisions were made”.The parents of Chan’s victims have been promised answers in the form of a repeatedly delayed safeguarding review, led by an independent reviewer appointed by Camden council. But many expressed fury that they only learned the review had been pushed back to 2027 in the Guardian article.“Expressions of regret are meaningless,” said the parents in a statement. “Families deserve the truth about what happened, accountability for the decisions that were made, and action to make sure this cannot happen again. We cannot wait until 2027 for answers.”Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe families also restated their calls for Camden council to consider prosecuting Bright Horizons under health and safety legislation. “The Guardian’s report also strengthens the case for a criminal investigation,” they said.The row over the decision to clear Chan to return to work has overshadowed the Labour MP Sagal Abdi-Wali’s first week as an MP after her byelection victory in Holborn and St Pancras last week. Before becoming an MP, Abdi-Wali was leader of Camden council, presiding over the delayed review.Earlier on Tuesday Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Kilburn, wrote to Camden council, asking it to commit to publishing the documentation relating to the 2021 investigation.“These revelations are causing significant distress to parents in my constituency, particularly the families directly affected by Chan’s crimes,” Siddiq wrote.“Families should not have to wait any longer for these answers,” she added.Camden council said: “We know the parents of the children who attended the nursery, and the wider public, will be concerned that a complaint was made about Vincent Chan to Bright Horizons in 2021 – and will want to know how this was responded to.“In 2021, Camden council’s local authority designated officer (LADO) provided advice to Bright Horizons, after Bright Horizons informed them (the LADO) of a complaint.“We have shared all relevant documents and information with the independent review team. We want families to get the answers they deserve, in full, through the outcome of the independent review.”A Bright Horizons spokesperson said: “We remain appalled by Vincent Chan’s crimes, and our thoughts are first and foremost with the children and families affected.“We strongly encourage parents to share all their concerns with the child safeguarding practice review (CSPR), which is being led by an independent reviewer and will rightly examine this case in full.“As the review is ongoing, we are unable to comment without the express written authorisation of the committee.”Explore more on these topicsChild protectionChildrenLondonCrimeChildcareLocal governmentEarly years educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park named | South Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: William Chapman was pronounced dead at scene on Saturday after scaling fence and entering enclosure
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: William Chapman was pronounced dead at scene on Saturday after scaling fence and entering enclosure
Content: Chapman (pictured) was heard shouting ‘stop’ after walking up to the 200kg male Siberian tiger.View image in fullscreenChapman (pictured) was heard shouting ‘stop’ after walking up to the 200kg male Siberian tiger.South YorkshireMan killed by tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park namedWilliam Chapman was pronounced dead at scene on Saturday after scaling fence and entering enclosureRobyn VinterNorth of England correspondent andNadeem BadshahTue 13 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man killed by a tiger at a zoo inSouth Yorkshirehas been named locally as William Chapman.Chapman scaled the fence and entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park nearDoncasteron Saturday afternoon. Witnesses described seeing Chapman, who has not been officially named by police, walking up to a 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai, which attacked him.The incident lasted only a couple of minutes and Chapman, who is believed to have been in his 20s, was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after.Chapman had “suffered from significant mental illness”, his family said in a statement, describing him as a “bright, warm and engaging young man”.The family said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened.“The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.“William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back.“Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.“It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process.”Videos in which onlookers urged him not to approach the tiger and to “play dead” during the attack were shared online in the aftermath, as well as a number of AI-generated fakes. Police advised members of the public to avoid sharing them. They said the man’s family was being supported by specialist officers.Donald Trump reposted a silent 41-second video apparently showing the attack on his Truth Social account on Tuesday, captioning it: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.”A minute later, he posted a 24-second video compilation of lion attacks on people, this one accompanied by jaunty music.Chapman was a child actor who appeared in the ITV programme May Contain Nuts and in the BBC’s True Stories series, according to the website IMDb.He previously attended Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire.In a tribute shared on Facebook, the school said: “We are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of our former student, William Chapman.“Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.“We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us.“It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.“William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.”Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated on Saturday and will remain closed on Wednesday.Dan Swaine, the executive director of place at Doncaster council, said: “As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation.“We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident.“At this time, we won’t be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time.”The park said staff were receiving specialist support and that Altai, a member of an endangered species, would not be euthanised.Wildlife and zoo experts told the Guardian it was unlikely the wildlife park would have been able to prevent the incident.Amy Dickman, a professor of wildlife conservation and the director ofWildCRUat the University of Oxford, said: “I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.”Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at the University of Reading, who until recently sat on the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ zoos expert committee, said: “It’s simply not possible … at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.”He added: “If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house. You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.”A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an “urgent review” of “how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next”.Explore more on these topicsSouth YorkshireYorkshireDoncasterEnglandZoosNorth of EnglandShareReuse this content

title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over Tupac Shakur’s murder | Tupac Shakur | The Guardian
description: ‘You don’t get to take a man from his family … and just walk away from it,’ judge says as former gang leader sentenced
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: ‘You don’t get to take a man from his family … and just walk away from it,’ judge says as former gang leader sentenced
Content: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis appears in court during his murder trial in Clark county district court in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 20 August.Photograph: Steve Marcus/ReutersView image in fullscreenDuane ‘Keffe D’ Davis appears in court during his murder trial in Clark county district court in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 20 August.Photograph: Steve Marcus/ReutersTupac ShakurDuane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over Tupac Shakur’s murder‘You don’t get to take a man from his family … and just walk away from it,’ judge says as former gang leader sentencedTupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the caseUwa Ede-OsifoTue 13 Oct 2026 15.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leaderconvictedof murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapperTupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing … ‘Yeah, I was involved in this. But I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now,’” Judge Carli Kierny said Tuesday as she delivered the sentence.“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it,” Kierny continued.On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near theLas Vegasstrip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.For decades, hismurder remained unsolvedand one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries. Davis is the only person to beconvicted in connection to Shakur’s murder.“It was hard sitting, listening over and over and over again to someone describe – bit by bit, how they hunted Tupac Amaru Shakur down,” the rapper’s sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, said on Tuesday minutes before Davis was sentenced.She described her brother as a father figure. “He was who God trusted to take care of me,” she told the court.The grief from her brother’s murder led Sekyiwa Shakur to be hospitalized several times for depression, suicidal ideation and PTSD, she said.She and the rapper’s stepbrother, Maurice Shakur, called for Davis to face the maximum penalty.“Time to sit down and contemplate what you’ve done to the world, not just to me,” Sekyiwa Shakur said.Davis stared intently, but appeared stoic as the relatives spoke. He vowed earlier during the hearing to appeal the case.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘It always comes around’: fans react to conviction in Tupac Shakur’s murder 30 years laterRead moreA confluence of several factors hindered the investigation. The code of silence within street culture made some witnesses averse to police cooperation. Las Vegas police were skeptical about leads from their Compton counterparts, given that the head of security for Shakur’s record label was a former Compton cop.Orlando Anderson, a gangster and Davis’s nephew, was on law enforcement’s radar as the possible gunman. The night Shakur was killed, the young rap star got into an altercation with Anderson. Las Vegas police interviewed Anderson, but he was never arrested. Anderson later died in 1998.But then, in 2023, Davis wasarrestedon a murder charge.It was Davis’s own media tour, touting his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, and a 2019 “tell-all” memoir that led to the breakthrough.Davis had felt emboldened by a 2008 backdoor deal he brokered with police. He spoke candidly to investigators about Shakur’s shooting, who had actually been seeking information about the death of Christopher Wallace, known as Biggie Smalls or The Notorious BIG. Under a proffer agreement, Davis was not to face charges for any offenses he shared.In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that he and a group of other men targeted Shakur and his entourage, seeking retribution for the scuffle with his nephew.The memoir and the interview became central to prosecutors’ case. They argued the details amounted to a confession and that his public remarks voided the proffer agreement.During Davis’s murder trial, his defense team maintained that these details were embellished. They also argued, during the trial, that there was no physical evidence, such as a murder weapon, tying Davis to the Las Vegas slaying.Ultimately, jurors sided with the state.Explore more on these topicsTupac ShakurUS crimeWest CoastCaliforniaNevadaLas VegasnewsShareReuse this content

title: British and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’ | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups
Content: A UVF mural on Newtownards Road in east Belfast, since replaced with images of Edward Carson.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyView image in fullscreenA UVF mural on Newtownards Road in east Belfast, since replaced with images of Edward Carson.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyNorthern IrelandBritish and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groupsRory CarrollIreland correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups inNorthern Irelandto negotiate their disbandment, according to a report.A “window of opportunity” exists to establish a formal transition mechanism for loyalist and republican groups, provided certain conditions are met, it said.The Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment, commissioned by both governments and published on Tuesday, said groups should not receive financial rewards for engaging in the process.Fleur Ravensbergen, a Dutch conflict resolution expert who authored the report, said in Belfast: “I have concluded that there is sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition.”Ravensbergen said she found “significant willingness to engage” among paramilitaries during a year-long scoping exercise.She added: “There was limited support for the term ‘disbandment’ as the endpoint of a transition process. However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording.”Paramilitary groups were expected to fade after the1998 Good Friday agreement, but some endured and evolved into lucrative enterprises involved in drug dealing, extortion and coercive control.Agreeing a transition process was more important than the terminology used to describe disbandment, said Ravensbergen, a lecturer in conflict resolution and governance at the University of Amsterdam.She said: “I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process. Inaction is not a neutral option. My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.”Chris Bryant, theNorthern Irelandsecretary, thanked Ravensbergen and said the government was committed to ending paramilitarism.Bryant said: “While these groups may pose as protectors of their communities, they are largely engaged in criminality including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation, blighting the very communities they perversely claim to protect. Their continued influence is a stain on our collective conscience.”He said the government would consider the report and liaise with authorities in Dublin before responding to the proposed transition mechanism.He added: “It is evident from the report that the implementation of any process will face challenges and will need the support from across the political community in Northern Ireland.”Naomi Long, Northern Ireland’s justice minister and a member of the Alliance party, criticised Ravensbergen’s appointment as an interlocutor last year, saying engagement with paramilitaries and criminal gangs risked giving them a veneer of legitimacy.Long said at the time: “The idea that paramilitary groups can transition into law-abiding entities has long since moved beyond the point of credibility. They cannot continue to be treated as if they are genuinely committed to reform – that moment passed long ago.”The report did not identify individuals or specific organisations because discussions were held on a confidential basis.It said: “The nature, extent and impact of paramilitary influence vary considerably between paramilitary groups, communities and geographical areas. However, it is clear that residual paramilitary structures continue to cause harm in some communities.”Ravensbergen said a transition mechanism would need credible monitoring and verification of progress and robust law enforcement.She declined to comment on the recent standoff between the Orange Order and nationalist residents at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it was outside the report’s remit. There is speculation that renewed tension over theDrumcree parademay boost paramilitary recruitment.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandNorthern Irish politicsGood Friday agreementnewsShareReuse this content

title: Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing
Content: Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a residential area in Kyiv.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenUkrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a residential area in Kyiv.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineAllies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says ZelenskyyUkrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharingLuke Harding, andAndrew Rothin KyivTue 13 Oct 2026 17.54 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine received no early warning from its partners about a second night of Russian ballistic missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, including a critical power plant struck after dark,Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid on Tuesday.The Ukrainian president had earlierdescribed an attack involving five missiles on Mondayas “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” hewrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.More ballistic missiles were then launched at Kyiv on Tuesday night, striking a key power plant in the capital despite a purported energy ceasefire claimed byDonald Trump. One person also died in a strike on a high-rise apartment building, according to the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said apartments were on fire and being evacuated. A further 13 injuries were reported.“Once again, ‌no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No 4,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media app Telegram, again without explaining why he thought there had been no warning.US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that theTrump administrationwas on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv.On Tuesday, however, Trump denied intelligence sharing had stopped. He told reporters: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them andRussiaon getting the war to end.”Trump hasdemanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineriesand has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?Read moreAsked on Tuesday whether Russia could use proceeds ​from the ​sale to purchase ​more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s ​a diesel ‌deal, not ​for ​us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said.Earlier the president claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyydescribed as “news to me”. Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said.“Russia did not heed the president … the Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted on Tuesday.Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.“It is deeply unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine receives no warnings about ballistic missile launches,” Zelenskyy said in a statement after the Tuesday strikes. “It is vital that the world does not remain silent about this. And it is crucial that America clearly sees what is happening and who is responsible for the continuation of the war.”The blasts could be heard in centralKyivas Ukraine’s air defences failed to stop the high-speed Russian missile targeting the capital. The missile strikes on Ukraine’s left bank targeted a thermal power plant, Zelenskyy said, and also struck an apartment building leaving both dead and injured in the latest strike on the capital.Zelenskyy warned on Tuesday evening that Russia was planning further strikes with ballistic missiles, telling Ukrainians: “Please take care of yourselves tonight and tomorrow.”In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. It has particularly stepped up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, cutting power and water in large parts of Ukraine’s capital as emergency workers race to restore basic utilities. Ukraine, meanwhile, has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.According tothe Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.Speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation with the US was continuing and said the lack of warning about the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.On Monday, Russia also bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.Meanwhile, 11 sailors were missing after their ship was sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria. The incident prompted Bulgaria to summon Russia’s ⁠ambassador.Two cargo ships were hit ⁠by drones overnight and one ​was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but the prime minister, Rumen Radev, said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House.Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strongEurope, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaVolodymyr ZelenskyyTrump administrationUS foreign policyKyivDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on record | Birds | The Guardian
description: Nearly half of species are in decline, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit, conservation bodies say
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Nearly half of species are in decline, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit, conservation bodies say
Content: The sound of skylarks could become only a memory, says one expert.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe sound of skylarks could become only a memory, says one expert.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyBirds‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on recordNearly half of species are in decline, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit, conservation bodies sayMatthew PearceTue 13 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWild bird populations in the UK have fallen to their lowest level since records began, figures show, with nearly half of species in decline.Figuresproduced by leading nature conservation bodies for the government show that average populations across 132 native breeding species fell by 19% between 1970 and 2025, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit in recent years.Prof Richard Gregory, the head of monitoring at theRSPB, called the overall findings “shocking and sobering”.View image in fullscreenSwift populations have declined by about 25% in five years.Photograph: Stephen Kill/Alamy“Birds are indicators of the way we’re looking after the countryside and the world around us,” he said. “We’re losing the birds that people are so emotionally connected to and want to protect.”Average populations of turtle doves have fallen by more than half in five years, showing no sign of the bird recovering from thebrink of extinction. Tree sparrows, wood warblers and capercaillie were among the birds with the next biggest average annual decreases between 2019 and 2024.Wild bird populations between 1970 and 2025,Swifts, whose arrival for many marks the beginning of summer, have declined by about 25% in five years, an average of nearly 6% a year across the UK. Bullfinches fell at a similar rate nationally, and by an average of 11% a year in England.Of the 132 native breeding species tracked, 45% have declined over the past five years, while just 27% have increased. In England, 55% of monitored species have declined.Seabirds are the worst hit group, down by more than a fifth over the past five years. Dr Ailidh Barnes, who helps build the index at the British Trust for Ornithology, said avian flu had “decimated” species such as Arctic skuas and terns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionListen to Britain’s dawn chorus of 1976: the dramatic loss of birdsong in 50 yearsRead moreThe disease spread quickly, she said, because seabirds nested shoulder to shoulder, and each year a different species appeared to suffer. “There’s a lag of data collection and then data analysis, and now we’re actually seeing that effect coming through,” she said.View image in fullscreenRed kite numbers have risen by 48% since 2019.Photograph: James Manning/PAFarmland bird populations have decreased by 63% since 1970 and 12% since 2020. Defra attributes the long-term decline to changes in farming since the 1950s, including the loss of mixed farming (crops and livestock), increased pesticide and fertiliser use, and the removal of hedgerows.Gregory said if the trend continued, the songs of farm birds such as skylarks and yellowhammers would become only “memories” of what the countryside used to be like.Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?Read more“It’s a familiar story of declining farmland [birds],” he added. “That’s not showing any upturn. We need to do more there to get nature-friendly farming right and help support farmers.”Despite the general decline, some populations are booming. Red kite populations have risen by 48% since 2019, and firecrests are up 300% over the same period. Gregory also highlighted the number of cranes “really coming back from extinction in the UK”,rising to 87 pairsnationally.Gregory said these examples proved concerted efforts to save species worked. “We know the main drivers of change and we can bring about recovery, but we need to massively scale up our conservation intervention,” he said. “We need more funding to support these conservation measures and they need to be at a larger spatial scale.”A Defra spokesperson said: “We are committed to the recovery and protection of our native birds. There are multiple pressures on wild bird populations, including avian flu. We are acting to protect them, from supporting farmers to manage their land in a way that benefits farmland birds, to working with fishers to prevent the accidental catch of seabirds.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsAnimalsWildlifeRSPBConservationEndangered speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Coastal erosion in England has claimed at least 183 homes in past 16 years | Coastlines | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Homes demolished along east coast after being deemed too vulnerable to live in, figures reveal
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Exclusive: Homes demolished along east coast after being deemed too vulnerable to live in, figures reveal
Content: The scene after a cliff collapsed on 6 December 2013 in Hemsby, England.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe scene after a cliff collapsed on 6 December 2013 in Hemsby, England.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesCoastlinesCoastal erosion in England has claimed at least 183 homes in past 16 yearsExclusive: Homes demolished along east coast after being deemed too vulnerable to live in, figures revealMatthew PearceTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeaside communities along the east coast ofEnglandhave lost at least183 homes to coastalerosion and landslides over the past 16 years, figures obtained by the Guardian reveal.After councils judged properties across the Yorkshire and East Anglian coasts too vulnerable to remain safely occupied, the homes were proactively demolished.The demolitions cost £1.1m, with theEnvironment Agencycontributing about £482,000 towards clearing 61 homes at risk of collapsing and the rest paid for by councils and at times by homeowners themselves.Coastal erosion is the gradual wearing away and retreat of the sea shoreline, which can destabilise cliffs and eventually force homes and infrastructure to be demolished before they collapse. While it is a natural process, scientists said the climate crisis was accelerating the retreat of the UK’s shores.The Guardian requested data from nine councils noted in a House of Commonsenvironment, food and rural affairs committee (EFRA) reportas being some of the most vulnerable to coastal erosion.East Riding of Yorkshire council, which includes vulnerable communities in Skipsea, Aldbrough and Mappleton, has demolished 66 homes since 2010 – the most of these nine local authorities.Great Yarmouth borough council (GYBC) has demolished 64 homes since 2010, with all the houseslocated in the village of Hemsby. Since December 2025, the council has removed 41 properties in the seaside resort.A GYBC spokesperson said: “Last winter, the dunes in Hemsby saw about 50% of the erosion predicted for the entirety of the next 30 years. More than 10 metres of land was lost in just over 12 months.“Council staff continue to liaise with people to make sure residents and the public are safe and work closely with people to offer support and advice and explain the options available.”North Norfolk council has proactively demolished 21 homes over the same period.East Suffolk council, which only held data for the past six years, recorded a sharp rise in demolitions last year.Eight homes were demolished between 2020 and 2024, and 16 between May last year and April this year.Most of East Suffolk’s homes demolished this year are understood to be in Thorpeness. Hilary Lightfoot’s home, in which she lived and raised a family for 20 years, was demolished this year. “I’ve lost £650,000 – that was what my flat was worth,” she said. “I’ve had to dig into my pension savings to buy a house, of which I still owe money on. I’ve borrowed money. It’s just disastrous.”The Environment Agency estimates that3,500 properties in England are at risk from coastal erosionby 2055, increasing to more than 10,000 properties by 2105.More than 6 miles (10km) of major roads, 107 miles of minor roads and 3.5 miles of railway – many serving small, coastal communities – are also at risk from erosion over the next 80 years, according to the EA.Unlike flood damage, which can be covered by the Flood Re scheme, there is no UK insurance product for coastal erosion because insurers treat coastal retreat as a “virtual certainty” for some seaside homesrather than an accidental risk, according to the EFRA committee’s report.East Suffolk council said that although some government funding was available towards demolition, “there are currently limited mechanisms to support the wider costs of adaptation and relocation” for residents.The authority said it had invested about £1.5m in short-term measures designed to slow erosion and give residents more time to prepare, while also testing new approaches through the government’s flood and coastal innovation programme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSophie Day, senior research associate at the University of East Anglia, said because the east coast was made up of “very sandy, gravelly, silty material”, it was more vulnerable to erosion.She said wetter winters, made more likely by the climate crisis, would saturate and destabilise soft cliffs such as those on the east coast, while increased storminess and rising sea levels would worsen the impact of high tides and leave beaches with less time to recover between storms.While councils have increased spending on sea defences over the decades, Day said these protections have created an “illusion of permanence” for what is an accelerating issue. The scale of the threat from coastal erosion meant “we are going to have to shift to more of an acceptance of not intervening any more and enabling retreat”, she added.Day said adapting to a retreating coastline meant planning for the loss of homes and infrastructure before the next emergency, while working more closely with communities.“Having skilled people who are able to engage, who have the time, the training, the skills, to go and sit at somebody’s kitchen table and talk to them about the fact that, in a year, even five months’ time, their home may not be livable. What are the options? How can we find ways of giving people choices and support?”North Norfolk district council (NNDC) said: “Households in all 21 homes were supported by NNDC. Nineteen of these properties were proactively demolished before they reached the cliff edge and became an emergency.“NNDC continues to work with the Environment Agency and Defra … to better prepare communities. A number of pilot opportunities are under development. It is hoped that through this work, more targeted support for those impacted can become part of the business as usual and supported by government for the whole coast into the future.”A spokesperson for East Riding council said: “East Riding of Yorkshire has some of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, resulting in the loss of homes, businesses and roads. Through the Changing Coasts East Riding project, the council is working directly with residents, businesses and communities to find out the full economic, environmental and social impacts of these losses.”An Environment Agency spokesperson said it was “very aware” of how erosion was affecting coastal homeowners and communities.They said: “While local authorities are best placed to support affected residents, we’re backing them with £36m for coastal erosion adaptation pilots, slashing planning regulation red tape in vulnerable areas and offering £10,000 grants to fund the safe demolition of affected properties – with scope to go further for more complex jobs.”Explore more on these topicsCoastlinesEnglandSea levelClimate crisisLandslidesEnvironment AgencyEast Riding of YorkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not glamorous’: the volunteers counting flushed wet wipes on the banks of the Thames | Pollution | The Guardian
description: A Thames21 charity citizen science project helps track plastic pollution in the capital’s river
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: A Thames21 charity citizen science project helps track plastic pollution in the capital’s river
Content: Volunteers looking for flushed wet wipes on the Thames foreshire near Hammersmith Bridge.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenVolunteers looking for flushed wet wipes on the Thames foreshire near Hammersmith Bridge.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianPollution‘It’s not glamorous’: the volunteers counting flushed wet wipes on the banks of the ThamesA Thames21 charity citizen science project helps track plastic pollution in the capital’s riverMatthew PearceTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a pale-blue Sunday morning on the foreshore of the River Thames, 40 people are searching for what others have tried to lose. Dotted across a 250-metre stretch under Hammersmith Bridge, they are combing through layers of silt, seashells and dirty driftwood to find one of the river’s most stubborn problems: wet wipes.“People come and walk here and it looks just like mud, at a distance,” says the organiser, Dr Felicity Rhodes. “And then you get closer in and see.”The dig forms part a citizen science project that has tracked sanitary litter on the banks of the Thames for nearly a decade. Set up by the environmental charity Thames21, volunteers are recruited to help map out the amount of wipes that are flushed down the toilet and washed up along the river. Findings are added to adatabase that quantifies plastic pollutionon the banks of the Thames.View image in fullscreenAt first glance the wipes blend in with the silt on the riverbed.Photograph: The Guardian“It’s not glamorous,” says Rhodes, the programme manager atThames21. “But through this data generation, we’ve created this dataset of really robust, accurate data that’s given us an understanding of the wet wipes here on the foreshore.”Hydrographic surveyors from the Port ofLondonauthority (PLA) are assisting the project, and are riverside before the volunteers arrive, having meticulously marked out channels of the foreshore based on where the last count took place. Volunteers lay quadrats, square frames, on the riverbed and drag metal sticks through the mud. One drag can pull up a clump of flushed wet wipes from what had appeared to be just silt to the naked eye; they are counted, recorded and deposited into a bucket for disposal, along with the plastic, vapes and other rubbish curios that come up.View image in fullscreenElio Gregori is a regular volunteer.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianJim Powell, an operations manager and hydrographic surveyor at the PLA, explains why Hammersmith is such a hotspot for grime. “You’re on the inside of a bend of the river so the water velocities are slower,” he says. Material builds up on the inside because the water flows faster on the outside. “As soon as you get bits of wood and tyres, they start to trap sediment and other things start getting caught, like plastic wipes. Then it just snowballs from there.”Elio Gregori, 66, has attended about 300 sessions since he retired. “You can look at a place like this and assume that it’s mostly nice and clean, but under the surface is a wet wipe,” he says, fishing a knot of rotten-brown wipes out of his bucket as an exhibit. “When it’s in the environment, you wouldn’t really recognise it as a wet wipe. If you look down, it opens your eyes to how much of this stuff is around.”Many wet wipes contain plastic fibres and are designed to stay intact when wet – even some marketed as biodegradable. When London’s wipes are flushed down the toilet, they can end up on the riverbanks, mostly through storm water overflow and sewage outfall. Thames Water estimates 3.8bn wipes are flushed into its network each year – enough to build more than 10 wet and stinking Big Bens.“Plastic here on the foreshore has the potential to make its way into the ocean and into our ocean food system as well,” says Rhodes. “We want to remove plastic here so that it doesn’t become microplastic in the ocean.”A young refugee from Sudan attended the count with the community centre West London Welcome. “It’s really a shame for people to throw bad things through toilets,” he said. “This waste is in this nice area … people should have to be more careful in the environment where these things ended up.”View image in fullscreenA flushed sanitary item in the silt of the riverbed.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianSome relief arrived last year when thedelayed Thames Tideway Tunnelopened – the £4.6bn project designed to reduce sewage discharges into the river.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThen diggers came to this part of the foreshore a few months later to remove the infamous “Wet Wipe Island”, the 180-tonne amalgamation of wipes that had grown so large it had begun to alter the shape of the river.Thames21estimates the work removed 5m wipes that had congealed into a 250-metre island.Now, Thames21 is back to assess what the Tideway Tunnel – the “super sewer” – and removing Wet Wipe Island has done. “Will we see fewer wet wipes? Most likely,” says Rhodes. “Are they re-accumulating? We might be able to start to see any changes and that’s why it’s really important to keep monitoring.”View image in fullscreenWaste collects near Hammersmith Bridge due to the bend in the river.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianLast December,the government announcedthat selling single-use wet wipes containing plastic will be illegal by May 2027. It was a win for Thames21, who had for years been banging the drum and sharing their data with Fleur Anderson, the MP for Putney, who campaigned on the issue in parliament.By the end of the weekend’s count, Thames21 said volunteers had found 733 wipes in 50 sampling squares, compared with 1,584 found in the same spots in April. It is a substantial drop in the recorded count, although the PLA says it is still early days, and two surveys cannot yet establish precisely how much of it is due to the cleanups, the Tideway tunnel or changing conditions on the river.But for now, Thames21 volunteers plan to keep counting. “We expect that they’ll still wash up on the river for a time,” says Rhodes. “What we’re doing here is tracking the ongoing change in that.”Explore more on these topicsPollutionPlasticsThe ThamesWasteRiversLondonEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs? | Birds | The Guardian
description: When populations fall, fledglings can struggle to learn the right notes to attract mates. But research on how birds communicate offers hope for species’ survival
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: When populations fall, fledglings can struggle to learn the right notes to attract mates. But research on how birds communicate offers hope for species’ survival
Content: A rufous-collared sparrow. The bird’s songs, some of which are no longer heard, have been recreated with a computer from annotations made in the 1960s. About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds, such as finches, sparrows and blackbirds.Photograph: Martín BenchimolView image in fullscreenA rufous-collared sparrow. The bird’s songs, some of which are no longer heard, have been recreated with a computer from annotations made in the 1960s. About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds, such as finches, sparrows and blackbirds.Photograph: Martín BenchimolThe age of extinctionBirdsTrill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?When populations fall, fledglings can struggle to learn the right notes to attract mates. But research on how birds communicate offers hope for species’ survivalSupported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleListening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area.That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect”, they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory and ultimately survive.If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers.Birdscan begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species, jeopardising their chances of breeding.Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well – which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo.“When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who co-authored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds.Butanimals’ learned behaviour or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin.13:49Guardian-produced documentary Dream of BirdsThe rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist.About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider group of passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds,has identified common “motifs”or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes and harmonic notes.The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range.View image in fullscreenRecreations of hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs made in the 1960s. Some of the themes recorded decades ago have died out.Photograph: Martín BenchimolThe song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out.It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined.Birds’ songs can change naturally over time – for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes.Songbirds learn from other members of their species - such as a father or neighbours –which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge.View image in fullscreenA male cirl bunting with chicks – the birds are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the ‘notes’ used in their songs.Photograph: José B Ruiz/naturepl.com“There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behaviour at the University of Plymouth, whostudied a group of cirl buntingsthat were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project.Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal.A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says.Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated.Aseparate study in Australiatracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation.The secret call of the wild: how animals teach each other to surviveRead more“Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins.Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that AI could help provide live tutoring in the future.View image in fullscreenA pair of critically endangered regent honeyeaters in New South Wales, Australia.Photograph: RCAustralia/AlamyDialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarising birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this.A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.”In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsBirdsThe age of extinctionWildlifeEndangered speciesAnimalsConservationAnimal behaviourBirdwatchingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Farage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Farage’s intervention comes as Reform chair Zia Yusuf criticises ‘everybody’ in former Tory government that included Jenrick and Suella Braverman
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Farage’s intervention comes as Reform chair Zia Yusuf criticises ‘everybody’ in former Tory government that included Jenrick and Suella Braverman
