Content: Jenrick had said Reform would deploy the Royal Marines to take boats back to France, and ‘if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so’.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenJenrick had said Reform would deploy the Royal Marines to take boats back to France, and ‘if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so’.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAReform UKFarage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claimFarage’s intervention comes as Reform chair Zia Yusuf criticises ‘everybody’ in former Tory government that included Jenrick and Suella BravermanJessica ElgotDeputy political editorTue 13 Oct 2026 10.49 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel, hours after one of his MPs said the Royal Marines should be permitted to fire on the boats.Farage overruledRobert Jenrick, a Reform UK MP who defected from the Conservatives, who had told TalkTV that the party would deploy the marines to take boats back to France.In a day of party splits where a poll showed the party had fallen to third place behind the Conservatives, theReform UKchair, Zia Yusuf, also suggested he would not trust Conservative defectors such as Jenrick – and criticised another Reform MP, Suella Braverman, for her suggestions that she could not be considered English because of her ethnicity.The initial row was sparked by Jenrick saying his was the only party prepared to use force against people crossing in small boats. “What we are going to do, and we’re the only political party that has the courage to say this, is deploy the Royal Marines into the Channel. If they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so,” he said.But speaking on LBC, Farage said he would not authorise routine use of force, that it would be used only if soldiers were fired at, and that Jenrick was being “utterly misconstrued”.Children and women included in Reform plan to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekersRead more“Anybody wearing British military uniform who gets fired at has the right to respond. That’s what he was saying,” he said. “Remember, in these camps, every week there are shootings, there are stabbings.“We are dealing here with very, very serious international criminal organisations, and what we’re saying is, we will, if we win the next election, pick these people up and take them back to France.“There is a possibility that initially that might be met with some force. If it is, force will be met with force. But I tell you something: within two weeks of boats being taken back to France, the boats will stop coming.”Jenrick had said that allowing the use of force would mean the problem would end “in just a few days”. He said using force was “obviously not what we want to see happen”, adding: “We want to see these individuals picked up off the boats in a sensible and reasonable way, and taken straight back to France.”The defence minister Luke Pollard called the comments “disgusting and illegal”, and said the armed forces were not allowed to accept “an illegal order”.“We do not shoot unarmed civilians. We do not take military action against civilians,” Pollard told Times Radio. “The idea of this is a soundbite designed by Reform to distract from their sleaze and their scandal … it’s abhorrent to military values, it’s abhorrent to British values.“I don’t think anyone should give this any truck. We can all see what this is: an attempt to distract from Reform’s internal woes.”Yusuf, who himself has previously promised that “lethal force” would be used to stop migrants on boats reaching Britain, also rowed back on the comments on Tuesday. But he said on BBC Breakfast that it would only be used “in extremely limited circumstances where it is necessary to protect innocent life”.“In the event there are people on those boats with weapons, with firearms, who think nothing of shedding innocent life, throwing people overboard, we need to be ready to respond.”But Yusuf also opened up new splits with Jenrick and Braverman – a former Conservative home secretary – in interviews on Tuesday. Asked if he still considered them to be “quislings” because they had been part of a Tory cabinet, as he had once posted on X, Yusuf told Sky News: “Everybody in that Conservative government – that did things that were not only damaging to the country, but were literally the opposite of the things that they promised to do – need to take responsibility for that.“I was looking on, as the Tories claimed they were going to cut immigration to the tens of thousands and then did the complete opposite. And I do think there is collective responsibility for that.”View image in fullscreenZia Yusuf said he did not agree with comments made by Suella Braverman that her south Asian heritage meant she was not English.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersHe said he did not agree with controversial comments made by Braverman that her south Asian heritage meant she was not English. “In my view Ashley Cole is the best English fullback in history, and I won’t take any other position. So in my view, Ashley Cole is English. The argument that he’s not English doesn’t hold water with me,” he said.“I do think it is important that we listen to people who are worried about some of the demographics in this country. I think that there are some legitimate arguments that they can make about that. But I will also say … whether it’s [Bukayo] Saka, Ashley Cole, Rio Ferdinand, Nasser Hussain, who I grew up watching when I went to the cricket, the idea that those people aren’t English is an alien concept to me. I would respectfully disagree with people, who make the opposite argument.”A new poll for the Times on Tuesday showed Reform had dropped to third place behind Labour and the Tories, in a boost for Kemi Badenoch’s party, which has its highest rating since she became Tory leader.Explore more on these topicsReform UKRobert JenrickNigel FarageImmigration and asylumMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds of early-release prisoners in England and Wales not being tagged, say MPs | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: MPs question monitoring of released offenders as Serco denies failures and probation union warns of strain on staff
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: MPs question monitoring of released offenders as Serco denies failures and probation union warns of strain on staff
Content: ‘If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all,’ said one senior probation worker.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all,’ said one senior probation worker.Photograph: Mark Richardson/AlamyPrisons and probationHundreds of early-release prisoners in England and Wales not being tagged, say MPsSerco denies tagging failures as police and probation officers struggle to cope with influx of released offendersRajeev SyalandJamie GriersonTue 13 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of prisoners released early acrossEnglandand Wales, including stalkers and violent offenders, are not being tagged, MPs have said, despite promises of the “toughest supervision in British history”.As the government begins releasing a second tranche of 650 offenders to relieve prison overcrowding, police and probation officers have said they are struggling to cope with a new influx of offenders who are supposed to be monitored in the community.Speaking during an urgent question in the Commons on Tuesday, the Labour MP Clive Efford asked why the outsourcing company Serco had failed to tag prisoners as they leave prison. Serco has denied any such failure.“They are not actually fulfilling their contracts. It can’t be beyond the tech firm’s ability to tag people on release. So what are these companies going to do about it?” he said.The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said most prisoners were not being tagged before release, despite assurances from the government that the tagging system would be the “toughest in history”.Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releasesRead more“The justice secretary told the country that proper safeguards would be put in place with a presumption that all released prisoners would be tagged. He called it the toughest tagging regime in history, but that was nonsense,” he said.Jake Richards, the justice minister, replied: “We are working closely with Serco and have seen an improvement in the implementation since March this year. Although there is a presumption of every person being tagged, ultimately it is an operational decision.”A Serco spokesperson said it is “delivering an excellent service, tagging a record number of people, and consistently meeting all our contractual measures”.The spokesperson added: “The Ministry of Justice has publicly recognised the quality of our performance and our team has successfully delivered four early release schemes.“We attempt to fit an electronic monitoring device to every person required to wear one. Where it is not possible to fit a device, or where the person breaches the conditions of their release, the individual is reported to the relevant authorities, who are responsible for considering and taking any further action.”About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after anintervention by Andy Burnham.Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.But the probation service union, Napo, said the releases were putting enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community.The union held a pre-ballot meeting on Tuesday concerning taking strike action over pay and workloads.Pay negotiations ended earlier in October with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early in 2022.A senior Prison and Probation Service source said a failure to place tags on released offenders as they left prison meant it could then be up to a month before they were tagged.“If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all before they reoffend,” they said.Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, said many of those who breached their tagging conditions – by consuming alcohol or drugs, or by breaching a curfew, for example – were not facing sanctions if arrested.“We’re seeing 95%-plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition. So there is zero sanction,” he said.The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England andWaleswas at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has said released offenders will be monitored under the“toughest supervision in British history”.New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure their victims.However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan was “not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’ | Construction industry | The Guardian
description: Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits
Content: Bellway is aiming to build between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAView image in fullscreenBellway is aiming to build between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAConstruction industryBurnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admitsJulia KolleweTue 13 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe newYour First Home programmefor first-time buyers could increase the number of houses British builder Bellway produces each year by 10%, its boss has said.Faced with a chronic shortage of homes, the government has made housing one of its top priorities and Andy Burnham’ssurprise announcement of theYFH schemea fortnight agosent housebuilders’ shares soaringby more than 10%.Jason Honeyman, who has ledBellwaysince 2017, welcomed the new programme, which will be more targeted than previous help-to-buy initiatives. It features household income caps to exclude those with big salaries, and price caps to ensure people can only buy modest houses.How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fencesRead moreFull details, including the launch date, are expected be announced by John Healey in his first budget as chancellor on 28 October.YFH applies only to England and is for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. They will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price and the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%.While the scheme has the potential to “provide significant support for first-time buyers”, it could weigh on the market in the near term, Honeyman said, as some will want to wait for the initiative to be launched.However, he added that it could drive Bellway’s annual completions back to 10,000 homes, in the 12-month period from next September at the earliest.“Based upon our past experience with help to buy, the new scheme has the potential to boost volumes by around 10%, and with a market recovery, provide a path back to at least 10,000 homes a year and a return on equity of 15%,” Honeyman said.Bellway is targeting between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year, ​down from 9,695 ​last year, ‌given a lower order book and “ongoing pressures on customer demand” coupled with higher construction costs, running at between 3% and 4%.It has a forward order book of 4,981 homes worth £1.4bn, compared with 5,285 homes with a value of £1.5bn a year earlier. Bellway also expects the average selling price to be flat over the coming year at about £325,000.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chief executive’s comments came after the company beat analysts’ expectations with revenue of £3.16bn for the year to 31 August, up 13% from the previous year. This lifted underlying profits before tax by 5.7% to £305.7m.Bellway shares rose 2% on Tuesday but are still down by more than a quarter so far this year.YFH is expected to give a shot in the arm to most big housebuilders, such as Persimmon, MJ Gleeson, Taylor Wimpey and Bellway.However, the upmarket builder Berkeley Group, which is focused on London, where prices are higher, and Vistry Group, which has pivoted towards building affordable and social homes, are not expected to get much help from the initiative.Explore more on these topicsConstruction industryBellwayPropertyFirst-time buyersnewsShareReuse this content

title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’ | Economics | The Guardian
description: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year
Content: John Healey makes his speech at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJohn Healey makes his speech at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last month.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEconomicsIMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next yearIMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’Heather Stewartin BangkokTue 13 Oct 2026 03.58 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’Read moreTenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before thesharp rise in energy bills expected in January.IMF GDP growth forecast chartBut in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMFRead moreThe IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from itsmost recent update in July.UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies sincethe Middle East conflictre-escalated in the summer.The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting,echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.Speaking to the Atlantic Councilat the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS)warned this weekthat the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Budget deficitBudget 2026John HealeyEconomic policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Cornell suspends fraternity parties amid backlash over alleged sexual assault | US universities | The Guardian
description: University bans parties at frat houses for rest of academic year to conduct ‘thorough review’ of campus Greek life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: University bans parties at frat houses for rest of academic year to conduct ‘thorough review’ of campus Greek life
Content: A Cornell University student sits with a sign during a campus wide sit-in after a student was sexually assaulted at a campus fraternity house in 2024, on 7 October 2026 in Ithaca, New York.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Cornell University student sits with a sign during a campus wide sit-in after a student was sexually assaulted at a campus fraternity house in 2024, on 7 October 2026 in Ithaca, New York.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesUS universitiesCornell suspends fraternity parties amid backlash over alleged sexual assaultUniversity bans parties at frat houses for rest of academic year to conduct ‘thorough review’ of campus Greek lifeGuardian staff and agenciesTue 13 Oct 2026 14.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCornell University has announced that it is suspending parties and other social gatherings at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid intensifying backlash over its handling ofallegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.The university has also said that Cornell will involveNew Yorkstate police in investigating sex crimes on campus.Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, announced the measures on Tuesday.Fraternities are the most likely place for unwanted sexual contact. Should they be shut down?Read moreThe suspension of all parties and social gatherings at houses governed by Cornell’s interfraternity council is meant to be in effect through the end of the academic year ending in the spring of 2027 – and it is subject to a “zero tolerance” policy that would lead to the immediate emergency suspension of any chapter found to be in violation, Kotlikoff said.“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.Kotlikoff also committed to adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the Ivy League institution navigate the processes. Kotlikoff also pledged to work with the New York state police to allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators – who are independent of Cornell University – to investigate allegations.Such allegations otherwise have been handled by Cornell’s campus police force.A civil lawsuit filed in September by a woman identified by the pseudonym of Jane Doe alleges that several men assaulted her at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house after she went there in an intoxicated state looking for a friend.Two of the accused men were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while others were allowed to resume their studies after writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a short suspension.None were ever arrested or charged by local authorities, and disgust over the treatment of the alleged offenders grew when the woman’s lawsuit was made public.Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, on 2 Octoberannouncedthat she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, to take over Jane Doe’s case as a special prosecutor.If warranted, James would present evidence to a grand jury that could lead to criminal charges, Hochul said.Two of the men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit have challenged James’s appointment. Hochul said James’s appointment is necessary because local police and prosecutors who were obligated to protect Jane Doe “failed” her.The Associated Press contributed reportingInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesNew YorkLaw (US)Rape and sexual assaultFraternities and sororitiesLetitia JamesKathy HochulnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle ousted as US ambassador to Greece after alleged misconduct | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: White House told Guilfoyle, who is alleged to have sought a bill payment from a Trump donor, to resign from post
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: White House told Guilfoyle, who is alleged to have sought a bill payment from a Trump donor, to resign from post
Content: Kimberly Guilfoyle and Marco Rubio in Athens, Greece, on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersView image in fullscreenKimberly Guilfoyle and Marco Rubio in Athens, Greece, on 7 October 2026.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersTrump administrationKimberly Guilfoyle ousted as US ambassador to Greece after alleged misconductWhite House told Guilfoyle, who is alleged to have sought a bill payment from a Trump donor, to resign from postUS politics live – latest updatesJoseph Gedeonin Washington andHelena Smithin AthensTue 13 Oct 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.The decision, announced by the White House on Tuesday morning, ends the diplomatic career of one of Donald Trump’s longest-standing political allies. It came after the US president and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, werereportedto have grown furious over the allegations.“We have asked Ambassador Guilfyole to resign, she has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” said Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, during her first briefing on Tuesday.Guilfoyle – the former fiancee of Trump’s eldest son,Donald TrumpJr – later confirmed her departure from the post, which she described as the “honor of a lifetime”, and denied what she described as “false” allegations.Pledging to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity” in a post on social media, she wrote: “While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.”The most serious claim,first reportedby the Wall Street Journal on 8 October, centers on the donor Eric Deters.Citing Signal messages, the paper reported that in July 2025, days before her Senate confirmation hearing, Guilfoyle pressed Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill, assuring him the transfer would not show up anywhere. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote, according to the report.Guilfoyle offered to use her influence on his tax and legal problems in return and told him she had contacted the IRS commissioner and the justice department on his behalf.He has also said he paid Guilfoyle about $300,000 over the years without receiving “one favor”, andtold MS Nowthe request “absolutely was a quid pro quo”.Guilfoyle also expressed concern about the exchanges becoming public, according to the Wall Street Journal. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” she wrote in one message. In another, she told him: “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.” She urged him to call her on Signal instead.The Journal has also reported that Guilfoyle accepted improper gifts and services, made an alleged threat to a host-country official, and promoted the interests of a Greek company, Aktor, during official engagements. A lawyer for Guilfoyle, Jesse Binnall, said she disputes the authenticity of the messages.Guilfoyle, 57, a former San Francisco prosecutor who was married until 2006 to Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, became a fixture of Trump’s political orbit after leaving Fox News in 2018 as she began dating Trump Jr. The couple became engaged in late 2020, and she was a prominent speaker at Trump’s campaign events, including the 2024 Republican national convention, before breaking up soon after in September 2024.Trump, as president-elect, then named her for the Athens post in December 2024, weeks after his election win, calling her “a close friend and ally”. That month, Trump Jrhad been photographedholding hands with Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite, and Guilfoyle was absent from the family’s post-election portrait, which did include Trump Jr’s ex-wife and their children. Trump Jr married Anderson in May.The nomination stalled for months in the Senate until Republicans used the “nuclear option” in September 2025 to overcome a Democratic filibuster and confirm her by simple majority. She was sworn in as the first woman to represent the US in Greece, succeeding the Biden appointee George Tsunis, and arrived in Athens in late October 2025.It ends a tenure that lasted less than a year. Hours before Tuesday’s announcement, the Greek government had denied any suggestion the ambassador was on her way out. “There has been no relevant request, nor has it been discussed with Greek authorities,” said Pavlos Marinakis, a government spokesman, when asked if she would resign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut speculation had been rife. The allegations of misconduct engulfing the envoy were not only embarrassing for Guilfoyle. The Greek media had begun to speak of the US embassy being “headless” and dysfunctional only days after Rubio’s high-profile visit to the country. “If truth be told, she is not respected in Athens,” one well-placed insider confided.Alec Mally, a former senior US diplomat who had handled Greek affairs at the US state department, told the Guardian the US embassy in Athens had been put “in an impossible situation because the ambassador had increasingly come across almost as if she were representing an old-style Balkan country”.“With allegations multiplying daily, the question was whether her Trump family Teflon was anywhere near sufficient to keep her in the job,” Mally said. “It would not surprise me if the Greek public reacts with joy to the news of her resignation.”Although there were some who argued the direct access to Trump “outweighed all the negatives” there were many who thought her appointment had been “an insult to the country’s reputation”, he added.In recent weeks Guilfoyle had done what she had rarely done in the whirlwind 11 months since she assumed the post: remained out of sight. But reported claims she had told Greece’s energy minister that Washington was capable of toppling any government – including the center-right administration in Athens – if they didn’t toe the line had stirred outrage. On the left where many have still not forgotten Washington’s support of the 1967-74 military dictatorship, Guilfoyle’s comments had caused widespread consternation.On 9 October in a stormy debate in parliament, Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greece’s foreign minister, was forced to deny the claim – one of several surrounding the US envoy’s alleged improper behavior reported by the Wall Street Journal – beforeSia Anagnostopoulos, the prominent leftwing politician and former deputy foreign minister, who had said it was “a question of national dignity that the American ambassador is called to give an explanation”.Within hours of arriving in Greece, Guilfoyle was seen at a bouzouki music club, attending a party thrown by a popular singer who would go on to be one of her closest friends in Athens. “I think we can safely say she was like no ambassador Greece has ever seen before,” said one official, speaking on condition of anonymity. “I don’t think that in these uncertain times many will be shedding tears at the news of her departure.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks following deadly strike on Riyadh airport
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks following deadly strike on Riyadh airport
Content: Smoke over Sana’a during a reported Saudi-led coalition airstrike on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital on 9 October 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSmoke over Sana’a during a reported Saudi-led coalition airstrike on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital on 9 October 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQCivilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks as conflict between Riyadh and Houthi forces escalatesPatrick WintourTue 13 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?Read moreThe strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthiattack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturdaythat killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. An evacuation order ​for the building ‌had been ‌issued, four sources told Reuters. There was no official comment ​or ​confirmation ​from ​Aramco.The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while theHouthishave to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.View image in fullscreenA map released by the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition shows the targeted site of the Yemeni Oil Company and Al-Sabaha Central station in Sana’a.Photograph: @CJFCS.Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown princeMohammed bin Salmanis prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisDonald TrumpMohammed bin SalmanIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Retailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Retailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget
Content: A barista prepares a drink at a Costa Coffee outlet.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyView image in fullscreenA barista prepares a drink at a Costa Coffee outlet.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyRetail industryUK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young peopleRetailers call on John Healey to reduce national insurance contributions threshold in his first budgetSarah ButlerandRichard PartingtonTue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have metJohn Healeyto urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics).Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and arise in youth unemployment.They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said.Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills.Another attender, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium trade body which represents most big retailers, said:“Retail is a major driver of growth, supporting jobs, investment and communities across the country, and providing vital first jobs and career opportunities for young people.“But after whacking up retailers’ taxes by 20% in two years, including an extra £6.5bn in new employment costs, any new costs will be paid by consumers at the till and make it harder for retailers to create jobs.“The chancellor recognised these pressures, and we had a positive discussion about our shared ambition for growth and tackling youth unemployment. His first budget is the chance to turn that ambition into action by easing costs, making tax fairer and unlocking investment.”Meanwhile it was reported that Healey has rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed.He has come under pressure to increase the rates of capital gains tax (CGT), which is levied on the sale of assets – including second homes and shares – at significantlylower rates than wages.In her first budget in 2024, Reeves increased the rate of CGT from 10% to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers, and from 20% to 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. That compares with a 20% basic rate of income tax, a 40% higher rate and 45% additional rate for top earners.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEconomists have suggested an equalisation of the rates could raise £11.3bn a year for the exchequer. However, according to the Financial Times, Healey has dismissed such calls because of fears it could deter inward investment, but may yet opt for a smaller increase in CGT short of equalisation.It comes after senior Labour figures floated CGT increases among options to repair the government finances while funding priorities ranging from public services, support for households and long-term infrastructure projects.The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, suggested the idea of equalisationduring his ill-fated May pitch to be the party leaderas a “wealth tax that works”.And the first secretary, Louise Haigh, a close ally of Andy Burnham, argued in an article in the journal Renewal in May – while on the backbenches before her return to cabinet – that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”.A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryBudget 2026John HealeyTax and spendingYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Content: Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEmployers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisCompanies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling backTaylor TelfordRapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality workSupported byAbout this contentTue 13 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTShareEmployers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors,Reuters reported. And after thinning its workforce,especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widelyinternally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recentlypubliclylamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”.Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance,Business Insider reported.Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses thatstarted off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.”Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserveworking paper. And anErnst & Young surveypublished last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions.Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamiltonand Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies,Reutersreported.Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.“We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recentblogpostabout the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.”Expertise gaps and errorsAI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to anIndeed surveypublished in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”.Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managersare balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added.Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said.Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity.One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.“This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif.Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. AtWalmart, frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported.Employees described bots that set unreasonable standards for human workers while introducing a host of their own inefficiencies and errors. AI tools plotted nonsensical routes for fulfilment workers that made it harder to fill orders quickly, pumped out useless safety alerts and set unrealistic schedules that left store employees cutting corners to keep up.These bots assume that workers are “going to be perfect every single time”, one manager told Business Insider. “We’re not going to hold people to these impossible standards.”Walmart declined to comment.Rising risksNeil Elan, attorney at Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP, said he had observed “a growing gap” between how his corporate clients think AI is being used and how it is actually being used, which is creating issues with confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee conduct.It’s also creating headaches for companies when workers’ use ofChatGPTspills into public view.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe night before Will Moye was set to face 3M in court over a 2020 gas explosion at a Houston manufacturing plant that killed three and damaged hundreds of homes and businesses, the attorney received a report from the company’s independent expert witness.Skimming on his iPad, Moye noticed telltale signs of AI: strange formatting and fonts and time stamps showing that 14,500 pages were assembled in a matter of hours. Moye suspected that the author, Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering, lacked expertise and had relied on ChatGPT, despite billing 3M $90,000 for a report arguing the company was not liable.Autenrieth’s chat logs, which Moye requested and shared in court, show he prompted ChatGPT, “What am I looking at?” after uploading a picture of the gas detector at the heart of the case.The jury found that 3M had failed to properly inspect the gas detection system and ordered the company to pay $61.5m to 24 homeowners. Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”.“[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.”A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”.Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”.Performance boost? Not so muchAs companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive.In a studypublished in May, University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff.Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states.More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according toReuters. Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews,the Information reported.Meta did not respond to a request for comment.Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”.But companies’share prices tend to dipafter they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.”“A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedMetaMicrosoftWalmartPalantirNvidiaChatGPTanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Hobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer data | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Cyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackers
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Cyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackers
Content: Whistles and Hobbs stores remain open but some of their IT systems are unavailable.Photograph: William Barton/AlamyView image in fullscreenWhistles and Hobbs stores remain open but some of their IT systems are unavailable.Photograph: William Barton/AlamyRetail industryHobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer dataCyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackersSarah ButlerTue 13 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles has said its websites and IT systems have been hit by a cyber-attack that may have compromised customers’ personal data.The South-African listed TFG London said it identified the “cybersecurity incident” at the three UK-based retail chains on Sunday. Its two other UK brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected.TFG said its stores had stayed open and trading but some of its IT systems “remain unavailable” and it had paused all online orders as a “precautionary measure”.Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bnRead moreAn “investigation is ongoing, including establishing whether any personal or other sensitive information has been compromised,” the company said.If the investigation establishes that any personal information has been accessed by hackers, TFG said it would “notify affected individuals or organisations”.“Some of our brand’s website capabilities may not be available as the investigation continues. We apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate,” the company added.In an email to Whistles customers, the company said any orders placed on or after 11 October may be delayed. Orders placed before that date are being processed normally. Returns can only be made via stores at present and Whistles told customers it was “working on a solution for postal returns”.TFG has engaged external cybersecurity specialists to contain the incident, which has been reported to the relevant UK authorities.The group’s operations in Africa or Australia run on separate systems and are not affected.The attack on the three UK fashion brands comes less than a week after acyber-attack affected the online fashion seller Asos, in which the names, addresses and recent search data of millions of customers was accessed.H&M said on Monday that it was also investigating claims that its systems had been attacked. However, the fast fashion retailer said: “We have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Monday, it emerged that hackers had forced the temperature ofmany French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight, in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores.Several other British retailers, includingMarks & Spencer, theCo-opandHarrods, were hit by damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op faced stock shortages and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean.Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the digital security firm NordVPN, said: “Coming so soon after the Asos incident, this latest attack on TFG London is another reminder that the retail sector is firmly in hackers’ sights. These attacks are becoming a recurring nightmare for businesses, and there’s every reason to believe we’ll see more of them.“Retailers are particularly attractive targets because they hold valuable customer information and rely on a sprawling network of payment systems, suppliers and third-party technology providers. Every connection is a potential weak point, and attackers are increasingly adept at exploiting stolen credentials, human error and gaps in security.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryCybercrimeHackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds
Content: Nova Icaria beach in Barcelona. The number of British holidaymakers who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36% this year.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenNova Icaria beach in Barcelona. The number of British holidaymakers who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36% this year.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PATravel & leisureFewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industrySpain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report findsGwyn TophamTransport correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 09.44 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned.Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday.Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026.Bedbug infestation forces Qantas to ground plane in RomeRead moreConfidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta.Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad.However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad.Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES).The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it had been a tough year for the travel industry. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.”Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer.“We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.”He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.”Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays.Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain.Travel to the convention was provided by AbtaExplore more on these topicsTravel & leisureAir transportFlightsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All Time | Music | The Guardian
description: Raised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndrome
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Raised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndrome
Content: ‘The universe rewards confidence’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyView image in fullscreen‘The universe rewards confidence’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyMusicInterview‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All TimeTiffany LaiRaised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndromeTue 13 Oct 2026 06.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time Sophia Stel came to London, she slept outside in the freezing cold. The Vancouver songwriter had finished a live set last autumn, then gone out until 3am with her then crush, but when they returned to their Airbnb, they found that Stel’s manager had dead-bolted the door and fallen asleep. Stel plus crush looked for a hotel but ultimately had no choice but to kip on the doorstep. “We hadn’t spent that much time together and I got to see how she was in a stressful situation,” Stel says, smiling at the memory. “She kept her vibe up and tried to solve it – I knew I was so in love then.”A lot has changed in Stel’s life in the year since. She opened her business bank account as an artist, and that crush is now her girlfriend. “It’s a lot of change, but maybe because of my Sagittarius moon, I’m fine with it to an extent,” she says, only half-joking, when we meet at her publicist’s office in south London, the 27-year-old Stel in her uniform of vintage hoodie and Adidas trackies.Stel started gaining attention last summer when her swaggering, lonely-dancefloor banger I’ll Take It exploded on TikTok, then honed her sound – AutoTuned vocals merging with hazy electropop – over two EPs. She recorded the second, How to Win at Solitaire, in the basement of the Vancouver club where she worked, and it seemed to absorb a bittersweet afterparty energy through the walls. She soon signed with chic film production company A24’s record label, andLordeinvited her to support her live.So having ticked off so many achievements so quickly, why shouldn’t she call her debut LP The Greatest Album of all Time? The title comes from an interview in which Stel joked that, like everyone else, she wanted to make the greatest album of all time. “They made it the cover of the Instagram carousel and I was like, ‘I did not mean that,’” she says. “This is the type of pressure I’m trying to avoid!” So the title is mostly tongue-in-cheek but not entirely. “I think the universe rewards confidence, and sometimes as a girl, you’re not allowed to be as cocky. It’s nice to try and have a louder voice. It’s something I’m working on in my life.”Becoming a pop star has been a lesson in overcoming imposter syndrome. This past year, Stel has balanced performing with odd jobs painting houses and bartending. “I was so broke but I had never been around so many crazy wealthy people at the same time,” she says. “Sometimes I struggle with overextending myself financially because I want to feel rich … who doesn’t?”Her debut, almost all of it self-produced, tackles all of this with typically sly humour. On the skittering, bratty anthem Bitches Talk Shit, she protests: “’Cause you’re a rockstar you should have a lot of money / Course I am a pop star but I’m still very up and coming,” while the narcotised drawl of On My Dick reflects the whiplash experience of her meteoric year: “Scarlet told me no new friends / Cause all they want is dividends.”View image in fullscreen‘Being sceptical has helped me keep my sanity’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mark HunterUnsurprisingly, Stel keeps her circle close. She lives with two of her younger brothers and her best friend in a Vancouver apartment, paying an enviable 650CA$ (£300) each. “They all come in and out of my room while I’m making music and I can tell if something’s fun because they’ll stick around for a while,” she smiles.For most of her life, Stel has lived with a lot of people. She grew up as one of 11 in an ultra-religious family, and describes her upbringing as “overstimulating” and “very extreme”. She found organised religion “really damaging” and has long since parted ways with it. “When you’re so indoctrinated growing up, you have to be conscious of what you believe in,” she says. “You learn a lot about listening to yourself and your body.”Strangely, that sounds like experience that could help her navigate her new career. “It has helped in industry decisions because if I’m told that things are one way, I’m sceptical,” she admits. “That’s proven to be really helpful in keeping my sanity.”View image in fullscreen‘One baby goat snapped in half and the other suffocated’ … the cover art for The Greatest Album of All Time.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyStel also works as a model, despite hating being photographed. “Though I do love that it allows me to become financially stable,” she says. The brutal casting process contributed to the bluster in her lyrics. “I wanted to make an album that gave me the energy to get up and go to castings where I’m sure I’m not going to be selected, and still be confident.”Modelling for it-girl brands such as Gimaguas is in stark contrast to how Stel presents herself. For the cover of Greatest, she chose a poetic image of herself aged seven cradling a dead baby goat – a dark riff on the “greatest of all time” acronym – on the family farm. “I was sleeping in the barn with my best friend every night in the weeks leading up to the birth,” she says. When it came, “one of the babies was sideways and got snapped in half so the other one suffocated inside. That’s the one I’m holding.”And despite early acclaim for the record, Stel doesn’t put much stock in the opinion of others. “I had a park day with my brother last year where we smoked a joint and played soccer,” she says. “I was so happy and it felt very similar to playing my biggest show. That’s made me really conscious of what I do – I’m not going to chase a feeling if it’s going to feel pretty similar to a really good day doing anything else.”The Greatest Album of All Time is released via A24 Music on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Home is where the jellyfish glows: Finland finally warms to nature-loving modernist Alvar Aalto | Architecture | The Guardian
description: His egalitarian homeland used to harbour reservation against the architecture star. But with 13 new Unesco listings and a new exhibition in Helsinki, Aalto’s work is finally getting the recognition it deserves
Author: Christian House
Headline: His egalitarian homeland used to harbour reservation against the architecture star. But with 13 new Unesco listings and a new exhibition in Helsinki, Aalto’s work is finally getting the recognition it deserves
Content: Sustainable ways of living: interior of the the Aalto House, HelsinkiPhotograph: 2026 Tuomas Uusheimo: www.uushView image in fullscreenSustainable ways of living: interior of the the Aalto House, HelsinkiPhotograph: 2026 Tuomas Uusheimo: www.uushArchitectureHome is where the jellyfish glows: Finland finally warms to nature-loving modernist Alvar AaltoHis egalitarian homeland used to harbour reservation against the architecture star. But with 13 new Unesco listings and a new exhibition in Helsinki, Aalto’s work is finally getting the recognition it deservesChristian HouseTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1950s, Alvar Aalto built a boat to get to his remote summer residence on an island in Lake Päijänne, about 200km north of Helsinki.But the celebrated Finnish architect was not a happy skipper. He named the boat – a title as cumbersome as his buildings were elegant – Nemo propheta in patria: “No man is a prophet in his own land”.The name was a dig atFinland, which the architectural maestro believed had taken him for granted. Other nations, he moaned, recognised his talent more than his own. Today, arriving in Helsinki, I find that Finland doesn’t just love Aalto, he’s a national treasure.Last month, 13 Alvar sites dotted around Finland gained Unesco world heritage status. In addition to this international honour, vast quantities of Finnish public funding are being spent on the restoration of his buildings, and his designs are currently being celebrated in the Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition at Helsinki’sArchitecture& Design Museum. Norman Foster could but dream of such public adoration. For many Finns today, Aalto’s buildings – light-filled, harmonious habitats created from the mid-1920s to his death in 1976 – speak of national pride at a time of geopolitical tension with Russia and, further afield, connect to global considerations about “wellness” in the built environment.View image in fullscreenGlacier-like: Finlandia Hall, HelsinkiPhotograph: © 2026 Kuvatoimisto Kuvio Oy and Helsinki PartnersBut was it true that Aalto was once underappreciated at home? “The boat’s name wasn’t entirely in jest,” notes Sofia Nivarti, author of Studio Aalto, a new survey of his work to be published later this month. “The more he succeeded internationally, the more a local audience turned against him – steeped in a social-democratic ethos of egalitarianism, Finnish architectural circles worried about the dominance of one name over all others.”In the first half of the 1950s, Aalto “wasn’t able to get a professorship from his alma mater, the Helsinki University of Technology,” explains Tommi Lindh, CEO of the Alvar Aalto Foundation. And a starchitect’s ego is a fragile thing, even in the cool egalitarian north.In Helsinki, Lindh gives me a tour of the National Pensions Institute – now home to the Finns’ social security system – a vast brick building designed by Aalto between 1953 and 1957. It is perfectly preserved, right down to its ingenious overhead heating panels, angled skylights and working paternoster lift. This monumental brick building is one of five Aalto sites in Helsinki to gain Unesco recognition, alongside the House of Culture (commissioned by the Finnish Communist party in 1952, with the goal of “making culture the property of the entire nation”), Finlandia Hall, the vast, glacier-like concert and conference centre, and both Aalto’s home and his studio.View image in fullscreenAs if it’s been bent by the wind … a chair by Aalto.Photograph: Foundation for the Finnish Museum of Architecture and DesignAt the Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition, curators have broadened out the Aalto story to include the work of Alvar’s first wife, Aino, and second wife, Elissa, both skilled architects in their own right. It also shows that the experiential – and nature-loving – considerations Aalto brought to buildings also shaped his approach to furniture and lighting systems: his pendant lights recall beehives and jellyfish, his wooden chairs look as if they have been bent by the wind. “As we reconsider our relationship with nature and seek more sustainable ways of living, Aalto Studio’s work offers a valuable perspective,” says Pilvi Kalhama, director of the Architecture & Design Museum.Naturally, Aalto’s domestic flourishes can also be found at his home in Munkkiniemi, Helsinki’s leafy, classy, equivalent of Hampstead. Completed in 1936, the Aalto House is a series of light-boxes overlooking a sports field, quiet but for birdsong and rippling with daylight. Aalto’s monochromatic abstract paintings still hang on the walls, his Homburg still sits in a wardrobe.View image in fullscreenWellness pioneer: a former patient room at Paimio Sanatorium, converted into a ‘retreat room’ for visitorsPhotograph: © Paimio Sanatorium FoundationIn contrast, Finlandia Hall – completed in 1971 and arguably his greatest masterpiece – introduces visitors to Aalto at his most symphonic. Standing in its concert hall – a jagged collection of white-on-white geometric planes – is like being inside an ice cube. A €136m renovation between 2022 and 2024 saw the building’s facade reclad in pristine Lasa Bianco Nuvolato marble and the opening of a permanent exhibition space dedicated to Aalto’s life and times.Following Finland’s independence from Russia in 1917, the built environment – and Aalto’s mark on it – played a significant role in the shaping a new national identity. “Aalto did not set out simply to create a national style, but through his work he expressed values that became closely associated with modern Finland,” says Pilvi Kalhama. “Functionality, purpose, aesthetic quality and a progressive outlook were all central to his architecture and design. These qualities still reflect a broader Finnish attitude towards everyday life.”View image in fullscreen‘Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core’ … Alvar Aalto.Photograph: Pertti IngervoAs his compatriots once feared, Aalto’s international success has largely overshadowed the achievements of other Finnish architects. But these days, Finns seem less oppressed by his legacy. “You can’t really grow up as a Finnish architect without Aalto being part of your thinking.
