But that doesn’t mean we all want to design like him,” says Asmo Jaaksi, founding partner of JKMM Architects, which refurbished and restored Aalto’s House of Culture and has won the international competition to design a new Museum of Architecture and Design on Helsinki’s South Harbour (planned to open in 2030). “What I admire most is Aalto’s independence of thought, his willingness to experiment and his instinct for putting people and nature first. I think he’d be rather disappointed if we were all still copying him.”At the height of Aalto’s career in the mid-20th century, he may have been sore at perceived slights, but his disgruntled state proved short-lived. “Aalto was a chameleonic persona,” says Sofia Nivarti. “Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core; moody and hilarious in turn; at times egotistical and at others deeply self-sacrificing and generous.” He was impossible to pigeonhole and his buildings embraced the contradictions of the human experience.Soon enough, the Finns acknowledged his vision. In 1955, just as he launched his scornfully named boat, Aalto was elected as a member of the Finnish Academy. “He is the only architect in Finland to have received this position,” says Lindh. “Meaning thenemo propheta in patriadays were over.”Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeingis at the Architecture and Design Museum Helsinki until 3 January 2027.Studio Aalto by Sofia Nivartiis published by Yale University Press on 27 October 2026Explore more on these topicsArchitectureExhibitionsFinlandEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Devil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpiece | FW Murnau | The Guardian
description: A rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneers
Author: Pamela Hutchinson
Headline: A rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneers
Content: Speak of the devil … Mephisto (Emil Jannings) looms over a village (created in miature) in FW Murnau’s 1926 expressionist film Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisView image in fullscreenSpeak of the devil … Mephisto (Emil Jannings) looms over a village (created in miature) in FW Murnau’s 1926 expressionist film Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFW MurnauDevil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpieceA rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneersPamela HutchinsonTue 13 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFW Murnau was one of the greatest of all silent film-makers, with a rare genius for making beautiful images on screen. His peers liked to say he “had a camera instead of a head”. The director of such stunning films as vampire tale Nosferatu (1922) and marital romance Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) died at the age of 42 in 1931, meaning that his career barely scraped into the talkie era. Still, Murnau’s tremendous run of silent pictures included some beautiful, often disturbing classics, in which he sent his camera roaming through changing vistas of shadows and light, and plumbed the depths of the human soul. Nowhere more so than in his tour-de-force Faust, released 100 years ago this month, based on Goethe’s play about a deal with the devil. And the making of Faust is depicted in a stunning new book, which is both a document of, and in a sense an artefact from, the production of this classic film.Murnau was also one of the most mysterious of directors: secretive about his methods, with an intense devotion to his work. Early collaborator Edgar G Ulmer called him “a great purist who worked under a sort of hypnosis”. Murnau banned producers from his sets, and executives from watching his rushes. Bar a few exceptions, he did not allow on-set photography to reveal the secrets of his camerawork and special effects. This mystique created room for speculation as to whether Murnau, or his talented crew, were responsible for the success of his films. The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece publishes unseen images from the shoot of one of his best films, and gives a rare insight into the collaborative way it was made.View image in fullscreenFW Murnau photographed on the set of Faust by Hans Natge.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFaust was Murnau’s final German film before he went to Hollywood, and at the time it was the most expensive, complex film that the Ufa studio had ever produced. It is an adaptation of Goethe’s tragedy about the scholar Faust (played by Swedish actor Gösta Ekman) who sells his soul to the devil, represented by the grinning, black-clad demon Mephistopheles (German star Emil Jannings). A commercial flop on its release, Faust is now acclaimed as one of the greats. French New Wave director Éric Rohmer, a Murnau devotee, wrote his doctoral dissertation on the film. The Faust Bible reveals how Murnau and his crew achieved some of the incredible shots and special effects in this film, but it is also an enhanced facsimile of an artefact from the film’s production, which has survived against all odds to spill its secrets.In the film, Faust owns a hefty, leather-bound Bible, which he throws on the fire in a moment of despair. But the prop was to become something more. Art directors Robert Herlth and Walter Röhrig pulled the book from the ashes and pasted designs, stills and behind-the-scenes photographs on to its blank pages so they could present the souvenir as a gift to the director at the end of the shoot. Murnau left it behind in his flat in Berlin when he went to Hollywood, not knowing he would never return to retrieve it. After his death, Murnau’s brother stashed his belongings in various city-centre basements, which were susceptible to flooding, and worse, once the bombs began falling on Berlin during the second world war.View image in fullscreenEmil Jannings and Gösta Ekman in costume as Mephisto and Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFilm scholar and archivist Lotte Eisner came to Berlin looking for Murnau’s archives in the 1950s, but found no sign of the Bible. It was not until the 1960s that a German curator from the city’s Akademie der Künste, Engelbert von Mallinckrodt, told Henri Langlois at the Cinématheque Française that he had bought some of Murnau’s photo albums for a small sum from a restaurateur called Rolf Conscienze, who had film industry connections. It turned out that these albums included the Bible – though no one knows how they ended up with Conscienze. Then, to deepen the mystery, Mallinckrodt vanished, and his flatmate became the book’s custodian for several decades: it was wrapped in brown paper sitting on top of a cupboard. Eisner searched for the Faust Bible her whole life but she was never to see it. She died in 1983.View image in fullscreenThe film-makers creating special effect clouds above a model mountaintop.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisNow the book is in the safekeeping of the Cinémathèque Française, which bought it in 2017, and there it remains, a memento of the once-contested collaborative nature of Murnau’s methods. I went to see it this summer, and it is appropriately grand in scale, an unusually majestic scrapbook. Restored by the cinema’s director of heritage Laurent Mannoni and his team, the book looks good for an abandoned, 100-year-old prop. The water-damage has been smoothed out, leaving only a few scuffs, and the shadows where some enterprising thief has prised the metal crucifix and corner pieces from the leather.double quotation markEach day on the set was a fresh opportunity to surpass ourselves in ingenuityArt director Robert HerlthInside, sketches for individual scenes are arranged opposite matching stills from the film. Turning these hallowed pages, you can see how the compositions of figures and objects by the designers known as “film architects” – the forced perspectives, contrasting arrangements of light and dark, sweeping shadows, steam and flames – were re-created on film by Murnau and his talented cinematographer Carl Hoffmann. The director encouraged his designer to draw not just the spaces, but the actors too, creating something closer to a storyboard image than a set design.View image in fullscreenMephisto appears in a still from the film.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris“The sketch became the equivalent of a contract,” Herlth later wrote. “[Murnau] insisted that every stroke of the pen should be faithfully rendered in the execution.” This meant not only building sets according to the designs but Murnau and Hoffmann making extensive adjustments to the lighting to produce the velvety shadows that the director demanded. Hoffmann then navigated these settings with bold, fluid camera movements in a technique calledentfesselte Kamera(unchained camera), originated by cinematographer Karl Freund when working with Murnau on The Last Laugh (1924). Murnau was not short of visual references. He had a strong interest in the occult, and his background was in art history. Albrecht Dürer’s Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse woodcut was a direct influence on the film’s opening scene.View image in fullscreenA behind-the-scenes photograph by Hans Natge. Faust was the most expensive and ambitious film the Ufa studio had ever produced.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisHerlth recalled the experience of working with Murnau as good-humoured, if challenging, as the director was cheerful but always ambitious to create shots and camera effects that had not been achieved before. The crew spent long days and nights discussing and experimenting with new ideas. “Each day on the set was a fresh opportunity to surpass ourselves in inventiveness and ingenuity,” he said.Leafing further through the Bible, the chiaroscuro sketches and stills give way to playful collages, images of the cast and crew having fun on set, the legendarily tall Murnau hunched over as he instructs Jannings how to leer malevolently. And there are pages that speak to that boundless technical ingenuity. One of the most celebrated moments in the film is the Weltflug (“flight around the world”) sequence, in which Mephistopheles flies Faust through the sky on his cloak, the world lurching below them. The Bible retains the diagrams that explain just how they achieved this uncanny flight simulation. The secret was a low wooden trolley moving along a plaster ramp, an idea that came to Herlth and Röhrig when they saw a truck being unloaded in the street.View image in fullscreenMurnau, left, directs a group of children on a grassy hillside during the filming of the Gretchen sequence.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisThe facsimile edition reprints the Weltflug diagrams on gatefold pages so you can study century-old secrets of film technique at your leisure. It also comprehensively reprints all the Bible’s images, with explanatory captions, enlargements, and quotations from the screenplay, which was written in epigrammatic, almost poetic prose. There are also essays and additional drawings from the Cinémathèque’s archives.We may never fully understand the workings of Murnau’s mysterious “camera-head” and his collaborations with his team. But this fascinating souvenir takes us close.The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece is published byMubi Editionson 17 October. Faust streams on Mubi from 14 October, with live-scored centenary screenings in Paris on 17 October, Munich on 25 October, and Los Angeles on 1 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFW MurnauJohann Wolfgang von GoethefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Girl in the River review – forensic psychologist police procedural thriller plays like noir parody | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ralph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenager
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Ralph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenager
Content: Devon Sawa and Maggie Grace in The Girl in the Water.Photograph: David WigginsView image in fullscreenDevon Sawa and Maggie Grace in The Girl in the Water.Photograph: David WigginsMoviesReviewThe Girl in the River review – forensic psychologist police procedural thriller plays like noir parodyRalph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenagerPhil HoadTue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis small-town police thriller sets its stall out intriguingly, with a murder that seems actively begging to be solved. The perp chose to dump his victim – the 14-year-old daughter of a local political bigwig – into a part of the Mississippi River where she was likely to resurface, and from a highly visible bridge. When veteran detective Alan Kramer (Devon Sawa) and rookie forensic psychologist Amelia Pembrock (Maggie Grace) show up to investigate, they are immediately alerted to a gun in the bushes just yards away. As a colleague observes: “This isn’t a clean-up. It’s a message.”But Brando Benetton’s debut film sadly fails to capitalise on the misdirection at play in this open-goal crime scene. Instead of using it to pry open community secrets, he gives us a ropey and implausible manhunt. As Kramer and Pembrock race to locate the girl’s twin, who is presumably still in the killer’s clutches, they zero in on local butcher Boris (Darron Dunbar). He has a sex-pest rap sheet and lives with his mother – which apparently ticks all the boxes for a profiling genius such as Pembrock. Kramer pulls her up for being unbothered by the lack of actual prosecutable evidence. But carping is about the only investigative contribution this seasoned criminologist makes here (and what’s a criminologist – a crime sociologist – doing out in the field anyway?).If the killer leaves behind a parody of a crime scene, The Girl in the River offers up its own parody noir, though in a cliche-strewn and far less careful fashion. We have the obsessive desk jockey, the boozy, trauma-harbouring vet halfway out the retirement door, Tiffany Haddish’s angry black captain (as satirised in the Jump Street franchise), and the affable town coroner (The Karate Kid’s Ralph Macchio). Whenever the detectives are floundering, the over-directed script is always on hand to put them back on the rails. The local media seem strangely willing to share their voluminous stash of damning evidence; a transparently staged mutiny among the townsfolk fires up Kramer and Pembrock just as they’re out of leads.Grace, with her twitchy defensiveness, and the frazzled Sawa manage to half-ballast this dubious sleuthing, and Benetton keeps the film moving fast enough so the many infelicities don’t register too horrifically. But with no time to accumulate any proper gravitas, Kramer’s capstone speech about universal corruption is, like the victim, dead in the water.The Girl in the River is on digital platforms on 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersCrime filmsTiffany HaddishreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows up  | Television | The Guardian
description: This peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US president
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: This peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US president
Content: Mike Tyson in the Netflix docuseries Tyson.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenMike Tyson in the Netflix docuseries Tyson.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewTyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows upThis peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US presidentHannah J DaviesTue 13 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s new four-parter onMike Tysonis one of the strangest sports documentaries it has ever released, or maybe just one of its strangest documentaries full stop. The streamer has form in sporting hagiographies – tales told with questionable distance from their subjects, and all the objectivity of cold war agitprop. Tyson is different, though: not only is it lopsided, but it also feels deeply icky. And that’s before Donald Trump arrives to defend its subject – a great catch for the programme-makers but a wholly baffling cameo that makes you wish he would stick with geopolitical meddling and golf.It ends – spoiler alert – with the former boxing champion taking thehallucinogenic drug DMT(or as he calls it, “the toad”, after the animal that produces it), while sobbing and inviting the show’s director to join him. Its episodes are peculiar, sometimes compelling, and – as many viewers will surely feel – truly irresponsible.It starts uncontroversially enough, recounting the extreme poverty and precarity of Tyson’s upbringing, when he would rob other kids for their wallets and chains. Now when he goes back to Brownsville, Brooklyn, he is mobbed by adoring fans. Tyson had a talent for knocking people out in his youth, which would later pique the interest of the coach Bobby Stewart, whom he met during a stint in a juvenile detention centre. At 13, Stewart put Tyson in front of the fabled manager and promoter Cus D’Amato, who told him that he would be heavyweight champion of the world one day; Lennox Lewis, an early sparring partner, says: “[Tyson] just ran over to me and took my head off!” A dazzling pro career followed, despite many tragedies – not least the loss of D’Amato, who died in 1985. But Tyson was on the brink of big titles and big fame. As he puts it: “It was awesome being young and having all of that attention.”View image in fullscreen‘It was awesome’ … Tyson with the boxing promoter Don King in Tyson.Photograph: NetflixBut Tyson the docuseries isn’t content with being a professional fable. It also delves into the man’s past in a way that feels grubby and careless. Much is made of his short-lived marriage to the actor Robin Givens, whose mother told the journalist Wallace Matthews that Tyson was beating her daughter (Givens declined an interview request from the programme-makers). Tyson, says Matthews, didn’t deny attacking her but said he didn’t hurt her and that “we fought”. (Here, Tyson says: “I know people say she can’t fight you, you’re Mike Tyson – but we fought.”)Givens was later to deny that her husband had beaten her. As for rumblings, after her denial, of assault and battery towards his then wife, Tyson says “it’s a bunch of bullshit”. There’s archive footage of Tyson telling the broadcaster Barbara Walters that he grabbed his wife but never hit her, while Givens is shown telling her that the union was “pure hell” and “torture”. In the present, Tyson calls Givens “a fucking bitch”. Headlines flash up on screen, among them: “Iron Mike dreamed of love, but all he got was [a] package of strife”. The episode ends with a disclaimer and mention of a website with resources for survivors of sexual violence.View image in fullscreenTyson celebrates his heavyweight win over Michael Spinks in 1988.Photograph: NetflixAn instalment on his rape conviction is no better, with Tyson – who denies that he sexually assaulted the then 18-year-old pageant contestant Desiree Washington – laughing about his reputation for being handsy. There are a few voices who don’t entirely discredit Washington, but many more who express scepticism that Tyson could have been guilty of the crime for which he was convicted and served three years in prison.Trump – a man who, at least, has some apparent experience in this area – says “[Tyson] is very truthful, and I think the truth hurt him in this case”. The media, he adds, was “rough on Mike, but it just made Mike harder. They’re rough on me, and I’m the president!”Interviewees talk about Tyson not as an athlete with a troubling past but as someone akin to Nelson Mandela. Tom Patti, a friend and former boxer, says: “You can knock him down, you can say bad things about him, you can take away his freedom, but guess what? [He’s] still here.” The same warning plays at the end of that episode.Sure, there’s much on the drugs and booze and the inadvisable face tattoo, and even the son (Miguel, now 24) who calls his dad a “deadbeat”. Tyson calls himself “a spoiled brat” for how he acted in the ring, when he bit Evander Holyfield’s ear not once but twice. And there is deep, horrifying tragedy in the form of the death of Tyson’s young daughter, Exodus, who perished in an accident aged four. But Tyson the docuseries is an exercise in not taking due accountability, and swerving your opponent’s punches. Tyson ends by talking about how “special” he is. Certainly, it takes a singular figure to star in a programme this gross.Tyson is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMike TysonSport TVDocumentaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Forever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with morals | Movies | The Guardian
description: Eamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition government
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Eamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition government
Content: One of the good guys … Eamon Ryan on the New York subway in Forever Is Now.Photograph: Soilsiú FilmsView image in fullscreenOne of the good guys … Eamon Ryan on the New York subway in Forever Is Now.Photograph: Soilsiú FilmsMoviesReviewForever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with moralsEamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition governmentCath ClarkeTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis fly-on-the-wall documentary about theformer Irish Green party leader and cabinet minister Eamon Ryanreminded me of the political satire The Thick of It – but without the cynical gags and hapless self-serving politicians. Even after you factor in the skewing effect of it being a favourable portrait, showing him in the best possible light, Ryan comes across as one of the good guys: principled, likable and extremely hard working. The film follows his final 18 months serving in Ireland’s coalition government as minister for the environment and transport before stepping down in 2025.The title is something that Ryan’s 25-year-old son Tommy repeats over and over. “Forever … forever … forever.” Tommy is autistic and requires full-time care. When Ryan resigns from government, one of his reasons is to spend more time with Tommy. We see the pair of them at the allotment picking raspberries and walking the dog. But other than a quick glimpse of his wife, Victoria, the rest of Ryan’s family life is kept firmly behind closed doors.Instead, the cameras trail him on the road, talking to angry residents of an Irish town submerged by flood waters (again), and hustling at the UN general assembly in New York and two Cop conferences. At his side is formidable media adviser Edel Hackett (Malcolm Tucker with morals), who sifts through the daily torrent of online abuse, harassment and intimidation slung Ryan’s way.The film is lacking a little context: perhaps an interview or two with Ryan might have been helpful, giving some background to the Cop conferences and – for those unfamiliar with Irish politics – the ambitious climate laws he pushed through in office. Something on the general election wipeout of Greens in November 2024 would have been useful too. But no explanation is necessary watching Ryan’s crumpled crestfallen face in January 2025 as he packs up his ministerial office, watching Donald Trump’s inauguration on TV.Forever Is Now is in UK and Irish cinemas from 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGreen partyIrelandAutismEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Beth Orton review – battered optimism from an artist making the best music of her career  | Beth Orton | The Guardian
description: Drawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowd
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Drawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowd
Content: Another instrument in the mix … Beth Orton performing at Concorde 2 in Brighton.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnother instrument in the mix … Beth Orton performing at Concorde 2 in Brighton.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianBeth OrtonReviewBeth Orton review – battered optimism from an artist making the best music of her careerConcorde 2, BrightonDrawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowdAlexis PetridisTue 13 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe audience at Brighton’s Concorde 2 largely look old enough to have first encountered Beth Orton’s music three decades ago, as it wafted around a smoke-filled living room in the post-club small hours. That was the primary means of transmission for her 1996 debut album Trailer Park, which smartly appended classic singer-songwriter tropes to misty electronics. But if they’re expecting an evening of nostalgia, they’re in for a shock. The title track from 1999’s Mercury-nominated Central Reservation aside, her set swerves the music that made her famous, drawing almost entirely from her two most recent albums: this year’s The Ground Above and 2022’s Weather Alive.This would count as a bold move from someone 30-odd years into their career, were it not for the fact that Orton’s recent albums are so good – the latest fruit of an artistic reboot that began in the mid-2010s, when she shifted a sound that had grown increasingly acoustic and traditional back towards something more experimental and dancefloor-adjacent.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianShe spends most of the gig seated behind a keyboard rather than playing guitar. The Ground Above’s title track floats clouds of ambient synth over drums that split the difference between jazz and drum’n’bass, while Cigarette Curls unexpectedly shifts its location from something approximating laidback soul into an echoey dubbed-out space. Both Haunted Satellite and Celestial Light venture into the realm of abstraction and there is much playing with the timbre of her voice, amping up its huskiness and fragility, wilfully mangling the lyrics until her singing sounds less like the songs’ focus than another instrument in the mix. You could, if you wished, draw a spiritual parallel with John Martyn’s approach to vocals on 1973’s Inside Out.‘AI isn’t going to have any beneficial influence on humans’: Beth Orton on creativity, craft and the inspirational power of David BowieRead moreAlways adept at picking collaborators, she is backed by a band heavy on players rooted in jazz and at home at London’s Cafe Oto – bassist Tom Herbert, pianist Sam Beste. But the key instrument on stage seems to be Christos Stylianides’s trumpet, its breathy tone shifting from colouration that vaguely evokes the late Jon Hassell to densely effected gusts of white noise.It’s both enrapturing and, when you can make out the lyrics, emotionally fraught in a middle-aged way – sleepless nights, the inexorable passing of time, sickness, loss – although the set closer Otherside gathers itself into a kind of optimism: battered but nevertheless anthemic, Orton’s voice dramatically changing gear and becoming soulful and full-throated. If the audience came to hear the old hits, they don’t evince any disappointment: at the show’s conclusion, they go nuts. Understandably, given that they’re in the presence of something rare: an artist in her mid-50s making the most adventurous, fascinating music of her career.Touring the UKuntil 22 OctoberExplore more on these topicsBeth OrtonPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus review – the zany follow-up to Lessons in Chemistry | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetry
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: This offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetry
Content: Sharp wit … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Sophia Spring/eyevineView image in fullscreenSharp wit … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Sophia Spring/eyevineBook of the dayFictionReviewPeck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus review – the zany follow-up to Lessons in ChemistryThis offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetryClare ClarkTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you have been into a bookshop since 2022, or perhaps even just breathed in and out, you could not have failed to clock the phenomenon that was Lessons in Chemistry. Bonnie Garmus’s debut remains a global sensation. The story of Elizabeth Zott, a gifted research chemist who, forced out of her lab by rampant 1950s misogyny, becomes the inspirational host of a TV cooking show, has so far sold a staggering 9m copies around the world. It spent the best part of two years on the Sunday Times bestseller list, was translated into more than 40 languages, and scooped numerous awards. In 2023 it became an Emmy-winning TV series; a year later New York Times readers voted it one of their top 100 books of the 21st century. Elizabeth Zott made such a splash that even her favoured brand of rowing machine saw a spike in sales.What was the key to its prodigious success? Timing helped. In the aftermath of #MeToo, readers embraced a heroine who refuses to be cowed by injustice, who, thanks to resilience, pragmatism and straight-up hard work, ultimately comes out on top. The book is smart and very funny, a propulsive mashup of feminism and fairytale that balances darkness with whimsy, heartbreak with hope. It is also carries a shamelessly inspirational message. “Do not allow your talents to lie dormant, ladies,” Zott exhorts her audience of housewives in the TV studio. “Design your own future. When you go home today, ask yourself what you will change. And then get started.”Garmus, then a copywriter, wrote the first chapter of Lessons in Chemistry in a fury after a meeting where a male colleague flagrantly took credit for her ideas: her anger “lit a fire under me about telling this story”. In Peck & Peck, her follow-up, there is less outrage crackling on the page but there are most definitely fires, and not metaphorical ones either. At the otherworldly New York offices of Peck & Peck, the most enigmatic, prestigious and dysfunctional poetry magazine in the world, the 39 editors have a single aim: to publish the world’s finest poems. Failed submissions – and every week there are thousands – are incinerated by the team of prison parolees who work in the mailroom.double quotation markIt is impossible not to be beguiled by Garmus’s irrepressible humour and the freewheeling exuberance of her imaginationGarmus’s sharp wit and gift for offbeat characters are both at full throttle in this quirky story of Batter Gray, a boy named for his mother’s improbably intrepid dog. Batter’s parents – his father teaches history, his mother designs typefaces – are eager for him to pursue a sensible, by which they mean lucrative, career; but Batter cares only for poetry. When by a marvellous fluke he lands a job at Peck & Peck, he is ecstatic, only to find himself in the basement churning out photocopies. Passionate about poems, pathologically unable to resist trouble, Batter is soon caught up in the bitter feud between the magazine’s two editors-in-chief, sworn enemies who just happen also to be twins.Corporate machinations at a cultish poetry magazine in the 1980s might seem to offer slim pickings for any mainstream novel, let alone the follow-up to a monster blockbuster. The endangered future of poetry does not exactly sit alongside feminism as a rousing call to arms. Even Batter’s truth-telling typeface-fixated mother Rainey (a ringer for Elizabeth Zott) cannot duck the fact that poetry “is the bottom of the barrel arts-wise” and poets “never make a dime”. And yet from this apparently rarefied premise Garmus constructs a zany office comedy with shades of Hogwarts (Peck & Peck’s office building, with its vast glass dome, pneumatic tube delivery system and alphabetised balcony topiary, is as fantastical as anything in Rowling’s oeuvre) and the gleeful originality of early John Irving.Though it sags a little in the middle, the result is a story that mostly zips along, and a resoundingly impassioned case for the importance of poetry in a profit-obsessed society that would gladly condemn it to extinction. Garmus’s riff on the poems that Peck & Peck sends straight to the incinerator is worth the price of admission alone: “anything on scented paper; anything written in only lowercase letters; anything that included a mention of self-publishing … poems that mentioned kittens, puppies, cooking, sandcastles, babies, sunrises, rainbows, running, beaches, cancer, or the word ‘namaste’ … Anything written on parchment … Anything using the word ‘methinks’”.This aversion to mawkishness does not prevent it from creeping into Garmus’s own work. Readers irked by Six-Thirty, Lessons in Chemistry’s preternaturally intelligent dog, will find themselves no less vexed by Batter’s namesake, a rescue mutt whose credulity-stretching acts of heroism leave Lassie in the shade. And yet it is impossible not to be beguiled by Garmus’s irrepressible humour and the freewheeling exuberance of her imagination. It is hard to imagine a novel with more laugh-out-loud jokes about typography, harder still to dismiss her fierce exhortation to all of us to make words count. Will it repeat the mind-boggling success of Lessons in Chemistry? Probably not, but there are lessons in this book too that, in this terrifyingly accelerating age of AI, feel just as vital. “When you’re interested in poetry, you’re interested in everything,” one of Peck & Peck’s longstanding editors tells Batter. Garmus shows us that in spades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Generation Maybe by Camilla Cavendish review – what’s really behind the fertility gap?  | Society books | The Guardian
description: An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to Iran
Author: Mythili Rao
Headline: An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to Iran
Content: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who has publicly disclosed that she is freezing her eggs.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who has publicly disclosed that she is freezing her eggs.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSociety booksReviewGeneration Maybe by Camilla Cavendish review – what’s really behind the fertility gap?An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to IranMythili RaoTue 13 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Don’t be weird about this,” representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez laughed into the camera as she prepared to jab a hormone-filled needle into her midsection, adding that she knew full well that, yes, people were definitely going to be weird about it. At 36, the congresswoman had begun freezing her eggs, and was making a point of bringing her online audience along with her as she did, stepping directly into the fraught question of how an ambitious woman should manage her fertility.It’s a live concern: around the world, birthrates are falling sharply. “Only the Black Death in the 14th century is comparable to what is happening now,” Financial Times journalist Camilla Cavendish notes ina new book examining why. Setting aside the most toxic gender-war narratives, “the standard explanation is that as women get educated, they choose freedom and autonomy over family”.As Cavendish explains, however, that is “not the whole story”.Drawing on a wealth of reporting, her book seeks to present a more nuanced picture. Cavendish begins with the “fertility gap” – the official name for the difference between the number of children people say they want and the number they actually go on to have – and works her way backwards, focusing on the lived experience of men and women who find themselves with fewer children than they expected. What stopped them?double quotation markCavendish shows the gulf between popular talking points about fertility and the actual conversations potential parents are havingFor some, the main barrier is finding the right partner in time. For others, it comes down to the increasing costs of raising a family (where housing specifically can be a factor) and the enormous difficulty of balancing a career with caregiving, particularly when it takes longer to establish a professional foundation in the first place. There’s more: a “rational pessimism about prospects for the next generation” in an unstable world, the stigma of embracing motherhood, the shortage of stories glorifying father­hood, a pressure to perform “intensive parenting”, the lure of well-compensated but all-consuming “greedy jobs”, and so on. There’s also the sheer exhaustion that comes with caring for a small child. The headwinds are strong.Taken together, “the joyous, messy, life-giving task of raising a family has become something that feels more like a daunting, lonely, and expensive chore,” Cavendish observes. “We’ve shifted, slowly but surely, into treating parent­hood like a self-indulgent lifestyle choice. The onus is on you to cope.” These aren’t abstract observations. Cavendish herself is a working mother of three, well acquainted with the difficulties of supporting a family and managing a career. She has no illusions about how hard it can be, and no interest in pretending otherwise. “I am struck by how little has changed in the workplace in the last 20 years, despite the rhetoric about flexibility,” she notes. “What has changed, I think, is how grimly realistic young women now are about the trade-offs.”“Reproduction is kind of the whole ballgame,” the trailblazing feminist Gloria Steinem told David Remnick in a 2015 interview, “and who controls it is the most fundamental question.” Generation Maybecharts how authoritarian governments in China, Russia, Iran and elsewhere have responded to falling birthrates with a variety of repressive pronatalist policies – sanctioning child marriage, making divorce more difficult and denying abortion access. The Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive rights and federal childcare funding follow this trend, conscripting women into domestic roles. A simple solution to the problem of birth deficit is to force women to breed.It may not be easy to create effective pronatalist policy interventions that encourage, rather than entrap – but it’s not impossible. Cavendish looks at what’s worked and what hasn’t in Singapore, Scandinavia and France, and outlines just shy of a dozen ways to help people choose children, from building more housing to offering parents benefits and even giving children themselves the vote: “Almost all policies which may help to lift birthrates are also ones which could enable human flourishing,” she notes.There is no hectoring or finger-wagging in this book. What’s offered instead is an empathic and curious approach to an entirely rational ambivalence. In so doing, Generation Maybe illuminates the enormous gulf between popular talking points about fertility and the actual conversations potential parents are having. For Cavendish, the real goal isn’t to persuade anyone to have kids; it’s simply “to make children a genuine choice”.Generation Maybe: Why We’re Having Fewer Children, and What It Means for Us All by Camilla Cavendish is published by Bodley Head (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsSociety booksPopulationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled | Games | The Guardian
description: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Content: A woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiView image in fullscreenA woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiGamesReviewCastlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilledEvil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, XboxThere are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dullHarper Jay MacIntyreTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed.Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull.To its benefit, Belmont’s Curse doesn’t pull any punches. Literally. The smallest minion can land a heavy blow and dodging even basic attacks, though occasionally counterintuitive, forces the player to intimately learn enemy habits. Every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled: bats burst into blood, demons burn to cinders. Every battle holds fresh twists and gimmicks.View image in fullscreenA significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges … Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.Photograph: KonamiExploration is less about remembering old, previously inaccessible routes then circling back, so much as mastering challenge rooms full of buzzsaws and blood pits. Learning how to juggle multiple tools at once becomes crucial, as some rooms start to resemble the notoriously tough platformer Super Meat Boy more than Symphony of the Night. Navigating these challenges requires acrobatics, air dashes and death-defying leaps. And while Castlevania veterans may expect something more subtle (secret-hunting and puzzle-solving is the classic stuff of the series), a significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges.As Rose progresses, she gains new magical attacks via tarot cards, and tools for reaching new areas. This is, however, an inconsistent game world. The castle library offers notebook-worthy puzzles, including a cathedral hidden within a cursed portrait that tasks you with playing music on a magic organ. After that, however, you might have to explore underground waterways packed with uninspired combat challenges. This may be the most virtually striking Castlevania since 2002’s Harmony of Dissonance and sometimes it’s also the most inventive and brain-teasing. In other moments, you’ll be bored to bloody tears.Belmont’s Curse improves considerably after an early twist forces Rose to grapple with the Belmont family legacy and her own anger. Once you’re out of the Parisian streets and into Dracula’s castle, there’s far more to love.The result is an earnest, likable game. There are undeniable shortcomings and moments of curse-worthy frustration, but every now and again, there is real cleverness on display, even if Belmont’s Curse can’t quite match contemporary peers such as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown or Hollow Knight: Silksong – the trendsetter now feels like something of a trend-chaser. For most Castlevania players, this will be more than enough. You have a whip, a castle, and a dark lord. Do you really need anything else?Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is released on 15 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesNintendo SwitchPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Larger Than Life review – Wallace, Gromit and the gang say cheeeese for hilarious Aardman origin story | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to follow
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: From Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to follow
Content: ‘At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay’ … visitors look up at the projections at Larger Than Life at Lightroom in London.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXView image in fullscreen‘At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay’ … visitors look up at the projections at Larger Than Life at Lightroom in London.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXArt and designReviewLarger Than Life review – Wallace, Gromit and the gang say cheeeese for hilarious Aardman origin storyLightroom, LondonFrom Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to followEddy FrankelTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNothing is safe from the scourge of immersification. They’ve turned Gustav Klimt and Vincent Van Gogh into vast, projection-mapped digital environments; they’ve told the stories of the moon landings and the dinosaurs and David Bowie as floor-to-ceiling electronic spectacles; and now they’ve come forAardman. For Wallace and Gromit and Shaun the Sheep, our national treasures. Is nothing sacred?The latest immersive cinematic experience at Lightroom is a big, eye-popping celebration of Aardman Animations, the company behind the world’s favourite claymation films and TV shows. It moves between documentary storytelling, behind-the-scenes insight and dazzling immersive renderings of all your wide-grinned, cheeky northern favourites.We get to hear about howPeter Lord and David Sproxtonmet in suburban Surrey and started messing around with clay, before joining forces withNick Parkand setting in motion a series of events that would take them from Woking to the stars. We get to hear about how they first made Morph out of a ball of clay, how the animators hilariously act out all the scenes to camera themselves before moving over to puppets, how they make the mouths form the “eeee” sound of the word cheese, all interspersed with Shaun the Sheep doing a barn-based talent show and clips from their biggest cinematic triumphs.View image in fullscreen‘When’s the movie starting?’ … a child reaches out to the screen at Lightroom.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXAnd it makes a pretty convincing argument for why Aardman is so important, so beloved by so many people. Early on, it cuts to a clip from 1989’s A Grand Day Out, the first Wallace & Gromit film. At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay, every finger print and smudge. It looks so real, so human. Director Lucy Izzard says in a voiceover: “I think people still crave imperfection,” and you think yes, that’s it, that’s why Aardman matters. It’s something incredibly human in an age when things feel so amazingly non-human so much of the time.Does that hand-made, imperfect, homely aesthetic rub up awkwardly against the technological wizardry of immersive cinema? Sure does. But the bigger issue is that this experience doesn’t really know what it wants to be.It ends up as half-documentary, half-clip show, becoming sort of neither in the process, and a bit hard to follow too. It doesn’t even take full advantage of Lightroom’s capabilities. It could be bolder, more fun, it could play with the immersive format a bit more.One good use of the tech are the side screens, which make you feel like you are inside various environments: Shaun the Sheep’s barn, Gromit’s cardboard box as he spies on Feathers McGraw, behind the recording desk as actors do their vocal takes. But it’s not quite enough.There’s some fun stuff here. It’s great seeing Creature Comforts recreated in living rooms and gardens, it’s nice to see all the concept art and storyboards come to life, it’s pretty joyful watching the amazing video forPeter Gabriel’s Sledgehammerat such an enormous scale. It just lacks the crowd-pleasing immersive thrills of Lightroom’s recent Prehistoric Planet: Discovering Dinosaurs.View image in fullscreen‘It’s sort of a documentary.’Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXAs a jaded, tired contemporary art critic, I may not be the target audience, so I brought along someone called Solomon. What are his qualifications? Well, he’s four, and yesterday he went to the cinema to seethe latest Shaun the Sheep movie, so you could say he’s something of a young cinephile. Also, his father (me) is a critic, so he is probably genetically predisposed to have opinions about this.Halfway through, I ask what he thinks. He says: “When is the movie starting? This is just ads.” He’s right – the whole thing just feels like an advert for Aardman. “When is the movie starting?” he asks again, more impatient this time, almost pleading. “This is it,” I say. “It’s sort of a documentary.” He stares at me, uncomprehending, and then yawns. Ouch, he really is a critic.Aardman’​s Peter Lord and David Sproxton: ‘At the Oscars, I went to the gents and had a pee with Jack Nicholson!’Read moreIt doesn’t really have enough for kids, and the storytelling isn’t strong enough for adults. It’s gimmick over narrative, as if they didn’t ask: “How can we make an amazing immersive experience?” but instead asked: “How can we tell our story in an immersive-ish way?” And those are two different propositions.This show doesn’t tarnish Aardman’s stellar reputation, nor detract from all the amazing, quirky, quaint, funny work that they’ve done, but it doesn’t add a huge amount to it either. More of a rubber glove on the head than a crowning achievement.Larger Than Life is at Lightroom, London, from 14 October to 4 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designAardmanArtExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Our Bodies Have Been Bridges review – riveting portraits and the story of the first woman on Earth | Art | The Guardian
description: The three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communities
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: The three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communities
Content: Quiet and minimal … Laura Aguilar, Motion #50, 1999.Photograph: © Laura AguilarView image in fullscreenQuiet and minimal … Laura Aguilar, Motion #50, 1999.Photograph: © Laura AguilarArtReviewOur Bodies Have Been Bridges review – riveting portraits and the story of the first woman on EarthAutograph, LondonThe three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communitiesCharlotte JansenTue 13 Oct 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 1990s, the late Chicana artist Laura Aguilar was living with depression. A friend took her on a road trip to New Mexico, where Aguilar made some nude self-portraits in the mystical landscapes. Those photographs evolved into a pivotal series shot in desert environments across the American south-west, Aguilar’s notable 1996 Nature Self-Portrait – considered an early work of intersectional feminist art, before the word had entered academic discourse.London gallery Autograph first worked on an exhibition of Aguilar’s in 1997, the year after she made Nature Self-Portrait, so this is something of a homecoming, a generation on. Aguilar’s contours, folds, and crevices sometimes disappear into the barren desert landscapes, assimilating the shapes of boulders or trees; at other times, her body is incongruous, soft flesh that can’t be held by the harsh, barren conditions. These images capture the paradox of a body that is both hypervisible and ignored.Several works from Nature Self-Portrait appear at the beginning of Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Autograph’s new three-person headline show. They’re so quiet and minimal, shot in black and white, they’d be easy to coast past – which is partly Aguilar’s point. Bodies like hers – large, queer, Chicana – had no visibility in culture at the time Aguilar made these works, while in real life her experiences were of an uncomfortable, scrutinised presence. Out here in the terrain of nowhere, Aguilar returns her body to the earth – a body wanting to just be a body, to not ache to fit in. A body with the same cracks, dents and curves as the land; hardy, wild and free. They’re photographs about rejection, but also embrace.View image in fullscreenRemembered scenes … Koyoltzintli, Mom curing me from the evil eye, c.1990 from Other Stories/Historias Bravas, 2011-2012.Photograph: © Koyoltzintli. Courtesy the artist.This is the beginning of three concurrent exhibitions at Autograph about rebellious bodies. In the first and largest, Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Aguilar’s story continues through two younger artists who also use their bodies as anchors, in pursuit of healing, truth and connection to ancestral female knowledge. In a diaristic, family album-style account of matriarchy and ritual, Other Stories/Historias Bravas, the artist Koyoltzintli re-enacts remembered scenes from her childhood in the Andean mountains of Ecuador.Her bare breasts are blessed by her aunt, for protection. In another picture, her mother braids her hair tenderly, the same way, the caption tells us, her grandmother had once done for her. Her mum takes her to sit among the iguanas at the local park, to cure her of her phobia of the reptiles. Routines of care passed down generations of women, through their bodies. Tangible, physical, felt knowledge and history is reflected in Koyoltzintli’s very direct, intimate approach to photography. In a group of works from the series Meda – indebted to Aguilar’s self-portraits – Koyoltzintli asked women to interact with the land as their ancestors might have, to trace a collective, imagined, silent story of the first woman on Earth. An alternative origin story.These works appear with Peruvian Tarrah Krajnak’s grainy, photocopied, archival images that focus on 1979 – the year the military regime ended in Peru, and also the year of the artist’s birth. The works explore the dissonance between women’s bodies portrayed in the country’s media and the private, personal experiences of living as a woman through that time and the years of armed conflict that followed. She takes images cribbed from newspapers and magazines published that year, and to query their veracity, photocopies, rephotographs, and interrupts them with her own image. The bodies here are agitated, unstable and unresolved.Upstairs, this dovetails seamlessly into Charan Singh’s Your Tongue in My Mouth. As the unforgettable title promises, Singh’s work is a joyful provocation, but also a serious meditation on desirability, sexuality and reciprocity – when certain bodies are seen by some as a burden, a threat.View image in fullscreenRiveting and regal … Charan Singh, Rasili, 2026.Photograph: © Charan SinghSingh’s lucid colour portraits of Hijra, Kothi and trans people combine a realist sensibility and theatricality – the subjects’ authenticity contrasts with choreographed poses; beautiful hand-painted backdrops behind them evoke a world of fantasy and escape. Riveting, regal portraits such as Umrao and Sonu have a timeless elegance: the subjects’ decision to wear traditional salwar kameez or anarkali-style dress, ornate brocade fabrics, their bodies adorned with henna and bindi, are intentional gestures that they also belong to a longer history in south Asia. These portraits are statements of dignity that claim their right to that place without words or apology.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe subtle tension between realism and artifice takes on a particular urgency against the backdrop of India’s deteriorating trans rights. In March 2026, legislative amendments to the country’s Transgender Persons Act 2019 rolled back protections for gender self-identification, raising profound questions about bodily autonomy, recognition and the right to define oneself. A timeline of transgender history and rights, displayed on a table at the centre of Singh’s exhibition, situates these intimate portraits within a longer struggle for visibility and legal recognition, grounding their gestures of self-fashioning and self-expression in a shifting and often hostile political reality.AtAutograph, Londonuntil 13 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtExhibitionsPhotographyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Georg Baselitz: The Heroes review – astonishing paintings take a savage swipe at history | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at
Content: Frankensteinian monsters … Georg Baselitz, 1. Kopf (1. Head), 1966.Photograph: Friedrich Rosenstiel, Köln. © Georg Baselitz 2026.View image in fullscreenFrankensteinian monsters … Georg Baselitz, 1. Kopf (1. Head), 1966.Photograph: Friedrich Rosenstiel, Köln. © Georg Baselitz 2026.Art and designReviewGeorg Baselitz: The Heroes review – astonishing paintings take a savage swipe at historyThaddaeus Ropac, LondonThe artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat atJonathan JonesTue 13 Oct 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the German painter Georg Baselitz died this year a chunk of Europe’s rapidly diminishing historical memory went with him. Baselitz was born in 1938, experienced Hitler’s Germany and the second world war as a young child, then found himself growing up in communist East Germany before escaping to the west and becoming an artist. His acidic, honest perceptions of the history he’d lived throughwill no longer be those of the living personI was lucky enough to encounter. But he has left us a gift: an exhibition in London he helped plan of his most astonishing history paintings, The Heroes.It’s a savage, merciless vision of modern history with feelings of horror, disgust and irreparable guilt hanging heavy in the poisoned air. But there’s a terrible joy too, the thrill of speaking the truth. You sense the liberation Baselitz must have felt when he set brush to canvas to start these paintings in 1965. Comparing the explosive rage and nihilism of his art to punk may be inadequate but the title of this series of colossal imaginary portraits is so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at.View image in fullscreenMit Roter Fahne (With Red Flag), 1965.Photograph: Ed Gumuchian/Courtesy private collection. © Georg Baselitz 2026.Mit Rote Fahne – or With the Red Banner – depicts a massive, square-shouldered yet exhausted soldier holding a half-lowered flag that is a smear of red and black. A banner of blood, the redness congeals to form black scabs that suggest the shadow of the swastika. All around the soldier is a wasteland. Do we owe him compassion? No, he had none. The devastated world at his feet was destroyed by Germany’s heroes who fought in the second world war. When Baselitz painted these furious homages in the mid-1960s, these men were running West Germany’s banks and car companies.Another long-haired Hero, in a uniform with shorts, stands in a trashed, blood-stained landscape. This bland-faced character balances two crimson mittens, preparing apparently to let them go and to live on without these gory encumbrances, with clean hands.It’s as if Baselitz was walking around the increasingly affluent streets of West Germany, seeing healthy, optimistic faces and retching at how easily the crimes of the second world war could be shoved into the past. The Holocaust only ended 20 years ago, these paintings scream, when the armies advancing on Hitler’s Reich discovered the places where six million Jews were systematically murdered – how can we Germans hold our heads high and strut on?View image in fullscreenEin Moderner Maler (A Modern Painter), 1966.Photograph: Courtesy Berlinische Galerie - Museum of Modern Art, Photography and Architecture. © Georg Baselitz 2026.But if Germany is mired in shame, what about German art? Baselitz and his artistic peers Joseph Beuys and Anselm Kiefer, all of whom face German history head on, were sometimes accused by critics of glorifying it, or feasting on it, but there’s no hint of Teutonic grandeur here. In Ein Moderner Maler – A modern painter – Baselitz depicts an artist who can’t work because both hands are caught in man-traps. He sits defeated on the ground in military-looking clothes with armbands, as guilty and mad as all the other Heroes. He literally spills his guts in a parody of inner angst: a curl of intestines lies between his legs, while another section of bowel emerges from his side and becomes a spiralling pig’s tail. This is what the German artist’s romantic inner life has become. It’s OK to laugh. His hair is flattened on his head and he has a hint of a square moustache to remind you that Hitler, too, fancied himself an artist.Georg Baselitz – a life in picturesRead moreBaselitz reserves his deepest disgust for his own artistic mastery: painting has been smashed, it is no longer possible, say these brilliant paintings. Their uncoordinated, lumpen figures look like Frankensteinian monsters, made from bits and pieces of mud and flesh pathetically sewn together. One soldier, sitting under the trees, has a square head on top of a slumped, square body as blood drips on his head from two branches. He is a ghost inside his garments, there and not there.View image in fullscreenSchwarzgrundig (Black Grounded), 1966.Photograph: Mick Vincenz, Essen/MKM Museum Küppersmühle for Modern Art, Duisburg, Ströher Collection. © Georg Baselitz 2026.This way of depicting the human figure makes Baselitz unique. He has little in common with British postwar figurative artists such as Bacon and Freud for whom there is always a real, pulsing body they’re trying to record. Baselitz’s bodies are abstract, designed with irony and black humour, their sufferings absurd. Another Hero stands with his flies undone, grey spurts of semen emerging from his black trousers as he towers over a shattered landscape. His ecstatic expression tells us he’s turned on by it all while at his feet is a Disneyish duck, an emblem perhaps of the innocence he will feign in postwar life.What has happened to the art of memory? After all the artistic reckonings, the history books and Holocaust memorials, the far-right AfD is winning one election after another in Germany. For extremists of all hues it isn’t even necessary to deny the Holocaust – nowadays you can shrug it off, trivialise it, dismiss it as belonging to the distant past. And the Heroes walk again. Baselitz paints one of them waving, or is it saluting, in blood-soaked trousers with a ghostly shadow of a face. Around him in the European night white flecks fall slowly, like snow or ashes.At Thaddaeus Ropac Gallery, London, until 18 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designGermanyEuropeExhibitionsPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The play that changed my life: ‘I was the badass queen in Titus Andronicus – we did it like A Nightmare on Elm Street’ | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effect
Author: Moira Buffini
Headline: Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effect
Content: Carnage … Flora Spencer-Longhurst (Lavinia) and William Houston (Titus) in Titus Andronicus at Shakespeare's Globe theatre, London, in 2014.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCarnage … Flora Spencer-Longhurst (Lavinia) and William Houston (Titus) in Titus Andronicus at Shakespeare's Globe theatre, London, in 2014.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe play that changed my lifeTheatreThe play that changed my life: ‘I was the badass queen in Titus Andronicus – we did it like A Nightmare on Elm Street’Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effectMoira BuffiniTue 13 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTitus Andronicus has to be among William Shakespeare’s worst plays. In fact TS Eliot called it “one of the stupidest and most uninspired plays ever written”. Yet it holds a very special place in my heart. It’s a bloody revenge-fest in which each act of violence is more grotesque than the last. Titus Andronicus returns from war with “barbarous” Tamora, “Queen of the Goths”, as his prisoner. She stealthily proceeds to kill and destroy his family, and when he discovers this, he murders her sons and serves them up to her in a pie. The play ends with gudgeons of fake blood and a sea of carnage. In Shakespeare’s day it was a huge hit, a kind of slasher film of the 16th century.Plays are very powerful things and I have spent my life watching them and writing them. Some have been revelatory but none has affected me likeTitus Andronicus. It was the first play, outside of school, that I was ever in – so I suppose this is about the transformative power of youth theatre.My family were going through some difficult years and I had been “asked to leave” my small-town Catholic school (it’s still hard to say I was expelled). I was feeling pretty low. When I got into the National YouthTheatre, it felt like someone had offered me a lifeline, away from the circumstances I was in. I got to escape from north Wales for a few weeks and I went to London for the first time.View image in fullscreenUtterly ruthless … Estelle Kohler as Tamora, centre, with Piers Ibbotson and Richard McCabe in Titus Andronicus at the Pit, Barbican, London, in 1988.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianI found myself in a diverse company of young people from all over the UK. We didn’t understand a word of Titus Andronicus. We could hardly say it aloud. But our director was adamant that we could do it, so we flung ourselves in. I discovered the level of collaboration that happens when you’re rehearsing a play. The camaraderie wasn’t like anything I had experienced before. It was exhilarating. Being thrown in at the deep end made me unafraid of Shakespeare. It made me instinctively appreciate the way his language worked. More importantly, I began to have faith in who I was.To see or not to see? Every single Shakespeare play – ranked!Read moreI got cast as Queen Tamora. I learned her lines on the tube, saying them over and over. She was wronged, she was utterly ruthless and depraved. She was a mature woman, not a teenager like me, and she had badass lines. She was an absolutely transgressional woman. Being Tamora made me straighten my shoulders and stand strong.We put on our production in a school gym. In the performances, we went for the grotesquerie, full-throttle. I remember the faces of my fellow cast members, playing the shock and horror of the play’s murders as if it was A Nightmare on Elm Street. I’ve got no idea what the experience was like for our audience but by the time the production was finished, something in me had shifted. I saw a new direction in life. I got my act together, applied to study drama and I moved down to London. A bit of barbarous Tamora had rubbed off on me.Flarestorm by Moira Buffini is published by Faber on 22 October.Order your copy from guardianbookshop.com.
