title: Lena Dunham’s Girls returning for limited run at HBO | Girls | The Guardian
description: Creator and star will return along with Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells for five-episode revival
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Creator and star will return along with Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells for five-episode revival
Content: The cast of Girls.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOView image in fullscreenThe cast of Girls.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOGirlsLena Dunham’s Girls returning for limited run at HBOCreator and star will return along with Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke and Andrew Rannells for five-episode revivalAdrian HortonTue 13 Oct 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGirls, the seminal HBO series on millennial strivers that launched the careers ofLena Dunham, Allison Williams, Adam Driver and more, will return for a limited run on HBO in 2027.The five-episode addendum, set to begin production next year – a decade after the series finale aired – will reunite creator and star Dunham, as aspiring writer Hannah Horvath, alongside Williams as Marnie Michaels, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna, Jemima Kirke as Jessa and Andrew Rannells as Elijah. Judd Apatow will also return as executive producer.“We always said we would only return toGirlsif there was a specific story we were burning to tell,” Dunham said in a statement. “I’ve missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn’t quite picture them in the present day. Then, right around my fortieth birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it’s pretty hard to get them to stop …“It’s rare that you get the chance to return to something that changed your life with the gift of hindsight and a whole new level of gratitude and understanding,” she added. “I love these girls (and boy), our friends atHBO, and all the people who have continued to discover the show and remind us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together … and the chance to wear yellow mesh …”“We’re thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one’s twenties to the milestone of turning forty,” said Amy Gravitt, the head of HBO comedy programming. “To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans – old and new – will be happy to see how they’ve grown and relieved to see that they’re still the Girls we knew way back when.”Over six headline-generating seasons, from 2012 to 2017, Girls received 19 Emmy nominations and two wins, including for best casting. Dunham, who became a media fixture after writing the show’s pilot at just 23, is returning to the series after the launch of her bestselling memoirFamesick, which dealt with the heady rush of responsibilities and fame during the show’s 2010s heyday. Dunham’s credits since the end of Girls also include the Netflix series Too Much and indie film Sharp Stick.Other details, including title, plot and additional casting, have yet to be announced. As Dunham wondered in a video teasing the announcement: “I have a question though – can we still call it Girls? Because we’re old as f-.”The news arrives asHBO becomes part of Skydanceas the result of the $111bn merger which was made official last week.Explore more on these topicsGirlsLena DunhamUS televisionTV comedyComedyTelevisionHBOnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netflix unveils first trailer for Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew | Greta Gerwig | The Guardian
description: The fantasy epic based on CS Lewis’s classic stars Daniel Craig, Carey Mulligan and Meryl Streep
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The fantasy epic based on CS Lewis’s classic stars Daniel Craig, Carey Mulligan and Meryl Streep
Content: A still from Narnia: The Magician's Nephew.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenA still from Narnia: The Magician's Nephew.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixGreta GerwigNetflix unveils first trailer for Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s NephewThe fantasy epic based on CS Lewis’s classic stars Daniel Craig, Carey Mulligan and Meryl StreepOwen MyersTue 13 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first look atGreta Gerwig’s vision for Narnia has been revealed.Today, Netflix is giving a first look at her vision forCS Lewis’s magical world in the trailer for The Magician’s Nephew, the first chronological book in the beloved series.With the soundtrack of Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven, the trailer opens with magician Andrew Ketterley (Daniel Craig) intoning that “sometimes one story is the beginning to all others”, as he gives a group of kids a magic ring that will transport them to strange and wonderful lands.Elsewhere, the trailer gives a first look at many locations and characters familiar to fans, including Jadis (Emma Mackey, the future White Witch) and Aslan, the mythical lion voiced byMeryl Streep.The Magician’s Nephew tells the story of two children in Edwardian England named Digory and Polly (newcomers David McKenna and Beatrice Campbell) who chance upon the Wood Between Worlds, a realm with many portals to different dimensions. There, they witness the birth of Narnia.Meryl Streep’s casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don’t they have more pressing issues?Read moreIn a trailer premiere event in New York this morning, Gerwig spoke of her longtime passion for CS Lewis’s series. “I don’t remember a time I didn’t know the books,” she said, perVariety. “I wouldn’t be who I am without these books.”The film, which is Gerwig’s first since her $1bn-grossing megahitBarbie, will open for an eight-week theatrical window on 12 February before it streams on Netflix starting 2 April, in the studio’s first global theatrical release.“I told Ted [Sarandos, CEO of Netflix] I only know how to make movies for the big screen,” Gerwig said. “He said: ‘Make the movie for the biggest screen and trust the process.’”The director added that she petitioned Led Zeppelin’s Robert Plant and Jimmy Page for permission to use Stairway to Heaven in the trailer.“I talked to them about a lot of the themes of the film,” Gerwig said, as reported byRolling Stone. “They saw the heart and the story and the drama in it.”“It’s an epic song,” she added. “It’s about the two paths of good and evil … It is a spiritual quest and a spiritual journey. So to me, this was a song that made sense to introduce the film to the world.”Explore more on these topicsGreta GerwigAction and adventure filmsNetflixDaniel CraigMeryl StreepCarey MulliganCS LewisnewsShareReuse this content

title: 50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about exclusion of minority ethnic artists
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about exclusion of minority ethnic artists
Content: Lauryn Pinard in Sonje at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026 in Leicester, hosted by the Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsView image in fullscreenLauryn Pinard in Sonje at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026 in Leicester, hosted by the Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsArt and design50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists?Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about  exclusion of minority ethnic artistsChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British arts establishment was first published, and the question of who and what counts as British continues to be contested.The Arts Britain Ignores – Khan’s groundbreaking 1976 report, commissioned by organisations including the then Arts Council of Great Britain, presented a vision of a pluralistic national culture, in which the creativity of Britons of diverse ethnic backgrounds – from bhangra music, to black painters and Ukrainian dance – should be recognised, supported and respected.Today, whenpolls,debates and cultural and political moments present differing notions of British identity – whether it is thediversity of the England football team, orhow political figures choose to define their own identities– Khan’s work retains its relevance.View image in fullscreenUndated photo of Naseem Khan.Photograph: Frank Martin/The GuardianOn Wednesday, Dawn Airey, the new chair of cultural funding and development agencyArts Council England, will give her inaugural speech at a conference celebrating Khan’s legacy – The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On – at Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage in Leicester.Today, the work of black and Asian British visual artists, such as Frank Bowling, Sonia Boyce and Anish Kapoor is critically acclaimed and in demand. But in 1976, Khan documented how grassroot arts and cultural practices that thrived in UK ethnic minority communities were largely ignored by funders and critics.This week’s conference, bringing together artists, organisations, experts and policymakers, will explore how much progress has been made in 50 years and comes at a time when community and independent cultural spaces face pressures over finances, redevelopment and gentrification.View image in fullscreenDancer and choreographer Tebandeke Joseph performing in TimeMachine at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsContributors to Wednesday’s conference include Khan’s daughter, Amelia Torode, the theatre director Jatinder Verma, the broadcaster Brenda Emmanus and the crossbench peer and chancellor of the University of Nottingham, Lola Young.View image in fullscreenCover of the new book The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On.Photograph: Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage / The Unloved.The conference also marks the launch of a new book, The Arts Britain Ignores at 50, published bySerendipity Institute, including essays and new research.Pawlet Brookes, the chief executive and artistic director of Serendipity Institute, said: “We had Cool Britannia, we’ve had the ‘ain’t no black in the union jack’. We’ve had all of that narrative. But the reality is British is diverse – whether that diversity is layered with colour or layered in other ways. We can go down a negative road, or we can celebrate what we have, which is fantastic, the best in Europe – although we still have some way to go.”View image in fullscreenBritish-Indian sculptor Anish Kapoor next to his installation Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto at the Hayward Gallery, London, in June.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersDescribing Khan’s work as “seminal”, Brookes said it was time to “see how far we’ve travelled, and what we need to do for the next 50 years.”She added: “We did a timeline investigation [for the new book] and what it shows is that, there has been funding for culturally diverse organisations, but what there hasn’t been is sustainability and growth.“We also need recognition for dance and theatre, in the way that progress has been made in the visual arts.”View image in fullscreenThe artist Frank Bowling at the launch of his  exhibition Seeking the Sublime, at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, in March.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAIn her speech, Airey is expected to say: “The journey Khan set us on remains one of the most important our sector is undertaking … [it] will sit at the centre of my work.”She praises Khan as having told institutions such as the Arts Council that “you have built an entire cultural establishment – its funding structures, its buildings, its critics, its canon – around a definition of British art that leaves whole swathes of it out.”View image in fullscreenDawn Airey, the new chair of Arts Council England, will be speaking at the conference.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianAirey is also expected to say: “It a hard time to be an artist in this country, whatever your background – but for many people in this room it is harder still.“Racism, Islamophobia and antisemitism are part of daily life for too many people in our sector: sometimes in crude and obvious ways, sometimes in subtle and deniable ones, but constantly there … So let me be emphatic. Those of us who don’t experience this – and I include myself – have a responsibility to stand with you: to stand up for the work you want to make, and to back that with action, not just words.”Explore more on these topicsArt and designBlack British cultureArts Council EnglandDawn AireyBritish identity and societyLeicesterArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Some things are worth dying for’: Karl Bushby’s incredible 28-year walk home, through deserts, kidnappers and polar bears | Life and style | The Guardian
description: On his record-breaking trek, Karl Bushby was held at gunpoint, arrested, menaced by a polar bear and left by two separate girlfriends. Now he’s nearing home after 28 years – and he has a few stories to tell
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: On his record-breaking trek, Karl Bushby was held at gunpoint, arrested, menaced by a polar bear and left by two separate girlfriends. Now he’s nearing home after 28 years – and he has a few stories to tell
Content: Making history … Bushby in Alaska in 2005.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyView image in fullscreenMaking history … Bushby in Alaska in 2005.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyThe big interviewLife and styleInterview‘Some things are worth dying for’: Karl Bushby’s incredible 28-year walk home, through deserts, kidnappers and polar bearsSimon HattenstoneThe ex-soldier has marched 36,000 miles since he left Hull in 1998. He’s crossed the Americas, Asia and Europe, fallen in love, been held at gunpoint and been deported, in between nearly drowning, nearly dying of thirst and nearly being eaten. But that’s just the start of it …Tue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s a big moment,” says Karl Bushby, who has had plenty of big moments in his life. He is recording himself on his phone for social media. “We’re in Dover, and I’m about to have my first fish and chips and mushy peas in 28 years. Mushy peas, my God, I forgot they even existed!” He points his phone at the plate in front of him. “It better be good.” And he tucks in. “Mmmm. See, this is a big chunk of fish and a decent bit of batter, and that’s something you don’t see in other parts of the world. I mean, come on! That. Is. Fish. And. Chips! You see, Britain is special.”It has been two days since Bushby swam the Channel to return to England. Tomorrow, he’ll start the walk home to Hull for the first time since he left in 1998. He hopes to get back on 1 November, the same date he set off all those years ago.Although Bushby is a man of military precision, timing is not one of his greatest traits. When the former paratrooper left the army, aged 29, to walk the world, he planned to be home 12 years later. What accounted for the extra years? “The real world. You can’t account for financial crises, pandemics, visa bans, wars and the bureaucracy you have to deal with. It took 28 years because of the rules and because we refused to compromise on the route.” I ask what he means by “we”? He smiles. “It’s the royal we. Me and the Beast.”Ah, the Beast. That’s the customised golf trolley he travelled with, containing essential survival equipment, camping supplies, electronics and food. The original Beast lasted three years before it broke down and had to be put out to grass. The Beast 2, an upgrade he built in Nicaragua, has survived 25 years.View image in fullscreenKarl Bushby on Shakespeare Beach in Dover.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianRather than circumnavigating the globe, which is impossible without transport, Bushby decided to walk about as far as he possibly could. As his starting point he chose the southernmost city on the South American continent, Punta Arenas in Chile (53 deg S), and planned to make his way across the Americas, Asia and Europe back to his home town, Hull (which is, at 53 deg N, the latitudinal mirror image of Punta Arenas).He was guided by two simple self-made rules: he could use no transport to advance, and there was no going home until he arrived on foot, mission completed. If he had to make a detour or pause his trip, by force or by choice, he would use transport, but always restart at the exact spot where he had stopped.Bushby has walked approximately 36,000 miles (58,000km), breaking the record for the longest unbroken foot journey and far exceeding the 25,000-mile circumference of the world. When he gets home he will be the first person to have walked continuously across the world, visiting 29 countries. En route, he broke other records (as part of the first teams to complete the crossing of the Bering Strait, from Alaska to Russia, on foot in modern times, and to swim the Caspian Sea, from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan). He has also almost died, spent years stuck in Mexico because he lost his sponsor, been convicted of being a spy, been held in custody in Russia and sentenced to deportation, been threatened at gunpoint and faced the prospect of predation by a polar bear. To many he’s a hero. To some, he’s a reckless chancer.double quotation markLuckily for me, when dealing with the gunmen, I had copies of newspaper clippings about me from South America. With them I could talk my way out of anythingWe meet at the White Horse in Dover, its walls graffitied with thetimes people have taken to swim the Channel. Bushby looks at them and says they show what an amateur he is. It took him 20 hours over three days to swim the 21 miles (34km) on his back. “There’s one over there who did it in 10 hours. Swimmers normally go twice the speed I did. Real swimmers are in trunks, caps and a pair of goggles. I’ve got a wetsuit, fins, paddles for my hands, a flotation vest, neck flotation. I don’t call what I do swimming, out of respect to real swimmers. I call it ‘floatimming’.”Bushby looks fit in the way that people who take regular constitutionals do. His face is tanned from the sun and the wind; his hair is still blond, his eyes sea blue. But he is also very different from the man who set out three decades ago. At 29, Bushby was skinny with shoulder-length hair – a dead ringer for Kurt Cobain. Once the media started reporting on his “Goliath expedition”, a joke/conspiracy theory went round that the former Nirvana frontman wasn’t really dead, he was just walking the world using the pseudonym Karl Bushby.View image in fullscreenIn Chile, 1999.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyToday, at 57, he is strong, with a bone-crunching handshake, a fuller face and a hint of middle-aged spread. He says people don’t expect him to look the way he does. They either imagine him as Gandalf, with a white beard down to his knees, or as a ripped athlete. “Everyone’s saying: if he’s been walking 28 years, why does he look so fat? But most of the time I’m eating out of gas stations, burger bars, sitting somewhere for three months waiting for a visa, getting older, eating biscuits and cookies.”He has brought along a friend, Angela Maxwell, a 44-year-old American who spent six and a half years walking the world, some of it alongside Bushby. She also swam the Caspian Sea with him over 31 days in 2024, accompanied by Anastasia Boborykina and Abdurrahman Rustamov,two young Azerbaijani champion swimmers.Maxwell tells me that in many ways she and Bushby are different, but they are similar in important ways. “We’re both introverts, even hermits in some way. We like our autonomy.” Maxwell is a funny and talkative introvert. Bushby is a more conventional introvert – quiet, understated, dry.View image in fullscreen‘I wouldn’t quit – I just won’t let go’ … Karl Bushby.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianBushby grew up in a military family. His father, Keith, is an SAS veteran who spent 24 years in the British army, and his younger brother, Adrian, is also an army man. His mother, another Angela, worked in a factory.School, Bushby says, was a “living hell”. Dyslexic (though undiagnosed), he was branded as “thick”, and found solace in birdwatching. He left school at 16 with no qualifications and joined the junior Parachute regiment. But he struggled with the physical demands, and took five attempts to pass the gruelling P Company training before eventually joining the 3rd battalion of the Parachute regiment. Some mocked him for his repeated failures, but others were impressed by his tenacity. “Normally, they’ll allow you two or three attempts.” Why did he get five? “Because I wouldn’t quit … that was probably one of the first signs. I just won’t let go. I’m a bit of a rottweiler.”Bushby remained an outsider in the paras, not least because he didn’t like booze. “I was never a beer drinker. And that’s very bad news in the army. Very difficult. It can be a problem.” Throughout his military career, he felt his peers didn’t trust or respect him.In his early 20s, stationed in Northern Ireland, he married a Belfast woman, yet another Angela. Five years later, when they were living in Hampshire, they divorced. She returned home to Belfast with their young son, Adam. At the time, servicemen were only allowed into Northern Ireland if they were serving there, so Bushby was effectively separated from Adam.There was another thing gnawing away at him. A professional, or existential, crisis. The world was at peace, which was catastrophic for those who had joined the military hoping to see action. Between 1990 and 1995, the British army was downsized from 160,000 to 120,000. Bushby kept his job, but he was bored and restless. “We were not being used. There was nothing going on. I was one of those guys looking for other challenges in life. We were all disillusioned because of the lack of action – the “peace disease”, as the Chinese refer to it. It’s hard to keep an army in combat fighting conditions when there’s nothing to do. As young soldiers, you’re up for the fight, and you end up in Northern Ireland on sentry on a gate every day. It’s not very appealing.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianEver since childhood, he had wanderlust, a longing for new horizons. “I used to dream about great big journeys on foot. I started drawing lines on maps, and the conversation spread between friends.” Had he ever done a big journey before? “No!Nothing.”In his mid-20s, he got a birthday card from his father that mentioned a group of SAS soldiers who were discussing the possibility of walking from London to New York. That was an epiphany, Bushby says. There was a map on the wall, and he took a black marker pen and drew a line from the UK to Europe, through Asia, over the Bering Strait. Then he thought: why stop in New York? So he extended the line down to the bottom of the Americas. He knew there were a few obstacles, but as far as he was concerned, the whole world was connected if he could get over the Bering Strait. Not that he knewwhat the Bering Strait was, or that nobody had successfully crossed it in modern times, since it had broken down into treacherous blocks of ice. (Some scientists believe Paleo-Indian people may havecrossed from Siberia into Alaska17,000 years ago, when ocean levels were lower.)For the next couple of years Bushby studied the route, working out how his dream could be turned into a reality. It meant swotting up on the subjects he’d flunked at school – maths, physics and geography. The more he studied, the more he told people he was going to do it. “Nobody took it seriously when I said I wanted to walk around the world. It was like, ‘Karl just had this crazy batshit idea of spending 12 years walking around the world. Yeah, whatever!’ That was the response from everybody, and that fuelled the fire. But I would look at the map, and think of what kind of life that would be. I couldn’t let go of that.”He was also motivated by poor mental health. He was a keen distance runner, and if he went a single day without running, he suffered anxiety attacks. It got so bad that he saw a behavioural psychologist. “It dominated my life. It really did.”Perhaps the biggest motivation of all was an overwhelming sense of his own mortality. “I took death seriously. You’re dying, you’ve got one life, and what are you going to do with it? That really resonated with me.”Once Bushby had made up his mind, he accepted that he would never see his son growing up. If everything went to plan, Adam would be 20 when he got back (as it is, he is 36).“That was a difficult decision,” Bushby says. “But the way I squared that circle was, ‘How would I be worth something to my son?’ Would I be worth more to him by doing something on this scale?’” He doesn’t sound wholly convinced by his argument.On 1 November 1998, Bushby set off from his mother’s house. He flew to Chile, hitching a lift to the Falkland Islands on an RAF military transport flight.From there, he took a short civilian flight to cross over to his official starting point in Punta Arenas,Chile. He set off from there with $500 (then equal to about £300) of savings and the Beast, speaking no Spanish, and was met immediately with a ferocious environment on the Patagonian steppe. Hurricane-force winds were raging. The freezing gales forced him to lean at a 45-degree angle just to stay on his feet, for days at a time, while dust and grit pelted his face. He experienced suffocating altitude sickness, breathing difficulties and starvation.Bushby soon realised that pushing his way across the wind-lashed, bone-dry plateau was a death sentence. He altered his route to cross the Andes and headed west towards the coast. The terrain was still hostile (at one point he survived on one banana for three days), but he began to meet people who transformed his view of humanity. When he needed warmth or food or simply contact, they provided it.“There are so many examples out there. Where would we be without some of the help we’ve had? Just the simple stuff. You’ll find people living in shacks on the side of the road built with car parts – hoods and doors taped together. These people are just scratching out an existence, but they’ll give you a bowl of rice and water.”View image in fullscreenCrossing the driest desert in the world … Bushby in Chile.Photograph: Tiktok: @karlcbushbyBy now he was beginning to speak Spanish, but often he didn’t even exchange a word with those who helped him. “I was walking through the Atacama desert in Chile. You’ve got one main highway, Route 5, so the truckers and coach drivers get to see the same guys over the months as you’re inching forward, and eventually they become your support network. You’re now in the driest desert in the world, and those trucks are passing me fruit, and bottles of water get thrown out for me. I don’t know who’s in that truck, but they’re looking after me.”He tells me about a Chilean family who would regularly drive hundreds of miles to give him provisions and spend time with him. Then there was the stranger who drove up to him on the highway, asked if he was Karl Bushby, and handed him an envelope containing a huge booklet of food vouchers for meals at the German-Chilean restaurant franchise Bavaria, whose outlets are dotted along the highway. The man, Michael Bier, also gave him $100 on condition that Bushby hand-deliver a postcard to a friend in Vienna, which he eventually did – 27 years later.Bushby admits he had a mean-spirited view of humankind before the walk. “Twelve years in the army, you don’t get to see the best of humanity, but the kindness of strangers …” He trails off. “I always say 99.999% of the people I met represented the very best of humanity. Every country has been the same.”And he met them just when he needed them most. In 2000, in Peru, he caught a severe stomach infection along with multiple secondary bacterial infections that left him fearing the worst. “This guy stopped me one day and said: ‘Come and stay with us when you get to the next town.’ His wife just happened to be a doctor running an analysis company. I walk in, sick as a dog, they take blood and samples, put me in bed for the week, quadruple-dose me on antibiotics, get me back on my feet and don’t want anything for it.” He shakes his head in wonder. “Another miracle,” he says.The one time he did meet with the 0.001% of people that weren’t the best of humanity was in Colombia. “At the time, the country was a lawless mix of insurgency, counterinsurgency, drugs and counternarcotics intelligence agencies. There was even MI6 chasing the IRA, who were teaching the leftwing guerrillas how to make bombs. Nobody trusted anything or anyone. I was a blond-haired gringo in the kidnap capital of the world. Pretty stupid.”But he fell in love with the country and with a woman called Catalina, whom he was with for seven years. “She struggled because there was no country north of Panama that would let her in, because she was a single woman and Colombian. She was a civil engineer, very intelligent.” But she couldn’t cope with the instability of their life. “Eventually, she was headhunted by an energy company in Spain and met someone there.” His heart was broken – not for the last time.View image in fullscreenGoing undercover in the Darién Gap.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyHe left Colombia in about 2000 via the notoriousDarién Gap,a 60-mile (97km) stretch of dense rainforest, swamps and mountains that served as cover for guerrilla groups such as the leftwing Farc and the rightwing AUC on the border between Colombia and Panama. The gap is the only break in the Pan-American highway (the world’s longest motorable road), and Bushby had to cross it because it was the only way of reaching Panama. He dressed as a vagrant to make himself less conspicuous, with maps, compasses and essential medicines stitched into secret pockets in his clothing. At times, he backstroked his way down rivers, disguised as detritus.Was it scary? “Oh yes, absolutely. I found myself at gunpoint a few times. People are often executed when caught by the revolutionary armed forces.”What happened when he was held up at gunpoint? Again, he says he was lucky. “These situations weren’t that bad. I’ve been held at gunpoint by someone who bumped into me in the dark and was scared. And normally it’s the police or army. There was a situation where you find yourself being confronted by a rightwing paramilitary organisation.” By now, his Spanish was decent. How did he talk his way out of being shot? “Keep smiling, play it down. Don’t get angry. Just a smile will get you through so much. Just defuse, defuse, de-conflict and you’re going to be all right.”With a Panamanian family.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyHe was also helped by a file he carried, documenting his journey. “Luckily for me, when dealing with those people, I had all these copies of newspaper clippings from South America. With them I could talk my way out of anything.”Between 2002 and 2005, he travelled through America, eventually reaching Alaska, where he confronted the most dangerous part of the expedition. To get from the US to Russia, he had to cross the Bering Strait, a narrow 51-mile (82km) frozen waterway connecting the Arctic and Pacific Oceans. The problem is that it is no longer all frozen. Bits are continually falling off as ice turns into sea and back again. Nobody had ever successfully crossed from Alaska to Siberia on foot (going the other way is easier because you are moving with the natural drift of the ice, whereas going towards Russia means you’re fighting against the ice). Bushby teamed up with the French-American adventurer Dimitri Kieffer – neither had experience of Arctic conditions.A BBC crew went out to film the mission, but had to return to base early because the trek was too dangerous. In the introduction, the presenter, Morland Sanders, said: “Karl Bushby, the ex-paratrooper on a mission that nobody has ever done before. To walk, swim, stumble across a semi-frozen sea. The chances are he won’t make it across alive.” Bushby told Sanders that throughout his life he’d constantly dealt with failure, and now he was out there proving himself. “Some people might think it’s ludicrous, some people might think it’s irresponsible, some people out there will understand the way I feel. Some things in life are worth dying for.” And he and Kieffer almost did.View image in fullscreen‘Chances are he won’t make it across alive’ … the Bering Strait.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyAt one point, the thin ice shelf beneath them gave way, and their 90kg supply sleds plunged into the sub-zero ocean water. Losing those sleds meant certain death from starvation or hypothermia in -30C temperatures. In terrifying footage filmed by the two men, we see them pulling the waterlogged sleds back up on to solid ice before they could be sucked under the shifting ice packs.They also came face to face with a polar bear. “We tried to scare it off, but all we had were fireworks and they were useless. So eventually we inched our way towards this bear. It stops and it’s looking at us. If it wanted us, we’re dead. There’s no escape at this point. It stood up to get a better look at us and it just rose into the sky like a freaking skyscraper. It was horrifying. They arehuuuuge. Massive.” The bear stared them out, then wandered off. He exhales loudly, the relief still fresh. “There was just no way you’re getting away from that.”Although the conditions were almost perfect, it looked as if they had insufficient food to last. Then, on one amazing day, they managed 12 miles, and after 14 days they made it across, just before running out. Another miracle, Bushby says. How did it feel to have made history? “It’s a pretty good feeling.”View image in fullscreenIn Siberia, 2008.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyOn reaching Siberia, the pair were arrested on suspicion of spying, charged and convicted. The authorities wanted them to serve a minimum of five years. In the end, they relented and sent them back to Alaska.But it wasn’t any of these challenges that Bushby found toughest to deal with; it was walking away from love. Or love walking away from him. In Mongolia, he met a Japanese woman called Rika. This relationship lasted three years, and again she eventually gave up on him. By that time, the pandemic had begun, and he had returned to Mexico because it was cheap to live there and Rika was in New Zealand. “She found someone else because we’d been separated for years. That is the hardest thing about this journey.”Did he never think love should come before the expedition? “No. Mission first,” he says. “If you look at my diaries from Hull, I write about how I’m going to fall in love, how I’m going to keep going and how I’m going to get burned by this. It was in the prophecy and it was foretold.”double quotation markMy son had to deal with those questions: why is my father out there and not home? As he matured, we’ve managed to have those conversationsTo be fair, I say, you didn’t make it easy for the women in your life. “Oh no. It was not the way to run relationships. But we knew we weren’t going to stop,” he says. I ask if he started referring to “we” to make him feel less alone. “I don’t know, but now it’s out of respect for everyone else who made this happen. I owe the world a lot. Don’t ever think it’s just me. It was never me. It is a ‘we’ thing. ‘We’ got me across the Channel to this beach in Dover. Me and a support network like no other. Before that, I just had the army behind me – now I have the world.”Bushby says he has led a selfish life. When he set off, he knew that if either of his parents died while he was away, he would not return for their funeral. When his son, Adam, almost died in a motorbike accident, he didn’t return home. He tells me he’s got a 12-year-old granddaughter he is yet to meet.Does he get on well with Adam now? “Yeah, me and Adam are great.” Did Adam ever ask why he hadn’t been there for him when he was growing up? “No, he accepted it. In those early years, he had to deal with those questions: why is my father out there and not home? As he matured, we’ve managed to have those conversations. To his credit, he rolled with the punches. He understands his father, and he’s one of my big fans.”View image in fullscreenKarl Bushby and Angela Maxwell in the waters off Baku 2024, preparing to swim the Caspian.Photograph: https://www.tiktok.com/@karlcbushbyMaxwell adds: “All adventure could be labelled selfish, because you’re going to hike the greatest mountain and someone dies from an avalanche and they’ve got a wife and kids back home. You explore something and then you die in the sea. To have an adventure is self-centred.”“Totally self-centred,” agrees Bushby. “This 28 years has been about keeping me. I have been the centre of my world. It has been about gettingmefrom A to B, looking afterme, givingmethe money so I can survive. Totally self-centred.”Has his family told him he’s been selfish? “Not family, no.”“Everyone else!” Maxwell says, laughing.“When you look at some of our great heroes, like Shackleton and Cook, they were the worst family men you could humanly imagine,” Bushby says. “They abandoned families left, right and centre. That’s the bit that people don’t think about. Those people had families back home, and they never saw their father.”View image in fullscreen‘My purpose for living is about to abruptly end.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianIn his decades on the road, there were so many other adventures: 11 years struggling to get through Russia because of tough immigration rules and extreme weather; buying a caravan of camels, and the aborted plan to walk the camels along the Silk Road to Europe; being given a police escort through the heavily monitored Xinjiang region of western China because they also thought he was a spy.There have also been periods of complete torpor. In 2005 he published a memoir after securing a substantial advance from Time Warner, who had also agreed to sponsor the rest of his journey. When the financial crisis hit, they pulled out. He retreated to Mexico and just about got by for two years through working as a waiter and helping to run a boat-racing school. In 2010, the House of Cards showrunner Beau Willimon offered to sponsor him, and he returned to the road. Then the pandemic came and he was forced to hole up in Mexico for another three years.View image in fullscreenDinner in Mongolia.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyAnd now, finally, he’s back in England, heading home to Hull. How does he feel? Terrified, he says – in a way he hasn’t been before. “My purpose for living is about to abruptly end.” You seem very calm, I say. “My world’s about to stop. I’m going to fall off the edge of the world in a minute.”“OhGod!” says Maxwell, as if he’s being dramatic, although she admits that she struggled when she got home.“I don’t know how to do the grownup stuff,” Bushby says. “I’ve got to get a job, I’ve got to grow up, and that’s scary. When I get home, I’m going to be living in my mother’s house.” Is he close to her? “Not as close as I should be. There’s a distance there.” He says he’ll have to put a lot of work into reconnecting. “It’s going to get tough for me. My solution for this is to get busy. Find your passion, your other mission, sink your teeth into that.”He knows he has changed and believes he may struggle to fit in with his family now. “Coming from the UK, and a military family, I was very much on the conservative side.” As a child he thought Britain was the centre of the world, but now he knows different. “My family is very patriotic and UK-centric. They are not lunatic rightwingers, but they’re Brexit voters and all the rest of it. This is their environment. It’s required for their jobs as soldiers and I understand the importance of that. But I’m not that guy any more.”Seeing the world can’t help but change you, he says. “The world is an incredible place. People are worth all the effort. The species is an incredible thing. I’ve got a different attitude to the world; a slightly softer, left-leaning approach compared to some of the staunch politics in the UK right now.”View image in fullscreenBushby (left) with Werner Herzog at Dover.Photograph: Zach GuglinFortunately for him, Bushby is not returning to a vacuum. There is so much going on in his life. The great German film-maker Werner Herzog is making a documentary about his journey; there is a book in the works; talks are lined up. He could probably make a good living just giving speeches about his 28-year odyssey.Could he see himself settling down with someone to a regular life, or is he post-relationship?“That’s a bit deep and dark,” he says. “I would be open to a relationship for sure. Who wouldn’t?”“OK, here we go. I’ll speak for Karl,” Maxwell says. “Karl is the most eligible bachelor and adventurer for someone who likes the unknown. He is loyal, he’s committed, he’s a good lover and he’s also committed to his mission.”Lover? Maxwell laughs, embarrassed. “I mean, he’s a good love person.”“How do you know that I’m a good lover?” Bushby asks. “Wait. What?”I ask them if they’ve been hiding something from me. “No,” she stumbles. “No, I just meant a great lover of life.”“Yeah, that’s what she meant,” says Bushby. “That one. We’re good friends. I like having her around. She makes life a lot more exciting.”“Wait a minute. You likehaving me around?” She sounds insulted.“Yeah, we get along great,” says Bushby. “You make life a lot cheerier.”“Yeah, all right,” says Maxwell, semi-pacified.View image in fullscreenIn Mexico, 2002.Photograph: Courtesy of Karl BushbyThe waitress removes our plates. Maxwell has left half her fish and chips. “I’ll take that to go,” Bushby says, pointing at her plate. He’s used to scrimping.“It does have tissue on it, if you don’t mind,” the waitress says.“I’ve eaten worse,” he says.He is still thinking about how he’s changed. Everybody in the UK seems so pessimistic about the future, he says, but not him. As a child he was a religious Christian, but then he became a militant atheist. Today, he says, he has more faith than he ever had – not in a god, or a prophet or the church, but in people.“I’m the eternal optimist. Right now, everyone seems to think we’re facing the end of humanity. Not me.” He is betting on survival. “For me, I look at the species rather than a nation state.”Does he think he’ll stay in Hull? “No,” he says instantly.Perhaps if he doesn’t want to settle in Hull, after a rest he’ll be ready for another walk?“I wish he would,” Maxwell says. “Can I answer this for him?”“No!”he bellows. “The answer’s no.”Maxwell bursts out laughing. ‘He doesn’t like walking. I love walking. Heactuallydoesn’t like walking.”Bushby nods. “For me, it was the journey in its entirety that was fascinating,” he says. “It was trying to get from A to B.”You genuinely don’t like walking, I ask, flabbergasted. “No, it’s boring as hell.” And now he’s got the giggles. “It’s really, really tedious.”This article was amended on 13 October 2026 to remove a detail.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothes | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively?
Author: Fleur Britten
Headline: Swamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively?
Content: Fleur Britten with a pair of torn black trousers donated to St Raphael's Hospice charity shop in Cheam, Sutton.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFleur Britten with a pair of torn black trousers donated to St Raphael's Hospice charity shop in Cheam, Sutton.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Fashion‘People sell their best stuff on Vinted’ – how charity shops became a dumping ground for unsellable clothesSwamped with ‘daily avalanches’ of soiled items and poor-quality fast fashion, secondhand stores are in crisis. What went wrong with people’s good intentions? And is it possible to donate more effectively?Fleur BrittenTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe small stockroom of St Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, south London, is rammed with donations. “On average, we get 30 to 50 bags a day,” says Caroline Worley, the commercial manager, “but it’s not unusual to receive over 100.” This might sound like a good problem to have, but the sheer volume of stuff is the shop’s biggest challenge. “Sometimes, there’s only [enough] floor space to tiptoe,” says 48-year-old store manager, Colin French.Rummaging through the donations, it’s clear that much is unsaleable: a smelly, soiled bathrobe, tatty trainers, heavily bobbled jumpers, old socks, an empty Swarovski jewellery case. “Absolutely typical,” says Worley. They’re also overwhelmed with deluges of low-quality fashion – a shift in donation habits that accelerated during Covid, because, says Worley, all that time at home enabled people to sell their best stuff on Vinted.The experience here echoes that of author Tansy Hoskins, whose latest book,Charity Shop World, paints a picture of a charity retail sector in crisis. She spent 16 months working in a London charity shop, sorting through “daily avalanches” of clothing, which swamped “all the other categories put together”.View image in fullscreenSt Raphael’s Hospice charity shop in Cheam, Sutton gets rammed with donations.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianEveryone Hoskins interviewed said similar: “quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste.” The problem is nationwide. Since the book came out, she’s “been contacted by managers of charity shops around the country – for example, Nottingham, Accrington, Newcastle – all saying that most of what they’re getting is waste.”It is, of course, our waste. According to Jose Baladron of Traid, which has 12 shops across London, shopping for new clothes is “through the roof –the UK is the highest consumer of clothing in Europe by far”. “That obviously translates to more donations, which is far too much to process in small shops.” Hoskins routinely found that ultra-fast-fashion donations would “still have tags on – it was clear people had received their online purchases and gone, ‘What the hell is this?’ It wasn’t even wearable so they’d just donate it.”On average, charity shops only manage to sell about 25% of clothing donations, according to Baladron (a figurereplicated by a University of Southampton study). “So they rely heavily on the ragman” to shift the rest. Yet the price of rag has “plummeted”, according to Merryn Haines-Gadd of the environmental action charity Wrap, “due to the saturation of low-quality fast fashion”. Ten years ago, a charity might have been paid 50-60p per kilo. “Now you’re lucky to get 10p,” says Baladron. Plus there’s only so much the ragman can take.View image in fullscreenBritten sorts through donations.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianFor anything they can’t take, charity shops have to pay to have it collected as waste. At St Raphael’s, some of that has included, according to Worley, saucepans with food still in the bottom, babies’ soiled sleep-suits and used sanitary products. “[Staff] can get a bit worn down when people are donating stuff that isn’t saleable,” says Libby Gordon, CEO of Fara, which has 39 charity shops in London. “Plus there’s a time cost for us to process it all.”Factor in rising utility costs and national insurance payments, and “charity shops are in a perfect storm”, says Hoskins. In June, the British Heart Foundation announced plans to close 150 of its 651 stores; its latest accounts indicate that its retail armlost £3.3mlast year.Cancer Researchis part-way through a 190-shop closure programme, and rumours are swirling that up to 100 Oxfam shops might close (which the charity hasdenied).Some are fighting back. Fara’s new in-store poster campaign advises would-be donators: “If you’d be happy to give it to a friend, we’d be delighted to receive it.” Items should be “clean, complete, and in good condition”,states their online guide.View image in fullscreen‘We get 30 to 50 bags a day’ … St Raphael’s Hospice commercial manager, Caroline Worley.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianBut just as people “wish cycle” by chucking unrecyclables into the recycling, so do people “wish give”. I certainly struggle to accept that something with life left in it, however worn, can’t be useful to someone. This mentality, however, creates unpleasant work and costs for charities – even more so when people leave donations outside a closed charity shop (technically, it’s fly-tipping, and charity shops do often check their CCTV, record numberplates and report such crimes). These bags are often soiled by foxes or dogs, ripped open and/or rained on. At St Raphael’s, staff have found soiled mattresses, ripped sofas and even an old toilet dumped outside: “It leaves us with a big problem,” says Worley.Disposal at scale is an expensive business. St Raphael’s, which as a charity costs around £7m a year to run, and supports more than 1,000 patients a year with free end-of-life care, ends up paying £30,000 a year to dispose of dud donations. That could fund a month of around-the-clock specialist care for an inpatient; their 13-bed inpatient unit can currently only afford to keep 10 spots open. It’s a similar story for other charities. “The public’s generosity is how we support our work in Romania,” says Gordon. “It’s how the British Heart Foundation funds their research; it’s how Mind supports their mental-health work.”French knows first-hand the difference money earned by charity shops can have. Last year his sister died, and in her final three weeks, received incredible care from Princess Alice Hospice in Esher, Surrey – as did the whole family. “My parents (still) go back every single week [for bereavement support] and don’t have to pay anything,” says French. “It’s not until those moments that you truly realise that this is vital for our communities,” he says.View image in fullscreenCharity shops have to pay for anything they can’t take as waste.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThe work a charity does can often feel a long way away when faced with a wardrobe in need of a clear-out. But, says Hoskins, try to “connect with why you like a charity, why it’s important – whether it’s the Red Cross or Cancer Research or an animal charity – and donate responsibly to them … It would be a complete tragedy if our charity shops vanished.”How can you make your good intentions go further?Resist virgin fast fashionThe fast-fashion business model is about making clothes quickly and cheaply to churn out trends. It’s bad news for our wardrobes, our purses and the charity shops that we pass them on to.‘Donate like you’re being reviewed’“Wash your clothes first, do simple mending tasks, or get it fixed at a freeRepair Cafe,” says Hoskins. There’s a perception, she adds, that “charity shops have laundries – they don’t. The number one reason we’d chuck something in the rag bag was because it was dirty.”Reframe how you view charity shopsThink of them not as convenient dumping grounds, but as places that deserve a little more thought. Plus, Hoskins says, “if you can afford it, donate your best bits instead of selling them on Vinted.”View image in fullscreenCharity shops deserve a little more thought.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianResearch what to do with ragDon’t bin those odd socks, greyed bras, or stained items, as many of us do – according to Wrap, almost half of all used textiles ending up in the bin. There are specialist recycling programmes for …UnderwearFor new pants and “gently worn, laundered” bras, trysmallsforall, which distributes them to those in need;Bravissimotakes bras from any brand in any condition, plus swimwear, for redistribution or downcycling (in-store only). For odd or holey socks, theLondon Sock Companyruns a “sock amnesty”, recycling them into fingerless gloves for the charity Give Your Best (free UK postage).CottonRemillwill recycle 100% cotton items (excluding bedlinen, denim and underwear) into new clothing, or where necessary, downcycle into cloths and insulation (free UK postage); plus you’ll receive a voucher for its recycled-cotton clothing.CashmereTheCashmere Centrewill recycle your used, pure cashmere into knits, and give you a £10 voucher.Sports shoesJogOn, on a mission to save 1m sports shoes from landfill, takes trainers, football boots etc in any condition, redistributing the usable ones to those in need (its “save” rate is 90%), and sustainably disposing of truly end-of-life ones (postage costs £2 for up to 30 pairs).General ragEase the processing burden on charity shops by taking end-of-life textiles to your local textile recycling bank (checkRecycle Now’s bin locator– you can also search which bins accept specific items; some take shoes). Ideally put your rag in a labelled bag to simplify sorting, tie pairs of shoes together, and if the bank is full, don’t dump your stuff – it will most likely be binned.Explore more on these topicsFashionRecyclingEthical and green livingWasteFashion industryVintage fashionShareReuse this content

title: The best concealers in the UK for camouflaging blemishes and dark circles – tested | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Searching for a concealer that can do it all? From creamy to crease-resistant, brightening to hydrating, these are the formulas that impressed us most
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: Searching for a concealer that can do it all? From creamy to crease-resistant, brightening to hydrating, these are the formulas that impressed us most
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterBeautyReviewThe best concealers in the UK for camouflaging blemishes and dark circles – testedSearching for a concealer that can do it all? From creamy to crease-resistant, brightening to hydrating, these are the formulas that impressed us mostThe best mascaras for longer, fuller and fluttery lashesThe best foundations – testedSarah MatthewsTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen life gets stressful, your face can often be the first place to show the telltale signs. Eye bags can get darker after sleepless nights, and breakouts can appear in protest. Whatever the cause, the best concealers can help to even out imperfections, so you look flawless regardless of what is going on behind the scenes.It might seem obvious, but not all concealers are the same. Some leave a cakey finish on the skin, while others settle quickly into fine lines or blend out and leave barely any coverage at all. Many modern concealers also include active skincare ingredients to combine the benefits of both products.I tested a huge variety of concealers for consideration here, including cult-favourite viral products and new formulas arriving to shake up the makeup game. Below, you’ll find the very best concealers from my testing, with options to suit every skin type, coverage preference and budget.Scroll further to find advice from professional makeup artists on how and when to apply concealer, as well as how to prolong its wear.At a glanceBest concealer overallNarsRadiant creamy concealer£27 at Cult BeautyBest budget concealerCollectionLasting Perfection concealer£4.99 at AmazonBest concealer for dark circlesCharlotte TilburyBeautiful Skin Radiant concealer£28 at John LewisBest concealer for dry skinBy TerryHyaluronic serum concealer£39 at John LewisBest lightweight concealerNYXBare With Me serum concealer£9.96 at AmazonBest concealer for comfortable coverageMilk MakeupHydro Grip gel concealer£26 at AsosWhy you should trust meI’ve spent the past five years testing and writing about beauty products, makeup included. In that time, I’ve come across bestsellers that fully deserve the hype, but also a fair share of concealers that crease immediately or cling to every dry patch on my face.I’m not a professional makeup artist, but I’ve been wearing makeup since my early teenage years. Because I don’t use fancy blending techniques, my tests show exactly how user-friendly each product is. If I ended up with a creasy, cakey mess under my eyes, chances are you might too.How I testedView image in fullscreenOur makeup expert applies concealer to her face during testing.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThere are three main areas to consider when testing concealer: coverage, creasing and the range of shades available. Before I sourced any concealers, I checked the available shade ranges and wouldn’t touch a formulation if it didn’t cater to a wide range of skin tones. Considering this has been a widely publicised issue for a decade or more, I was amazed by how many brands still hadn’t caught up.View image in fullscreenSharpie dots were used to test each concealer’s coverage.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianThe next thing I tested was coverage. Rather than guess how well each of the 17 concealers I tested covered up my ever-changing spots and dark circles, I judged this by using a red Sharpie to make small spots on my forearm. Once the spots had dried, I covered each with a small amount of concealer and lightly blended them with a small fluffy brush. This showed me how well each concealer could cover imperfections.The last and perhaps most important step was a wear test. This involved wearing each concealer for a full day and monitoring how well it covered spots and dark circles. Whenever a concealer settled into fine lines, it was marked down as being unsuitable for the eye area. I assessed how easy each product was to blend too, and noted any dryness, irritation or patchiness as the day went on.The best concealers for 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianBest concealer overall:Nars Radiant creamy concealerNarsRadiant creamy concealerfrom£27£27 at Cult Beauty£29.50 at NarsWhat we loveLarge shade range; long-wearing; comfy coverageWhat we don’t loveIt’s not hydrating and is expensive per mlView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£27 at Cult Beauty£29.50 at NarsThis is one of the most revered concealers on the market – and for good reason. It’s creamy, buildable and lasts all day without budging or settling into fine lines. It’s my top recommendation for anyone looking for a foolproof formula.Why we love itIt’s fairly pricey, but a little goes a long way with this formula. In my experience, a light layer worked hard to conceal dark circles and angry-looking spots alike. Applied in light layers, it’s also buildable, meaning you can get high coverage if you need it.Once blended into the skin, the concealer is almost imperceptible, especially if you find a perfect shade match from its 30-strong shade range. I also found it to be long-wearing and resistant to creasing.In my experience, the formula didn’t feel as hydrating as other creamy concealers, which means it’s better at keeping excess oiliness at bay. I didn’t find it remotely drying either, so it’s great if you’re looking for something to use on oilier skin without adding shine.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive, but you need only a tiny amount of product for a big impact. If you have very dry skin, though, other formulations provide better hydration.Size:6mlPrice/ml:from £4.50Coverage:mediumApplicator type:doe-footShades available:30(find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:noNarsRadiant creamy concealerfrom£27£27 at Cult Beauty£29.50 at NarsWhat we loveLarge shade range; long-wearing; comfy coverageWhat we don’t loveIt’s not hydrating and is expensive per mlBest budget concealer:Collection Lasting Perfection concealerCollectionLasting Perfection concealerfrom£4.99£4.99 at Boots£4.99 at AmazonWhat we loveBuildable; long-wearing coverage; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveIt needs to be blended quicklyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£4.99 at Boots£4.99 at AmazonAs an affordable-makeup fanatic, I’ve had this concealer in my collection for as long as I can remember. It’s super cheap, has a great shade range, and is a brilliant all-rounder for disguising all kinds of imperfections.Why we love itThis concealer gives a smooth, matt finish, which is perfect for brightening up the area under the eyes. If you’re concealing spots, the formulation lasts really well on oily and combination skin, and I found it offered buildable coverage when gently blended.Since it’s so affordable, you can easily justify buying two different shades – one for a perfect skin match and a brighter shade for use under your eyes. Although the packaging has changed in recent years, it’s still the same hard-working formula. The latest version arrives with a beauty blender for easier application on the go. I’m not convinced it’s a huge improvement – the blender is a little too firm to comfortably blend concealer under the eyes. Still, it costs the same, so I can’t complain too much.It’s a shame that …it needs to be blended out quickly, or it’ll settle in the place you applied it – a lesson I learned when I got distracted from my makeup one morning and ended up with stubborn splodges under my eyes.Size:3.5mlPrice/ml:£1.43Coverage:mediumApplicator type:doe-footShades available:20(find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:noCollectionLasting Perfection concealerfrom£4.99£4.99 at Boots£4.99 at AmazonWhat we loveBuildable; long-wearing coverage; sensible priceWhat we don’t loveIt needs to be blended quicklyBest concealer for dark circles:Charlotte Tilbury Beautiful Skin Radiant concealerCharlotte TilburyBeautiful Skin Radiant concealerfrom£28£28 at John Lewis£31 at Charlotte TilburyWhat we loveIts brightening performance and hydrating feelWhat we don’t loveIt’s pricey per mlView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianFrom £28 at John Lewis£31 at Charlotte TilburyTackling dark circles requires you to look after your skin, not just bury it beneath concealer. The Charlotte Tilbury Beautiful Skin Radiant concealer succeeds on both these fronts, combining comfortable coverage with hydrating, plumping and brightening skincare ingredients.Why we love itIf you’re wearing makeup anyway, why not invest in a multitasker? Packed into this concealer, you’ll find hyaluronic acid, niacinamide and vitamin C. These ingredients work to hydrate, soothe, plump and brighten the skin under the eyes in a product that offers medium coverage.In my tests, I found the concealer both buildable and easy to blend around the eye area. It didn’t settle into any of my fine lines, even when I really challenged it by squinting immediately after application. Better still, it left my skin with a natural-looking glow, without any dry, cakey-looking patches. Thanks to its large doe-foot applicator and blendable consistency, it’s perfect for busy mornings when you’re hoping to quickly achieve a lasting, radiant finish.It’s a shame that …it’s quite expensive, and those with very sensitive, acne-prone skin may find the vitamin C causes breakouts when used to conceal spots.Size:7.2mlPrice/ml:from about £3.89Coverage:mediumApplicator type:doe-footShades available:30(find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:noCharlotte TilburyBeautiful Skin Radiant concealerfrom£28£28 at John Lewis£31 at Charlotte TilburyWhat we loveIts brightening performance and hydrating feelWhat we don’t loveIt’s pricey per mlBest concealer for dry skin:By Terry hyaluronic serum concealerBy TerryHyaluronic serum concealerfrom£39£39 at John Lewis£39 at Space NKWhat we loveHydrating formula with a flawless natural finishWhat we don’t loveIt’s incredibly expensive; smaller shade rangeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£39 at John Lewis£39 at Space NKIf you’re tired of drying concealers that cling to patches of skin, the By Terry hyaluronic serum concealer will be transformative. Its hydrating ingredients and lightweight, buildable texture make it a great option for dry, mature skin and for use under the eyes.Why we love itBy Terry has packed eight different types of hyaluronic acid – a humectant that draws moisture into the skin – into this formulation. It uses three molecular weights to help plump and moisturise different layers of the skin, meaning the product won’t dry out or go patchy in a day’s wear.This rang true in my tests, with a light amount of concealer effectively minimising blemishes and brightening dark circles to create a natural-looking finish. You’ll also find caffeine and magnolia flower to help brighten and soothe the skin, making this great for stimulating healing in dry and irritated skin.It’s a shame that …it’s the most expensive concealer I’ve ever used – I’m almost annoyed at how nice it is to use for that reason. That said, the shade range isn’t as extensive as others, and if you want high coverage, this isn’t the concealer for you.Size:5.2mlPrice/ml:£7.50Coverage:light to mediumApplicator type:doe-footShades available:16(find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:noBy TerryHyaluronic serum concealerfrom£39£39 at John Lewis£39 at Space NKWhat we loveHydrating formula with a flawless natural finishWhat we don’t loveIt’s incredibly expensive; smaller shade rangeBest lightweight concealer:NYX Bare With Me serum concealerNYXBare With Me serum concealerfrom£9.96£11.49 at Cult Beauty£9.96 at AmazonWhat we loveLightweight consistency in a clean pump bottleWhat we don’t loveIts slightly dewy finish isn’t for everyoneView image in fullscreen£11.49 at Cult Beauty£9.96 at AmazonConfession time: I’ve worked my way through at least three tubes of this stuff. I first tried it when I was struggling with a nightmare combination of dry but spot-ridden skin, and pretty much stuck with it as a daily concealer from then onwards. It’s super lightweight and leaves the skin looking fresh, healthy and dewy.Why we love itWhen you have redness and uneven skin texture, it can be tempting to reach for heavier, full-coverage formulations. However, something with a serum-like consistency, like this product, can gently blur rough texture and disguise redness without exaggerating it or looking cakey. In my years of using this concealer, it’s never settled into any fine lines.Better still, it dispenses from a small pump, which helps minimise contamination, unlike concealers with a doe-foot that comes in contact with the skin. I have acne-prone skin, so I much prefer this design.It’s a shame that …with a full press, the pump dispenses far more product than I typically use. This is easily rectified by only using a half press, though. It also has a slightly dewy finish, which isn’t for everyone.Size:9.6mlPrice/ml:from about £1.04Coverage:lightApplicator type:pumpShades available:13(find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:yesNYXBare With Me serum concealerfrom£9.96£11.49 at Cult Beauty£9.96 at AmazonWhat we loveLightweight consistency in a clean pump bottleWhat we don’t loveIts slightly dewy finish isn’t for everyoneBest concealer for comfortable coverage:Milk Makeup Hydro Grip gel concealerMilk MakeupHydro Grip gel concealerfrom£26£26 at Asos£26 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveQuick application with comfortable coverageWhat we don’t loveIts packaging doesn’t wind downView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£26 at Asos£26 at Cult BeautyThis is the first stick concealer I’ve tried that hasn’t dragged across my skin during application or felt heavy and cakey. Its gel-to-cream formula glides on effortlessly, blending into a hydrated, blurred, skin-like finish.Why we love itLike Milk’s most popular hydro-grip primer, this concealer really does stay put, offering all-day coverage without any creasing or caking. The formula contains hyaluronic acid, aloe leaf extract, moisturising squalane and protective antioxidant vitamin E, which help hydrate and protect the skin while covering any flaws.Admittedly, coverage isn’t opaque, but I found the stick format made it easy to apply just the right amount of product, whether I wanted to conceal a spot precisely, or sweep more product over larger areas of redness or discoloration. The natural finish makes it a great option for those who prefer a minimal makeup look.It’s a shame that …it isn’t immediately obvious that the formula sits in a non-retractable stick. One or two clicks up should be enough for a day’s application. It’s also quite expensive per gram, but a little goes further than many standard liquid concealers.Size:3gPrice/g:about £8.67Coverage:mediumApplicator type:stickShades available:25 (find your shade)Vegan:yesCertified cruelty-free:yesMilk MakeupHydro Grip gel concealerfrom£26£26 at Asos£26 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveQuick application with comfortable coverageWhat we don’t loveIts packaging doesn’t wind downThe best of the restMac Studio Fix concealerMacStudio Fix concealer£25£25 at SephoraWhat we loveFast full coverage without settlingWhat we don’t loveIts paint-like smellView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£25 at SephoraBest for:full coverageThe Mac Studio Fix range is best known for its long-wearing soft matt foundation. This concealer is the foundation’s sister product, and it performed very well in my tests. It lasted all day without budging or smudging, even during a heatwave.Of all the concealers here, this one offers the fullest coverage, making it perfect for covering stubborn blemishes and dark spots. Still, despite its thicker formulation, it didn’t settle into any of my fine lines. Used with a light touch, it’s a good option for those who prefer a little extra coverage.It didn’t make the final cut because …it has an odd paint-like smell – the same smell as the Studio Fix foundation I used to wear in my late teens. I welcomed the nostalgia hit, but anyone hoping to avoid strong chemical scents may feel differently.Size:7ml;price/ml:£3.57;coverage:high;applicator type:doe-foot;shades available:34(find your shade);vegan:yes;certified cruelty-free:noMacStudio Fix concealer£25£25 at SephoraWhat we loveFast full coverage without settlingWhat we don’t loveIts paint-like smellLaura Mercier Secret Camouflage Complexion PerfectorLaura MercierSecret Camouflage Complexion Perfectorfrom£29£29 at Lookfantastic£29 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveClever camouflaging; flawless wear; easy to applyWhat we don’t loveStingy product size; small shade rangeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£29 at Lookfantastic£29 at Cult BeautyBest for:colour correctingColour-correcting concealers typically come in a rainbow of shades that can look odd if applied incorrectly. Laura Mercier’s Secret Camouflage Complexion Perfector takes a less colourful approach, pairing neutral, warm and cool shades in a single compact. You can mix and layer them to build coverage where you need it – without fear of ending up with an unnatural finish.The creamy consistency here was particularly easy to apply. I simply tapped it over blemishes and dark circles and blended it out to create a near-imperceptible finish. Unlike most concealers, which come as a single fixed shade, I liked that I could customise the colour to suit my skin each day. I found the warm-toned colour particularly effective after a sleepless night, quickly neutralising the blue undereye circles, and staying put all day without settling into fine lines.It didn’t make the final cut because …of the small amount of product you actually get. The warm and cool shades are tiny and could run out quickly. I was using the warm shade far more often, so I could end up with a lot of cool-toned concealer left over. The overall shade range could also be more inclusive.Size:3.2g;price/g:about £9.06;coverage:buildable;applicator type:compact;shades available:8 (find your shade);vegan:yes;certified cruelty-free:noLaura MercierSecret Camouflage Complexion Perfectorfrom£29£29 at Lookfantastic£29 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveClever camouflaging; flawless wear; easy to applyWhat we don’t loveStingy product size; small shade rangeMilani Conceal + Perfect concealerMilaniConceal + Perfect concealerfrom£11.80£11.80 at Boots£13 at MilaniWhat we loveHigh-end performance at an affordable priceWhat we don’t loveHard applicator and paint-like smellView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£11.80 at Boots£13 at MilaniBest for:a multi-use concealer at a mid-range priceThis mid-range concealer offers many of the benefits associated with high-end concealers at a much more palatable price. It has a lightweight, buildable formula that lasts well on the skin without creasing, caking or settling into fine lines.It’s marketed as a long-wear concealer, and I can confirm it didn’t budge during a long, hot summer day running errands. Like many of its competitors, it’s also infused with hydrating hyaluronic acid and antioxidant vitamin E to soothe the skin. That means it doesn’t become drying, despite being long-lasting.It didn’t make the final cut because …it has a paint-like, chemical smell, and its doe-foot applicator is less fluffy than other concealers, making it less comfortable to apply. You also need to blend out this concealer quickly, or it will settle in place.Size:5ml;price/ml:from£2.36;coverage:medium;applicator type:doe-foot;shades available:18(find your shade);vegan:yes;certified cruelty-free:yesMilaniConceal + Perfect concealerfrom£11.80£11.80 at Boots£13 at MilaniWhat we loveHigh-end performance at an affordable priceWhat we don’t loveHard applicator and paint-like smellWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenOnline shade finders can help you find your ideal concealer.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHow much should I spend on a concealer?“Concealer sits closely on your skin, often covering spots or sensitive areas, so quality really does matter,” says Jamie Genevieve, makeup artist and founder ofVieve. “It’s worth investing in a formula that performs well, wears comfortably and treats your skin kindly. But ultimately, choose one that fits your budget and meets your needs.”As you can see in the recommendations above, you can buy a great basic concealer for less than £10. However, if you want to invest in something that uses hydrating skincare ingredients, more innovative applicators or cruelty-free formulations, you may need to spend more.How do I know my concealer shade?This was far simpler in bygone days before online shopping, when pharmacies would stock testers of every concealer to help find your perfect shade. Sadly, in-store product testers have become a dying breed since the pandemic.However, many makeup brands now have their own shade finders online, which use either a phone camera or webcam to give the best guess for your perfect shade. Others will offer a short questionnaire that asks you for details about your skin undertone, texture and shade. Both work well in my experience.It helps to know your skin tone to help choose the right shade – if you have warm-toned skin and the shade finder recommends a cool-toned shade, think twice. For each concealer on this page, I’ve included a link to the shade finder.That said, concealer isn’t a one-trick pony. “Use a shade lighter than your foundation for brightening the undereye area, or a shade that matches your skin tone for seamless coverage elsewhere,” recommends Suzie O’Neill, founder ofAYU Cosmetics.How and when do I apply concealer?“Think of it as layering strategically based on the coverage you want,” says Genevieve. “I usually apply concealer after foundation to brighten and perfect specific areas. But if you’re covering dark spots or pigmentation, you can start with concealer as a base, then follow with foundation to even out everything.”Unlike Genevieve, I apply concealer after my eye makeup to clean up any fallout from the eye shadow I use. Most days, I prefer a lighter makeup look and don’t see the need to use foundation after applying concealer. This is an approach recommended by Karen MacDonald, founder ofBlomma Beauty, “for a barefaced, no-makeup look to let your natural skin shine through”.For more, read our guide to thebest foundationsHow do you keep concealer from creasing on older skin?“Prep is everything,” says O’Neill. “Hydrate the undereye area well, apply a nourishing eye cream and use a light hand – less is more.”I recommend giving any hydrating,anti-ageing skincareandeye creams15 minutes or so to settle into the skin before applying makeup. This should ensure the skincare products don’t mess with the formulation of the concealer, causing it to pill or settle into fine lines.When applying concealer, O’Neill recommends you “tap the concealer in gently and, if needed, set lightly with a touch of translucent powder to stop it from moving”.For more:The best eye creams for banishing bags, puffiness and fine linesThe best mascaras for longer, fuller and fluttery lashesThe best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatments, picked by Sali HughesShark FacialPro Glow + DePuffi reviewSarah Matthews is aconsumer journalist who specialises in giving health and beauty recommendations. She’s tested her way through more makeup, skincare and hair care than you can shake a stick at. Thanks to her stubborn hormonal acne, concealer is always a staple in her makeup bagThis article was originally published on 2 January 2026.
