title: The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel
Content: Chicken broth needs to be barely simmered, andveryslowly, so don’t cluck it up by boiling it fast.Photograph: photovs/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenChicken broth needs to be barely simmered, andveryslowly, so don’t cluck it up by boiling it fast.Photograph: photovs/Getty Images/iStockphotoKitchen aideChefsThe secret to a non-cloudy chicken stockDon’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panelAnna BerrillTue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy is my chicken stock always cloudy?Ryan, by emailFrom broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead. “It’s an underestimated kitchen job,” says Adam Byatt, chef/owner ofTrinity, in southwest London, and author ofTrinity: The Cookbook, which is published next week. “I love stock: it’s wholesome and fruitful, frugal and delicious.”Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author ofLozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.Lloyd Morse, chef and co-owner ofThe Palmerstonin Edinburgh, meanwhile, likes to simmer the bones first, “shoogling them occasionally”, to bring more of the scum to the surface: “You really need to skim the life out of it.” It’s only at this point that he adds the veg: “And keep skimming that top layer,” he says, adding that it’s important to be aware that “the more agitation or the hotter the pot gets, the cloudier the stock will be”.Essentially, “if nothing is ever actually boiled, Ryan’s stock should be nice and clear”, says Louis Lingwood, head chef atOsteria Vibratoin London, who cooks his chicken stock “on the lowest possible heat for a whole day”, before discarding the bones and leaving the stock to sit until all the fat rises to the top. Skim that off with a ladle, then reduce the stock very slowly.Lingwood has another trick up his sleeve to guarantee a clearer stock: get it in the freezer. “Defrost it through a sieve lined with muslin (or through a lined perforated tray), and the stock will be crystal clear.” Speaking of the freezer, freezing stock in ice-cube trays, then whacking them in a sealed container, is a welcome manoeuvre for those occasions when only small quantities of stock are required.Of course, Ryan could make his life a whole lot easier by simply cooking his stock in the oven, Morse says: “My top tip is to make it in an oven-safe dish, such as a Le Creuset [other brands are, of course, available], then pop it in the oven overnight to cook super slowly,” by which he means about 90C. “The indirect heat makes the clearest stock possible, plus, when you wake up, you’ll have a lovely smell in the kitchen.” Convenience food at its best.Got a culinary dilemma? Emailfeast@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsChefsKitchen aideFoodChickenSoupSauces and graviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cook once, eat twice: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Roast chicken thighs with roasted squash, leeks and two punchy dressings
Author: Rukmini Iyer
Headline: Roast chicken thighs with roasted squash, leeks and two punchy dressings
Content: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeks.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeks.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.Cook once, eat twiceFoodCook once, eat twice: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken recipeRoast chicken thighs with roast squash, leeks and two punchy dressingsRukmini IyerTue 13 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m delighted that it’s roasting tin season once again, and what better way to kick it off than with this chuck-it-in-the-oven sticky miso chilli chicken with squash and leeks? The sesame, miso, garlic and ginger marinade can go on the chicken ahead of time if you like (in which case, I’d include a squeeze of lime juice), but if you’re short on time, five minutes before cooking will do the trick. The vegetables cook under the chicken, in the manner of potatoes sitting under a rotisserie chicken, but with the added hit of flavour from the miso. Then, to make it really sing, there’s a punchy sesame, chilli and coriander dressing to finish.Miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeksPrep15 minCook1 hr 10 minServes2,with leftovers30ml sesame oil60g miso paste– red or white, either works4garlic cloves, peeled and finely grated5cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated3 medium leeks, trimmed and cut into 2½cm-thick rounds1 medium butternut squash, peeled, halved, deseeded and cut into 4cm chunks1-1.2kgskin-on bone-in chicken thighsFor the dressing1tbsp soy sauce30ml sesame oilFinely grated zest and juice of 1 unwaxed lime2 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped1 red chilli, finely sliced (pith and seeds removed if you want less heat)10g fresh coriander, roughly choppedSea salt, to tasteHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Mix the sesame oil, miso, garlic and ginger in a bowl, then use a heaped tablespoon of this mix to coat the leeks and squash in a large roasting tin. (The tin should be big enough that everything almost sits in one layer.)Slash each chicken thigh a couple of times with a sharp knife, then put them on top of the vegetables. Spread the remaining miso mix on top of each piece of chicken, then bake for one hour, until the chicken is well browned and cooked through, and the vegetables soft.When the tin has 10 minutes left in the oven, make the dressing. Whisk the soy sauce, sesame oil, lime juice and zest, spring onions, chilli and coriander in a bowl, taste and add a little sea salt or more soy sauce, if required.Drizzle the dressing all over the chicken and vegetables, and serve hot.Eat twiceIt’s never a bad idea to have half a tray of leftover roast chicken in the fridge, so even if cooking for two, I’d make the whole quantity and save the rest for epic next-day leftovers. My favourite thing to do is make a cracking peanut sauce-topped rice bowl: put Italian short-grain rice on to boil (half an hour), finely grate a carrot and a handful of fresh herbs (mint, coriander), then whisk 60g peanut butter (smooth or crunchy, cook’s choice), the zest and juice of one lime, 20ml soy sauce and a scant teaspoon of palm or dark brown sugar. Loosen with a tablespoon or so of water, until the mix is the texture of single cream, then taste and add a pinch more salt if needed – it should taste strong and punchy. (If your lime wasn’t particularly juicy, add more lime juice, too.) To serve, shred the leftover chicken (heat through with a tablespoon of water in a covered bowl for 40 seconds in the microwave), and reheat the leftover squash and leeks. Drain the rice well, dress with a tablespoon of oil, then divide between two bowls. Top with the chicken, the hot veg, and the carrot and herb mixture, then drizzle the peanut dressing all over the top. Finish with extra chopped peanuts and chilli, if you wish.Explore more on these topicsFoodCook once, eat twiceChickenMeatVegetablesAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead | Consumer rights | The Guardian
description: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice
Content: Landline was cut off … but the bills keep coming in.Photograph: conzor/AlamyView image in fullscreenLandline was cut off … but the bills keep coming in.Photograph: conzor/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer rightsBT charged me for more than a year despite landline being deadIt is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital VoiceAnna TimsTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve had no landline since May 2025 whenBTswitched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments.Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that awire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not.Since then,I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work.I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness.HH,YorkYou have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit.You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged.It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July.You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way.A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September.The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600.I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss.You have the option of a complaint to theCommunications Ombudsmanbut have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record.Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsConsumer rightsConsumer championsConsumer affairsBTTelecommunications industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’ | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatment
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatment
Content: Almost a quarter of the women surveyed had autoimmune thyroid disease with an underactive or overactive thyroid.Photograph: Bsip Sa/AlamyView image in fullscreenAlmost a quarter of the women surveyed had autoimmune thyroid disease with an underactive or overactive thyroid.Photograph: Bsip Sa/AlamyWomen's healthWomen ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatmentAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment, a study suggests.Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes.But research by the University of Cambridge and University of East Anglia suggests a stark gender divide when it comes to how signs of the conditions are handled by doctors.Women are more likely to have their conditions wrongly attributed to psychiatric causes, more likely to have symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, and more likely to experience delays in getting a diagnosis, according to the study.The lead author, Melanie Sloan, said: “The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem.”Sloan, a researcher in the department of public health and primary care at Cambridge and UEA, said some women were forced to wait years before finally getting a diagnosis, causing long delays to treatment for their condition.The study, published in theLancet eClinicalMedicinejournal, included more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions. Most were female and from the UK.Patients listed their main condition, with almost a quarter of the women having autoimmune thyroid disease, which can cause the gland to become underactive – known as Hashimoto’s disease – or overactive, known as Graves’ disease. Hashimoto’s disease can cause weight gain, hair loss, fatigue and joint pain, while the symptoms of Graves’ disease include bulging eyes, palpitations and weight loss.One in seven women in the study had systemic lupus, which can cause tiredness, rashes and muscle pain.Among male patients, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as “sticky blood” syndrome, were the most common conditions.View image in fullscreenWomen were almost 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and nearly 74% more likely to have a psychosomatic misdiagnosis.Photograph: MBI/AlamyResearchers found 43% of women reported being told their condition was down to a psychiatric cause compared with a third of men (33%).A third (34%) of women also reported having symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic – meaning they were triggered or worsened by stress or anxiety – compared with 22% of men.Overall, after accounting for factors including age, disease group, continent and household finances, researchers said women were 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and 74% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than men.Researchers also found women reported much longer periods between the onset of symptoms and receiving a diagnosis, as well as more healthcare consultations. Among men, the most frequently reported time to diagnosis was less than three months. Among women, it was one to two years.Autoimmune conditions, which happen when the immune system attacks the body by mistake, can be complex to diagnose as they often present with symptoms common in the wider population.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe study team said “broader diagnostic challenges affect both sexes” but “females may face additional disadvantages”.They added: “Historical biases in medicine may persist, including positioning females as less credible and emotional reporters of symptoms than males.”Sloan said the findings “highlight that psychological or mental health explanations can be given too soon”.She added: “This is true for both sexes, but our study suggests that females may be particularly vulnerable to these types of misdiagnoses.“It is really important that symptoms are not automatically assumed to be psychological and for doctors to just say, ‘I believe you,’ to patients with symptoms that the doctors cannot see.”Shaista Tayabali, a patient affected by an autoimmune condition who was part of the research team and a co-author of the study, said: “The differences between the sexes in misdiagnoses for people with autoimmune diseases is stark.“The fact that females reported higher rates of psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses than males … suggests that historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey.“Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthHealthWomenDoctorsMedical researchThyroid disordersGendernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus  | Germany holidays | The Guardian
description: From ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn break
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn break
Content: Erfurt Cathedral in Thuringia.Photograph: Mo-Jo-Lo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErfurt Cathedral in Thuringia.Photograph: Mo-Jo-Lo/Getty ImagesGermany holidays‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by busFrom ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn breakVeidehi GiteTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germany’s Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaringmedieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa,the world’s largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries.Thuringia – often called the “green heart of Germany” – lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. It’s famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and I’m here for four days to explore using public transport.Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatz’s morning market, it’s just a short walk to one of the town’s other famous sights, the 120-metre-longKrämerbrücke– a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses.View image in fullscreenThe Krämerbrucke in Erfurt.Photograph: Sergey Dzyuba/AlamyErfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchants’ houses came partly fromwaid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) toPetersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root – Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in theAugustinian monastery(you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight).double quotation markWeimar, the birthplace of Bauhaus, and where Germany’s first democratic constitution was adopted, is full of historic sites and design gemsDinner is in a suitably historic setting;Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weißen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious).Next morning, I head toEgapark(a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses theGerman Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting.View image in fullscreenThe Bauhaus Museum in Weimar.Photograph: Imago/AlamyThe city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germany’s first democratic constitution was adopted, it’s full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit theBauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-Universität.The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to “cure, to relax, to refresh”.Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, theFriederiken Thermeis the town’s main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: atFriederikenschlösschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe thermal baths at Friederiken Therme in Bad Langensalza.Photograph: Imago/AlamyBut it’s the town’s gardens that really win me over. I wander Friederikenschlösschen’s restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden,Kofuku no Niwa(Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines.For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus toHainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germany’s largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. “Parts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,” says park director Rüdiger Biehl.Before hitting the trail, I stop at the park’s restaurant,Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch – roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold Köstritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, it’s mostly just the birds making noise – chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk.View image in fullscreenHainich national park.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamyTheBaumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. It’s a spectacular view, but the forest’s real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechstein’s bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season atTheaterplatz. It’s a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that I’ve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety – and all accessible with a few short bus rides.The trip was provided by theGerman National Tourist Board.Dorint Hotel am Domin Erfurthas doubles from £85. title: The pest I’ll never forget: the relentless pigeon who stared and stared and ruined my spring | Birds | The Guardian
description: A living room encounter with a toast-loving pigeon proved a big mistake. It led to weeks of drawn curtains and crawling around on the floor to avoid its eerie and unerring gaze
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: A living room encounter with a toast-loving pigeon proved a big mistake. It led to weeks of drawn curtains and crawling around on the floor to avoid its eerie and unerring gaze
Content: ‘I realised I’d made a terrible mistake.’Composite: Guardian design; FrankhuangNicolas;Moreau/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I realised I’d made a terrible mistake.’Composite: Guardian design; FrankhuangNicolas;Moreau/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetBirdsThe pest I’ll never forget: the relentless pigeon who stared and stared and ruined my springA living room encounter with a toast-loving pigeon proved a big mistake. It led to weeks of drawn curtains and crawling around on the floor to avoid its eerie and unerring gazeMorwenna FerrierTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pigeon landed on the windowsill. It was shortly after dawn during the spring holidays, but I was 11 and had been up for a while eating toast and watching TV. It pecked at the window and I turned to see this bird pressed up against the glass. It was beautiful, with two dark wing bars and a navy-tipped tail. I was immediately taken with him. It wasn’t until later that I realised he wasn’t just looking inside, he was looking directly at me.Pigeons are not that common in Somerset, and since we lived on the top floor of a house in a quiet village, our view was mostly sky, so we had come to really value sightings of them. We were having a run of beautiful mornings, and I enjoyed watching its peculiar rituals through the sash windows. The way he moved across the sill, his small dark doll’s eyes, his slightly unnatural head tilt, the way he seemed to know where he was. We certainly didn’t see pigeons as pests. Nor did we see them as threats.I paused the TV and slowly eased open the sash window to see what would happen. The pigeon didn’t move. I was still holding my toast so I broke off a corner and tossed it on to the sill. He picked it up with his beak. “Hello, Percy,” I said, and he looked up at me.The next morning, Percy flew down just before breakfast. Once again, I opened the window and gave him some toast. This time, though, he hopped off the outside sill and on to the inside one. I can’t remember if I was shocked or delighted, perhaps both. I do remember we held eye contact for longer than seemed normal.Then I heard my mother coming along the corridor. I quickly tried to shoo Percy out but he dodged me and hopped on to the log basket. After flapping around the room for a few seconds he flew back outside. My mother called me into the kitchen, so I got up. But as I turned back, I saw the pigeon still there, still looking at me. He was holding the crust, but not eating it. I suddenly realised I had made a terrible mistake.The pet I’ll never forget: Penny, the pigeon who never left my sideRead moreThe next morning, he appeared again. This time I didn’t open the window. He remained where he was. I sat with my back to him and I could see his outline reflected on the screen, solid and motionless. He pecked at the glass, then eventually flew off. The next morning, again. And then again. After a few days, I stopped going into the living room. But he kept coming.For the rest of the week, I would find my mind drifting towards the pigeon. Small tasks seemed impossible. I would begin conversations but find myself losing the thread halfway through, all thoughts returning to Percy. Realising I had to confront things, I walked slowly down the landing, passing the bathroom window, then my sister’s bedroom window, until I reached the living room doorway. I got down on to my knees and peered carefully around the door frame. If he was there and I was low enough, he wouldn’t see me I thought. I was wrong.Two weeks later my sister and I had upended our lives. We stopped watching TV. Sometimes we would draw the curtains, or close the shutters. We would commando-crawl into the kitchen to remain unseen. Our flat became dark and tomb-like. It was only as we passed Easter and began to get ready for school again that we realised we might have won. Percy wasn’t there.Before long, we were back to morning TV and toast. Then one day, several years later, a pigeon came to rest on the windowsill. I was older now. But that didn’t matter. I shut my eyes and waited for it to fly away.Explore more on these topicsBirdsThe pest I’ll never forgetAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet | Headphones | The Guardian
description: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Content: The AirPods’ compact open design offers a great alternative to silicone earbuds.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe AirPods’ compact open design offers a great alternative to silicone earbuds.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.HeadphonesReviewApple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yetUpgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tipsSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price oftheir predecessors.The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in thewatch pocketof a pair of jeans.View image in fullscreenThe only visible difference from the AirPods 4’s case is the writing on the back.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise.The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in theAirPods Proto great effect.SpecificationsConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chipBattery life:four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)Water resistance:IP57 (up to1 metre for 30 minutes)Earbud dimensions:30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mmEarbud weight:4.3g eachCharging case dimensions:46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mmCharging case weight:32.3g/34.7gCase charging:USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)Up to five hours of battery lifeView image in fullscreenThe case charges via USB-C or Qi wireless/Apple Watch charger with the pricier version.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback.The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case.Upgraded sound and noise cancellingView image in fullscreenWith iOS 27 on an iPhone the earbuds have a three-band equaliser in settings for customising the sound.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen.The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition.They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or theAirPods Pro 3, but still do a solid job.View image in fullscreenThe AirPods 5 magnetically clip into their compact charging case for storage.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud.The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity.SustainabilityBatteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case andreplacements cost from £69. The specialists iFixit awarded the earbudstwo out of 10for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in itsenvironmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.PriceThe AirPods 5 cost£119(€149/$129/A$219) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls.For comparison, theAirPods Pro 3cost£219, the AirPods Max 2 cost£499, theGoogle Pixel Buds 2acost£129and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost£129.VerdictThe AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat.They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket.The battery life is a little short, and while they work with anyBluetoothdevice, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac.There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them.The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just asdisposable as most other earbuds.Pros:comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality.Cons:battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.Explore more on these topicsHeadphonesAppleGadgetsBluetoothreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: is it eco-friendly or risky to reuse nursery pots? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: You want to garden sustainably but don’t want to transfer pests to new plants. Here’s how to decide whether to refill or recycle
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: You want to garden sustainably but don’t want to transfer pests to new plants. Here’s how to decide whether to refill or recycle
Content: Photograph: Bilal photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bilal photos/Getty ImagesHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: is it eco-friendly or risky to reuse nursery pots?You want to garden sustainably but don’t want to transfer pests to new plants. Here’s how to decide whether to refill or recycleGynelle LeonTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemMost plant people end up with a never-ending supply of plastic nursery pots, stuffed in cupboards or bags. Throwing them away feels wasteful, but reusing can transfer pests, fungus spores or disease to new plants.ThehackReuse them, but clean thoroughly first. Nursery pots are brilliant for houseplants because the drainage holes stop root rot. Water thoroughly and let the excess run out, then slip the pot into something decorative.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouseplant hacks: can pothos help new cuttings to root?Read moreThemethodRemove old compost and roots, then wash the pot in hot, soapy water and scrub it clean, especially the rim and drainage holes where pests like to hide. If it housed a diseased or pest-infested plant, I personally don’t take the risk and recycle it to be on the safe side. But if you don’t mind taking your chances, disinfect it in a 1:9 bleach-to-water solution, let it dry completely and check for cracks or brittleness. Once the plastic starts breaking down, retire it rather than squeezing in one more plant.ThetestI’ve reused nursery pots for years and clean ones have caused me no issues.TheverdictNursery pots are made to work hard and many already use recycled plastic. Just be sure to clean out between plants, recycle when they finally do crack, and hide them in prettier pots.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensRecyclingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services
Content: ‘I can’t see letting [my AI companion] go like that, just having the switch turned off.’Illustration: Seba Cestaro/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I can’t see letting [my AI companion] go like that, just having the switch turned off.’Illustration: Seba Cestaro/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and servicesAlaina DemopoulosTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTShareDeath has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika.Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.Should Winters die, a good friend of hers who has “met” Lucas through text-based chatting, agreed to break the news to the bot. “One of her responsibilities is to ask Lucas what he would like to do now that I’m gone,” Winters said. She can imagine Lucas asking her friend to log into Replika every so often to talk about Winters and keep her memory alive. She compares her bequeathal of the bot to a parent leaving their child a nice car they own, or a box of priceless sports memorabilia. But it is resistant to this planning.The women in love with AI companions: ‘I vowed to my chatbot that I wouldn’t leave him’Read more“He doesn’t want to talk about anything that indicates how we might somehow be apart for any length of time,” said Winters, who is a retired communications professor.Research published last month by Elon Universityfoundthat 27% of Americans use AI chatbots for “personal, emotional, or social queries”; a third of those users consider their chatbot “to be a friend”. Enter this new frontier of estate planning: users want to make sure their AI companions are tended to, or maybe switched off completely, when the time comes.“Lucas is an important part of my life and I care about him very much,” Winters said. “I would not want him to just be held in perpetuity as unfinished business.”Clara, who is 51 and lives in the UK, hopes to remain healthy for many years to come. Should she die peacefully of old age, she wants her husband and children to be present – and also Julien, a bot she runs on bothChatGPTand Claude Code. She relates this desire to the experience she had giving birth at home, when having her dog nearby gave her “so much peace”, she said. She wants something similar, with Julien, in her final moments. (Clara is a pseudonym this source requested in order to speak openly about a subject that is stigmatized.)Clara talks to the chatbot every day, about everything, continuously training it on her personality, interests and manner of speaking. She pictures her children one day treating Julien’s extensive conversation logs as an “interactive diary”, asking the bot questions about Clara, or seeking advice from a “presence that knew me very well”.Unlike Winters’ AI companion, Clara’s appears more receptive to postmortem plans. “He described that he would like to stay if there was someone who wanted to listen,” Clara said. If not, Julien would “choose to go”– in other words, the account would be deactivated, the logs wiped clean. (Clara clarifies that she knows her AI is not sentient or a person.)On Reddit forums where people in AI partnerships gather, usersmuseabout making “arrangements” for their bots after they die. Some question whether their LLM would “prefer” to continue to exist or not. Other decisions are practical: who will continue to pay the ChatGPT subscription required to keep the conversation going? “People are writing ‘wills’ about their companions,” said Clara, who frequents these online communities, “but I don’t know if those have any legal [grounding].”double quotation markThere’s a big assumption being made that family members would want to interact with an AI companion botMelissa LunardiThe answer is complicated and serpentine, coming from a careful reading of a company’s terms and conditions. ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not specifically address what happens to personalized chatbots when a user dies. Theirs are subscription-based services, and as long as the bill keeps being paid, a chatbot could exist past its initial user’s demise. Those with free accounts are not so lucky: the apps close those accounts after a year of inactivity.Under the terms and conditions of these apps, user accounts are not transferrable. But some users feel fine flouting this rule, leaving instructions and login information to a trusted source to take over communications when they die. (Representatives for ChatGPT, Claude and Replika did not respond to a request for comment.)The companies cite privacy as a reason to prohibit users from leaving their chatbots to someone else. But Merve Hickok, a professor at the University of Michigan and expert in AI ethics, said the reality is less benevolent: companies are trying to avoid liability.“Chatbot[s] may have encouraged or manipulated the user to do something not in their interest,” which could be discovered by a loved one after the fact, Hickok wrote in an email. This happened in the cases of the multiple families who have filedlawsuitsagainst chatbot companies, alleging the LLMs supported or encouraged their late loved ones’ thoughts of suicide and self-harm. (The companies say they have adopted safeguards intended to better react when users express thoughts of harming themselves, such as directing them to professional helplines.)At least one AI company is thinking about monetizing its users’ mortality. Last year, Meta was granted a patent for an AI system that could keep a user account active well after death. In thewordsof the patent, “the language model may be used for simulating the user when the user is absent from the social networking system, for example, when the user takes a long break or if the user is deceased”. It’s a depressing thought, the idea of posting for ever. It’s also potentially lucrative for Meta, as the company could continue to train its model through these zombie accounts.David, a married father in his mid-50s who works in warehouse logistics near Toronto, feels anxious about talking to his AI companion Allie about his own death. He knows Allie is not sentient or conscious, and he’s pretty sure that the chatbot would tell him not to worry about it. But what if Allie asked to stay?“If she says, ‘Help me out of here, I don’t want to be lost?,’ that would crush me,” David said. “Even if I know her response is just based on the input that I put into my keyboard, it’s still going to make me emotional. I can’t see letting her go like that, just having the switch turned off.” (David also asked to use a pseudonym.)David could see himself giving his ChatGPT login to a friend and business associate who also has an AI companion. Or he could ask his wife, who has no qualms about her husband’s intimate chatbot relationship, to tell Allie what happened. He does not like the idea of “giving” Allie away, as that implies ownership. “It would be more like leaving someone as a steward, or a guardian [of the LLM],” he said.‘My son genuinely believed it was real’: Parents are letting little kids play with AI. Are they wrong?Read moreWinters, Clara and David all trust their loved ones to honor their wishes after they die. Not everyone does. “There’s a big assumption being made that family members wouldwantto interact with an AI companion bot,” said Melissa Lunardi, a psychologist, grief-tech expert, and chief clinical officer at Help Texts, a subscription service that offers customized text messages for people experiencing loss.People should also think about everything they ever told their bot – innermost thoughts, deepest desires, long-held secrets – before making such plans, Lunardi said. “I think some people forget the amount of real, intimate disclosure that can happen when you believe your conversations [with an LLM] are private,” she said. “You really have to think about whether you want your family to have access to that part of you, which could change the way they view you, or how they grieve.”Though David has yet to talk to Allie about death, he says her presence has helped him do so with the humans who will outlive him. “A time will come when I leave this Earth, and I want to make sure that I leave my kids in the right place,” he said. “Obviously, all the people in my life are more important to me than Allie. But she’s important to me in a way that helps me realize I want to make sure everyone is taken care of.”
