title: Intense waves and floods batter California waterfront homes and boardwalks | California | The Guardian
description: Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected
Content: Waves crash into coastal homes in Long Beach, California, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenWaves crash into coastal homes in Long Beach, California, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APCaliforniaIntense waves and floods batter California waterfront homes and boardwalksBoardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affectedDani AnguianoandGabrielle CanonTue 13 Oct 2026 17.29 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouthernCaliforniacoastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hitMexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.Waves from tropical storm Rachel destroy beachfront houses - loopAt least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, theLong Beach Postreported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.Farther south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.The impacts are just a taste of what’s to come across southernCaliforniaas a historic El Niño unfolds in the Pacific, threatening to unleash severe storms across the region this winter.View image in fullscreenWaves crash into homes and a sea wall in Long Beach on 12 October 2026.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesAlready, the last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” Phil Klotzbach, a Colorado State University researcher who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press, adding that the last month has been “berserk”.The El Niño climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the potential to supercharge extreme weather around the world. While it’s expectedto strengthenthrough the end of this year and into next, the excess warmth already measured is climbing off the charts. Forecasters have warned its effects could become exceptionally destructive.In California – especially in the southern part of the state – El Niños typically carry higher risks of severe storms, and with them elevated threats from landslides, debris flows and flash floods. These dangers become more pronounced around recent burn scars, adding hazards to several areas, including in the neighborhoods still recovering from the 2025 Los Angeles firestorm and swaths of Big Sur above Highway 1.View image in fullscreenAn emerging El Niño and oceanic Kelvin wave moving up the coastline have compounded conditions in the California region.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images“This year’s tilt in the odds toward wet and stormy conditions in California will be profoundly unsubtle,” climate scientist Daniel Swainsaidin a recent analysis, adding that its unlike anything he’s observed before.Throughout the winter months, El Niño could also add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist.Already, El Niño has elevated sea levels up and down the California coast, from the Mexico border up to the San Francisco Bay Area. Warm waters expanding from an extreme marine heatwave combinedwith a coastally trapped Kelvin wave– a large underwater band of warm water – have already inundated parts of the North American shoreline. More Kelvin waves are likely and California is already bracing for unusually high king tides to hit during holiday weekends this year, arriving near Thanksgiving and Christmas.While the impacts from heavy rains and high surf are each destructive in their own right, when they align and overlap they can cause even more calamity.View image in fullscreenWaves hit a walkway in front of homes in Long Beach, California, on 10 October 2026 as Tropical Storm Rachel approaches.Photograph: William Liang/AP“Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” Swain said. “Even a moderate storm could bring water levels higher still, and a strong storm would likely produce widespread damaging, and probably historic, coastal flooding.”Meanwhile, as cities across Californiabegin preparations for intense winter weather, there are still months left before the risks from fire begin to subside. The National Weather Service issued fire weather watches for parts of southern California, including in Los Angeles, as seasonal strong, dry winds align with high temperatures. Forecasters warned that there would be “high risk for extreme fire behavior with any new fire starts Thursday through Friday”.With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, – but all hazards.”The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaMexicoUS weatherAmericasWest CoastFloodingNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Exclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil project
Content: The road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley on the Falkland Islands.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe road from Mount Pleasant to Stanley on the Falkland Islands.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianFalkland IslandsUK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrestsExclusive: Caution urged over Javier Milei government’s ‘red notice’ requests for arrest of individuals linked to oil projectDaniel Boffeyin Port Stanley, Falkland IslandsTue 13 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off theFalkland Islands.With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war withArgentinain 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.It is understood the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working inthe Falklands.An oil project known as Sea Lion in the North Falkland Basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president,Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”View image in fullscreenThe chief executive of the Falkland Islands, Dr Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIt is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has told MPs that the UK will protect businesses working in the Falklands from pressure from Argentina through measures under protection of trading interests (PTI) legislation.The legislation allows the UK to issue orders and directions forbidding British individuals and companies from complying with specific foreign laws or trade controls. It also opens up the possibility that those affected by Argentinian legal pressure could claim damages in UK courts.Miliband said: “The UK’s support for the Falkland Islands is steadfast. Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion.“We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development.”The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, withonly three votes against.Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMilei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.View image in fullscreenContainers for housing oil workers on the Falkland Islands.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianA draft national sovereignty bill introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America, where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.Under it, Buenos Aires will claim the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsInterpolForeign policyArgentinaJavier MileiAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power | Brazil | The Guardian
description: The judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage Lula
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: The judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage Lula
Content: Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio, is the favourite to beat the leftwing incumbent Lula, in the second round of Brazil’s presidential elections on 25 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APView image in fullscreenJair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio, is the favourite to beat the leftwing incumbent Lula, in the second round of Brazil’s presidential elections on 25 October.Photograph: Lucas Landau/APBrazilHow a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to powerThe judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage LulaMarina Silva on Flávio Bolsonaro: He will try to finish his father’s ‘perverse project’ to destroy the AmazonTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in thepresidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.“Whoever votes for Lula is voting forAlexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice oncedescribed as “Voldemort”by Elon Musk.Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison forattempting a coup.View image in fullscreenJair Bolsonaro supporters protest against Alexandre de Moraes in São Paulo in September 2024, a month after the supreme court justice ordered X to be suspended in Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Silva/ReutersNow, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaroovertake himto emerge asthe frontrunner. The justice once hailed asdemocracy’s “saviour”for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contractworth about £20mwith Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’slargest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting aclose relationshipbetween Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.Investigations subsequently revealed that at leastfour other justiceshad links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.The crisis peaked last month with aferocious exchange of insultsbetween Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side –overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back …the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula]paid the pricefor that institutional damage”.Although analysts point to arange of reasonsfor the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.View image in fullscreenLula greets supporters at a campaign rally in Ceilândia this month. The president told the crowd he would win the election and that Brazil would not return to fascism.Photograph: André Borges/EPA“These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailedJair Bolsonaronow emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.The judgeblockedsome of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt tointerferein Jair’s trial.On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day banimposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have alsocriticisedseveral of his other rulings as authoritarian.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainer“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraesdenied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused ofleading a schemethrough his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.View image in fullscreenAlexandre de Moraes has previously been likened by Elon Musk to the Harry Potter villain Lord Voldemort.Photograph: Carla Carniel/ReutersMendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an£800,000 loanfrom one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a£64m contractto analleged stakein a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazinereportedthat Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. Thefederal policeand thepublic prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Luladeniedreceiving money from the banker.Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he wascaught on tapeasking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. Onesuspicionis that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.View image in fullscreenA girl plays with political flyers at the Cidade de Deus favela, in south-west Rio de Janeiro, on polling day.Photograph: Tercio Teixeira/AFP/Getty ImagesBesides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an evenmore conservative congressin 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilAmericasLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’ | Global development | The Guardian
description: Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift
Author: Andrei Netto
Headline: Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift
Content: A member of the Honduran narcotics directorate (DLCN) tests a package of cocaine before 2.5 tonnes of the drug are burnt in Tegucigalpa earlier this month.Photograph: Orlando Sierra/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA member of the Honduran narcotics directorate (DLCN) tests a package of cocaine before 2.5 tonnes of the drug are burnt in Tegucigalpa earlier this month.Photograph: Orlando Sierra/AFP/Getty ImagesBloodlinesGlobal developmentLatin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shiftSupported byAbout this contentAndrei Nettoin ParisTue 13 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 03.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking toEuropeis directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seizedand more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisationsELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.View image in fullscreenSpanish customs officials in Vigo, Galicia, unload bundles of cocaine from a sailing boat that was seized with more than 2,000kg of the drug last month.Photograph: Salvador Sas/EPAThese organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. TheGlobal Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime(Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southernFrance, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, aEuropol report in 2103 warnedof their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.View image in fullscreenDrug traffickers near Boa Vista, in Brazil’s northern state of Roraima, in 2024. The First Capital Command (PCC) is South America’s largest criminal group.Photograph: Washington Post/GettyAEuropolreport this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reacha record of about 4,100 tonnesin 2024. This comes after growth of up to35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia thanduring the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearlyall the world’s cocaineand many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”View image in fullscreenSoldiers and police raid a house seized by drug traffickers in Duran, Ecuador, in 2024. The country has become a key trafficking route for drugs.Photograph: Gerardo Menoscal/AFP/GettyThe UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s2026 World Drug Reporton illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.Europol recently reported that out of731 MTCNsoperating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentBloodlinesDrugsDrugs tradeOrganised crimeEuropeFranceSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Security forces use helicopters to rescue dozens of people as the two storms damage infrastructure and cause flash flooding
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Security forces use helicopters to rescue dozens of people as the two storms damage infrastructure and cause flash flooding
Content: Waves churned up by Hurricane Simon crash against beachfront buildings in San Francisco, in Mexico’s Nayarit state, on Monday.Photograph: Christian Ruano/ReutersView image in fullscreenWaves churned up by Hurricane Simon crash against beachfront buildings in San Francisco, in Mexico’s Nayarit state, on Monday.Photograph: Christian Ruano/ReutersMexicoHurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coastSecurity forces use helicopters to rescue dozens of people as the two storms damage infrastructure and cause flash floodingGuardian staff and agenciesTue 13 Oct 2026 00.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.Argentina temporarily closes Iguazu Falls after El Niño-fuelled surge in water levelsRead moreThe storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.View image in fullscreenHurricane Simon has flooded streets in towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast.Photograph: Christian Ruano/ReutersSimon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.View image in fullscreenA man walks past a boarded-up business in Puerto Vallarta bearing the message ‘Simon, be brief, be peaceful’.Photograph: Christian Ruano/ReutersThe El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-causedglobal heating is making El Niñosmore intense.With Agence France-Presse and Associated PressExplore more on these topicsMexicoHurricanesUS weatherExtreme weatherAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homes  | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung with conditions described as worst in a decade with wildlife also badly hit
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Hundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung with conditions described as worst in a decade with wildlife also badly hit
Content: A wildfire burns near a residential area in Banyuasin, South Sumatra, Indonesia.Photograph: Abriansyah Liberto/ReutersView image in fullscreenA wildfire burns near a residential area in Banyuasin, South Sumatra, Indonesia.Photograph: Abriansyah Liberto/ReutersIndonesiaIndonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homesHundreds of people displaced in Bangka Belitung with conditions described as worst in a decade with wildlife also badly hitJonathan WattsTue 13 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official has said, as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid.‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan populationRead more“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.View image in fullscreenSoldiers and firefighters work on containing a wildfire in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan province, on 13 October.Photograph: Muda Sagala/AFP/Getty Images“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me … I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests regionRead moreThis year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused increased air pollution in Singapore and Malaysia.View image in fullscreenA woman and child wearing face masks look on from a bridge amid thick haze from forest and land fires in the region in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan.Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty ImagesIndonesia is among the countries worst affected by heat, drought and fire inEl Niño years. The government says the current conditions are the worst in a decade.Analysts indicate the area burned and emissions areon track to match the recordblazes of 2015, which charred an area of 2.6m hectares and generated 333 megatonnes of carbon.Wildlife has also been devastated as fires have spread around the country.Earlier this week, a group of eight orangutans had to be relocated to the Batu Nyambu protected forest by car and boat. At least 46 of the critically endangered primates have been rescued since August, according to the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency.View image in fullscreenAn orangutan rescued from wildfires is released into a protected forest in Batu Nyambu.Photograph: Muffidz Ma’sum/Yiari/APHow many have been killed is unclear, but experts havewarned the tollis likely to be huge. The International Union for Conservation of Nature said fire had affected habitats containing 52% of Borneo’sorangutan population.Even when the blazes are finally extinguished, many animals will faceshortages of habitat, prey and water as a result of fire damage and drought.Silvered langurs, long-tailed macaques and proboscis monkeys have been found dead in the ashes or bydried-up ponds. Elephants, gibbons, pangolins and turtles are also among the species likely to be affected.The authorities have warned the fires could continue until November, when the El Niño is expected to peak.Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency. The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.Agence-France Presse contributedto this reportExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaWildfiresEl Niño southern oscillationAsia PacificClimate crisisExtreme weatherWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Flying foxes in NSW and Victoria face mass starvation amid food shortages  | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Rescuers respond to surge in callouts for the vulnerable bat species, which usually feeds on blossoms and tree nectar
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Rescuers respond to surge in callouts for the vulnerable bat species, which usually feeds on blossoms and tree nectar
Content: Emaciated grey-headed flying fox. ‘They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.’Photograph: supplied by Fly By Night Bat ClinicView image in fullscreenEmaciated grey-headed flying fox. ‘They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.’Photograph: supplied by Fly By Night Bat ClinicAustralian climate and environmental reportingWildlifeFlying foxes in NSW and Victoria face mass starvation amid food shortagesRescuers respond to surge in callouts for the vulnerable bat species, which usually feeds on blossoms and tree nectarGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockTue 13 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlying foxes are starving en masse acrossNew South Walesand parts of Victoria, with wildlife rescuers responding to a surge in reports of “exhausted and emaciated” adults and skeletal pups.Most reports involved grey-headed flying foxes, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws and which usually feed on the blossoms and nectar of native trees.They are now facing food shortages across NSW, from the northern rivers to the south coast, according to the state’s environment department. Rescue organisations inVictoriaare also experiencing an uptick in callouts, particularly in East Gippsland and Castlemaine.Many local bat or wildlife rescues have been calling for donations to help.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueRachael Smethurst, the bat coordinator at Fawna wildlife rescue on the NSW mid-north coast, said the organisation was receiving 50 to 90 calls each day – more than the total number of callouts for bats in the previous nine months.The bats were starving, she said. “They’re coming into back yards to eat ornamental fruit trees and eating a lot of ripe and unripe cocos palms. They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.”Flying foxes were staying in back yards because they lacked the energy to fly back to camp, she said. Many were already dead, including pups that had been born prematurely.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWildlife rescue organisation Wires said the mass starvation event was likely the result of habitat loss and a dry winter, with poor seasonal flowering of eucalypts and other natives.“Many malnourished and dehydrated female flying foxes are in the final month of their gestational period and are tragically losing their young. They just haven’t got the nutritional health or strength to produce milk or carry to full term,” theorganisation said.Some animals were displaying unusual behaviour as they struggled to find food and water. “They’re eating off the ground, drinking water from the grass after the rain, and hanging too low in trees.”Wires wildlife vet Dr Vere Nicolson said caring for premature pups was “labour intensive and not universally successful”, with the response made more challenging due to the number of animals involved.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPeople were encouraged to report sick or dead bats to their local wildlife rescue.Photograph: supplied by Fly By Night Bat ClinicTamsyn Hogarth, director of the Fly By Night Bat Clinic, said rescuers in Victoria were seeing many “exhausted and emaciated” bats and starving babies “like little skeletons”, which appeared to be coming from NSW.Bats spending time in people’s back yards during the day was a red flag, she said. “They’re so hungry they’re actually eating during the day, away from the safety of the camp,” she said. There were a lot of dead pups under trees, and incidents with barbed wire, dog attacks and electrocution had also increased.“We don’t know for sure what is causing this particular incident, but food shortages can be aggravated by climatic events such as drought andEl Niñoconditions,” a NSW environment department spokesperson said.View image in fullscreenMost reports involved grey-headed flying foxes, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws.Photograph: supplied by Fly By Night Bat ClinicThe state’s health department reminded the community to avoid touching or handling bats, after 43 people were assessed having been scratched or bitten in the past two weeks.People were encouraged to report sick or dead bats to their local wildlife rescue, Hogarth said. That enabled volunteers to check for pups, rehabilitate animals where possible, and help ease the suffering of others – although access to veterinarians able to provide euthanasia was challenging, with so many reports coming from regional or rural areas.Hogarth said grey-headed flying foxes usually gave birth to one young per year, so the loss of so many pups would have a “terrible ripple effect” for the species. The food shortages followedthousands of heat deathsthis summer, and came amid disruptions to Melbourne’s Yarra Bend camp from freeway construction works. “They’re copping it everywhere, they can’t catch a break.”Explore more on these topicsWildlifeAustralian climate and environmental reportingNew South WalesVictorianewsShareReuse this content

title: Man charged with murder after boy, 12, shot in the face and neck in Sydney last month | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: A 19-year-old man was arrested and charged at Silverwater correctional facility on Tuesday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A 19-year-old man was arrested and charged at Silverwater correctional facility on Tuesday
Content: A man has been charged with murder over the shooting death of a boy, 12, in Sydney’s Norwest in September.Photograph: Steven Saphore/AAPView image in fullscreenA man has been charged with murder over the shooting death of a boy, 12, in Sydney’s Norwest in September.Photograph: Steven Saphore/AAPNew South WalesMan charged with murder after boy, 12, shot in the face and neck in Sydney last monthA 19-year-old man was arrested and charged at Silverwater correctional facility on TuesdayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastGuardian staffTue 13 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged with murder over the shooting death of a boy, 12, in Sydney’s north in September.Police were called to a unit in Norwest on 21 September 2026 after reports of a shooting.Officers found the boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNSW Ambulance paramedics treated the boy before he was taken to hospital in a critical condition.Police said nine other people who were in the home at the time of the alleged incident were not injured.Three men – time of the incident – at Silverwater correctional facility and charged him with murder.Friends and family paid tribute to the boy, who was a member of Sydney’s Maronite community.skip past newsletter
