title: ‘Manosphere’ warnings as rates of family and sexual violence against Australian children rise sharply | Crime - Australia | The Guardian
description: Study authors say increase cannot be attributed to any one factor and list income inequality and reporting increases due to growing awareness as other likely reasons
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Study authors say increase cannot be attributed to any one factor and list income inequality and reporting increases due to growing awareness as other likely reasons
Content: A new study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open found rates of violence against Australian children are rising.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenA new study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open found rates of violence against Australian children are rising.Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAPCrime - Australia‘Manosphere’ warnings as rates of family and sexual violence against Australian children rise sharplyStudy authors say increase cannot be attributed to any one factor and list income inequality and reporting increases due to growing awareness as other likely reasonsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciTue 13 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sexual assault of Australian children has accelerated sharply since the pandemic, surprising researchers who expected rates to have fallen but instead found attacks on boys had risen 15.7%.Researchers expected rates to have dropped in line with other countries around the world and warn the troubling findings show an urgent need to prevent the suffering of children.The University of Sydney research published on Wednesday found a significant increase in violence against children between 2014 and 2024 that could be attributed to a range of factors, including income inequality and the manosphere.An increase in reporting due to growing awareness could also partially explain the higher rate of violence, it found.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe study found a steady increase in rates of sexual assaults against girls aged up to nine (2.8% per year) and aged 10 to 17 (4.2%), with rates among boys aged 10 to 17 accelerating sharply after 2021 (15.7%).Family violence-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter.MPs v the manosphere: ministers battle misogyny as they take a different message to men and boys across AustraliaRead moreAssault-related hospitalisations and child maltreatment were generally stable.“In Australia, income inequality is at its highest point in 20 years, with substantial increases from 2021, coinciding with the acceleration of rates found in the current study,” researchers found.“Economic stress may be especially salient in the post-2020 period, when pandemic-related financial disruptions intensified for many families, while government benefits providing economic relief, such as the JobKeeper payment scheme in Australia, ended in March 2021.“Shifts in gender norms and online cultures may also play a role … traditional gender attitudes that favour male authority within households are resurging among young men [and] the expansion of misogynistic online communities and broader toxic masculinity narratives are associated with hostility toward women and girls.”The research,published in the media journal JAMA Network Open, was based on an analysis of a decades-worth of Australian data from multiple sources.These sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalisations, and child protection data from three Australian national agency databases.The study’s lead author, Dr Lucy Grummitt, said researchers expected to find that the rate of violence against children had fallen, given evidence recorded in other high-income countries over the past decade regarding child protection.That they found the opposite was impossible to attribute to any one factor, she said, but it did show the need for a less siloed approach to the issue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“All these different departments that are involved in the bigger picture of violence against children are just focused on one particular subset, and we don’t actually have a very clear picture of what young people are being exposed to, and how has that changed over the last decade,” Grummitt said.“So that was kind of the rationale … I expected to see that things were kind of improving, I suppose. But that’s not really what we found.“Violence against children is a human rights issue, it shouldn’t be falling to one government department to be monitoring this … it really is a whole-of-government issue and currently our data and our monitoring really doesn’t reflect that.”Grummitt said that it was frustrating for researchers to discover that in some cases entire datasets they hoped to use in the triangulation were missing.This data included one year of missing child maltreatment data for NSW and Queensland, and family violence-related assault data for Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia also being incomplete.The data that did exist was also not directly comparable across states, Grummitt said.“Family domestic violence data is improving, but it’s pretty striking that in 2024 when we finished extracting the data that there weren’t already these nationally consistent definitions.”In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help at Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helpline InternationalExplore more on these topicsCrime - AustraliaDomestic violenceSexual harassmentChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing
Content: Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a residential area in Kyiv.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenUkrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a residential area in Kyiv.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineAllies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says ZelenskyyUkrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharingLuke Harding, andAndrew Rothin KyivTue 13 Oct 2026 17.54 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine received no early warning from its partners about a second night of Russian ballistic missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, including a critical power plant struck after dark,Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid on Tuesday.The Ukrainian president had earlierdescribed an attack involving five missiles on Mondayas “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” hewrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.More ballistic missiles were then launched at Kyiv on Tuesday night, striking a key power plant in the capital despite a purported energy ceasefire claimed byDonald Trump. One person also died in a strike on a high-rise apartment building, according to the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said apartments were on fire and being evacuated. A further 13 injuries were reported.“Once again, ‌no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No 4,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media app Telegram, again without explaining why he thought there had been no warning.US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that theTrump administrationwas on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv.On Tuesday, however, Trump denied intelligence sharing had stopped. He told reporters: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them andRussiaon getting the war to end.”Trump hasdemanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineriesand has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?Read moreAsked on Tuesday whether Russia could use proceeds ​from the ​sale to purchase ​more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s ​a diesel ‌deal, not ​for ​us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said.Earlier the president claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyydescribed as “news to me”. Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said.“Russia did not heed the president … the Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted on Tuesday.Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.“It is deeply unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine receives no warnings about ballistic missile launches,” Zelenskyy said in a statement after the Tuesday strikes. “It is vital that the world does not remain silent about this. And it is crucial that America clearly sees what is happening and who is responsible for the continuation of the war.”The blasts could be heard in centralKyivas Ukraine’s air defences failed to stop the high-speed Russian missile targeting the capital. The missile strikes on Ukraine’s left bank targeted a thermal power plant, Zelenskyy said, and also struck an apartment building leaving both dead and injured in the latest strike on the capital.Zelenskyy warned on Tuesday evening that Russia was planning further strikes with ballistic missiles, telling Ukrainians: “Please take care of yourselves tonight and tomorrow.”In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. It has particularly stepped up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, cutting power and water in large parts of Ukraine’s capital as emergency workers race to restore basic utilities. Ukraine, meanwhile, has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.According tothe Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.Speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation with the US was continuing and said the lack of warning about the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.On Monday, Russia also bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.Meanwhile, 11 sailors were missing after their ship was sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria. The incident prompted Bulgaria to summon Russia’s ⁠ambassador.Two cargo ships were hit ⁠by drones overnight and one ​was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but the prime minister, Rumen Radev, said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House.Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strongEurope, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaVolodymyr ZelenskyyTrump administrationUS foreign policyKyivDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump
Content: Andy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August.Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham chose Ukraine for his first foreign visit after taking office, meeting Volodymyr Zelenskyy at his residence in Kyiv in August.Photograph: Future Publishing/Getty ImagesForeign policyBurnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ supportPrime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald TrumpPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will hostVolodymyr Zelenskyyat Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect itfrom attacks bya new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyyvisited a naval basein Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnhamtravelled to Kyivin August.Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trumpmade a dealto buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraineto have a new leader, and announced asupposed ceasefireconnected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.Trump is an often wayward ally forUkraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin.UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. Hemet Keir Starmerat Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance,publicly beratedthe Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.During that trip Zelenskyy was also hostedby King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones.These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace inEurope.“It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourAndy BurnhamVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgery | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Vatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in Rome
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Vatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in Rome
Content: Pope Leo arrives at Gemelli hospital in Rome for surgery to remove a lung nodule on Wednesday.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo arrives at Gemelli hospital in Rome for surgery to remove a lung nodule on Wednesday.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersPope Leo XIVPope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer as growth removed during surgeryVatican says pontiff had lower lobe of right lung removed in ‘successful, on schedule and as planned’ operation in RomeAngela Giuffridain RomeTue 13 Oct 2026 16.32 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leohas lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday.Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, theVaticansaid in a medical bulletin, which followed an earlier statement saying the pope’s operation had concluded “successfully, on schedule and as planned”.The Vatican added that the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.Leo was in the operating theatre for about three hours and the operation itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo, said during his angelus prayer on Sunday thatdoctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, adding that it was “well-contained” and detected early.“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it,” he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square.Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted his arrival earlier on Tuesday.The Vatican said that Leo had “now returned to his room” following the operation.All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October.Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. “We spoke with great serenity,” Parolin toldRai News. “He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.”Leo is staying in the 10th-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated.The Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals – the authority that presides over papal conclaves.The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high-security papal suite.Leo’s predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis, which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVVaticanCatholicismChristianityItalyEuropeReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain
Content: Armed officers stand guard on a road outside the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase on 28 September after police declared a major incident at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenArmed officers stand guard on a road outside the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase on 28 September after police declared a major incident at the base.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK security and counter-terrorismAnalysisFar-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AIDan SabbaghDefence and security editorAnnual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for BritainTue 13 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTShareMI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongsideRussiaas a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK.“There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,”MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said, although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.”A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures.It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk arekeen to sow division in the UK too, as they post about flashpoint events such as the June riotingin Belfast and Southampton.View image in fullscreenKen McCallum, MI5’s director general.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAA second trend is that seemingly far-off conflicts, such as the wars the UK did not start in Ukraine orIran, have a habit of rippling back home.It is less than eight months since the US and Israel attacked Iran, subsequently with a little help from Britain, but already Iran is trying to direct terror plots in the UK.BothMI5and the counter-terror police may have to do a little better to explain precisely what five men from London were doing in a village next to RAF Fairford in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, given that nothing of significance was found in the vans and nobody has been charged.But McCallum warned that Iran had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites” – a likely reference to Fairford. That came a day after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind the episode. It would be surprising if both were wrong.That is not the only possible example. At the beginning of October,two Iranians from Liverpool and Salford were charged, accused of trying to make a chlorine powder bomb to target Jewish sites in Manchester. Prosecutors alleged they were directed by a third party, believed to be in Iran. The two have not yet pleaded to the charges; a trial at the Old Bailey is scheduled.Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief saysRead moreYet, if these fast-emerging threats were not enough, the normally sober McCallum decided to reference AI.He warned that AI could refine terror plots, supercharge hackers, produce individually targeted propaganda – and even help develop a novel bioweapon. This, he added, with emphasis, was a subject on which they were “particularly focused”, as if it was episode one of a TV thriller.While concerns were recently raised about scientists who have used AI to design viruses, as Anthropic warned offive examples of scientistswho had used Claude for researching novel pathogens, both instances provokeda scientific debateas to what is actually possible. And what McCallum did not mention was that AI is also an extraordinary and potentially intrusive tool for MI5 to seek out threats.There is already enough for the intelligence agencies to think about, as the MI5 review makes clear: a country made more dangerous by blowback from strongmen starting what they think will be short wars; a rising tide of hatred that may start online but is morphing into violent intent in real life; a complex cocktail of external and internal threats that could have real-life consequences.As McCallum himself recognised: “The protection of democracy – its institutions, its representatives, its principles – has never felt more vital.”Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismMI5Counter-terrorism policyIranRussiaThe far rightEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: At least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protests | France | The Guardian
description: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools
Content: Students and union members march in Montpellier on Tuesday.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAView image in fullscreenStudents and union members march in Montpellier on Tuesday.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAFranceAt least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protestsSwedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schoolsJon HenleyandAngelique Chrisafisin ParisTue 13 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 160,000 schoolchildren, students and trade unionists have marched in cities acrossFranceas protests over high school education continued into a third week and many demonstrators denounced policing tactics.Riot police fired teargas at the end of Tuesday’s marches in Nantes and near the Montparnasse area of Paris, but most of the demonstrations overteacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling school buildingsheld in cities including Lyon, Lille and Marseille were peaceful.The Swedish climate activistGreta Thunbergjoined an early morning protest outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.“Young people are not being included in the conversation,” said Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis.As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils afteraccusations of police brutality, Thunberg said: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.”View image in fullscreen‘Young people are not being included in the conversation,’ said Thunberg.Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/ShutterstockStudents outside the high school said Thunberg had encouraged them to continue with peaceful demonstrations.The protests – backed by trade unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French stateRead moreFrance’s interior ministry said 161,500 people had turned out across the country on Tuesday, while similar marchesdrew more than 260,000 last Tuesdayand75,000 on Thursday.“They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them,” the university students’ union UE – many of whose members are also demonstrating in solidarity, with an estimated 90% of France’s universities disrupted on Tuesday – posted on social media. High schools in Paris, Marseille and elsewhere were again blockaded.French authorities hope the protests, some of which have resultedin violent clashes with riot police, will peter out during the two-week half-term school holiday that starts this weekend.View image in fullscreenPolice use water cannon in an attempt to disperse protesters in Paris on Tuesday.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersLouis Létoublon of the student organisation Les Lycéens! said the protest movement had begun indeprived areas outside Pariswhere families were unable to afford holidays, so the autumn school vacation would not dampen anger.“We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging,” Naouel, a high school student in Brest, told Agence France-Presse.Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, said: “Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don’t get it.”France is braced for more nationwide protests on Saturday, which could be joined by people angry at rising fuel and energy prices as well as the cost of living.Jérôme Rodrigues, a high-profile member of thegilets jaunes(yellow vests) protest movement in 2018 and 2019, was present at the Paris march on Tuesday, and there was speculation thatgilets jaunescould return to the streets on Saturday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPeople march in Rennes on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeremías González/AP“There is a lot of anger,” Rodrigues told journalists. He said people felt the government had not answered their concerns, offering only “crumbs” – whether on fuel prices or demands for more funding for schools.Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT union, said: “Our youth is determined …While there is no answer to demands, the mobilisation will continue.”How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?Read moreThe education minister, Édouard Geffray, who has said 3,000 substitute teachers are being deployed in schools facing the most severe staff shortages, said on Tuesday that 214 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were completely closed.French media have reported, however, that at least some classes have been cancelled or disrupted in many more schools, and some lycées – for pupils mostly aged between 15 and 18 – have switched wholly or partly to online learning.The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called for restraint on Monday, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”, as government figures showed more than 6,800 people – mainly minors – had been detained during the protests.About 1,500 people are being prosecuted, the justice ministry has said, while 24 allegations of police brutality against demonstrators are under investigation. More than 200 teenagers, 100 school staff and 700 police officers have been injured.One young protester lost a handfrom a police stun grenade, prompting the government to ban their use during the protests, while another lost the use of an eye and a third many of his teeth from a teargas canister fired at close range.Rights groups and students have accused the police of a disproportionate use of force.The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, defended the policing. “When demonstrations take place peacefully, there is no police intervention,” he said.Six months from a crucial presidential election to replace Macron, rival politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests.The far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, has highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills, while her radical-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.Explore more on these topicsFranceGreta ThunbergProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks following deadly strike on Riyadh airport
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks following deadly strike on Riyadh airport
Content: Smoke over Sana’a during a reported Saudi-led coalition airstrike on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital on 9 October 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSmoke over Sana’a during a reported Saudi-led coalition airstrike on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital on 9 October 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQCivilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks as conflict between Riyadh and Houthi forces escalatesPatrick WintourTue 13 Oct 2026 13.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?Read moreThe strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthiattack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturdaythat killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. An evacuation order ​for the building ‌had been ‌issued, four sources told Reuters. There was no official comment ​or ​confirmation ​from ​Aramco.The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while theHouthishave to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.View image in fullscreenA map released by the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition shows the targeted site of the Yemeni Oil Company and Al-Sabaha Central station in Sana’a.Photograph: @CJFCS.Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown princeMohammed bin Salmanis prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisDonald TrumpMohammed bin SalmanIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’ | International Monetary Fund (IMF) | The Guardian
description: World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026
Content: The ExxonMobile refinery near Joliet, Illinois, US. The plant has been receiving crude from the US strategic reserve to make up shortfalls in imports.Photograph: Tannen Maury/EPA-EFEView image in fullscreenThe ExxonMobile refinery near Joliet, Illinois, US. The plant has been receiving crude from the US strategic reserve to make up shortfalls in imports.Photograph: Tannen Maury/EPA-EFEInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’World Economic Outlook says states’ oil stocks are low and budgets are overstretched, as it upgrades UK GDP growth forecast for 2026Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMFHeather Stewartin BangkokMon 12 Oct 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soarRead moreHowever, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”IMF GDP growth forecast chartThe International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, andpromised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month.But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal withVladimir Putinto temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, whichanalysts saidwould have little “meaningful” effect.The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF andWorld Bankare holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.Are global stock markets heading for a crash?Read moreLaunching the report in Bangkok, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said “the global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits”. She urged policymakers to “move from just coping, to rebuilding”.Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva,urged governments to tighten their belts, amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from itsmost recent update in July– in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is poised to arrive in Bangkok later this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts sayRead moreThe Fund cautioned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.Explore more on these topicsInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)World BankEconomicsGlobal economyOilCommoditiesInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage | World news | The Guardian
description: Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of the mundane
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of the mundane
Content: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) take part in a protest demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) take part in a protest demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter-roll irregularities.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Is IndiaWorld newsShock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrageMarches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of the mundaneDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 13 Oct 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonths of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.Over the weekend, Delhi was effectivelyunder lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authoritiesdeployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.The founders of the Cockroach party wereremoved from an Air India flightshortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were alsoswept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police,his shirt tornin the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav,who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramaticimages of police personneldetaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasadaccusing the oppositionof weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.While suppression of protests is not new,what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns inIndian-administered Kashmirhave been far more severe,particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after therevocation of Article 370.View image in fullscreenAn activist tries to stop a police bus carrying detained protesters during a demo seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersThe ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after anIndian Express investigation reportedthat the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in aKafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed tobenefit the ruling regime.Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as aduty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissionerslegal immunityfor actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenSouth African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel peace prize.Photograph: Daniel Karmann/DPA/APHuman rights| South African jurist and former international criminal court judge,Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage,has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person accountpublished in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.Technology| The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, includingtop Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announcedwater cuts of at least 10%across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque.Photograph: Mayank Austen SoofiWith Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned toMayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenKoushila Markam holds a photo of her daughter, Bamita Markam, who died from measles during an outbreak in Balaghat.Photograph: BBC News32At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June,the Indian Expressreported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenA quiet moment between Arbab Kamal Khan’s parents, whose everyday intimacy features in his photographs.For Mumbai-based cinematographer,Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – theirfeet across each otherbesides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or hisdad resting under his wife’s dupattaas she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? title: Fostering in crisis: can flexible care models fix England’s child placement shortfall? | Fostering | The Guardian
description: New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care places
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care places
Content: The number of fostering households in England has dropped 10% since 2021, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over.Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe number of fostering households in England has dropped 10% since 2021, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over.Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/AlamyFosteringFostering in crisis: can flexible care models fix England’s child placement shortfall?New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care placesJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleViennetta Basterfield, 67, spent two decades fostering more than 100 children in her west London home before she and her husband handed in the reins during Covid.Her own mother had died when she was nine and she was brought up by another woman who took her in. There was no doubt in her mind that she wanted to dedicate her life to passing that gift on to others.“I can’t say I wasn’t frightened. Every single placement I was frightened because you think, are we going to be OK? Are they going to accept us?” she said. “But it was the most rewarding thing I’ve ever done. We still have a full house for Sunday dinners, for christmas, for birthdays.“The greatest gift you can give a child is to show them that they matter.”But she worries about the future of fostering – she said the bureaucracy around the process was putting people off, and younger generations had more reservations about doing it, especially juggling it with caring for their own children.On Wednesday, the government is launching the country’s first nationalfoster carerrecruitment campaign, due to declining numbers at a time when there is a growing number of children in care.The number of fostering households has dropped 10% since 2021, and the foster care population is ageing, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over.The appeal will target adults in their 30s and 40s, urging them “to open their hearts and homes to some of the most vulnerable children in society”, with the aim of creating 10,000 new foster care places by the end of this parliament.It will run alongside trials of new foster care models, such as short-term “respite fostering” or fostering at weekends, which the government hopes will make it accessible to a wider range of people.The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said he wanted the public to respond to the campaign in the same way many did to the Homes for Ukraine scheme, when hundreds opened their homes to refugees.“There was this massive national moment where we understood that something was happening and people asked themselves, could we help? We need that kind of moment, to prompt people to have conversations in their homes,” he said.“Lots of families won’t be able to do it, but we’re trying to open up fostering to a wider group of people, by making it intergenerational or part-time, for instance.”He urged families not to wait for the “perfect moment”. “You’ve already got a lot of what it takes. Just step forward and start the process and see where you go,” he said.“Unless we rapidly, dramatically expand the foster care system, we will end up with children waking up every single day in residential care who could be in a family home, and children who are sent to live miles away from where they’ve grown up.”Speaking at an event ahead of the campagin at Downing Street on Tuesday, Marie-France van Heel, the prime minister’s wife, revealed for the first time that she had wanted to foster children.She was put off the idea because of her husband’s job and feeling she had to “transform myself into a different type of person to be able to give foster care”. “This campaign is really trying to dispel some of those myths and misconceptions,” she said.Fostering is the primary form of care for looked-after children in England. Out of 81,770 looked-after children, there are about 56,400 children in foster care at any one time.New research by the Coram Institute forChildrenfound over half a million adults want to foster and an estimated 3.4 million are interested.Dame Carol Homden, CEO of Coram, said there was a “substantial pool of people who are open to becoming foster carers” and the charity welcomed the government’s ambitious plans to recruit more.Their research has identified certain groups with a higher fostering propensity who could be targeted, including women, larger households and those from minoritised ethnic backgrounds, particularly black households.But there also needs to be a focus on retaining current foster carers as well as recruiting new ones, Homden said.Research has shown a number of factors are pushing foster carers to leave the sector, including feeling undervalued or ignored by social workers, and financial strain – the Fostering Network foundonly 33% of carers report their allowances fully cover the cost of raising a child.“We need to see a focus on targeting key areas and groups, clear information and practical support to boost both recruitment and retention of foster carers,” said Homden.Polling by the Department for Education found that two-thirds (66%) of people believe they could be a good foster carer if practical barriers were removed.Explore more on these topicsFosteringChildrenEnglandSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20m | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Former investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct Authority
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Former investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct Authority
Content: BitMEX cofounder Ben Delo donated £36m to Reform, saying he wanted to see a ‘level playing field’.Photograph: Anne Schwarz PhotographyView image in fullscreenBitMEX cofounder Ben Delo donated £36m to Reform, saying he wanted to see a ‘level playing field’.Photograph: Anne Schwarz PhotographyReform UKCryptocurrency exchange founded by Reform donor Ben Delo sued for £20mFormer investor alleges BitMEX sold products in UK despite not being regulated by Financial Conduct AuthorityDaniel BoffeyChief reporterTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cryptocurrency exchange founded by the billionaireReform UKdonor Ben Delo is being sued for £20m over claims that the company mis-sold financial products in the UK.Lewis Barber, who is a software engineer, alleges that BitMEX offered crypto derivative products to investors in the UK, despite not being regulated or approved to do so by theFinancial Conduct Authority(FCA).The claim filed at the high court but not yet served on BitMEX contends that under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 such contracts are void and that consumers are entitled to restitution of any bitcoin lost on those trades.Barber claims that he lost bitcoin between 2018 and 2022 to the value of £20m through trading the derivatives offered by BitMEX, which amplified gains or losses for investors depending on the changing value of the cryptocurrency.View image in fullscreenThe Seychelles-based company BitMEX closed in September 2026.Photograph: dennizn/AlamyBarber’s lawyers allege he may be one of thousands of non-professional investors in the UK who sustained heavy losses after being sold derivative products by BitMEX in breach of FCA rules and consumer protection laws.Barber’s claim is against HDR Global Trading Limited, the owner and operator of the BitMEX cryptocurrency derivatives exchange which has been shut down.Barber’s statement of claim says that BitMEX “conducted promotional campaigns on a worldwide basis and did not exclude the United Kingdom from their reach”.It goes on: “The Defendant placed at least one advertisement in the Times (published on 3 January 2019) which promoted the Defendant”.The claim alleges that “the financial products that it was offering to [Barber] in the United Kingdom did not fall within the scope of financial services regulation in the United Kingdom”.It adds: “On or around 3 March 2020, the FCA issued a warning that the Defendant may have been conducting trading in regulated investments in the United Kingdom without FCA authorisation.”A spokesperson for BitMex said: “No such claim has been served on HDR Global Trading Limited.”Gareth Keillor, a partner at Seladore Legal which is representing Barber, said: “This is a substantial claim concerning losses sustained by Lewis over a number of years.“Lewis’s case is that BitMEX entered into these transactions without the authorisation required under UK law, and that the Financial Services and Markets Act therefore entitles him to recover the bitcoin he lost, or equivalent damages.“The proceedings may also have wider relevance. Other UK-based persons may have entered into similar contracts with BitMEX, although whether any individual has a claim will depend on the particular facts and trading history.”Details about the case have emerged after BitMEX’s voluntary closure on 23 September 2026, after what it described as a strategic review of the business.The Seychelles-based company faces a number of actions internationally. In New York, investors are suing BitMEX for alleged theft of bitcoin and insider trading in a multimillion-dollar class action. The claims have been vigorously denied.In Britain,Delo has been in the spotlight over a record-breaking £36m donationto the Reform party. Delo wrote in the Daily Telegraph that he was making the gift to Reform because he wanted a “fair fight and a level playing field”.Delo, alongside cofounders Arthur Hayes and Samuel Reed, pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges in the US for violating the Bank Secrecy Act due to alleged failures to comply with anti-money-laundering procedures.They were fined and given custodial sentences, but were granted a pardon by Donald Trump in March 2025.In 2024, BitMEX itself pleaded guilty to violations of the Bank Secrecy Act in failing to maintain adequate anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer programmes, and in January 2025 was required to pay $100m (£75m) to the US Department of Justice.In his claim, Barber seeks the return of all bitcoin he lost in trading with BitMEX, or damages for trades going back a number of years. Should Barber be successful in his claims, the bill for BitMEX could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, it is claimed by his lawyers.Explore more on these topicsReform UKFinancial Conduct AuthorityCryptocurrenciesBitcoinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests | Language | The Guardian
description: Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
Content: Learning a language effectively requires prolonged exposure to its sounds.Photograph: Dimitrios Symeonidis/AlamyView image in fullscreenLearning a language effectively requires prolonged exposure to its sounds.Photograph: Dimitrios Symeonidis/AlamyLanguageStop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggestsResearch shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech soundsAnna BawdenTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests.A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words.Normally, when people learn a language, they try to understand it through the sounds of their native tongue. The more different the foreign language’s sounds and pronunciation are from the native language, the harder the new language will probably be to learn.But the best linguists master even the trickiest pronunciation much more easily. ​To find out why, researchers at UCL and Tohoku University, Japan, compared the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight changes in pitch, length and tone, in non-speech sounds. Using functional MRI scans, they measured participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between English vowel sounds that do not occur in Japanese.They found that those with higher auditory precision mastered the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners and relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Instead, their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds.With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds.In contrast, those with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native language when processing unfamiliar sounds.The latest findings challenge stereotypes that Britons are less adept at languages. Prof Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, the lead author and professor of second language education at UCL Institute of Education, said: “I do not think British people are biologically bad at languages. The problem is more likely to be that many people receive too little meaningful exposure, combined with teaching methods that do not necessarily train the auditory skills needed to make the most of that limited exposure.“If you only hear and use the language for a small number of hours each week, having a good ear may make a much bigger difference. Learners with high auditory precision can make very effective use of relatively sparse input, whereas others may need much more exposure before unfamiliar sounds begin to become established,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAçaí, chipotle and gnocchi – and other words you are probably mispronouncingRead moreThe findings also suggest schools should focus on sounds much more than just grammar and vocabulary when teaching modern languages, he added.“Foreign language education should move beyond an approach based on ‘more practice’ and towards one that develops learners’ ear for language learning in line with their auditory characteristics,” he said.Responding to the findings, Prof Padraic Monaghan, professor of cognition at Lancaster University, said: “Traditional language learning relies on structured practice, but our brains are naturally attuned to acquire languages through exposure. This study confirms how vital listening is to learning, though learners vary in their sound sensitivity at least in the early stages of hearing new language sounds.”​Explore more on these topicsLanguageLinguisticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rules, London’s oldest restaurant, donated to National Trust | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Historic eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 years
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Historic eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 years
Content: Rules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRules in Covent Garden. Owner JP Mayhew donated the restaurant to the National Trust, saying it will ‘protect this place in a way that no one else could’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianRestaurantsRules, London’s oldest restaurant, donated to National TrustHistoric eatery in capital’s theatreland given to heritage charity after changing hands only three times in 228 yearsEsther AddleyandGeorge Francis LeeTue 13 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Thomas Rule served his first oyster to diners on Maiden Lane in London’s Covent Garden, “mad” George III was on the throne of England, John Adams was US president and William Pitt the Younger had just come up with a wheeze called income tax to pay for the Napoleonic wars.More than two centuries later,Rules, the restaurant Thomas founded in what became the capital’s theatreland, has outlasted nine British monarchs and45 prime ministers– but has changed hands only three times. The interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century, nor has the tone of its determinedly meaty menu – think rabbit rillettes, shin of veal and roast guinea fowl.View image in fullscreenEstablished in 1798, Rules was once frequented by the likes of Charles Dickens, Laurence Olivier and Charlie Chaplin.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianRules was beloved by Dickens and Thackeray, inspired Graham Greene and was a favourite of Charlie Chaplin, Laurence Olivier and Ava Gardner. But even London’s oldest restaurant can feel vulnerable to the winds of change, leading the man who bought Rules in 1984 to take perhaps the most significant step in its long history. JP Mayhew has now donated the restaurant’s historic home to theNational Trust, assured that the heritage charity will “protect this place in a way that no one else could”.“With many years of hard work, and some extraordinary strokes of luck, Rules has survived everything from redevelopment plans and changing tastes to the blitz ,” Mayhew said. By taking on the historic and listed 34-35 Maiden Lane, he added , the National Trust would “[safeguard] its bricks and mortar, its famous interior and its invisible atmosphere too. I am grateful to them for believing in this idea and for protecting this building and two centuries worth of stories for people to enjoy forever”.View image in fullscreenThe interior of its four-storey home, stuffed with historic playbills and vintage caricatures and gilded antlers, is little changed from the 19th century.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThe £11m “landmark” gift is one of the most valuable in the National Trust’s recent history, and will mark its first entry into the restaurant business – although its portfolio includes 39 historic pubs and a number of country house hotels, includingClivedenin Buckinghamshire.Not that the heritage charity will be taking on the napkin-folding and the slow cooking of pork cheeks. While Mayhew is donating the historic building and its contents, he sold the restaurant business toRicky McMenemy, its longstanding general manager, in 2022; McMenemy will become a commercial tenant of the National Trust.View image in fullscreenDiners can expect little change to the menu, said  Lucy Porten from the National Trust: ‘It’s not a National Trust menu … there will be no scones.’Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian“Our involvement, day to day, will probably be very light touch,” said Lucy Porten, a national curator for the charity. “It will always be run as a restaurant.
