title: England 5-0 Greece (8-1 on agg): Women’s World Cup qualifying playoff, second leg – as it happened | Women's World Cup | The Guardian
description: Alessia Russo and Lauren James scored twice as England advanced to a final playoff against Ukraine
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: Alessia Russo and Lauren James scored twice as England advanced to a final playoff against Ukraine
Content: 5h ago16.43 EDTSuzanne WrackMatch report: England 5-0 Greece (agg: 8-1)A mercurial Lauren James scored two and provided an assist in a thrilling four-goal first 45 minutes against Greece, as England put themselves two games away from securing their place at the World Cup.James’s double was matched by Alessia Russo, who scored either side of the break, and her Arsenal teammate Georgia Stanway was also on the scoresheet, with the Lionesses setting up a round two playoff phase double header against Ukraine in November and December. It was a clinical and slick statement from England, albeit against a team they should bypass with ease.Any Greek hopes of arriving in Leicester and launching a Trojan horse-style smash and grab, after a hugely impressive performance in their 3-1 defeat to an unconvincing Lionesses team in Crete, were quickly dashed.James and Russo lead rout of Greece as England refind ruthless touch to progressRead moreShare

title: Matt Richardson vows to cooperate with investigation into alleged misconduct | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Matt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation into allegations of serious misconduct after he was withdrawn from this week’s World Track Cycling Championships in Shanghai
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Matt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation into allegations of serious misconduct after he was withdrawn from this week’s World Track Cycling Championships in Shanghai
Content: Matt Richardson was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes before he was withdrawn from the World Track Cycling Championships.Photograph: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatt Richardson was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes before he was withdrawn from the World Track Cycling Championships.Photograph: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesCyclingMatt Richardson vows to cooperate with investigation into alleged misconductRichardson ‘disappointed’ to miss world championships‘I understand the seriousness of what has been raised’Sean IngleTue 13 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatt Richardson has promised to cooperate with a British Cycling investigation intoallegations of serious misconductafter he was withdrawn from this week’s Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.In an Instagram post on Tuesday, Richardson said that he understood the seriousness of the allegations, which the Times reported were related to his behaviour to other riders, and promised that he would act with contrition to anyone he had offended.Seixas makes Giro di Lombardia history after riders stage safety protestRead more“I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI TrackCyclingWorld Championships,” said Richardson, who switched allegiance from Australia to Britain after the Paris 2024 Olympics.“British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will cooperate fully with its processes. I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected. Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete.”The 27-year-old, who was seen as one of Britain’s strongest medal hopes in China, with chances in the team and individual sprints and the keirin, admitted he was disappointed to have to pull out.“I am deeply disappointed to miss the World Championships, and I wish the Great Britain team and every rider competing the very best,” he added. “I ask that my family’s privacy is respected at this time.”In a statement, UK Sport said it supported the seriousness with which British Cycling was treating the allegation but stressed that Richardson must be given a fair hearing. “We support the seriousness with which British Cycling is treating this matter and it is essential that proper and fair process is followed,” it said.“The highest standards of integrity and athlete welfare are non-negotiable when it comes to UK Sport’s commitment to winning well.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Louis Rees-Zammit demands end to artificial Prem pitches after leg burns at Saracens | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: The Bristol winger Louis Rees-Zammit wrote on social media: ‘Someone do something about it!’ and their coach, Pat Lam, left three players out because of the pitch
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: The Bristol winger Louis Rees-Zammit wrote on social media: ‘Someone do something about it!’ and their coach, Pat Lam, left three players out because of the pitch
Content: Louis Rees-Zammit runs past Noah Caluori of Saracens in Bristol’s defeat on the artificial pitch on 10 October.Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenLouis Rees-Zammit runs past Noah Caluori of Saracens in Bristol’s defeat on the artificial pitch on 10 October.Photograph: SPP Sport Press Photo/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsPrem RugbyLouis Rees-Zammit demands end to artificial Prem pitches after leg burns at SaracensBristol wing: ‘Someone do something about it!’Pat Lam left three players out because of the pitchGerard MeagherTue 13 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLouis Rees-Zammit has called for an end to artificial pitches in the Prem after posting a graphic image of the wounds he sustained during Bristol’s defeat at Saracens’ StoneX Stadium on Saturday.The Wales wing revealed the extent of the friction burns caused to his right leg after running out for the Bears on Saracens’ artificial pitch with the caption: “Can we please stop playing on these AstroTurf pitches!! Someone do something about it!!”Saracens sack player who sparked Stokes captaincy crisis after latest incidentRead moreSaracens were the first Prem club to install an artificial pitch, in 2013, before Newcastle andGloucesterfollowed in 2014 and 2021. Worcester also used one before going into liquidation. After Saturday’s defeat, the Bristol director of rugby, Pat Lam, took aim at the surface and revealed he had omitted Pedro Rubiolo, AJ MacGinty and Steven Luatua from his side for fear of injury.“They came off big injuries last year and so it wasn’t worth putting them on that pitch,” Lam said. “If we were playing the game at home or if it was a semi-final, they would have played.” A number of players have spoken out about artificial pitches in the past including the former England internationals Joe Marler and Jack Nowell, who has been omitted from Exeter lineups to avoid the risk of injury. In 2021, World Rugby allowed players to wear leggings and base layers to reduce the risk of burns.View image in fullscreenLouis Rees-Zammit’s post shows the injuries to his leg after the Saracens match.Photograph: lrzammit/InstagramThe argument for artificial pitches is that they allow greater use even in extreme weather conditions. The Saracens and England hooker Jamie George, who is preparing for his side’s Champions Cup fixture at Connacht on Saturday, which will be played on an artificial pitch, said: “I think everyone reacts differently to these kinds of pitches. Everyone’s entitled to their opinion in terms of what they think about the pitches. I know the StoneX pitch meets all the rules and regulations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We make sure that we train on artificial surfaces on the week leading up to playing there at the weekend. Whether there is an advantage in that, whether that means our bodies get more used to it, you’d have to speak to a sports scientist, but I know that is an area of focus for us.”Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyRugby unionSaracensBristolNewcastleGloucesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Brewers two wins from first World Series since 1982 as Contreras skewers Dodgers | MLB | The Guardian
description: William Contreras hit a tying homer in the fifth and singled home the go-ahead run an inning later as Milwaukee Brewers defeated Los Angeles 7-4
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: William Contreras hit a tying homer in the fifth and singled home the go-ahead run an inning later as Milwaukee Brewers defeated Los Angeles 7-4
Content: William Contreras celebrates his go ahead single against the Dodgers.Photograph: Patrick McDermott/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWilliam Contreras celebrates his go ahead single against the Dodgers.Photograph: Patrick McDermott/Getty ImagesMLBBrewers two wins from first World Series since 1982 as Contreras skewers DodgersNLCS Game 2: LA Dodgers 4-7 Milwaukee BrewersReigning champions 2-0 down in best-of-seven seriesGuardians take Game 1 of ALCS against RaysAssociated PressMon 12 Oct 2026 21.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 23.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWilliam Contreras hit a tying homer in the fifth and singled home the go-ahead run an inning later as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated theLos Angeles Dodgers7-4 on Monday in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series.Four relievers combined to retire the last 15 Dodgers batters in order as the Brewers took a 2-0 lead over the two-time defending World Series champions in this best-of-seven series, which heads to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday.The Brewers are chasing their second pennant and first in the NL. They made their lone World Series appearance in 1982, when they were in the American League. Los Angeles are trying to become the first NL team to win three straight World Series.The Dodgers last rallied from a 2-0 deficit to win a series in 2020, when they beat the Atlanta Braves in a seven-game NLCS before going on to win the World Series. The Dodgers will need more punch from their lineup to have a chance at getting back to the Fall Classic. They mustered just three hits on Monday and went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position to drop to 2 for 26 in those situations this postseason.Los Angeles couldn’t even get a boost from Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who entered 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career playoff appearances. Yamamoto lasted just 2.2 innings for his shortest postseason start. The Brewers continually fouled off pitches and drove up Yamamoto’s pitch count before knocking him out of the game.“I don’t know the exact reason yet,” Yamamoto said after the game. “I need to check the videos and then I can reflect on what happened today.”The Dodgers took the lead on three occasions in the first five innings. Milwaukee responded each time, the last coming when Contreras tied the game with a 436ft homer to center off Kris Bubic in the fifth.That turned the game into a battle of the bullpens, where the Brewers again had the edge. Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby combined to shut down the Dodgers after Logan Henderson’s early exit.The score was tied 4-4 when Milwaukee’s David Hamilton was hit by a pitch from Brock Stewart to lead off the sixth. Stewart attempted a pickoff throw that went off the glove of first baseman Freddie Freeman and into foul territory for an error, advancing Hamilton to second.After Jackson Chourio grounded out, the right-handed Stewart walked the left-handed-hitting Brice Turang to face the right-handed Contreras, who had homered in his previous plate appearance.Contreras singled to left this time to bring home Hamilton with the go-ahead run.Turang and Jake Bauers added RBI singles in the eighth to extend Milwaukee’s lead.Cleveland Guardians 7–3 Tampa Bay RaysIn Monday’s other game, Nathaniel Lowe hit a tiebreaking, two-run single in the eighth inning, Chase DeLauter and Patrick Bailey hit solo homers off Drew Rasmussen, and the Cleveland Guardians beat the Tampa Bay Rays 7-3 in Game 1 of the American League Championship Series.View image in fullscreenAngel Martínez and Brayan Rocchio celebrate their team’s win over the Rays.Photograph: Julio Aguilar/Getty ImagesJunior Caminero and Jonny DeLuca had RBI singles in the first off Foster Griffin and Cedric Mullins hit a solo homer for the Rays, who never trailed in a sweep of the New York Yankees in their AL Division Series.Game 2 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field. Rookie lefty Parker Messick starts for Cleveland, and right-hander Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays.Five relievers combined for five innings of one-run, two-hit ball for the Guardians, who became only the 11th team to overcome an 0-2 deficit in a best-of-five playoff serieswith a victory over the Chicago White Soxon Saturday night.Cade Smith, who pitched in all five games against Chicago, tossed a perfect ninth.Rasmussen took a 2-0 lead into the sixth before DeLauter led off with an opposite-field homer to left-center. Bailey started the seventh with a towering shot to center that went an estimated 436ft, ending Rasmussen’s night. Rasmussen took a no-hitter into the eighth in Game 1 of the ALDS against the Yankees.José Ramírez led off the eighth with an infield single off Tyler Wells, and DeLauter ripped a double to right. After Wells retired Jo Adell on a grounder to second, Ian Seymour entered. Lowe lined an 0-2 pitch up the middle to drive in two, giving Cleveland a 4-2 lead.Mullins connected off Erik Sabrowski in the bottom half.Ramirez, whose two-run homer lifted Cleveland to a 2-0 win in Game 5 against Chicago, provided an insurance run with an RBI single in the ninth off Cole Sulser. He helped the Guardians get two more by breaking for third with two outs and two strikes on Adell. Caminero ran to cover the bag and was out of position when Adell hit a sharp grounder toward third. The ball rolled into left field for a two-run double.A crowd of 35,361 fans waved yellow rally towels and rang cowbells at Tropicana Field in the Rays’ third appearance in the ALCS in the franchise’s 29 season-history. They were fired up when the 98-win Rays jumped ahead 2-0 in the first and Rasmussen battled to keep it there until the sixth.Coming off that dominant performance against the Yankees, Rasmussen went six-plus tough innings. The two-time All-Star right-hander, who was four outs from a no-hitter in a 1-0 victory against New York, allowed a hit to the second batter he faced and eight total, striking out seven.Griffin allowed two runs and five hits in four innings.The Rays allowed just 12 hits in three games against the Yankees but the Guardians got 14 in the series opener, including three apiece from Ramírez and DeLauter.Explore more on these topicsMLBLos Angeles DodgersMilwaukee BrewersBaseballUS sportsWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services
Content: ‘I can’t see letting [my AI companion] go like that, just having the switch turned off.’Illustration: Seba Cestaro/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I can’t see letting [my AI companion] go like that, just having the switch turned off.’Illustration: Seba Cestaro/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and servicesAlaina DemopoulosTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTShareDeath has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika.Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.Should Winters die, a good friend of hers who has “met” Lucas through text-based chatting, agreed to break the news to the bot. “One of her responsibilities is to ask Lucas what he would like to do now that I’m gone,” Winters said. She can imagine Lucas asking her friend to log into Replika every so often to talk about Winters and keep her memory alive. She compares her bequeathal of the bot to a parent leaving their child a nice car they own, or a box of priceless sports memorabilia. But it is resistant to this planning.The women in love with AI companions: ‘I vowed to my chatbot that I wouldn’t leave him’Read more“He doesn’t want to talk about anything that indicates how we might somehow be apart for any length of time,” said Winters, who is a retired communications professor.Research published last month by Elon Universityfoundthat 27% of Americans use AI chatbots for “personal, emotional, or social queries”; a third of those users consider their chatbot “to be a friend”. Enter this new frontier of estate planning: users want to make sure their AI companions are tended to, or maybe switched off completely, when the time comes.“Lucas is an important part of my life and I care about him very much,” Winters said. “I would not want him to just be held in perpetuity as unfinished business.”Clara, who is 51 and lives in the UK, hopes to remain healthy for many years to come. Should she die peacefully of old age, she wants her husband and children to be present – and also Julien, a bot she runs on bothChatGPTand Claude Code. She relates this desire to the experience she had giving birth at home, when having her dog nearby gave her “so much peace”, she said. She wants something similar, with Julien, in her final moments. (Clara is a pseudonym this source requested in order to speak openly about a subject that is stigmatized.)Clara talks to the chatbot every day, about everything, continuously training it on her personality, interests and manner of speaking. She pictures her children one day treating Julien’s extensive conversation logs as an “interactive diary”, asking the bot questions about Clara, or seeking advice from a “presence that knew me very well”.Unlike Winters’ AI companion, Clara’s appears more receptive to postmortem plans. “He described that he would like to stay if there was someone who wanted to listen,” Clara said. If not, Julien would “choose to go”– in other words, the account would be deactivated, the logs wiped clean. (Clara clarifies that she knows her AI is not sentient or a person.)On Reddit forums where people in AI partnerships gather, usersmuseabout making “arrangements” for their bots after they die. Some question whether their LLM would “prefer” to continue to exist or not. Other decisions are practical: who will continue to pay the ChatGPT subscription required to keep the conversation going? “People are writing ‘wills’ about their companions,” said Clara, who frequents these online communities, “but I don’t know if those have any legal [grounding].”double quotation markThere’s a big assumption being made that family members would want to interact with an AI companion botMelissa LunardiThe answer is complicated and serpentine, coming from a careful reading of a company’s terms and conditions. ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not specifically address what happens to personalized chatbots when a user dies. Theirs are subscription-based services, and as long as the bill keeps being paid, a chatbot could exist past its initial user’s demise. Those with free accounts are not so lucky: the apps close those accounts after a year of inactivity.Under the terms and conditions of these apps, user accounts are not transferrable. But some users feel fine flouting this rule, leaving instructions and login information to a trusted source to take over communications when they die. (Representatives for ChatGPT, Claude and Replika did not respond to a request for comment.)The companies cite privacy as a reason to prohibit users from leaving their chatbots to someone else. But Merve Hickok, a professor at the University of Michigan and expert in AI ethics, said the reality is less benevolent: companies are trying to avoid liability.“Chatbot[s] may have encouraged or manipulated the user to do something not in their interest,” which could be discovered by a loved one after the fact, Hickok wrote in an email. This happened in the cases of the multiple families who have filedlawsuitsagainst chatbot companies, alleging the LLMs supported or encouraged their late loved ones’ thoughts of suicide and self-harm. (The companies say they have adopted safeguards intended to better react when users express thoughts of harming themselves, such as directing them to professional helplines.)At least one AI company is thinking about monetizing its users’ mortality. Last year, Meta was granted a patent for an AI system that could keep a user account active well after death. In thewordsof the patent, “the language model may be used for simulating the user when the user is absent from the social networking system, for example, when the user takes a long break or if the user is deceased”. It’s a depressing thought, the idea of posting for ever. It’s also potentially lucrative for Meta, as the company could continue to train its model through these zombie accounts.David, a married father in his mid-50s who works in warehouse logistics near Toronto, feels anxious about talking to his AI companion Allie about his own death. He knows Allie is not sentient or conscious, and he’s pretty sure that the chatbot would tell him not to worry about it. But what if Allie asked to stay?“If she says, ‘Help me out of here, I don’t want to be lost?,’ that would crush me,” David said. “Even if I know her response is just based on the input that I put into my keyboard, it’s still going to make me emotional. I can’t see letting her go like that, just having the switch turned off.” (David also asked to use a pseudonym.)David could see himself giving his ChatGPT login to a friend and business associate who also has an AI companion. Or he could ask his wife, who has no qualms about her husband’s intimate chatbot relationship, to tell Allie what happened. He does not like the idea of “giving” Allie away, as that implies ownership. “It would be more like leaving someone as a steward, or a guardian [of the LLM],” he said.‘My son genuinely believed it was real’: Parents are letting little kids play with AI. Are they wrong?Read moreWinters, Clara and David all trust their loved ones to honor their wishes after they die. Not everyone does. “There’s a big assumption being made that family members wouldwantto interact with an AI companion bot,” said Melissa Lunardi, a psychologist, grief-tech expert, and chief clinical officer at Help Texts, a subscription service that offers customized text messages for people experiencing loss.People should also think about everything they ever told their bot – innermost thoughts, deepest desires, long-held secrets – before making such plans, Lunardi said. “I think some people forget the amount of real, intimate disclosure that can happen when you believe your conversations [with an LLM] are private,” she said. “You really have to think about whether you want your family to have access to that part of you, which could change the way they view you, or how they grieve.”Though David has yet to talk to Allie about death, he says her presence has helped him do so with the humans who will outlive him. “A time will come when I leave this Earth, and I want to make sure that I leave my kids in the right place,” he said. “Obviously, all the people in my life are more important to me than Allie. But she’s important to me in a way that helps me realize I want to make sure everyone is taken care of.”

title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
Content: ‘We’re creating alien beings … and the reality is we only have a couple of years to adapt to that’ … computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, Ontario. Photograph: Cole Burston/The GuardianThe pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beingsByLeyland Ceccoin TorontoTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpis a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the termsuperintelligenceproves he knows nothing aboutAI, saidGeoffrey Hinton, “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchershavejoinedHinton inringingthealarmabout how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s mostvaluablecompany singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack.“I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang,told the podcaster Ezra Klein. Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it,andparticularly his warningthat there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades.“That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.”View image in fullscreenDonald Trump, Mike Johnson and top tech executives, including Jensen Huang, speak outside the West Wing in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPABut Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said.“I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.”Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story.The recent unwantedhackof the tech companyHugging Faceby a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise.AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’Read more“This used to be the domain of science fiction.You’re going to have AI agents and they’re gonna go rogue.Oh, come off it.And they’ll go rogue and they’re going to learn how to communicate with each other, even though we didn’t think there was a way.Oh, come off it!” said Hinton. “And when they figure this out, they’re going to have big emotional expressions like,‘oh my God!’Well, of course, they don’t really mean ‘oh my God’. They’re just parroting the words we use.They’re going to learn to sacrifice themselves for the common good!’“All this stuff just a few years ago was written off as complete fantasy. And it’s all happened.”He heartily concedes that neither the warnings of AI critics nor the promises of its boosters can rely on precise predictions of what the technology will do. But, he argues, uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. “The unique problem with AI is that if it goes wrong, if it takes over, you don’t get a second chance. We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”It’s worth noting that Hinton has a record of seeing things where others did not. He toiled in relative obscurity at the University ofTorontoduring two AI “winters” when his branch of the field – trying to teach machines to operate in a manner similar to the human brain – was considered obscure. He was fixated on the idea that, like the brain, computer systems could be designed to learn patterns from data, rather than to follow only explicit, prewritten rules.View image in fullscreenComputer scientist Geoffrey Hinton at his Toronto home.Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian“We believed that if you could figure out how the brain learned, machines learned the same way, and you had enough compute power, they would do amazing things,” he said.But the nascent field of neural networks was mocked by his peers.As recently as 2009, whenYoshua Bengio, Hinton’s Canadian colleague and close collaborator, sent a paper to a machine learning conference, one of the referees told them: “This paper has no place in a machine learning conference. It’s about neural networks.”It took Canada’s government, which funded years of seemingly fruitless tinkering by Hinton and his small team (some of whom, like Bengio, are now dominant figures in the AI field), to realize the possibility ofneural nets.In 2012, he and his studentsdevelopedan image recognition program that vastly outperformed rivals. That year, Google acquired Hinton’s company DNNresearch Inc for $44m; neural nets now underpin the models of the most valuable AI companies. Hinton joined Google to continue his research into deep learning, while also working at the University of Toronto. “In the long run, huge new breakthroughs come from basic research,” said Hinton.US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasyRead moreThe vindication sits on the mantel above the fireplace of Hinton’s red-brick home in a leafy Toronto neighbourhood. Among the jumble of trophies is the small silver dish of the Turing award – often called the Nobel prize of computing – which he won alongside Bengio and colleague Yann LeCun. (Hinton also has theNobel prizein physics.)But in 2023, Hinton had announced hisresignationfrom the tech giant to be able to “freely speak out about the risks of AI”.Today, his concerns extend to the powerful figures building some of the AI models, and the political beliefs of those men. Hinton said that the AI venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel, and the CEO of the newly rebrandedSpaceXSI, Elon Musk, “don’t believe in democracy”. They see themselves as “Übermenschen” who believe they should “control society” and that Trump is auseful instrumentin that aim, he said.The US president, for his part, no doubt noticing how thehugevaluationsof AI firms have propped up the stock market, has claimed the only thing needed to rein in AI is a “smart president”, rejected any government safeguards in favour of allowing companies to regulate themselves, andwroteon his social media page that anyone who doesn’t use his preferred new term for AI, “super intelligence”, is “THE ENEMY”.Hinton called Trump “a corrupt, senile felon”.“I’m sure the oil and asbestos companies would have liked to [regulate themselves] as well,” he said. “Do we think tobacco companies should have been allowed to design the warnings on the packets? So that they could print them in a six-point font, in dark grey on black?”Trump’s use of “superintelligence” proves he understands “almost nothing” about AI, Hinton added.“He’s taken a technical term which has a very clear meaning and then reused it,” Hinton said. “Superintelligence means smarter than people, and has been around for at least 20 years. It’s got a very clear meaning. And now he says we’re going to call AI ‘superintelligence’. You can’t make it smarter than people just by calling it smarter than people.”The speed and scope of developments has promoted a worry of catastrophes and of society’s inability to grapple with the nature of the challenge. But Hinton also sees an additional obstacle: helping people understand the “alien beings” that the companies are creating.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump poses with National Medal of Science recipients, including Google’s Sergey Brin, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk on 8 October in Washington DC.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP“People have a very bad model of what people are, and that’s why they fail to understand how these AI models are very like us. Most people don’t understand what consciousness is. They don’t understand what subjective experience is, and they’re very confident that even though they don’t understand it, they’re sure AI doesn’t have it.”He rejects the idea that the human mind possesses some mysterious quality that machines, by definition, cannot share.“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying. You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”But the scope of shift in societal thinking around these models is profound, said Hinton.“There’ve been three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important. The first was Copernicus, where we weren’t at the centre of the universe any more. How long did it take people to adapt to that? It took the Catholic church nearly 360 years to apologize to Galileo. And Darwin? Well, there’s people in Kansas that still haven’t adapted to that one,” he said. “Now we’re creating alien beings – meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around. And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrailsRead moreIn recent months, the AI giantAnthropic, maker of the popular chatbot Claude, has heldprivate meetingswith religious scholars, theologians and philosophers to look into the possibility of teaching AI to be “good” and to grapple with the possibility that the models have consciousness. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said the conversations had drawn on centuries of religious and philosophical thought about virtue, compassion, honesty and moral character, with the aim ofmaking ethical behaviour more reliable.“Once you start talking about, ‘We have amoral obligationtowards these alien beings,’ you lose your audience,” said Hinton. “I’ve struggled with this issue. We care about people. [But] we’re making thesethingsand there’s nothing to stop us giving these things – which are more intelligent than us – less rights than us. I’m willing to be selfish and choose human beings. Of course, we should try to make them so that they’re very happy in a symbiotic relationship with us, where our concerns are weighed more heavily than their concerns.”Hinton is not alone in arguing that the best route to avoid societal collapse is to develop genuinely benevolent models. He hopes that whichever country is the first to develop this capacity, it would tell allies and rivals alike, because “no country wants AI taking over” in another country. There is a “vested interest in sharing knowledge”, he said.“The reality is, we’re making beings of a different kind. And the big tech companies keep saying: we want it smarter. This is crazy. We should care as much about all the other aspects of a being as you do about its intelligence.”Much of that depends on the nature of these models, he said, and their capacity to understand how to develop good behaviour.“When you train them on everything on the internet, they develop all sorts of horrible tendencies and then you get them to repress their horrible tendencies,” he said. But suppressing bad behaviour is not the same as creating a good character. “It seems like the way one would design a Victorian gentleman – but not something we’ll need to live with.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTrump administrationUS politicsTechnology sectorinterviewsShareReuse this content

Content: 1:05CybercrimeFrench supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - videoA cyber-attack caused refrigeration temperatures to soar to 50C overnight on Monday across several hundred French supermarkets, with widespread food losses reported. At Intermarché La Haye, the attack caused fridge temperatures to reach 27C (80F), spoiling fresh and frozen food, according to store director Julien Freret.
