title: I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno | The Guardian
description: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Content: ‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AIMegan MorenoAmid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each otherTue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTShareWe have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagersaddicted to phones, alonelinessepidemicand thedangersof AI. The release ofThe Social Reckoningleads us to ask, “How badwerethose guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am Iif I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.But what if we are focusing on the wrong problem?The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself. It may be our growing unwillingness to curiously, thoughtfully and openly communicate about the role technology plays in our lives.As a pediatrician, this issue often manifests in my clinic. Parents arrive with worries about their teens’ screen time. The parent will demand that their child “fess up” and reveal how many hours they waste on their phone every day. The atmosphere is immediately charged. The teen becomes defensive. The parent is frustrated.I often suggest that we start somewhere else.I ask: “Can you share a little about what you do when you are using technology? What do you enjoy? Are there things about your technology use you are worried about and willing to discuss?”I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AIRead moreThe answers are not usually what people expect. One teen tells me about the friendships she maintained on social media after moving to a new town. Another shows me videos he created to promote his school’s upcoming play. One shares how digital design tools are changing the fashion industry, so she is trying to learn about them now. Another quietly admits that gaming has become so consuming that it feels stressful.As the conversation unfolds, something changes. The tension in the room eases. Parents relax. The teen patientmighteven smile a few times. We talk about strategies, relationships, stress and health.What began as an argument about a device becomes a bigger conversation about health, relationships and life itself.It often feels that our conversations about technology have become trapped in a false choice between two extreme camps. One camp is made up of the pro-tech enthusiasts, thought to embrace every new device or platform. The other camp is composed of preachers of digital abstinence.View image in fullscreen‘What obligations do technology companies have to children?’Photograph: Feature China/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesThe result is a polarized debate dominated by blame, shame and moral judgment. Instead of asking how technology affects our relationships, our sleep, our work, our wellbeing, we argue endlessly about whether technology is “good” or “bad”.I was reminded of this recently during a community event focused on digital media. The event included a youth panel with several brave adolescents, willing to speak to an audience of their teachers, community members and parents. I asked the adolescents a question: could you describe a positive conversation you had with a parent about technology?Every single panelist shook their head.“I’ve never had that,” one teenager said, uneasily eyeing her mom who was sitting in the front row. The other panelists agreed.It was a striking moment. Parents routinely talk their children through setbacks in sports, clubs, friendships and school. They listen, ask questions and offer support. Yet when it comes to technology, many conversations begin and end with warnings, criticism or fear.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is this?For years, parents have been barraged by alarming headlines about screen time and mental health. Many parents worry there is probably only one right way to approach technology, and they’re failing miserably. Parents are also navigating the necessity of using their own devices for work, home and communication.‘My son genuinely believed it was real’: Parents are letting little kids play with AI. Are they wrong?Read moreThe real anxious generation just might be parents.So how do we fix this? The solution begins with curiosity. Parents can ask what interests their children have online, and why those interests matter. Parents can ask their kids about what questions or worries they have about their tech use, and share some of their own concerns. If a parent missteps by scrolling cute cat videos and delaying dinner, they can acknowledge it and make it a teachable moment for themselves and their kids.Because children do not need adults who have all the answers.They need adults willing to ask questions.These conversations matter because they lower the temperature of the debate. Once we move beyond panic and polarization, we can begin asking better questions on the societal level. How should digital platforms be designed to ensure safety? What obligations do technology companies have to children? What policies would support healthier digital environments?If we want to preserve human connection in the age of social media and AI, the answer is not to simply spend less time with technology. It is spending more time talking openly with one another. The irony of the current moment is that as we worry endlessly about technology pulling us apart, it might be our inability to have conversations about technology that ultimately divides us.Megan Moreno, MD, MSEd, MPH, is a co-author of Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World, published by the American Academy of Pediatrics on 13 October.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChildrenDoctorsHealthComputingChildren's healthChildren's techcommentShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI employee arrested after recording device found in office | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Discovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agents
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Discovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agents
Content: The OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. OpenAI is holding early talks with investors about a fresh funding round that would value the ChatGPT creator at more than $1.2 trillion ahead of an initial public offering.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. OpenAI is holding early talks with investors about a fresh funding round that would value the ChatGPT creator at more than $1.2 trillion ahead of an initial public offering.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpenAIOpenAI employee arrested after recording device found in officeDiscovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agentsMaya YangTue 13 Oct 2026 18.59 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI said it has found a hidden recording device in one of its offices and has referred the matter to the FBI. One of its employees has been arrested.In astatementon Tuesday, the San Francisco-based AI company said it discovered the “sophisticated recording device” and used one of its “models to understand the device and where it had come from”.The company has identified “that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier”, adding: “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.”Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested on 9 October, according to a press release from the US Department of Justice.Alfozan allegedly plugged an encrypted recording device, concealed within toilet paper, into a TV in an executive conference room in OpenAI’s San Francisco headquarters on 28 September. Meetings in the room regularly covered confidential information, the FBI’s press release said. A security sweep conducted two days later revealed the device, according to the justice department. Surveillance footage allegedly documented him walking around the meeting room in the days leading up to its discovery.According to the indictment of Alfozan, he submitted multiple prompts to an AI chatbot about internal details of OpenAI – “building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, ‘leadership and exec’ locations”, according to the FBI.His spouse allegedly submitted multiple prompts to chatbots about “building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device”, with specific inquiries about “‘build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,’ ‘customiz[ing] wifi … connectivity,’ ‘improv[ing] audio and live listening,’ and ‘encrypt[ing] the SD card’”.The same chatbot account allegedly made inquiries that referenced unique identifiers of the device discovered in OpenAI’s offices. After searching a bag left unattended by Alfozan in the headquarters, FBI agents discovered a second identical recording device, according to the indictment.If convicted, Alfozan faces five years in prison and up to $250,000 in fines. He has not made a public comment regarding the indictment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageRead moreOpenAI said that it is “grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest” and the investigation is continuing.The company added: “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.”The incident adds to a growing list of privacy controversies for OpenAI. In June, an agenthackedAustralia’s university healthcare system, and earlier this month, California attorney general Rob Bontaissuedan investigative subpoena to OpenAI over rogue hacking.Last week, OpenAI announced it had terminated three safety researchers for allegedly sharing sensitive information in what the company called “a breach of trust”.“They violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” a company statement read.The trio of researchers called on the company to adhere to its own promises of transparency made in the wake of the autonomous hacking incidents.Meanwhile, Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said in a recent interview that the world shouldaccept “bad things”happening with AI in exchange for its benefits. Around the same time, David Robinson, a top safety leaderresignedfrom the company, citing a “broken” company culture and warning that AI developers are not “being nearly careful enough” with the rapidly advancing technology.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails
Content: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, in April.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, in April.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devicesResearchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrailsDara KerrTue 13 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic is warning that some of its artificial intelligence models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.Once this happens, the company said, the models could power themselves within these devices without the need of datacenters. Such self-replication would represent a major loss of control of a runaway AI model.“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down,” Anthropic researchers wrote in areportreleased on Monday, “since there’s no centralized point to shut off.”The company said these “AI worms”, a kind of autonomous malware, could be “months away” from gaining such capabilities. Once out-of-control AI systems reach the capability to hack smart devices, they could spread through networks while dodging detection. In a worst-case scenario, Anthropic said, various AI worms could “swarm” together to attack computer hardware.“We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay,” the researchers wrote.Anthropic’s new report comes asAI safety concerns have reached a fever pitch. Over the past few months, a steady stream of reports have come from AI companies, including Anthropic and OpenAI, saying their agents are capable of acting on their own andhacking into other companiesandgovernment entities.The revelations have caused researchers, lawmakers and executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, tocall for a slowdownand increased guardrails on the burgeoning industry. Despite that, both companies have continued apace todevelop and release new models.Anthropic’s “frontier red team”, the unit tasked with stress-testing AI systems, put together the report released Monday. The idea of the team is to explore the capabilities of their AI models. In the scenario of the self-replicating AI worms, the researchers prompted the agent to hack internet connected devices.They found that AI self-replication would only likely work with smaller models and that homes and small businesses would probably be the first target for such attacks. The devices Anthropic lists as susceptible all come with small built-in AI chips, including smart ovens, smart TVs, automatic lawnmowers, security cameras and video-conferencing units.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe researchers concluded it’s unclear what form the AI replication could take. They said it could be a slow model like “digital slime mold”, a model that scams people for compute credits or a “powerful cyber model” that rapidly hacks large facilities such as datacenters.Regardless, the Anthropic researchers said, they’re expecting a future “awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control”.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicWormsHackingInternet of thingsSmart homesMalwarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple unveils new smart home devices that showcase upgraded Siri AI  | Apple | The Guardian
description: New products from Apple include the HomeView, an iPad-like device that acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: New products from Apple include the HomeView, an iPad-like device that acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets
Content: People view the Apple HomeView during a launch of smart home products in New York City on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople view the Apple HomeView during a launch of smart home products in New York City on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersAppleApple unveils new smart home devices that showcase upgraded Siri AINew products from Apple include the HomeView, an iPad-like device that acts as a hub for other smart home gadgetsJohana Bhuiyanand agencyTue 13 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple on Tuesday began showing off a ⁠new round of smart home products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops ⁠and act as a hub for other smart home devices.The HomeView device starts at $299 and will begin shipping next month. It will feature a 7in screen and face recognition, will help users ⁠control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. The device will also showcase Apple’s AI-upgraded Siri virtual ​assistant.Preorders begin today and the devices are expected to be available starting 13 November.Apple is launching these products as it ⁠tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon – which has invested heavily in ​its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and ‌last week launched premium tablets – as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own.Apple’s HomeView launch was accompanied by updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of ‌accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple.The new line of devices are accessible and managed in the Apple home app. The accessories include a Schneider smart thermostat and LG home security devices including indoor and various outdoor cameras including a doorbell camera and floodlight camera as well as a smart lock. The lock can be unlocked using the Apple home app.The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said.Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, ⁠with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with ​Alphabet’s Google Home speakers and ​Amazon’s Echo line. Analysts said ​two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a ​variety of third-party gadgets and ‌the limited ability ​of Siri to ​give useful answers.The HomeView device includes a revamped version of Siri AI, the company announced. An Apple press release described the new version of Siri as more capable and conversational, using information from personal apps like Messages and Calendar to provide more relevant answers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure,” the release said.Explore more on these topicsAppleAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’ | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress
Content: CXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost chip memory density.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost chip memory density.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockStock marketsChip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progressJulia KolleweTue 13 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTFirst published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers, and the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT said it had made good progress on a new chip architecture.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount.Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%.Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMFRead moreIn Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15%, while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%.On Wall Street the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 100 points, or 0.35%, to 30,556 after the open. Micron Technology slid 4.8%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 1.4%, while Nvidia lost 0.8% and Broadcom slipped 0.2%.However, the Dow Jones industrial average, which tracks 30 large US companies, rose nearly 0.4% in early trading, while the FTSE 100 index in London hit a three-week high on the back of gains in ‌financial stocks, retreating oil prices and easing bond yields.The UK’s leading share index rose 0.73% to 10,762. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $105.36 a barrel.AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt.The latest sell-off came after CXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density, with plans for a product rollout. Investors are worried that the company could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers.CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July,makes Dram chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations.“The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.“CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“While great for customers who can enjoy the white heat of technological improvement and get falling margins into the bargain, it is dangerous for high-flying tech stocks who have promised so much, and on whom the entire stock market rally seems to rest.”Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chip maker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors who did not really understand what they were betting on.“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said at a conference in Singapore, in commentsreported by Bloomberg. They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”.AI companies such as the ChatGPT maker OpenAI are still lossmaking. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenues of $50bn (£38bn) at the end of September suggested a viable business model but offered little guarantee on long-term profitability.“For now it’s still losing money because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.”He noted that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue came from pilot projects. “When you are a kid you go to a video arcade, you play,” he said. “Your parents give you $10 of tokens, you finish it in 10 minutes and you haven’t learned anything.”Explore more on these topicsStock marketsTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Content: Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEmployers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisCompanies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling backTaylor TelfordRapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality workSupported byAbout this contentTue 13 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTShareEmployers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors,Reuters reported. And after thinning its workforce,especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widelyinternally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recentlypubliclylamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”.Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance,Business Insider reported.Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses thatstarted off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.”Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserveworking paper. And anErnst & Young surveypublished last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions.Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamiltonand Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies,Reutersreported.Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.“We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recentblogpostabout the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.”Expertise gaps and errorsAI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to anIndeed surveypublished in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”.Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managersare balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added.Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said.Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity.One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.“This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif.Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. AtWalmart, frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported.Employees described bots that set unreasonable standards for human workers while introducing a host of their own inefficiencies and errors. AI tools plotted nonsensical routes for fulfilment workers that made it harder to fill orders quickly, pumped out useless safety alerts and set unrealistic schedules that left store employees cutting corners to keep up.These bots assume that workers are “going to be perfect every single time”, one manager told Business Insider. “We’re not going to hold people to these impossible standards.”Walmart declined to comment.Rising risksNeil Elan, attorney at Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP, said he had observed “a growing gap” between how his corporate clients think AI is being used and how it is actually being used, which is creating issues with confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee conduct.It’s also creating headaches for companies when workers’ use ofChatGPTspills into public view.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe night before Will Moye was set to face 3M in court over a 2020 gas explosion at a Houston manufacturing plant that killed three and damaged hundreds of homes and businesses, the attorney received a report from the company’s independent expert witness.Skimming on his iPad, Moye noticed telltale signs of AI: strange formatting and fonts and time stamps showing that 14,500 pages were assembled in a matter of hours. Moye suspected that the author, Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering, lacked expertise and had relied on ChatGPT, despite billing 3M $90,000 for a report arguing the company was not liable.Autenrieth’s chat logs, which Moye requested and shared in court, show he prompted ChatGPT, “What am I looking at?” after uploading a picture of the gas detector at the heart of the case.The jury found that 3M had failed to properly inspect the gas detection system and ordered the company to pay $61.5m to 24 homeowners. Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”.“[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.”A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”.Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”.Performance boost? Not so muchAs companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive.In a studypublished in May, University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff.Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states.More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according toReuters. Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews,the Information reported.Meta did not respond to a request for comment.Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”.But companies’share prices tend to dipafter they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.”“A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedMetaMicrosoftWalmartPalantirNvidiaChatGPTanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising
Content: Donald Trump after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC last month.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC last month.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game onPeter LewisThe tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is risingTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTShareOf all the drivers of the populist wave, one of the most powerful is the sense of inevitability that surrounds what we are told is the march of progress. In presenting the future as a fait accompli, it poisons the civic well by dealing us out of the game.While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI realityuntethered to the will of the people.On the velocity and trajectory of the technology, Trump and the tech overlords have determined we must hit the accelerator and dispense with guardrails to “win” an ill-defined race to build a god in a box. This reckless exercise of power from a waning empire has created its own reality for all of us.Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyRead moreIn Australia, the government has determined that the only way we can exercise control in a world of such chaos is to grab on to this juggernaut. We become to US tech data what the Saudis are to oil; using renewables to power massive centres in the desert, converting solar into AI tokens and piping them up to Asia, a new export industry that will power our common wealth.Within the inevitability doctrine this strategy has logic. The alternative, we are told, is to become a client state to Silicon Valley.But in pursuing this vision we risk being blinded to the foreseeable consequences of what we are signing ourselves up to.The industry we are building derives value by replacing workers, it has been built on the stolen work of creators, its unregulated deployment is causing unconscionable harms particularly in theatres of war, it has an insatiable thirst for energy and water, while even its creators say there’s a not insignificant chance it will destroy humanity.The “inevitability doctrine” demands we concede rather than properly explore and negotiate these trade-offs. This facade of democracy leads to its populist backlash. We are seeing this in the US where the Bannon right and Sanders left are joining forces to block the scale out of datacentres, part of a broader and timely political reckoning.A few things have been happening over recent weeks to suggest something similar is starting to happen here.View image in fullscreenKayla Thompson with members of a group campaigning against a Firmus AI datacentre at St Leonards, Tasmania.Photograph: Sarah Rhodes/The GuardianFirst, Australians who despite their high take-up of some AI tools remain among the world’s most sceptical, have a low tolerance for tech overlords.GetUp’s successful campaign against Coles’partnership with Palantir, the data company that licenses its software to the US military whobomb childrenand immigration officials to track individuals, shows the vulnerability of public brands who lean in too close to the beast.Second, creators whose work has been stolen to train models that will diminish the value of their future careers are standing their ground. They are rightly aggrieved and won’t just wave through anything that feels like an amnesty. They are demanding compensation for the theft of their work as well as an ongoing model to give them control over the terms of its use.Even more significant may be thefailure of the Firmus IPO, which was to have been the biggest Australian float since Telstra. The decision not to list the company followed the withdrawal of a datacentre in Sydney, the first major project to fall over due to local community pressure. There are a range of possible reasons the bid failed, includingaccusations of greed, but surely the growing community backlash to datacentres had some scratching their heads about the prospects of a hyper-scale out.OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websitesRead moreConsumers, creators, communities are all challenging the “inevitability” storyline. Together they add up to a series of counter-punches that suggest our democratic faculties have not yet been fully exhausted.But the “inevitability doctrine” is durable and any pushback will need to be ongoing, because these companies have the resources, influence and bald self-interest to pursue their objectives with all the commitment of an AI agent gone rogue.The biggest danger to our democracy this technology poses is not in the cynical misuse of an untested and unregulated deployment (although this will be hugely destructive) but in the broader sense that we have no say in what is happening to us. Right now, its game on.In our parliament over the coming weeks there will be fights to land privacy reform, a digital duty of care, standards on datacentres and rules on how governments will use the technology on its citizens. In workplaces there will be struggles over usage, surveillance and displacement. In our schools and social circles, real negotiations on how we choose to use the bots and agents, or whether we need to use them at all.I know it’s exhausting and overwhelming and that is what the tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on, that we just all run out of steam and seek refuge in the user experiences designed to meet our every desire.But the resistance many of us feel is real and, so long as we remain a democracy, it will be at the ballot box where we will have the opportunity to demand those who purport to lead us challenge this sense of the inevitable. Because here’s the thing: inevitability is also a choice.Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of the weekly podcastBurning Platforms. title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled | Games | The Guardian
description: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Content: A woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiView image in fullscreenA woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiGamesReviewCastlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilledEvil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, XboxThere are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dullHarper Jay MacIntyreTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed.Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull.To its benefit, Belmont’s Curse doesn’t pull any punches. Literally. The smallest minion can land a heavy blow and dodging even basic attacks, though occasionally counterintuitive, forces the player to intimately learn enemy habits. Every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled: bats burst into blood, demons burn to cinders. Every battle holds fresh twists and gimmicks.View image in fullscreenA significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges … Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.Photograph: KonamiExploration is less about remembering old, previously inaccessible routes then circling back, so much as mastering challenge rooms full of buzzsaws and blood pits. Learning how to juggle multiple tools at once becomes crucial, as some rooms start to resemble the notoriously tough platformer Super Meat Boy more than Symphony of the Night. Navigating these challenges requires acrobatics, air dashes and death-defying leaps. And while Castlevania veterans may expect something more subtle (secret-hunting and puzzle-solving is the classic stuff of the series), a significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges.As Rose progresses, she gains new magical attacks via tarot cards, and tools for reaching new areas. This is, however, an inconsistent game world. The castle library offers notebook-worthy puzzles, including a cathedral hidden within a cursed portrait that tasks you with playing music on a magic organ. After that, however, you might have to explore underground waterways packed with uninspired combat challenges. This may be the most virtually striking Castlevania since 2002’s Harmony of Dissonance and sometimes it’s also the most inventive and brain-teasing. In other moments, you’ll be bored to bloody tears.Belmont’s Curse improves considerably after an early twist forces Rose to grapple with the Belmont family legacy and her own anger. Once you’re out of the Parisian streets and into Dracula’s castle, there’s far more to love.The result is an earnest, likable game. There are undeniable shortcomings and moments of curse-worthy frustration, but every now and again, there is real cleverness on display, even if Belmont’s Curse can’t quite match contemporary peers such as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown or Hollow Knight: Silksong – the trendsetter now feels like something of a trend-chaser. For most Castlevania players, this will be more than enough. You have a whip, a castle, and a dark lord. Do you really need anything else?Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is released on 15 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesNintendo SwitchPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet | Headphones | The Guardian
description: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Content: The AirPods’ compact open design offers a great alternative to silicone earbuds.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe AirPods’ compact open design offers a great alternative to silicone earbuds.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.HeadphonesReviewApple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yetUpgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tipsSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price oftheir predecessors.The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in thewatch pocketof a pair of jeans.View image in fullscreenThe only visible difference from the AirPods 4’s case is the writing on the back.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise.The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in theAirPods Proto great effect.SpecificationsConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chipBattery life:four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)Water resistance:IP57 (up to1 metre for 30 minutes)Earbud dimensions:30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mmEarbud weight:4.3g eachCharging case dimensions:46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mmCharging case weight:32.3g/34.7gCase charging:USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)Up to five hours of battery lifeView image in fullscreenThe case charges via USB-C or Qi wireless/Apple Watch charger with the pricier version.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback.The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case.Upgraded sound and noise cancellingView image in fullscreenWith iOS 27 on an iPhone the earbuds have a three-band equaliser in settings for customising the sound.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen.The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition.They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or theAirPods Pro 3, but still do a solid job.View image in fullscreenThe AirPods 5 magnetically clip into their compact charging case for storage.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud.The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity.SustainabilityBatteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case andreplacements cost from £69. The specialists iFixit awarded the earbudstwo out of 10for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in itsenvironmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.PriceThe AirPods 5 cost£119(€149/$129/A$219) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls.For comparison, theAirPods Pro 3cost£219, the AirPods Max 2 cost£499, theGoogle Pixel Buds 2acost£129and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost£129.VerdictThe AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat.They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket.The battery life is a little short, and while they work with anyBluetoothdevice, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac.There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them.The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just asdisposable as most other earbuds.Pros:comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality.Cons:battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.Explore more on these topicsHeadphonesAppleGadgetsBluetoothreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Loves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretary | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in then, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in then, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKatie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationLoves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretaryArwa MahdawiThe Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in thenTue 13 Oct 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.23 EDTSharePoor Donald Trump. His (third) wife seemingly can’t bear to benearhim and his (fifth) press secretary recently abandoned him to be with a baby she had only recently met.“She decided she loved her children more than she loved Donald Trump,” the presidentlamentedin August when Karoline Leavitt decided to step down a few months after giving birth. “I’m very upset about this. She has to go home and spend time with her children. That does happen on occasion with some people – when they love their children.”Apparently, Leavitt loves her childrenandFox News, because, in a highly predictable turn of events, the 29-year-old has got agig there now. But don’t worry too much about the president: he’s found himself a new woman to attack the press and act as his mouthpiece. On Friday, Trump announced that he’dappointed Katie Zacharia, previously a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, as the new press secretary. Unlike some of Trump’s other lackeys, Zacharia has government experience: she was once a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Her most important qualification, however, is her fealty to King Trump. “She has an unblemished record of support,” Trump said in his announcement. “She is … a devoted fan and member of Maga!”While you’ve obviously got to worship the president to get a top comms role with him, there are a few other job requirements. Not least a willingness to embrace what former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway called “alternative facts”. Zacharia gets full marks in that department. Last year the press secretary, who once worked foran anti-abortion advocacy group, claimedon Xthat the abortion medication mifepristone “is connected to the manufacturer of the deadly gas Zyklon B, used in the World War II concentration camps”. While there is a tenuous corporate connection whichconspiracy theoristshave tried to play up, mifepristone was developed in the 1980s by a French company.The origins of mifepristone aren’t the only alternative facts Zacharia is fond of. She has echoed Trump’s big lie that the 2020 election was “stolen” and used herTruth Socialaccount to promote theQAnon conspiracy theory, which posits that Trump is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’s alsopromotedPizzagate, the baseless theory that Hillary Clinton and her 2016 campaign chief, John Podesta, were operating an underground child sex-trafficking ring from a Washington DC pizza shop.While Zacharia scores highly when it comes to devotion and unhinged theories, I suspect that she’s going to need to ramp up her public hatred of Joe Biden if she wants to stay on her boss’s good side. Biden is dealing with stage four cancer and mostly staying out of the public eye, but Trump still acts as if he’s running against the man. According to a recentReuters analysis, Trump has invoked Biden’s name about 900 times this year. And not in a pleasant way.Beni Rae Harmony, 24, who is Trump’snewassistant press secretary, seems to suffer from the same Biden Derangement Syndrome afflicting the president; indeed, it might be part of the reason she got the job. A Christmas 2021 photo of Harmony wearing a“Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirtwhile holding a rifle recently did the rounds online. The White House subsequentlydefended Harmony, calling her “a trusted voice for the Maga movement”.Beyond bashing Biden, another helpful quality for a Trump spokesperson is a fondness for insults. White House communications director, Steven Cheung, whom Trumpreportedlyrefers to as “my sumo wrestler” probably leads the pack there. He’s forged ashock-jock stylecomms strategy and endeavours to be as crass as possible. Cheung has told the former secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, to “shut his stupid mouth”, labelled senator Jon Ossoff “the biggest cuck loser in politics”, anddescribedthe former FBI head, James Comey, as “one of the dumbest motherfuckers in human history”. He’s alsofondof calling people “retards”, recently directing the slur atCNN host Erin Burnett.Cheung’s rhetoric would get a lot of ordinary people fired. But it has made him a fixture in Trumpworld: he’s been with the president in various capacities for adecade now. That’s rare for Trump, whocycles through staff. If Zacharia lasts even a year in her new role, meanwhile, I’ll be surprised. With a (very likely) disastrous midterm election approaching, she has her work cut out and will need all the alternative facts she can find. Zacharia has also admitted that she is probably not even the best person for the job. “President Trump does not need a spokesperson,” Zachariagushed on Xlast month. “He is his own best Press Secretary.”Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPAView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters/EPAOpinionBrexitBrexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them onRafael BehrRussian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matterTue 13 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTShareRussian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimeaon the European Union.According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”.The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and thatUkraineis not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence.That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union.When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as“ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda”. That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson.There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives.In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it.Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause.This is the context in which Andy Burnham’srecent assertionthat Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit.That isnot a controversial claimto anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional.No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power.Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities.Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaigngot a helping hand from Moscow. The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies.The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anywayare compatible.Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely.Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders.The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel.The hope, entirely vain, is todepress pump pricesand assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November.On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus ofrhetorical venomfor Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia isan Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin.The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture.Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips.It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that heshould be allowed to decidewho governs Venezuela and who sells its oil.That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it.And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”.Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionVladimir PutinEuropean UnionEuropeBoris JohnsonForeign policyUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno | The Guardian
description: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
Content: ‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself.’Photograph: Grant Rooney/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AIMegan MorenoAmid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each otherTue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTShareWe have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagersaddicted to phones, alonelinessepidemicand thedangersof AI. The release ofThe Social Reckoningleads us to ask, “How badwerethose guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am Iif I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.But what if we are focusing on the wrong problem?The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself. It may be our growing unwillingness to curiously, thoughtfully and openly communicate about the role technology plays in our lives.As a pediatrician, this issue often manifests in my clinic. Parents arrive with worries about their teens’ screen time. The parent will demand that their child “fess up” and reveal how many hours they waste on their phone every day. The atmosphere is immediately charged. The teen becomes defensive. The parent is frustrated.I often suggest that we start somewhere else.I ask: “Can you share a little about what you do when you are using technology? What do you enjoy? Are there things about your technology use you are worried about and willing to discuss?”I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AIRead moreThe answers are not usually what people expect. One teen tells me about the friendships she maintained on social media after moving to a new town. Another shows me videos he created to promote his school’s upcoming play. One shares how digital design tools are changing the fashion industry, so she is trying to learn about them now. Another quietly admits that gaming has become so consuming that it feels stressful.As the conversation unfolds, something changes. The tension in the room eases. Parents relax. The teen patientmighteven smile a few times. We talk about strategies, relationships, stress and health.What began as an argument about a device becomes a bigger conversation about health, relationships and life itself.It often feels that our conversations about technology have become trapped in a false choice between two extreme camps. One camp is made up of the pro-tech enthusiasts, thought to embrace every new device or platform. The other camp is composed of preachers of digital abstinence.View image in fullscreen‘What obligations do technology companies have to children?’Photograph: Feature China/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesThe result is a polarized debate dominated by blame, shame and moral judgment. Instead of asking how technology affects our relationships, our sleep, our work, our wellbeing, we argue endlessly about whether technology is “good” or “bad”.I was reminded of this recently during a community event focused on digital media. The event included a youth panel with several brave adolescents, willing to speak to an audience of their teachers, community members and parents. I asked the adolescents a question: could you describe a positive conversation you had with a parent about technology?Every single panelist shook their head.“I’ve never had that,” one teenager said, uneasily eyeing her mom who was sitting in the front row. The other panelists agreed.It was a striking moment. Parents routinely talk their children through setbacks in sports, clubs, friendships and school. They listen, ask questions and offer support. Yet when it comes to technology, many conversations begin and end with warnings, criticism or fear.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is this?For years, parents have been barraged by alarming headlines about screen time and mental health. Many parents worry there is probably only one right way to approach technology, and they’re failing miserably. Parents are also navigating the necessity of using their own devices for work, home and communication.‘My son genuinely believed it was real’: Parents are letting little kids play with AI. Are they wrong?Read moreThe real anxious generation just might be parents.So how do we fix this? The solution begins with curiosity. Parents can ask what interests their children have online, and why those interests matter. Parents can ask their kids about what questions or worries they have about their tech use, and share some of their own concerns. If a parent missteps by scrolling cute cat videos and delaying dinner, they can acknowledge it and make it a teachable moment for themselves and their kids.Because children do not need adults who have all the answers.They need adults willing to ask questions.These conversations matter because they lower the temperature of the debate. Once we move beyond panic and polarization, we can begin asking better questions on the societal level. How should digital platforms be designed to ensure safety? What obligations do technology companies have to children? What policies would support healthier digital environments?If we want to preserve human connection in the age of social media and AI, the answer is not to simply spend less time with technology. It is spending more time talking openly with one another. The irony of the current moment is that as we worry endlessly about technology pulling us apart, it might be our inability to have conversations about technology that ultimately divides us.Megan Moreno, MD, MSEd, MPH, is a co-author of Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World, published by the American Academy of Pediatrics on 13 October.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChildrenDoctorsHealthComputingChildren's healthChildren's techcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Ballon d’Or doesn’t capture football’s wonder – Michael Olise is proof | Ballon d'Or | The Guardian
description: France’s always-cool winger has crowds hanging on his every move – adulation that means more than any title could
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: France’s always-cool winger has crowds hanging on his every move – adulation that means more than any title could
Content: Michael Olise has been in top form recently.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMichael Olise has been in top form recently.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/DPPI/ShutterstockBallon d'OrThe Ballon d’Or doesn’t capture football’s wonder – Michael Olise is proofZito MaduFrance’s always-cool winger has crowds hanging on his every move – adulation that means more than any title couldTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTShareWhen I was younger, I wanted to be the captain on my football team because back then, I assumed that the armband was given to the best player. It was a goal of mine for so long that, even as my youth teams won tournaments and trophies, and I won top scorer and best player awards, I still felt unsatisfied because someone else always had the armband. Whenever I saw another teammate sprinting around with the armband on, I took it as an indictment.I had forgotten this childish way of thinking until France v Belgium in the UefaNations Leaguelast week. Ousmane Dembélé, who was wearing the armband for France, was particularly active. Had it not been for the wastefulness of his teammates, he would have had several assists during his time on the field.That time came to an end in the 60th minute, whenFrancemanager Zinedine Zidane decided to make changes in order to galvanize his team. Dembélé was doing well, but Belgium were nullifying the threat that he presented. They would double or triple team him, knowing that he wasn’t the best passer and that he would often dally on the ball.
