Those extra touches and extra dribbles allowed the Belgium defenders time to close in, or to recover before the pass made it to a teammate.Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan WilsonRead moreOn came Michael Olise as Dembélé’s direct replacement, with Dembélé handing Olise the captain’s armband. There’s a clip online of the moment zoomed in, which shows what the broadcast cameras seemed to miss. When Dembélé gave Olise the armband, Olise accepted it with a look of confusion, seemingly not understanding why he was being given the honor, since he is not usually the captain or vice-captain. Seeing this, I remembered that I used to believe that the best player on the team is – and should be – the one who wears the armband and in that moment, the exchange made perfect sense.You can always tell the quality of a player by how the crowd reacts to them. When Olise came on, the crowd roared, behaving as if victory was inevitable, even though France were down when he made his entrance. Whenever he touched the ball, they rose and took a deep breath in anticipation. He had wowed them throughout the World Cup, where he provided seven assists and innumerable moments of magic, and he had already scored a late goal to beat Belgium at the end of September. The French crowd expected great things, because he had delivered for them over and over again.The first goal would actually come not from Olise but from Désiré Doué, who had subbed on for Bradley Barcola before Olise came on. But once things were back level, Olise took over and ended the game as a contest. In the 80th minute, he beat his man with ease down the line and cut the ball back for Rayan Cherki to slot past the keeper. Seven minutes later, he got the ball on the right side of the box from Doué. Surrounded by several defenders who were grabbing him all over, he managed a weak shot with his right foot that took the goalkeeper by surprise and went in the bottom left corner. Then three minutes after that, in the 90th minute, he made a run through the middle where Doué once again found him with the ball. With one touch Olise slotted the ball home through the keeper’s legs. His fourth goal in the last four matches. He didn’t just win the game, he turned a tough match between two of the best teams in the world into a rout in the span of 10 minutes.Olise is often accused of performing nonchalance. Maybe that’s true, and maybe it’s a case of social anxiety and shyness being so unusual in the professional football ranks that fans have to see it as something insincere. Regardless, if you watch Olise play closely, beyond the YouTube highlights of isolated moments, it’s impossible to accuse him of nonchalance. His playing style is one of ease and grace, but that is not a consequence of pretending not to try. His style is so similar to that of Zidane, in the sense that the grace comes from both a sense to entertain the crowd but also from an economy of movement.View image in fullscreenMichael Olise looked confused after being given the armband.Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/Getty ImagesIf the danger of Dembélé comes from the innumerable ways that he can beat you, options that are so numerous that they tend to sometimes weigh him down when he tries to do too much, Olise beats defenders and teams by doing the simple things extremely well. When he controls the ball, he sets it to lead up to his next move. When he runs with the ball, he pushes it with the exact amount of force that allows him to either get by the defender or set up a pass. And when he’s presented with a number of options of what to do in front of goal or to find a teammate on the run, he usually chooses the best one. That doesn’t mean that everything he does ultimately leads to success – his inability to score during the World Cup eventually made it seem as though he were under a curse – but he is usually making the right choices with the ball at his feet.Armbands don’t actually signify the best player on the field or in the world. Rather, that conversation is now centered around the Ballon d’Or. Players and their teams openly campaign to be crowned, and fans of each player attack the other sides, with each denigrating the opposing side’s favorite player in order to boost the campaign for their own. The obsession with the award has completely atrophied how we understand and appreciate players, replacing it with a destructive kind of comparison where great players are torn down as being bad if they haven’t won enough, or scored enough goals, or had more assists than the others that they’re up against.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis kind of engagement is intellectually silly and insincere, and leaves us no space for one of the best parts of watching football: The sense of wonder that players give us. And in the effort to boost one over the others whether through tribalism or idol worship, we miss the beauty of such a diverse group of players at the top of their game doing the ridiculous, match after match.The joy that I get from watching Olise and Dembélé (or Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappé, Raphinha, Harry Kane, Rodri, and others) doesn’t come from the possibility that they might win the Ballon d’Or. What is wonderful to me is seeing how each player solves the same questions presented to them on the football field. How each one interprets the game, its constraints, and faces it with their own strengths and weaknesses. What matters is how each of them makes magic from a collection of rules and chaos of 22 people on the field.When Olise steps out onto the field after checking the length of the grass, and looking in bemusement at the armband, my thoughts aren’t about whether he can prove that he’s the best player in the world. No, like everyone else who stands and gasps whenever he tries the spectacular, what I’m looking and hoping for is to be impressed by a player expanding what is possible on the field. And more often than not, he delivers.Zito Madu is a writer living in Brooklyn, New York. He is the author of the surrealist memoir The Minotaur at Calle Lanza.Explore more on these topicsBallon d'OrFrance (World news)Nations LeagueFrance (Football)commentShareReuse this content

title: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising
Content: Donald Trump after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC last month.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC last month.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game onPeter LewisThe tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is risingTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTShareOf all the drivers of the populist wave, one of the most powerful is the sense of inevitability that surrounds what we are told is the march of progress. In presenting the future as a fait accompli, it poisons the civic well by dealing us out of the game.While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI realityuntethered to the will of the people.On the velocity and trajectory of the technology, Trump and the tech overlords have determined we must hit the accelerator and dispense with guardrails to “win” an ill-defined race to build a god in a box. This reckless exercise of power from a waning empire has created its own reality for all of us.Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre companyRead moreIn Australia, the government has determined that the only way we can exercise control in a world of such chaos is to grab on to this juggernaut. We become to US tech data what the Saudis are to oil; using renewables to power massive centres in the desert, converting solar into AI tokens and piping them up to Asia, a new export industry that will power our common wealth.Within the inevitability doctrine this strategy has logic. The alternative, we are told, is to become a client state to Silicon Valley.But in pursuing this vision we risk being blinded to the foreseeable consequences of what we are signing ourselves up to.The industry we are building derives value by replacing workers, it has been built on the stolen work of creators, its unregulated deployment is causing unconscionable harms particularly in theatres of war, it has an insatiable thirst for energy and water, while even its creators say there’s a not insignificant chance it will destroy humanity.The “inevitability doctrine” demands we concede rather than properly explore and negotiate these trade-offs. This facade of democracy leads to its populist backlash. We are seeing this in the US where the Bannon right and Sanders left are joining forces to block the scale out of datacentres, part of a broader and timely political reckoning.A few things have been happening over recent weeks to suggest something similar is starting to happen here.View image in fullscreenKayla Thompson with members of a group campaigning against a Firmus AI datacentre at St Leonards, Tasmania.Photograph: Sarah Rhodes/The GuardianFirst, Australians who despite their high take-up of some AI tools remain among the world’s most sceptical, have a low tolerance for tech overlords.GetUp’s successful campaign against Coles’partnership with Palantir, the data company that licenses its software to the US military whobomb childrenand immigration officials to track individuals, shows the vulnerability of public brands who lean in too close to the beast.Second, creators whose work has been stolen to train models that will diminish the value of their future careers are standing their ground. They are rightly aggrieved and won’t just wave through anything that feels like an amnesty. They are demanding compensation for the theft of their work as well as an ongoing model to give them control over the terms of its use.Even more significant may be thefailure of the Firmus IPO, which was to have been the biggest Australian float since Telstra. The decision not to list the company followed the withdrawal of a datacentre in Sydney, the first major project to fall over due to local community pressure. There are a range of possible reasons the bid failed, includingaccusations of greed, but surely the growing community backlash to datacentres had some scratching their heads about the prospects of a hyper-scale out.OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websitesRead moreConsumers, creators, communities are all challenging the “inevitability” storyline. Together they add up to a series of counter-punches that suggest our democratic faculties have not yet been fully exhausted.But the “inevitability doctrine” is durable and any pushback will need to be ongoing, because these companies have the resources, influence and bald self-interest to pursue their objectives with all the commitment of an AI agent gone rogue.The biggest danger to our democracy this technology poses is not in the cynical misuse of an untested and unregulated deployment (although this will be hugely destructive) but in the broader sense that we have no say in what is happening to us. Right now, its game on.In our parliament over the coming weeks there will be fights to land privacy reform, a digital duty of care, standards on datacentres and rules on how governments will use the technology on its citizens. In workplaces there will be struggles over usage, surveillance and displacement. In our schools and social circles, real negotiations on how we choose to use the bots and agents, or whether we need to use them at all.I know it’s exhausting and overwhelming and that is what the tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on, that we just all run out of steam and seek refuge in the user experiences designed to meet our every desire.But the resistance many of us feel is real and, so long as we remain a democracy, it will be at the ballot box where we will have the opportunity to demand those who purport to lead us challenge this sense of the inevitable. Because here’s the thing: inevitability is also a choice.Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of the weekly podcastBurning Platforms. His columns are accreditedProudly HumanExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Cheesy? Yes. Cringe? Absolutely. That’s why High School Musical is still our secret passion  | Rachel Chang | The Guardian
description: I watched the filming of the first jazz-hands epic. Two decades on, its sparkle hasn’t faded – and now it’s back on the London stage, says journalist Rachel Chang
Author: Rachel Chang
Headline: I watched the filming of the first jazz-hands epic. Two decades on, its sparkle hasn’t faded – and now it’s back on the London stage, says journalist Rachel Chang
Content: Zac Efron and Vanessa Hudgens in the 2006 Disney Channel movie High School Musical.Photograph: Fred Hayes/Disney/AllstarView image in fullscreenZac Efron and Vanessa Hudgens in the 2006 Disney Channel movie High School Musical.Photograph: Fred Hayes/Disney/AllstarOpinionTelevisionCheesy? Yes. Cringe? Absolutely. That’s why High School Musical is still our secret passionRachel ChangI watched the filming of the first jazz-hands epic. Two decades on, its sparkle hasn’t faded – and now it’s back on the London stageTue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.18 EDTShareWhenever I watch basketball, I come away disappointedthat the players’ shoe squeaks didn’t jumpstart a choreographed dance number, just like in High School Musical. Whether it was a lunch break turning into a confession of closeted passions or a pep rally evolving into a flashmob, the 2006 Disney Channel movie proved that teen drama can always be solved through song.Quality entertainment? Meh. The corniest of lines? Oh, for sure. But the cheesiness was the point. Its 98 minutes became a deliciouslyenduring slice of pop culturenot despite the cringe, but because the film embraced it so wholeheartedly.Now, 20 years later, Troy Bolton’s dribbles and Sharpay Evans’s sparkles have sashayed their way into the London spotlight as anew stage adaptationopens at the Troubadour Wembley Park theatre this week, complete with throwback stars such as McFly’s Harry Judd and the original film’s “pop-and-lock girl” Kaycee Stroh.No one is as shocked and exuberant as I am. In August 2005, I was an editor for the US teen magazine Popstar!,and the only journalist on the first movie’s Salt Lake City set. I hung out at East High (the real school has the same name) as a fresh-faced Zac Efronand a charming Corbin Bleu taught me the Wildcats dance in the cafeteria. In the gym one day, when the weather was particularly gloomy, I watched so many takes of Get’cha Head in the Game that I eventually opted to sit outside in the rain.This was a time when Disney Channel movies debuted every other month, so the production seemed low key. Even so, I was keenly aware that being in my late 20s then, I was maybe three times the age of the intended audience. Paired with its TV distribution,it would likely be a niche kids’ movie at best.So when HSMpremiered to 7.7m US viewers – at the time, Disney Channel’s highest-rated broadcast ever – I was stunned. Those catchy upbeat songs that I thought played on repeat only in my head started climbing the Billboard charts as the soundtrack became theNo 1 album of 2006. By the end of the year, the little TV movie had notched up100m global viewers.View image in fullscreenRachel Chang with Corbin Bleu and Zac Efron on the set of High School Musical in 2005Of course,High School Musical 2 was fast-tracked. In tandem, I had graduated to entertainment editor at CosmoGIRL!, and visited the more guarded set in St George, Utah, in spring 2007, where everything was bigger and more dazzling. By now, Efron and Vanessa Hudgens’s real-life romance was a source of speculation – and I caught a clue, spotting a Troy button pin on Hudgens’s bag. The film’s director, Kenny Ortega, invited me to sit in the chair next to him, and this time I knew I was watching pop history unfold before my eyes.Expectations were shattered once again. HSM2’s US debut in August 2007 garnered a whopping 18.6m viewers, securing aGuinness world recordas the most-watched US cable TV movie.My trip back to Salt Lake City for High School Musical 3: Senior Year – now upgraded to the silver screen – was far more calculated. I was restricted to the studio where we shot Hudgens for CosmoGIRL!’s cover, and only some of the supporting cast were brought over for interviews as I sat in a nearby coffee shop. To no one’s surprise, the October 2008 US premiere marked the biggest opening for a musical film at the time, eventually raking in more than$250m globally.While some may roll their eyes at the bubblegum trilogy, many people were devouring the sappy storylines and bopping (to the top) with the earworms – a formula that translates as perfectly on stage as it did on the screen. The franchise has previously been made into a London stage show in 2008, with a tour of the UK, but this fresh immersive rendition promises a new interactive element, along with the songs ingrained in our muscle memory, primed for live theatre. It has already played in Salford this summer, and the run was extended due to demand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat HSMdid best was blend American high-school social hierarchy with the simplest of storylines: a jock who moonlights as a theatre geek represents the most universally relatable dilemma of embracing passion despite perception. It ushered in a new era of musicals, from other Disney productions such asCamp Rockand Descendants to Glee and Wicked.The brand has splashed into all areas: Hallmark ornaments, Disney park parades, licensed high-school productions, the mockumentaryHigh School Musical: The Musical: The Series(which introduced the world to Olivia Rodrigo), and a long list of appearances onSaturday Night Live US, the mostrecentof which was just three weeks ago.HSM may never be the cool kid, but it will always be the popular one. By breaking free and embracing its goody-goody reputation, it has grown into the sugary dose of innocent nostalgia that reminds us that when it comes to guilty pleasures, we’re all in this together. And if you’re not on board, get’cha head in the game.Rachel Chang is a journalist and author specialising in travel and pop culture. Her book Unforgettable Walks: 52 Places to Stroll Around the World is published next yearExplore more on these topicsTelevisionOpinionHigh School Musical 3: Senior YearcommentShareReuse this content

title: One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson | The Guardian
description: Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs, says Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Author: Jane Martinson
Headline: Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs, says Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs MimsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Anaïs MimsOpinionPoliticsOne thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemyJane MartinsonFarage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costsTue 13 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTShareWhile the merits of aso-called Britannia shieldto protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system wereenthusiastically heraldedby the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with abanner headlinecalling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile,hailed the Toriesfor seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to anall-expenses paid tripto Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in the runup to the Makerfield byelection in June 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAThe search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since theJune byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may havedubbed Burnham’s first conference speech“the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.This coverage reminds Alastair Campbellof his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”,wrote thatthe country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of itscoverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people.According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. Hisshort-form videoson fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which hasbarred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front pagewith the headline“Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”.But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacityExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionConservativesAndy BurnhamNewspapersRupert MurdochKemi BadenochcommentShareReuse this content

title: In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay? | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Preparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workers, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Preparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workers, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Louise Casey speaking at a care home in north London in July 2026Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenLouise Casey speaking at a care home in north London in July 2026Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAOpinionSocial careIn Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?Polly ToynbeePreparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workersTue 13 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTShareResidents with advanced dementia lined the day room, glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape, with that terrible human vacancy everyone most fears for their own end days.This was Millvina House in Anfield,Liverpool, which I visited withLouise Casey, who is heading the commission on social care in England, last week. Here is a snippet of what she saw: an angry man jolting into life, shooting out his arm at her and bellowing: “Out! Get out! Get out!” A young care assistant went to stroke his back and calm him down. It’s a hard job, and part of it is watching for warning signs of aggression, one of dementia’s dreadful symptoms. “People don’t want to know,” Casey said, “but if you are born, you will die. Chances are you will need care, and dementia is the biggest killer.”In her travels she has been appalled by the standards of social care she has found in some places, with so many people getting far too little help. The evening before this visit, she had been out with care workers attending to people at home. She said she had come away “profoundly, deeply shocked”. She had photographed an elderly man with diabetes, swollen legs and a stroke affecting his left side, who was unable to open a bottle of water. He had no relatives nearby. “He couldn’t afford more care, so he’d just cut their visits by half.” Then there was a woman with early dementia and an untreated, infected stoma bag, which she said had looked “so sore”.Casey’s shock at this “hidden misery” was matched by her admiration for care workers: “Only young girls, going into unknown homes, paid just £6.50 for a half-hour visit; it’s grim. But they are so patient.” She noted they were being paid about £4,000 a year less than if they had become healthcare assistants in the NHS. With better care, Casey thinks many more people should stay in their own homes – indeed, most would prefer to. “Even at four visits a day,” she said, it would be cheaper than residential homes such as Millvina House.Millvina is a good symbol for the tangle of problems facing Casey. It is rated “requires improvement”, struggling out of a troubled “inadequate” past and hoping the results of its latest inspection will be better. The nursing home used to be privately run but was put into special measures afterthe Care Quality Commission (CQC) reporteda lack of staff, shortage of medicines, unlawful restraint, dangerous neglect of residents with diabetes, incorrect doses of antibiotics and doubts on adequate feeding and hydration. After gaininginterim controlin July 2024, Liverpool city council officially took it overin September 2025, fearing its collapse would mean the loss of 60 much-needed beds – in the previous two years, 187 beds in Liverpoolhad already been lost. Its sister home, Brushwood, has also been insourced back to the council: here,the CQC founddirty baths and toilets, staff using disrespectful and dehumanising language, agency staff who didn’t know residents’ names and multiple safeguarding failures.Casey urges insourcing to council or voluntary services: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.” She wants to stop private-equity ownersprofiteering from care homesat one end, but at the other she sees services barely surviving unless better-off residents subsidise those on too-low state funding.Now council-owned, Millvina costs a lot more to run at a better standard, the council leader tells me. Local authority staff are better paid – something private providers, contracted to cut costs, have little incentive to match. That was the logic behind Margaret Thatcher’s privatisation of social care, but perversely the state ended up with a far higher bill. To force councils to privatise, central government paid for those entering a private residential home, but not if they used domiciliary care or council-owned care. The result was an explosion of people entering private residential care instead of staying in their own homes. The state’s bill for nursing homes and residential careshot upfrom £20m in 1979 to £459m in 1986. That misguided privatisation is likely to feature in Casey’s imminent report outlining the sector’s history. Expect a brutal description of its current state.Soon comes Casey’s first of several reports, this one on finance, which will lift the lid on where wealth resides. Overwhelmingly it is older people who have most wealth, a foundational fact underpinning whatever Casey’s final plans will be for a national care service. The people needing the care are better able to pay for it than working-age taxpayers. Expect that generational truth to shape her conclusions.Lest some misunderstood Andy Burnham’spromise of universal free care at the point of use, it is unlikely that better-off people will be significantly freed from their current residential payments, which amount to £14bn. That contribution can’t be magicked away into general taxation, though liabilities could be capped.Creating a fair system for elderly people may be easier than solving the inadequate state of care for working-age adults in need of support, which absorbs nearly half of councils’ care costs (Casey is writing separate reports about this). But political heat focuses on older people using family inheritances on care, a situation unresolved asnearly 30 years of forgottensocial care commissions, white papers and select committee inquiries gather dust.“Everything is on the table,” Casey says. Does that include Burnham’sown 2010 plan, in which everyone with capital would pay in a lump sum on retirement (or a lien on their home) and thereafter get free care? “Everything.” She and the government are examining a care plan by Steve Webb, a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister, forauto-enrolmentof 1p in the pound on income tax for over-40s, politically saleable as people can opt out.What of the clash with Burnham’s devolution plans? Some councils with similar profiles of deprivation, disability prevalence and median income provide up to twice the care of others, reportsthe King’s Fund. Voters want power devolved to councils – yet they hate an unfair postcode lottery between localities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLook at the conflicts Casey faces: public v privately run services, taxpayer funds v family payments, the NHS v council funding for different disabilities, and local v national standards.Her report will also collide with Toryinheritance tax promisesto the rich. The right to pass on property to family is at the heart of passionate feelings about people being obliged to sell homes (that they will no longer use) to pay for residential care. Should young working people, many unable to afford a home themselves, pay more taxes so others can pass theirs to their children?A third of first-time buyersrely on the help of family. The wealth gap is worsening, asthe Institute for Fiscal Studies reportsa “growing importance of inherited wealth” for some, while others will get next to nothing.Casey wants to set off an alarm on the miserable quality of care she finds, but her fiercest fight may be over inheritance and generational justice. How will she cut through these political knots? It’s easy to believe her when she replies: “I will do what’s right, however controversial. That’s it.”Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSocial careOpinionOlder peopleLocal governmentLiverpoolEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything | Nathalie Tocci | The Guardian
description: If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Author: Nathalie Tocci
Headline: If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Content: Marine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential electionPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen blows a kiss to supporters in La Fleche, in the Sarthe department, a day after announcing her candidacy for the 2027 French presidential electionPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersOpinionThe far rightEurope’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everythingNathalie TocciIf far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tiltTue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTShareWhen it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country inEuropewe have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week,calling a snap electionfor next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his bighousing reform packagein parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.In addition to Spain,France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able toform a majorityin the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party waspunished at the pollsand the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, afterViktor Orbán was oustedin a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats,scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’srecent victoryin eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times.But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirmGiorgia Melonias Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Friedrich Merz in Berlin after  Burnham ‘opened the door to Britain rejoining the EU’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAAnd it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outsideItalyis that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade,publicly recognisethat Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone.Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnistExplore more on these topicsThe far rightOpinionEuropeSpainItalyFranceMarine Le PenGiorgia MelonicommentShareReuse this content

title: If you’re over 55 and too tired to make it into the office, these two Fair Work decisions are required reading | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: The industrial tribunal is where the human experience of fatigue and the mythologies of outdated management cultures are brought into sharper view
Author: Van Badham
Headline: The industrial tribunal is where the human experience of fatigue and the mythologies of outdated management cultures are brought into sharper view
Content: ‘In 2000 the average age of Australian retirement was about 53 but in 2024 it was 63.8,’ Van Badham writes.Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In 2000 the average age of Australian retirement was about 53 but in 2024 it was 63.8,’ Van Badham writes.Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty ImagesOpinionIndustrial relationsIf you’re over 55 and too tired to make it into the office, these two Fair Work decisions are required readingVan BadhamThe industrial tribunal is where the human experience of fatigue and the mythologies of outdated management cultures are brought into sharper viewMon 12 Oct 2026 23.02 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 00.05 EDTShareA decision last week about work-from-home accommodations carries implications far beyond the modern workplace and into the realm of a refreshingly material understanding of existential limitation.It was only in July that Australia’sFair Work Commission rejected the requestfrom a full-time council employee, Steven Polak, to reduce his days in the office from two a week to one. Polak argued that as he was over 55 and experiencing a work-related fatigue his obliged commute was exacerbating.Fair Work sided with his employer, accepting the council’s argument that substantial turnover in his team and a dearth of long-serving employees were reasonable business grounds to oblige the continued maximisation of Polak’s in-person presence.That decision just three months ago stands innotable contrast to last week’s. Here, a 63-year-old Victoria University student adviser, Michele Duffy, sought approval to work from home two days a week, arguing that a reduced commute would alleviate enough physical fatigue to improve her productivity. The university denied the request, arguing that Duffy’s job was to deal with students face-to-face. While the commission accepted that there was business merit to VU’s claim, it ordered that the institution allow Duffy one day a week working from home – without Duffy having to prove a medical condition.Why not? Herein lies the commission’s transformative realisation. While it had acknowledged that Polak’s commute was depleting, it now accepted that over 55 that depletion was exhausting and therefore Duffy’s request for some relief was … fair enough.Sure, we could conclude that the change is merely the outcome of different circumstances weighed against a commissioner’s professional discretion. Alternatively, we might muse on theBritish politician Tony Benn’s claim that “the exhaustion of old age is something people who are younger don’t fully appreciate”, with the observation that the last three months of US news would be enough to shrivel the freshest-faced ingenue into a fossilised prawn.I prefer to fantasise that someone nominated the French philosopher Simone Weil’s Gravity and Grace for the FWC book club and the quote “no poetry concerning the people is authentic if fatigue does not figure in it” provoked a sudden emotional recommitment to the social project of realism.There is no better place than an industrial arbitration tribunal for bold stands against inauthentic poetry. Fair Work is precisely where the clash between the human experience of work fatigue and the delusional mythologies of outdated management cultures are brought into sharper view.Studiespublished in 2016andin 2021found that sleep problems and their daytime consequences “are endemic among Australian adults” while almost half of Australian adults reported at least two sleep-related problems. In 2016, 29% of the adults surveyed attributed errors made at work in the previous three months due to sleep-related tiredness.Is work to blame? Not solely, although 16% of survey respondents reported working until bedtime, and we’ve had a decade since then of technological advancement allowing more work to colonise our private lives.Australia’s “right to disconnect” legislation introduced in 2024 is a recognition of how thoroughly the boundaries between work and everything else have been eroded.Health impacts of the intrusion and the recovery from stress it denies arewell understood– from increased cardiovascular stress to cognitive impairment to susceptibility to infection. The World Health Organization doesn’t consider burnout a medical issue but anoccupational phenomenon, resulting from workplace stresses that can include long hours, time pressure, shift work, insecure conditions and inadequate support.Consider this in the context of a revolution in labour force participation and you can grasp the evolution in FWC’s thinking. In 2000 the average age ofAustralian retirementwas about 53 but in 2024 it was 63.8. Age doesn’t just arrive with new physical demands but with demands of life situation. The year Duffy was born,barely a third of Australian womenwere in the workforce, while the representation of their 60+ cohort wasin far lower figures.By 2020, 51.7% of Australian women aged 60 to 64 were working, despite being born into a world that hadn’t imagined they’d exist.Were gendered expectations surrounding care commitments, family responsibilities and the home similarly revolutionised? Were they, bollocks – the workplace got an overthrow but everything around it has beenon a long march.Managerial culture, meanwhile, is stuck ina hundred-year-old modeldemanding the visibility and supervision of workers, assessing performance by presence rather than productivity and refusing to imagine commitments outside it. Work-from-home has emerged as an imperfect instrument to address the disconnect; despite management’s resistance to change,studies reportworkers who are at home providecomparable productivityand less absenteeism.The most meaningful criticismof the arrangement is that working from home intrudes even further into the hours and realms of a separate existence.While individuals and unions fight for a responsive, staff-centred workplace, the dogged employer resistance at Fair Work to an overdue paradigm shift has exploded the most ancient myth of industrial relations; that workers have no value.Clearly, we do. Maybe someone could write a poem about it – if only we weren’t all so bloody tired.Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsIndustrial relationsOpinionWorking from homeAgeingHealth (Australia news)Health (Society)BusinessProductivitycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain Clayface | Movies | The Guardian
description: He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?
Content: Hunky gory … Rhys Harries in full rock’n’roller mode.Photograph: Austin HargraveView image in fullscreenHunky gory … Rhys Harries in full rock’n’roller mode.Photograph: Austin HargraveMovies‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain ClayfaceHe cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?Ryan GilbeyTue 13 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violentDC Comicssupervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”double quotation markThe audition lasted three months. How did I stay sane? I didn'tHarries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but thenthese,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”View image in fullscreenLooksmaxxing … Naomi Acki and Rhys Davies in Clayface.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesHarries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross betweenDarkman, in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, andThe Substance, the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.View image in fullscreenIf the face fits … as Matt Hagen in Clayface.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros. PicturesA perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horrorCrow, where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”View image in fullscreen‘He may ultimately be the star here’ … in Hunky Dory in 2011.Photograph: Aegis Film Fund/Kobal/ShutterstockThe son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedySlaughterhouse Rulez, where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunitSuspicion, opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mysteryWhite Lines, then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche inThe Return, a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such asThe Marvels,Joker: Folie à DeuxandSupergirl, Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which ispredicted to lose more than $100m, indicate that fatigue has set in.On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”It seems unlikely, in the wake ofthe costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Diggerand the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.Clayface is in cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDC ComicsHorror filmsSuperhero moviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Larger Than Life review – Wallace, Gromit and the gang say cheeeese for hilarious Aardman origin story | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to follow
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: From Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to follow
Content: ‘At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay’ … visitors look up at the projections at Larger Than Life at Lightroom in London.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXView image in fullscreen‘At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay’ … visitors look up at the projections at Larger Than Life at Lightroom in London.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXArt and designReviewLarger Than Life review – Wallace, Gromit and the gang say cheeeese for hilarious Aardman origin storyLightroom, LondonFrom Shaun’s barn to Gromit’s box, these immersive behind-the-scenes renderings of the wide-grinned, cheeky characters are joyful, enormous – and a bit hard to followEddy FrankelTue 13 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNothing is safe from the scourge of immersification. They’ve turned Gustav Klimt and Vincent Van Gogh into vast, projection-mapped digital environments; they’ve told the stories of the moon landings and the dinosaurs and David Bowie as floor-to-ceiling electronic spectacles; and now they’ve come forAardman. For Wallace and Gromit and Shaun the Sheep, our national treasures. Is nothing sacred?The latest immersive cinematic experience at Lightroom is a big, eye-popping celebration of Aardman Animations, the company behind the world’s favourite claymation films and TV shows. It moves between documentary storytelling, behind-the-scenes insight and dazzling immersive renderings of all your wide-grinned, cheeky northern favourites.We get to hear about howPeter Lord and David Sproxtonmet in suburban Surrey and started messing around with clay, before joining forces withNick Parkand setting in motion a series of events that would take them from Woking to the stars. We get to hear about how they first made Morph out of a ball of clay, how the animators hilariously act out all the scenes to camera themselves before moving over to puppets, how they make the mouths form the “eeee” sound of the word cheese, all interspersed with Shaun the Sheep doing a barn-based talent show and clips from their biggest cinematic triumphs.View image in fullscreen‘When’s the movie starting?’ … a child reaches out to the screen at Lightroom.Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXAnd it makes a pretty convincing argument for why Aardman is so important, so beloved by so many people. Early on, it cuts to a clip from 1989’s A Grand Day Out, the first Wallace & Gromit film. At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay, every finger print and smudge. It looks so real, so human. Director Lucy Izzard says in a voiceover: “I think people still crave imperfection,” and you think yes, that’s it, that’s why Aardman matters. It’s something incredibly human in an age when things feel so amazingly non-human so much of the time.Does that hand-made, imperfect, homely aesthetic rub up awkwardly against the technological wizardry of immersive cinema? Sure does. But the bigger issue is that this experience doesn’t really know what it wants to be.It ends up as half-documentary, half-clip show, becoming sort of neither in the process, and a bit hard to follow too. It doesn’t even take full advantage of Lightroom’s capabilities. It could be bolder, more fun, it could play with the immersive format a bit more.One good use of the tech are the side screens, which make you feel like you are inside various environments: Shaun the Sheep’s barn, Gromit’s cardboard box as he spies on Feathers McGraw, behind the recording desk as actors do their vocal takes. But it’s not quite enough.There’s some fun stuff here. It’s great seeing Creature Comforts recreated in living rooms and gardens, it’s nice to see all the concept art and storyboards come to life, it’s pretty joyful watching the amazing video forPeter Gabriel’s Sledgehammerat such an enormous scale. It just lacks the crowd-pleasing immersive thrills of Lightroom’s recent Prehistoric Planet: Discovering Dinosaurs.View image in fullscreen‘It’s sort of a documentary.’Photograph: Justin Sutcliffe/LIghtroom KXAs a jaded, tired contemporary art critic, I may not be the target audience, so I brought along someone called Solomon. What are his qualifications? Well, he’s four, and yesterday he went to the cinema to seethe latest Shaun the Sheep movie, so you could say he’s something of a young cinephile. Also, his father (me) is a critic, so he is probably genetically predisposed to have opinions about this.Halfway through, I ask what he thinks. He says: “When is the movie starting? This is just ads.” He’s right – the whole thing just feels like an advert for Aardman. “When is the movie starting?” he asks again, more impatient this time, almost pleading. “This is it,” I say. “It’s sort of a documentary.” He stares at me, uncomprehending, and then yawns. Ouch, he really is a critic.Aardman’​s Peter Lord and David Sproxton: ‘At the Oscars, I went to the gents and had a pee with Jack Nicholson!’Read moreIt doesn’t really have enough for kids, and the storytelling isn’t strong enough for adults. It’s gimmick over narrative, as if they didn’t ask: “How can we make an amazing immersive experience?” but instead asked: “How can we tell our story in an immersive-ish way?” And those are two different propositions.This show doesn’t tarnish Aardman’s stellar reputation, nor detract from all the amazing, quirky, quaint, funny work that they’ve done, but it doesn’t add a huge amount to it either. More of a rubber glove on the head than a crowning achievement.Larger Than Life is at Lightroom, London, from 14 October to 4 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designAardmanArtExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wow, dude. You’re an idiot’: why Kelly Clarkson is fighting over a $15,000 bird on social media | Kelly Clarkson | The Guardian
description: After having a Pretty Woman moment in a Brooklyn store, the singer-songwriter let rip on X
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After having a Pretty Woman moment in a Brooklyn store, the singer-songwriter let rip on X
Content: ‘I never blast people – but you, my friend, were an exception’ … Kelly Clarkson.Photograph: NBC/Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I never blast people – but you, my friend, were an exception’ … Kelly Clarkson.Photograph: NBC/Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesPass notesKelly Clarkson‘Wow, dude. You’re an idiot’: why Kelly Clarkson is fighting over a $15,000 bird on social mediaAfter having a Pretty Woman moment in a Brooklyn store, the singer-songwriter let rip on XTue 13 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Kelly Clarkson.Age:44. Born in 1982. In Fort Worth, as it happens.Is that relevant?Not really, but ask how much she’s worth.How much is she worth?Celebritynetworth.com estimates the singer, songwriter and TV personality has a net worth of $60m.Good forClarkson. And is that relevant?Well, it just means she can afford stuff.What kind of stuff?A $15,000 mechanical bird called Molly.Great! So has she got one?No.Whyever not?In Clarkson’s version of events, she visited aBrooklyncuriosity store, enquired about the bird and was treated like a Julia Roberts character.Erin Brockovich? Respect!No, Vivian Ward in Pretty Woman.They thought she was on a“date” with Richard Gere?No! But you’ll remember in the movie Roberts’s character is snubbed in a bijou Beverly Hills boutique. Clarkson says the same happened to her at Art of Play, where when she inquired about Molly, a member of staff looked at her “as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me”.So she had a makeoverand returned triumphantlyto the store, just like in the movie?That was 1990, dear – Clarkson reacted the modern way.Which is?Shetook to social media. “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” she posted on X, to her 8.8 million followers.What did Art of Play do?Took to social media too, of course.To apologise?Not really. “Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store,”they said on Instagram. They also said that Molly wasn’t even for sale.Just a little misunderstanding, then, and all cleared up now?Hmm. “Sure, it wasn’t for sale,” said Clarkson. “So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag … didn’t happen … Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar.”Ouch!She goes on to say she loves and supports small businesses: “I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t.”No olive branch fromClarkson, then. What about the store?The Times reported that Art of Play said a worker told Clarkson that while Molly was not for sale, her “twin” made by an artist in Seattle was, for $15,000. They say they’ve reached out directly to try to clear the air. “We really do wish her the best and hope that someday we can all laugh about this misunderstanding.”But we’re already laughing. Snobby shop, celebrity strop, a pile-onand a very expensive bird called Molly.True, what’s not to love?Do say:“There’s amechanical bird on Temufor £11.27.”Don’t say:“Shall we discuss the questionable sexual politics of Pretty Woman?”Explore more on these topicsKelly ClarksonPass notesBrooklynfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beth Orton review – battered optimism from an artist making the best music of her career  | Beth Orton | The Guardian
description: Drawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowd
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Drawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowd
Content: Another instrument in the mix … Beth Orton performing at Concorde 2 in Brighton.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnother instrument in the mix … Beth Orton performing at Concorde 2 in Brighton.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianBeth OrtonReviewBeth Orton review – battered optimism from an artist making the best music of her careerConcorde 2, BrightonDrawing almost entirely from her last two albums, and backed by a band rooted in jazz and experimentation, Orton performed her emotionally fraught songs to a rapturous crowdAlexis PetridisTue 13 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe audience at Brighton’s Concorde 2 largely look old enough to have first encountered Beth Orton’s music three decades ago, as it wafted around a smoke-filled living room in the post-club small hours. That was the primary means of transmission for her 1996 debut album Trailer Park, which smartly appended classic singer-songwriter tropes to misty electronics. But if they’re expecting an evening of nostalgia, they’re in for a shock. The title track from 1999’s Mercury-nominated Central Reservation aside, her set swerves the music that made her famous, drawing almost entirely from her two most recent albums: this year’s The Ground Above and 2022’s Weather Alive.This would count as a bold move from someone 30-odd years into their career, were it not for the fact that Orton’s recent albums are so good – the latest fruit of an artistic reboot that began in the mid-2010s, when she shifted a sound that had grown increasingly acoustic and traditional back towards something more experimental and dancefloor-adjacent.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianShe spends most of the gig seated behind a keyboard rather than playing guitar. The Ground Above’s title track floats clouds of ambient synth over drums that split the difference between jazz and drum’n’bass, while Cigarette Curls unexpectedly shifts its location from something approximating laidback soul into an echoey dubbed-out space. Both Haunted Satellite and Celestial Light venture into the realm of abstraction and there is much playing with the timbre of her voice, amping up its huskiness and fragility, wilfully mangling the lyrics until her singing sounds less like the songs’ focus than another instrument in the mix. You could, if you wished, draw a spiritual parallel with John Martyn’s approach to vocals on 1973’s Inside Out.‘AI isn’t going to have any beneficial influence on humans’: Beth Orton on creativity, craft and the inspirational power of David BowieRead moreAlways adept at picking collaborators, she is backed by a band heavy on players rooted in jazz and at home at London’s Cafe Oto – bassist Tom Herbert, pianist Sam Beste. But the key instrument on stage seems to be Christos Stylianides’s trumpet, its breathy tone shifting from colouration that vaguely evokes the late Jon Hassell to densely effected gusts of white noise.It’s both enrapturing and, when you can make out the lyrics, emotionally fraught in a middle-aged way – sleepless nights, the inexorable passing of time, sickness, loss – although the set closer Otherside gathers itself into a kind of optimism: battered but nevertheless anthemic, Orton’s voice dramatically changing gear and becoming soulful and full-throated. If the audience came to hear the old hits, they don’t evince any disappointment: at the show’s conclusion, they go nuts. Understandably, given that they’re in the presence of something rare: an artist in her mid-50s making the most adventurous, fascinating music of her career.Touring the UKuntil 22 OctoberExplore more on these topicsBeth OrtonPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I knew I was being followed’: Keira Knightley on her hacking nightmare – and new Stasi spy play The Lives of Others | Theatre | The Guardian
description: As the Oscar-winning Stasi surveillance film hits the stage, Knightley and co-star Luke Thompson talk about the paranoia at its heart, the cost of theatre tickets nowadays – and their fury at ringtones in the stalls
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As the Oscar-winning Stasi surveillance film hits the stage, Knightley and co-star Luke Thompson talk about the paranoia at its heart, the cost of theatre tickets nowadays – and their fury at ringtones in the stalls
Content: ‘It’s almost musical’ … Luke Thompson (Georg Dreyman) and Keira Knightley (Christa-Maria Sieland) during rehearsals for The Lives of Others at the Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreen‘It’s almost musical’ … Luke Thompson (Georg Dreyman) and Keira Knightley (Christa-Maria Sieland) during rehearsals for The Lives of Others at the Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanTheatreInterview‘I knew I was being followed’: Keira Knightley on her hacking nightmare – and new Stasi spy play The Lives of OthersRyan GilbeyAs the Oscar-winning Stasi surveillance film hits the stage, Knightley and co-star Luke Thompson talk about the paranoia at its heart, the cost of theatre tickets nowadays – and their fury at ringtones in the stallsTue 13 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnpacking assorted tubs of carrot sticks and salad, Keira Knightley winces apologetically. “I just realised I’ve got very crunchy food,” she says. How apropos that she should consider the impact that her lunch might have on my audio recording when we are here to discussThe Lives of Others, a new play in which the characters are divided between the spies and the spied-upon.Based onthe Oscar-winning 2006 filmand set in East Berlin in 1984, the play stars Knightley as Christa-Maria, a theatre actor in a relationship with a playwright, Georg, played by Luke Thompson. Earwigging on them is Wiesler (Stephen Dillane), the Stasi officer whose principles are gradually challenged and weakened by his round-the-clock exposure to this cultured couple.View image in fullscreenParanoia … Sebastian Koch and Martina Gedeck in 2006 film The Lives of Others.Photograph: Sony Picture Classics/Sportsphoto/AllstarFlorian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s original movie opens with an interrogation scene in which a persecuted citizen is grilled relentlessly for 40 hours – the length of time it takes, according to Wiesler, for a suspect to crack under questioning. I have only been allotted one-fortieth of that time with Knightley and Thompson, who has brought along his own leafy lunch to the north London town hall where rehearsals are under way. But I am still hopeful of extracting a few details about what the play’s visionary writer-director Robert Icke has up his sleeve. This is the man who introduced Sliding Doors-style alternate-reality scenes intoRomeo and Juliet, put a countdown clock on stage inOedipus(and others), andadded the Beach Boys to Oresteia.View image in fullscreenOresteia by Aeschylus at the Almeida, directed by Robert Icke, in 2015.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianInterrogation techniques turn out not to be necessary today. “It’s quite a technical show,” volunteers Thompson, the 38-year-old Bridgerton star who worked with Icke previously on Hamlet (with Andrew Scott as the Prince) and Oresteia. “Rather than different scenes, it’s like one big set-piece with people coming in and passing batons. It’s almost musical.” Which is odd, laughs the 41-year-old Knightley, “because Rob hates dancing. He is not a man who dances.”She has some beans of her own to spill. “We’re on a revolving stage,” she says, “so we’re always on the move.” This will enable the audience to see Christa-Maria and Georg at the same time as their Stasi eavesdropper. Thompson believes this lends the stage version an advantage over the movie: “Bringing a story about watching into the theatre is maybe even better, because the audience is literally peering in on what’s happening. Whereas in a film, there’s the barrier of the screen.”View image in fullscreenCompromised … Ulrich Mühe as a Stasi operative in the 2006 film.Photograph: Buena VistaOnly when I ask whether they are using the play’s new Max Richter score during rehearsals does Thompson become remotely tight-lipped: “I don’t know if I’m allowed to say that.” Knightley throws caution to the wind: “We are using it in rehearsal, yeah. It’s very beautiful. Everyone’s in the room: we’ve got the sound designer, the costume designer, the video designer …” Video, eh? Another hint. Icke used screens in the penetrating version of Orwell’s1984which he co-adapted with Duncan Macmillan; in his Hamlet, the Ghost turned up on CCTV. It’s a convention that risks seeming passe now. “Video can feel gimmicky,” Thompson concedes. “But it’s relevant here because it’s all about surveillance.”View image in fullscreenBig Brother is watching … Icke’s stagingof 1984.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe nature of surveillance in society has changed markedly, even in the two decades since the movie opened. “You want there to be a camera at the bus stop when your bag’s been nicked,” reflects Knightley, displaying a touching faith in police priorities. “You feel safer because of that surveillance.
