But then you ask: ‘Who is surveying me?’”In the same year thatThe Lives of Otherswas released, she became part of the first wave of public figures to discover that their phone messages had been hacked by tabloids. How far has that helped her understand the sort of paranoia that dominates the play? “I do have a personal experience of what that is. Then again, I knew that my phone was being hacked because I had something tangible to show for it. There were stories. Or for me, it was mostly pictures. I knew I was being followed and then I couldseethat I was being followed. I didn’t feel like I was going mad. Whereas the characters are in a funny world where they don’t know when or if they’re being monitored.”View image in fullscreen‘The best way to create surveillance is for people to do it themselves’ … Thompson at the rehearsals for The Lives of Others.Photograph: Manuel HarlanModern parallels have been part of the rehearsal room discussions. I mention the likelihood that visitors to the US now have their social media accounts probed at immigration, and Knightley’s eyes light up. “Ah, but did that ever happen?” she asks. “Or is it enough that yousayit’s going to happen for people to self-censor? You don’t even have to follow through on the threat. You just have to put it out there.” Thompson agrees: “It’s what’s so clever and efficient about the Stasi. The best way to create surveillance is for people to do it themselves.” And not only through self-censorship: estimates are that there wasone informant for every 6.5 citizensin East Germany.Top of the cast’s reading list for the play is Stasiland, Anna Funder’s 2003 account of life in the GDR. Funder has called Von Donnersmarck’s film “superb” but also “a fantasy narrative that could not have taken place (and never did) under the GDR dictatorship”. The Lives of Others, she wrote in 2007, “doesn’t accurately portray the way totalitarian systems work, because it needs to leave room for its hero to act humanely (something such systems are designed to prevent).” Another of her charges is that the movie inadvertently legitimised the ongoing campaign by former Stasi agents to launder their reputation.View image in fullscreenVisionary director … Robert Icke, who once added the Beach Boys to Oresteia.Photograph: Dim BalsemIn at least one documented instance, however, the movie has had a real-world benefit.In 2014, 43 veterans of an elite, clandestine Israeli military intelligence unit withdrew from participating in “the state’s actions against Palestinians”, protesting that their government was guilty of “political persecution” in refusing to distinguish “between Palestinians who are and are not involved in violence”. One Israeli whistleblower singled out The Lives of Others as the catalyst for his own awakening. He and his colleagues, he realised, “were similar to the kind of oppressive intelligence in oppressive regimes”.Not everyone regards von Donnersmarck’s picture as a force for good. When a journalist recommended it to the actor Julie Christie in 2007, she replied: “I’m not sure I can bear to see a film they gave the Oscar to, that tells you what awful people communists are.” Thompson mulls this over. “There are characters who are mouthpieces for something along those lines,” he says. “But it’s not just a politics play. Part of the fun, I think, is that the characters are mysterious and you never know quite which way they’re going to go. If what audiences take from the play is ‘Communists are awful’, then I’d feel like we’d failed.”Audiences can take what they like from it – as long as they don’t take photographs. It was the sight of phone cameras being whipped out for the curtain call at Icke’s Oedipus that sent its star, Lesley Manville, into a huff. (“Clap or don’t clap,” she later said, “but don’t just stick your phone in our face.”) Despite starring on stage inIvo van Hove’s four-hour adaptation of Hanya Yanagihara’s A Little Life, where a phone ban failed to prevent the leaking of nude snaps of hisco-star James Norton, Thompson trusts the audience. “I think people broadly follow the no-phone rule,” he says. Knightley may not have set foot on stage for 11 years (“Small children, no sleep” is her pithy explanation for the hiatus) but, as a punter, she notes approvingly the “absolute fucking fury from everyone if somebody’s phone goes off in the theatre”.View image in fullscreen‘I knew that my phone was being hacked because I had something tangible to show for it’ … Knightley at the rehearsals.Photograph: Manuel HarlanI wonder how they both feel about the standing ovations which have become ubiquitous to the point of meaningless atWest Endproductions. Knightley thinks ticket prices might explain it. “I took my kids to see a musical recently and we really did enjoy it, but it cost so much that I was, like, ‘Wearegoing to love this!’” With tickets for The Lives of Others peaking at £225, she and Thompson can expect to see audiences springing to their feet every night.“In a strange way, though, the exchange that happens between actors and an audience during the clapping is the least important or interesting moment of it,” says Thompson. “If people see something good, it stays with them. Perhaps we’ve been missing that – andthat’swhy people get so excited.”“I like your optimism,” says Knightley, clearing away the lunchtime detritus. “There’s me going, ‘Maybe it’s because the tickets are expensive.’ And you’re like, ‘It’s because the play transports you!’”The Lives of Others is at theAdelphi theatre, London, from 14 October until 9 JanuaryThis article was amended on 13 October 2026. An earlier version said the character Georg was a director; in fact, he is a playwright.Explore more on these topicsTheatreKeira KnightleyThe Lives of OthersRobert IckeGermanyWest EndPolitical theatreinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: 50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about exclusion of minority ethnic artists
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about exclusion of minority ethnic artists
Content: Lauryn Pinard in Sonje at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026 in Leicester, hosted by the Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsView image in fullscreenLauryn Pinard in Sonje at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026 in Leicester, hosted by the Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsArt and design50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists?Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about  exclusion of minority ethnic artistsChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentTue 13 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British arts establishment was first published, and the question of who and what counts as British continues to be contested.The Arts Britain Ignores – Khan’s groundbreaking 1976 report, commissioned by organisations including the then Arts Council of Great Britain, presented a vision of a pluralistic national culture, in which the creativity of Britons of diverse ethnic backgrounds – from bhangra music, to black painters and Ukrainian dance – should be recognised, supported and respected.Today, whenpolls,debates and cultural and political moments present differing notions of British identity – whether it is thediversity of the England football team, orhow political figures choose to define their own identities– Khan’s work retains its relevance.View image in fullscreenUndated photo of Naseem Khan.Photograph: Frank Martin/The GuardianOn Wednesday, Dawn Airey, the new chair of cultural funding and development agencyArts Council England, will give her inaugural speech at a conference celebrating Khan’s legacy – The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On – at Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage in Leicester.Today, the work of black and Asian British visual artists, such as Frank Bowling, Sonia Boyce and Anish Kapoor is critically acclaimed and in demand. But in 1976, Khan documented how grassroot arts and cultural practices that thrived in UK ethnic minority communities were largely ignored by funders and critics.This week’s conference, bringing together artists, organisations, experts and policymakers, will explore how much progress has been made in 50 years and comes at a time when community and independent cultural spaces face pressures over finances, redevelopment and gentrification.View image in fullscreenDancer and choreographer Tebandeke Joseph performing in TimeMachine at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026.Photograph: Leesha WilliamsContributors to Wednesday’s conference include Khan’s daughter, Amelia Torode, the theatre director Jatinder Verma, the broadcaster Brenda Emmanus and the crossbench peer and chancellor of the University of Nottingham, Lola Young.View image in fullscreenCover of the new book The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On.Photograph: Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage / The Unloved.The conference also marks the launch of a new book, The Arts Britain Ignores at 50, published bySerendipity Institute, including essays and new research.Pawlet Brookes, the chief executive and artistic director of Serendipity Institute, said: “We had Cool Britannia, we’ve had the ‘ain’t no black in the union jack’. We’ve had all of that narrative. But the reality is British is diverse – whether that diversity is layered with colour or layered in other ways. We can go down a negative road, or we can celebrate what we have, which is fantastic, the best in Europe – although we still have some way to go.”View image in fullscreenBritish-Indian sculptor Anish Kapoor next to his installation Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto at the Hayward Gallery, London, in June.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersDescribing Khan’s work as “seminal”, Brookes said it was time to “see how far we’ve travelled, and what we need to do for the next 50 years.”She added: “We did a timeline investigation [for the new book] and what it shows is that, there has been funding for culturally diverse organisations, but what there hasn’t been is sustainability and growth.“We also need recognition for dance and theatre, in the way that progress has been made in the visual arts.”View image in fullscreenThe artist Frank Bowling at the launch of his  exhibition Seeking the Sublime, at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, in March.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAIn her speech, Airey is expected to say: “The journey Khan set us on remains one of the most important our sector is undertaking … [it] will sit at the centre of my work.”She praises Khan as having told institutions such as the Arts Council that “you have built an entire cultural establishment – its funding structures, its buildings, its critics, its canon – around a definition of British art that leaves whole swathes of it out.”View image in fullscreenDawn Airey, the new chair of Arts Council England, will be speaking at the conference.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianAirey is also expected to say: “It a hard time to be an artist in this country, whatever your background – but for many people in this room it is harder still.“Racism, Islamophobia and antisemitism are part of daily life for too many people in our sector: sometimes in crude and obvious ways, sometimes in subtle and deniable ones, but constantly there … So let me be emphatic. Those of us who don’t experience this – and I include myself – have a responsibility to stand with you: to stand up for the work you want to make, and to back that with action, not just words.”Explore more on these topicsArt and designBlack British cultureArts Council EnglandDawn AireyBritish identity and societyLeicesterArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Devil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpiece | FW Murnau | The Guardian
description: A rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneers
Author: Pamela Hutchinson
Headline: A rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneers
Content: Speak of the devil … Mephisto (Emil Jannings) looms over a village (created in miature) in FW Murnau’s 1926 expressionist film Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisView image in fullscreenSpeak of the devil … Mephisto (Emil Jannings) looms over a village (created in miature) in FW Murnau’s 1926 expressionist film Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFW MurnauDevil in the detail: 100 years on, FW Murnau’s Faust scrapbook reveals the secrets of his silent masterpieceA rediscovered collection of drawings and on-set photos finally reveals the intricate on-set mysteries of one of early cinema’s most gifted pioneersPamela HutchinsonTue 13 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFW Murnau was one of the greatest of all silent film-makers, with a rare genius for making beautiful images on screen. His peers liked to say he “had a camera instead of a head”. The director of such stunning films as vampire tale Nosferatu (1922) and marital romance Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) died at the age of 42 in 1931, meaning that his career barely scraped into the talkie era. Still, Murnau’s tremendous run of silent pictures included some beautiful, often disturbing classics, in which he sent his camera roaming through changing vistas of shadows and light, and plumbed the depths of the human soul. Nowhere more so than in his tour-de-force Faust, released 100 years ago this month, based on Goethe’s play about a deal with the devil. And the making of Faust is depicted in a stunning new book, which is both a document of, and in a sense an artefact from, the production of this classic film.Murnau was also one of the most mysterious of directors: secretive about his methods, with an intense devotion to his work. Early collaborator Edgar G Ulmer called him “a great purist who worked under a sort of hypnosis”. Murnau banned producers from his sets, and executives from watching his rushes. Bar a few exceptions, he did not allow on-set photography to reveal the secrets of his camerawork and special effects. This mystique created room for speculation as to whether Murnau, or his talented crew, were responsible for the success of his films. The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece publishes unseen images from the shoot of one of his best films, and gives a rare insight into the collaborative way it was made.View image in fullscreenFW Murnau photographed on the set of Faust by Hans Natge.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFaust was Murnau’s final German film before he went to Hollywood, and at the time it was the most expensive, complex film that the Ufa studio had ever produced. It is an adaptation of Goethe’s tragedy about the scholar Faust (played by Swedish actor Gösta Ekman) who sells his soul to the devil, represented by the grinning, black-clad demon Mephistopheles (German star Emil Jannings). A commercial flop on its release, Faust is now acclaimed as one of the greats. French New Wave director Éric Rohmer, a Murnau devotee, wrote his doctoral dissertation on the film. The Faust Bible reveals how Murnau and his crew achieved some of the incredible shots and special effects in this film, but it is also an enhanced facsimile of an artefact from the film’s production, which has survived against all odds to spill its secrets.In the film, Faust owns a hefty, leather-bound Bible, which he throws on the fire in a moment of despair. But the prop was to become something more. Art directors Robert Herlth and Walter Röhrig pulled the book from the ashes and pasted designs, stills and behind-the-scenes photographs on to its blank pages so they could present the souvenir as a gift to the director at the end of the shoot. Murnau left it behind in his flat in Berlin when he went to Hollywood, not knowing he would never return to retrieve it. After his death, Murnau’s brother stashed his belongings in various city-centre basements, which were susceptible to flooding, and worse, once the bombs began falling on Berlin during the second world war.View image in fullscreenEmil Jannings and Gösta Ekman in costume as Mephisto and Faust.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisFilm scholar and archivist Lotte Eisner came to Berlin looking for Murnau’s archives in the 1950s, but found no sign of the Bible. It was not until the 1960s that a German curator from the city’s Akademie der Künste, Engelbert von Mallinckrodt, told Henri Langlois at the Cinématheque Française that he had bought some of Murnau’s photo albums for a small sum from a restaurateur called Rolf Conscienze, who had film industry connections. It turned out that these albums included the Bible – though no one knows how they ended up with Conscienze. Then, to deepen the mystery, Mallinckrodt vanished, and his flatmate became the book’s custodian for several decades: it was wrapped in brown paper sitting on top of a cupboard. Eisner searched for the Faust Bible her whole life but she was never to see it. She died in 1983.View image in fullscreenThe film-makers creating special effect clouds above a model mountaintop.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisNow the book is in the safekeeping of the Cinémathèque Française, which bought it in 2017, and there it remains, a memento of the once-contested collaborative nature of Murnau’s methods. I went to see it this summer, and it is appropriately grand in scale, an unusually majestic scrapbook. Restored by the cinema’s director of heritage Laurent Mannoni and his team, the book looks good for an abandoned, 100-year-old prop. The water-damage has been smoothed out, leaving only a few scuffs, and the shadows where some enterprising thief has prised the metal crucifix and corner pieces from the leather.double quotation markEach day on the set was a fresh opportunity to surpass ourselves in ingenuityArt director Robert HerlthInside, sketches for individual scenes are arranged opposite matching stills from the film. Turning these hallowed pages, you can see how the compositions of figures and objects by the designers known as “film architects” – the forced perspectives, contrasting arrangements of light and dark, sweeping shadows, steam and flames – were re-created on film by Murnau and his talented cinematographer Carl Hoffmann. The director encouraged his designer to draw not just the spaces, but the actors too, creating something closer to a storyboard image than a set design.View image in fullscreenMephisto appears in a still from the film.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, Paris“The sketch became the equivalent of a contract,” Herlth later wrote. “[Murnau] insisted that every stroke of the pen should be faithfully rendered in the execution.” This meant not only building sets according to the designs but Murnau and Hoffmann making extensive adjustments to the lighting to produce the velvety shadows that the director demanded. Hoffmann then navigated these settings with bold, fluid camera movements in a technique calledentfesselte Kamera(unchained camera), originated by cinematographer Karl Freund when working with Murnau on The Last Laugh (1924). Murnau was not short of visual references. He had a strong interest in the occult, and his background was in art history. Albrecht Dürer’s Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse woodcut was a direct influence on the film’s opening scene.View image in fullscreenA behind-the-scenes photograph by Hans Natge. Faust was the most expensive and ambitious film the Ufa studio had ever produced.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisHerlth recalled the experience of working with Murnau as good-humoured, if challenging, as the director was cheerful but always ambitious to create shots and camera effects that had not been achieved before. The crew spent long days and nights discussing and experimenting with new ideas. “Each day on the set was a fresh opportunity to surpass ourselves in inventiveness and ingenuity,” he said.Leafing further through the Bible, the chiaroscuro sketches and stills give way to playful collages, images of the cast and crew having fun on set, the legendarily tall Murnau hunched over as he instructs Jannings how to leer malevolently. And there are pages that speak to that boundless technical ingenuity. One of the most celebrated moments in the film is the Weltflug (“flight around the world”) sequence, in which Mephistopheles flies Faust through the sky on his cloak, the world lurching below them. The Bible retains the diagrams that explain just how they achieved this uncanny flight simulation. The secret was a low wooden trolley moving along a plaster ramp, an idea that came to Herlth and Röhrig when they saw a truck being unloaded in the street.View image in fullscreenMurnau, left, directs a group of children on a grassy hillside during the filming of the Gretchen sequence.Photograph: © La Cinémathèque française, ParisThe facsimile edition reprints the Weltflug diagrams on gatefold pages so you can study century-old secrets of film technique at your leisure. It also comprehensively reprints all the Bible’s images, with explanatory captions, enlargements, and quotations from the screenplay, which was written in epigrammatic, almost poetic prose. There are also essays and additional drawings from the Cinémathèque’s archives.We may never fully understand the workings of Murnau’s mysterious “camera-head” and his collaborations with his team. But this fascinating souvenir takes us close.The Faust Bible: The Making of FW Murnau’s Masterpiece is published byMubi Editionson 17 October. Faust streams on Mubi from 14 October, with live-scored centenary screenings in Paris on 17 October, Munich on 25 October, and Los Angeles on 1 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFW MurnauJohann Wolfgang von GoethefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ian McKellen to star in UK premiere of ‘mixed reality’ play – but not in person | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Audiences in Manchester will be asked to wear smart glasses for An Ark, which debuted in New York this year
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Audiences in Manchester will be asked to wear smart glasses for An Ark, which debuted in New York this year
Content: Ian McKellen in rehearsal for An Ark, which is coming to Manchester next spring.Photograph: Fiona FreundView image in fullscreenIan McKellen in rehearsal for An Ark, which is coming to Manchester next spring.Photograph: Fiona FreundTheatreIan McKellen to star in UK premiere of ‘mixed reality’ play – but not in personAudiences in Manchester will be asked to wear smart glasses for An Ark, which debuted in New York this yearHelena HortonTue 13 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan McKellen will star in a groundbreaking new play that gets its UK premiere in Manchester next spring. But the veteran actor will not set foot on stage.The Lord of the Rings star is taking part in An Ark, a“mixed reality” playthat had its debut in New York earlier this year. Theatregoers are asked to wear smart glasses, which project the actors into the room.John McGrath, the chief executive of Factory International, which is putting on the play, said: “Mixed reality is when you see both the virtual elements of an experience and also the real world around you.”He said it differed from virtual reality because rather than putting on “a set of goggles that exclude the physical reality you’re in”, these glasses “project into the space but also show the real world you are in”.Asked whether McKellen would have any physical role in the play, which will be on at Aviva Studios from 27 March to 10 April, he said: “His virtual presence will be there. He may well come and visit the play but you won’t see the real Ian McKellen performing.”View image in fullscreenFour actors were filmed by 52 cameras in one take for the play.Photograph: Tin DrumHe said the audience would be satisfied to pay to attend a play where the actors were not there in the flesh. “When people go to see a film, you don’t spend time explaining the lead actors in the film won’t be in the cinema. This is no different,” he said.The 47-minute production is billed as an exploration of life and death, during which “actors share stories about life to make it seem as if they are right before you, offering an intimate reimagining of live theatre. With that technology, actors share stories about how humans grow, connect, and grieve over a life.”While some may think going to the theatre is exciting because you see the actors performing live in front of you, McGrath said mixed reality plays had other benefits. “What you get is the intimacy with the actors, so you feel like they are sitting in front of you and talking directly to you.” He said this created a “very touching personal experience”.Four actors, including McKellen, were filmed by 52 cameras in one take at a studio in the French city of Grenoble. They appear seated just before the viewer as if they are putting on a private show.View image in fullscreenIan McKellen takes his turn during filming for the mixed reality play.Photograph: Tin DrumFor the actors, McGrath said, “it is far closer to being in a film than being on stage. It’s one for actors who enjoy a new challenge.”The theatre plans to hold public events to explore the future and ethics of this technology.Factory’s programme for 2027 celebrates 20 years of the organisation. Among the plans is a special production of Philip Glass’s opera Einstein on the Beach.McGrath said: “This will be one of the biggest opera performances anywhere in the year – it’s Philip Glass’s 90th birthday year, and this is the first time in 50 years there has been a full new production of it. It will be a way to experience that amazing score in a big, huge warehouse in a way that’s very different to an opera you’d usually see.”He added: “Most of the work in this programme, we are either the world premiere or the UK premiere and we have co-produced it.”Explore more on these topicsTheatreIan McKellenManchesternewsShareReuse this content

title: RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34 | RJ Mitte | The Guardian
description: Actor who played Walter White Jr and who advocated for disability representation is remembered by Bryan Cranston as ‘my sweet son’
Author: Mollie Reilly
Headline: Actor who played Walter White Jr and who advocated for disability representation is remembered by Bryan Cranston as ‘my sweet son’
Content: 1:00RJ Mitte's memorable moments in 'Breaking Bad' – videoRJ MitteRJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34Actor who played Walter White Jr and who advocated for disability representation is remembered by Bryan Cranston as ‘my sweet son’RJ Mitte – a life in picturesMollie ReillyandSian CainTue 13 Oct 2026 02.21 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr in the television seriesBreaking Bad, has died aged 34 in Brownsville, Texas.“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocateRJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”A publicist for the actor confirmed news reports that Mitte took his own life. No further details about the circumstances were given.RJ Mitte: ‘By 13, I was the main breadwinner for my family. It was scary but necessary’Read moreThe Brownsville police department said no foul play was suspected. The Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son ofBryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, Walter White, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which isoftencitedas one of the best television series of all time.In 2015, hespoke to the Guardianabout being a disabled actor who played disabled characters. “You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have,” he said.Mitte’s co-stars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke, including Cranston,who wrote a lengthy tribute on Instagram. Cranston described him as “my sweet son on Breaking Bad”, a “fine actor” and a “vocal advocate for performers with disabilities”.“It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life,” Cranston wrote. He said he and Mitte had been texting each other a few weeks ago about ​possibly meeting for lunch. “I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future,” Cranston wrote. “But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed. I’ll miss you, son.“He said Mitte “never – ever – allowed [his disability] to be an excuse for anything” during the show’s production. “He met the demanding shooting schedule head-on with great determination.”View image in fullscreenRJ Mitte, Bryan Cranston, Anna Gunn and Aaron Paul of Breaking Bad in 2013.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APAaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader,wroteon social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on other series including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Days before his death, he waspromotinghis new film, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRJ Mitte – a life in picturesRead moreEarlier this month, Mitteappearedon the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator,Vince Gilligan. “It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and he served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a2016 interviewwith the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face,” he said. “But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsRJ MitteTexasBreaking BadUS televisionTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendants | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Actor, who allegedly punched one Delta attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door, was charged for two separate assaults after the plane landed
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Actor, who allegedly punched one Delta attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door, was charged for two separate assaults after the plane landed
Content: Selma Blair leaving court in New York on Monday after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APView image in fullscreenSelma Blair leaving court in New York on Monday after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APSelma BlairSelma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendantsActor, who allegedly punched one Delta attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door, was charged for two separate assaults after the plane landedMaya Yangin New York andSian CainMon 12 Oct 2026 23.28 EDTFirst published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actorSelma Blairwas arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy airport inNew Yorkafter she allegedly attacked two flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, and separately charged with two counts of assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after landing.Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority ofNew Yorkand New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles.The 54-year-old “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.”Several news outlets on Mondayreportedthat Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door.The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicisttoldthe Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.”The FBI, which handles reports of crimes on airplanes, has issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter.View image in fullscreenSelma Blair attending Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersThose charges will be handled through the petty violations court in federal court in Brooklyn. No date has been set for Blair’s appearance.Separately, Blair was charged on Monday night at a court in Queens with two counts of second-degree assault, for allegedly assaulting a police officer who was taking her to hospital after the flight, as well as a nurse after she arrived there.In charging documents, a police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center alleged that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. A nurse who was moving Blair in hospital alleged the actor then kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain.On Monday night, a judge set Blair’s bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. Blair then left court with her lawyers.Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren’t immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”.An air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying “one flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks”.“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which waspublishedby NBC Los Angeles.The flight controller replied that paramedics were approaching the gate – and that law enforcement was already there.Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in an incident on a plane. In 2016, shereportedlybegan screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico.Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”.“That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time.The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018multiple sclerosisdiagnosis. And in February 2024, sheapologizedfor an Islamophobic comment on social media.Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.Explore more on these topicsSelma BlairNew YorkUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows up  | Television | The Guardian
description: This peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US president
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: This peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US president
Content: Mike Tyson in the Netflix docuseries Tyson.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenMike Tyson in the Netflix docuseries Tyson.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewTyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows upThis peculiar – some would say truly irresponsible – hagiography of boxing superstar Mike Tyson veers from psychedelics and sobbing to the inadvisable face tattoo via a cameo from the US presidentHannah J DaviesTue 13 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix’s new four-parter onMike Tysonis one of the strangest sports documentaries it has ever released, or maybe just one of its strangest documentaries full stop. The streamer has form in sporting hagiographies – tales told with questionable distance from their subjects, and all the objectivity of cold war agitprop. Tyson is different, though: not only is it lopsided, but it also feels deeply icky. And that’s before Donald Trump arrives to defend its subject – a great catch for the programme-makers but a wholly baffling cameo that makes you wish he would stick with geopolitical meddling and golf.It ends – spoiler alert – with the former boxing champion taking thehallucinogenic drug DMT(or as he calls it, “the toad”, after the animal that produces it), while sobbing and inviting the show’s director to join him. Its episodes are peculiar, sometimes compelling, and – as many viewers will surely feel – truly irresponsible.It starts uncontroversially enough, recounting the extreme poverty and precarity of Tyson’s upbringing, when he would rob other kids for their wallets and chains. Now when he goes back to Brownsville, Brooklyn, he is mobbed by adoring fans. Tyson had a talent for knocking people out in his youth, which would later pique the interest of the coach Bobby Stewart, whom he met during a stint in a juvenile detention centre. At 13, Stewart put Tyson in front of the fabled manager and promoter Cus D’Amato, who told him that he would be heavyweight champion of the world one day; Lennox Lewis, an early sparring partner, says: “[Tyson] just ran over to me and took my head off!” A dazzling pro career followed, despite many tragedies – not least the loss of D’Amato, who died in 1985. But Tyson was on the brink of big titles and big fame. As he puts it: “It was awesome being young and having all of that attention.”View image in fullscreen‘It was awesome’ … Tyson with the boxing promoter Don King in Tyson.Photograph: NetflixBut Tyson the docuseries isn’t content with being a professional fable. It also delves into the man’s past in a way that feels grubby and careless. Much is made of his short-lived marriage to the actor Robin Givens, whose mother told the journalist Wallace Matthews that Tyson was beating her daughter (Givens declined an interview request from the programme-makers). Tyson, says Matthews, didn’t deny attacking her but said he didn’t hurt her and that “we fought”. (Here, Tyson says: “I know people say she can’t fight you, you’re Mike Tyson – but we fought.”)Givens was later to deny that her husband had beaten her. As for rumblings, after her denial, of assault and battery towards his then wife, Tyson says “it’s a bunch of bullshit”. There’s archive footage of Tyson telling the broadcaster Barbara Walters that he grabbed his wife but never hit her, while Givens is shown telling her that the union was “pure hell” and “torture”. In the present, Tyson calls Givens “a fucking bitch”. Headlines flash up on screen, among them: “Iron Mike dreamed of love, but all he got was [a] package of strife”. The episode ends with a disclaimer and mention of a website with resources for survivors of sexual violence.View image in fullscreenTyson celebrates his heavyweight win over Michael Spinks in 1988.Photograph: NetflixAn instalment on his rape conviction is no better, with Tyson – who denies that he sexually assaulted the then 18-year-old pageant contestant Desiree Washington – laughing about his reputation for being handsy. There are a few voices who don’t entirely discredit Washington, but many more who express scepticism that Tyson could have been guilty of the crime for which he was convicted and served three years in prison.Trump – a man who, at least, has some apparent experience in this area – says “[Tyson] is very truthful, and I think the truth hurt him in this case”. The media, he adds, was “rough on Mike, but it just made Mike harder. They’re rough on me, and I’m the president!”Interviewees talk about Tyson not as an athlete with a troubling past but as someone akin to Nelson Mandela. Tom Patti, a friend and former boxer, says: “You can knock him down, you can say bad things about him, you can take away his freedom, but guess what? [He’s] still here.” The same warning plays at the end of that episode.Sure, there’s much on the drugs and booze and the inadvisable face tattoo, and even the son (Miguel, now 24) who calls his dad a “deadbeat”. Tyson calls himself “a spoiled brat” for how he acted in the ring, when he bit Evander Holyfield’s ear not once but twice. And there is deep, horrifying tragedy in the form of the death of Tyson’s young daughter, Exodus, who perished in an accident aged four. But Tyson the docuseries is an exercise in not taking due accountability, and swerving your opponent’s punches. Tyson ends by talking about how “special” he is. Certainly, it takes a singular figure to star in a programme this gross.Tyson is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMike TysonSport TVDocumentaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the advice columnist who sued Donald Trump twice – and won | Television | The Guardian
description: A riveting documentary about the journalist who took the US president to the cleaners. Plus: John Simpson celebrates 60 years at the Beeb. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A riveting documentary about the journalist who took the US president to the cleaners. Plus: John Simpson celebrates 60 years at the Beeb. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: She wouldn’t let it stand … E Jean Carroll in Storyville.Photograph: BBC/Miss Bingley LLCView image in fullscreenShe wouldn’t let it stand … E Jean Carroll in Storyville.Photograph: BBC/Miss Bingley LLCTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the advice columnist who sued Donald Trump twice – and wonA riveting documentary about the journalist who took the US president to the cleaners. Plus: John Simpson celebrates 60 years at the Beeb. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Phil HarrisonandGraeme VirtueTue 13 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStoryville: Ask E Jean10pm, BBC FourWhy did journalist and advice columnist E Jean Carroll decide to sue Donald Trump? “Because he called me a liar and I couldn’t let it stand.” This documentary follows her groundbreaking media career before retracing her journey to suing Trump twice in the civil courts over sexual abuse and defamation allegations (in 2019, and 2022), which she won both times.Hollie RichardsonThe Great British Bake Off8pm, Channel 4Bread is Paul Hollywood’s speciality, much to the chagrin of the contestants in bread week. For the first challenge, Tom and Gary are both making cheesy Chelsea buns, while Connie is creating Yum Yum-style bread with four different cheeses and chilli flakes. But which of the bakers can infuse the perfect amount of garlic into theirs?Priya ElanBlue Lights9pm, BBC OneThe day of Gerry’s murder trial is finally here, which means a quick return from former cop Jen (Hannah McClean), who was with him when he was shot. Prepare for the emotions to hit hard as Sandra (Andi Osho) sits through it. Meanwhile, Grace (Siân Brooke) pays a visit to the young woman who’s trying to ruin her life.HRJohn Simpson: Sixty Years at the BBC9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreen‘Affable, intelligent guide’ … John Simpson.Photograph: BBC / Robert CoxwellJohn Simpson’s BBC career covers an extraordinary span of time: this highlights package doubles as a history of the post-second world war era. Simpson is an affable, intelligent guide to events ranging from the Iranian revolution (“extremely frightening”) to the release of Nelson Mandela and the travails of Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Phil HarrisonBen Fogle: New Lives in the Wild9pm, Channel 5The Humbert family run a sustainable pearl-farming business on a far-flung Pacific atoll in French Polynesia. When Ben Fogle comes to visit he earns his keep by diving for oysters. But can he charm the clan’s 83-year-old grandpa, a salty Gallic sea dog who regards vegetables with contempt?Graeme VirtueThe Sky Arts awards 20269pm, Sky ArtsIt’s a classy affair as Grayson Perry and Rebecca Lucy Taylor (Self Esteem) host a night at London’s Roundhouse rewarding the best in this year’s culture. title: Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus review – the zany follow-up to Lessons in Chemistry | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetry
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: This offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetry
Content: Sharp wit … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Sophia Spring/eyevineView image in fullscreenSharp wit … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Sophia Spring/eyevineBook of the dayFictionReviewPeck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus review – the zany follow-up to Lessons in ChemistryThis offbeat tale of machinations at an eccentric poetry magazine in 80s New York is laugh-out-loud funny – and a paean to the power of poetryClare ClarkTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you have been into a bookshop since 2022, or perhaps even just breathed in and out, you could not have failed to clock the phenomenon that was Lessons in Chemistry. Bonnie Garmus’s debut remains a global sensation. The story of Elizabeth Zott, a gifted research chemist who, forced out of her lab by rampant 1950s misogyny, becomes the inspirational host of a TV cooking show, has so far sold a staggering 9m copies around the world. It spent the best part of two years on the Sunday Times bestseller list, was translated into more than 40 languages, and scooped numerous awards. In 2023 it became an Emmy-winning TV series; a year later New York Times readers voted it one of their top 100 books of the 21st century. Elizabeth Zott made such a splash that even her favoured brand of rowing machine saw a spike in sales.What was the key to its prodigious success? Timing helped. In the aftermath of #MeToo, readers embraced a heroine who refuses to be cowed by injustice, who, thanks to resilience, pragmatism and straight-up hard work, ultimately comes out on top. The book is smart and very funny, a propulsive mashup of feminism and fairytale that balances darkness with whimsy, heartbreak with hope. It is also carries a shamelessly inspirational message. “Do not allow your talents to lie dormant, ladies,” Zott exhorts her audience of housewives in the TV studio. “Design your own future. When you go home today, ask yourself what you will change. And then get started.”Garmus, then a copywriter, wrote the first chapter of Lessons in Chemistry in a fury after a meeting where a male colleague flagrantly took credit for her ideas: her anger “lit a fire under me about telling this story”. In Peck & Peck, her follow-up, there is less outrage crackling on the page but there are most definitely fires, and not metaphorical ones either. At the otherworldly New York offices of Peck & Peck, the most enigmatic, prestigious and dysfunctional poetry magazine in the world, the 39 editors have a single aim: to publish the world’s finest poems. Failed submissions – and every week there are thousands – are incinerated by the team of prison parolees who work in the mailroom.double quotation markIt is impossible not to be beguiled by Garmus’s irrepressible humour and the freewheeling exuberance of her imaginationGarmus’s sharp wit and gift for offbeat characters are both at full throttle in this quirky story of Batter Gray, a boy named for his mother’s improbably intrepid dog. Batter’s parents – his father teaches history, his mother designs typefaces – are eager for him to pursue a sensible, by which they mean lucrative, career; but Batter cares only for poetry. When by a marvellous fluke he lands a job at Peck & Peck, he is ecstatic, only to find himself in the basement churning out photocopies. Passionate about poems, pathologically unable to resist trouble, Batter is soon caught up in the bitter feud between the magazine’s two editors-in-chief, sworn enemies who just happen also to be twins.Corporate machinations at a cultish poetry magazine in the 1980s might seem to offer slim pickings for any mainstream novel, let alone the follow-up to a monster blockbuster. The endangered future of poetry does not exactly sit alongside feminism as a rousing call to arms. Even Batter’s truth-telling typeface-fixated mother Rainey (a ringer for Elizabeth Zott) cannot duck the fact that poetry “is the bottom of the barrel arts-wise” and poets “never make a dime”. And yet from this apparently rarefied premise Garmus constructs a zany office comedy with shades of Hogwarts (Peck & Peck’s office building, with its vast glass dome, pneumatic tube delivery system and alphabetised balcony topiary, is as fantastical as anything in Rowling’s oeuvre) and the gleeful originality of early John Irving.Though it sags a little in the middle, the result is a story that mostly zips along, and a resoundingly impassioned case for the importance of poetry in a profit-obsessed society that would gladly condemn it to extinction. Garmus’s riff on the poems that Peck & Peck sends straight to the incinerator is worth the price of admission alone: “anything on scented paper; anything written in only lowercase letters; anything that included a mention of self-publishing … poems that mentioned kittens, puppies, cooking, sandcastles, babies, sunrises, rainbows, running, beaches, cancer, or the word ‘namaste’ … Anything written on parchment … Anything using the word ‘methinks’”.This aversion to mawkishness does not prevent it from creeping into Garmus’s own work. Readers irked by Six-Thirty, Lessons in Chemistry’s preternaturally intelligent dog, will find themselves no less vexed by Batter’s namesake, a rescue mutt whose credulity-stretching acts of heroism leave Lassie in the shade. And yet it is impossible not to be beguiled by Garmus’s irrepressible humour and the freewheeling exuberance of her imagination. It is hard to imagine a novel with more laugh-out-loud jokes about typography, harder still to dismiss her fierce exhortation to all of us to make words count. Will it repeat the mind-boggling success of Lessons in Chemistry? Probably not, but there are lessons in this book too that, in this terrifyingly accelerating age of AI, feel just as vital. “When you’re interested in poetry, you’re interested in everything,” one of Peck & Peck’s longstanding editors tells Batter. title: Generation Maybe by Camilla Cavendish review – what’s really behind the fertility gap?  | Society books | The Guardian
description: An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to Iran
Author: Mythili Rao
Headline: An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to Iran
Content: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who has publicly disclosed that she is freezing her eggs.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who has publicly disclosed that she is freezing her eggs.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSociety booksReviewGeneration Maybe by Camilla Cavendish review – what’s really behind the fertility gap?An evidenced-based account of the difficult choices facing couples across the world – from America to IranMythili RaoTue 13 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Don’t be weird about this,” representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez laughed into the camera as she prepared to jab a hormone-filled needle into her midsection, adding that she knew full well that, yes, people were definitely going to be weird about it. At 36, the congresswoman had begun freezing her eggs, and was making a point of bringing her online audience along with her as she did, stepping directly into the fraught question of how an ambitious woman should manage her fertility.It’s a live concern: around the world, birthrates are falling sharply. “Only the Black Death in the 14th century is comparable to what is happening now,” Financial Times journalist Camilla Cavendish notes ina new book examining why. Setting aside the most toxic gender-war narratives, “the standard explanation is that as women get educated, they choose freedom and autonomy over family”.As Cavendish explains, however, that is “not the whole story”.Drawing on a wealth of reporting, her book seeks to present a more nuanced picture. Cavendish begins with the “fertility gap” – the official name for the difference between the number of children people say they want and the number they actually go on to have – and works her way backwards, focusing on the lived experience of men and women who find themselves with fewer children than they expected. What stopped them?double quotation markCavendish shows the gulf between popular talking points about fertility and the actual conversations potential parents are havingFor some, the main barrier is finding the right partner in time. For others, it comes down to the increasing costs of raising a family (where housing specifically can be a factor) and the enormous difficulty of balancing a career with caregiving, particularly when it takes longer to establish a professional foundation in the first place. There’s more: a “rational pessimism about prospects for the next generation” in an unstable world, the stigma of embracing motherhood, the shortage of stories glorifying father­hood, a pressure to perform “intensive parenting”, the lure of well-compensated but all-consuming “greedy jobs”, and so on. There’s also the sheer exhaustion that comes with caring for a small child. The headwinds are strong.Taken together, “the joyous, messy, life-giving task of raising a family has become something that feels more like a daunting, lonely, and expensive chore,” Cavendish observes. “We’ve shifted, slowly but surely, into treating parent­hood like a self-indulgent lifestyle choice. The onus is on you to cope.” These aren’t abstract observations. Cavendish herself is a working mother of three, well acquainted with the difficulties of supporting a family and managing a career. She has no illusions about how hard it can be, and no interest in pretending otherwise. “I am struck by how little has changed in the workplace in the last 20 years, despite the rhetoric about flexibility,” she notes. “What has changed, I think, is how grimly realistic young women now are about the trade-offs.”“Reproduction is kind of the whole ballgame,” the trailblazing feminist Gloria Steinem told David Remnick in a 2015 interview, “and who controls it is the most fundamental question.” Generation Maybecharts how authoritarian governments in China, Russia, Iran and elsewhere have responded to falling birthrates with a variety of repressive pronatalist policies – sanctioning child marriage, making divorce more difficult and denying abortion access. The Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive rights and federal childcare funding follow this trend, conscripting women into domestic roles. A simple solution to the problem of birth deficit is to force women to breed.It may not be easy to create effective pronatalist policy interventions that encourage, rather than entrap – but it’s not impossible. Cavendish looks at what’s worked and what hasn’t in Singapore, Scandinavia and France, and outlines just shy of a dozen ways to help people choose children, from building more housing to offering parents benefits and even giving children themselves the vote: “Almost all policies which may help to lift birthrates are also ones which could enable human flourishing,” she notes.There is no hectoring or finger-wagging in this book. What’s offered instead is an empathic and curious approach to an entirely rational ambivalence. In so doing, Generation Maybe illuminates the enormous gulf between popular talking points about fertility and the actual conversations potential parents are having. For Cavendish, the real goal isn’t to persuade anyone to have kids; it’s simply “to make children a genuine choice”.Generation Maybe: Why We’re Having Fewer Children, and What It Means for Us All by Camilla Cavendish is published by Bodley Head (£25).
