title: The Girl in the River review – forensic psychologist police procedural thriller plays like noir parody | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ralph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenager
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Ralph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenager
Content: Devon Sawa and Maggie Grace in The Girl in the Water.Photograph: David WigginsView image in fullscreenDevon Sawa and Maggie Grace in The Girl in the Water.Photograph: David WigginsMoviesReviewThe Girl in the River review – forensic psychologist police procedural thriller plays like noir parodyRalph Macchio and Tiffany Haddish feature in a ropey and implausible manhunt thriller as cops search for the missing twin of a murdered teenagerPhil HoadTue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis small-town police thriller sets its stall out intriguingly, with a murder that seems actively begging to be solved. The perp chose to dump his victim – the 14-year-old daughter of a local political bigwig – into a part of the Mississippi River where she was likely to resurface, and from a highly visible bridge. When veteran detective Alan Kramer (Devon Sawa) and rookie forensic psychologist Amelia Pembrock (Maggie Grace) show up to investigate, they are immediately alerted to a gun in the bushes just yards away. As a colleague observes: “This isn’t a clean-up. It’s a message.”But Brando Benetton’s debut film sadly fails to capitalise on the misdirection at play in this open-goal crime scene. Instead of using it to pry open community secrets, he gives us a ropey and implausible manhunt. As Kramer and Pembrock race to locate the girl’s twin, who is presumably still in the killer’s clutches, they zero in on local butcher Boris (Darron Dunbar). He has a sex-pest rap sheet and lives with his mother – which apparently ticks all the boxes for a profiling genius such as Pembrock. Kramer pulls her up for being unbothered by the lack of actual prosecutable evidence. But carping is about the only investigative contribution this seasoned criminologist makes here (and what’s a criminologist – a crime sociologist – doing out in the field anyway?).If the killer leaves behind a parody of a crime scene, The Girl in the River offers up its own parody noir, though in a cliche-strewn and far less careful fashion. We have the obsessive desk jockey, the boozy, trauma-harbouring vet halfway out the retirement door, Tiffany Haddish’s angry black captain (as satirised in the Jump Street franchise), and the affable town coroner (The Karate Kid’s Ralph Macchio). Whenever the detectives are floundering, the over-directed script is always on hand to put them back on the rails. The local media seem strangely willing to share their voluminous stash of damning evidence; a transparently staged mutiny among the townsfolk fires up Kramer and Pembrock just as they’re out of leads.Grace, with her twitchy defensiveness, and the frazzled Sawa manage to half-ballast this dubious sleuthing, and Benetton keeps the film moving fast enough so the many infelicities don’t register too horrifically. But with no time to accumulate any proper gravitas, Kramer’s capstone speech about universal corruption is, like the victim, dead in the water.The Girl in the River is on digital platforms on 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersCrime filmsTiffany HaddishreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Social Reckoning isn’t as angry or as potent as a Facebook drama should be | Drama films | The Guardian
description: Aaron Sorkin’s attempt to return to the success of The Social Network is a strangely dated and incomplete look at a world that needs a sharper eye
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Aaron Sorkin’s attempt to return to the success of The Social Network is a strangely dated and incomplete look at a world that needs a sharper eye
Content: Jeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APView image in fullscreenJeremy Allen White and Mikey Madison in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APDrama filmsThe Social Reckoning isn’t as angry or as potent as a Facebook drama should beJesse HassengerAaron Sorkin’s attempt to return to the success of The Social Network is a strangely dated and incomplete look at a world that needs a sharper eyeTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 16.32 EDTShareIn retrospect, David Fincher’s 2010 filmThe Social Networkwas a landmark for a quiet, even counterintuitive reason. Before the film was released, some questioned whether Aaron Sorkin, a writer not exactly known for his mastery of, nevermind obsession with, the technical sphere, was the right man to tell the origin story of Facebook. And while Sorkin may well have converted Mark Zuckerberg into terms he could better understand – namely, a motormouthed wiseass who deep down wants to impress a smart, serious-minded girl – he and Fincher also made one of the first internet-centric movies to treat online life as a natural extension of IRL dynamics, rather than the otherworldly tech portal seen in so many 90s internet movies.The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet ZuckerbergRead moreGranted, that’s the whole deal with Facebook: its viral spread of social networking, something so simple and addictive that aunts, grandpas and co-workers everywhere could understand it. Yet understanding its simultaneous extension and distortion of the real world wasn’t a given; four years later, for example, 2014’s Men, Women and Children was widely derided for taking an alarmist approach to the internet as a haven for adults seeking an affair, teenagers nursing porn addictions and fame-hungry strivers of all ages. The Social Network, on the other hand, is remarkably nonjudgmental about the basic mechanics ofFacebook, rooting its nascent flaws in the human weaknesses that birthed it. In retrospect, the movie only feels outdated to the extent that it underestimates Zuckerberg’s grasping for power and the potential for grim carelessness that his online kingdom was built on.The Social Reckoning, a sorta-sequel written and directed by Sorkin without Fincher’s involvement, aims to correct the record while still giving voice to a character who believes that the site has real utility. Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who works for the site’s civics team, is socially awkward and anxious, and when she notes that some people are better at a keyboard than they are in person, it’s clear she’s thinking of herself, even though she never says so. Frances is distraught to learn that Facebook is contributing to radicalization of some of its users, funneling them into extremist groups as a function of its give-the-people-what-they-want approach to free speech. She turns to a luddite-adjacent journalist (Jeremy Allen White) doing some digging on the company, and together they challenge the orthodoxy of Zuckerberg, last seen in The Social Network fruitlessly refreshing a Facebook page hoping for a reciprocated friend request.Appropriate for a movie set largely in the early 2020s, The Social Reckoning’s Zuckerberg is a completely different person, literally: famously intenseJeremy Strongsteps in for the comparably charming Jesse Eisenberg. But Zuck isn’t the main focus here anyway; though he is depicted as a sort of mutation of the aggrieved nerd from the first film, still issuing cutting sarcastic remarks, but in the voice of an empty-suit automaton, the movie wants to be about the ways that social networking has metastasized beyond Zuckerberg’s control. He can’t do anything about ill effects on real life – he laments the both-sides attacks he’ll face no matter what he does – so he might as well keep the profits churning in.It’s here where Sorkin both oversteps and falls short in his analysis of how online reality has bled into the real world. On one hand, he connects the radicalization of some Facebook users to the January 6 insurrection riots in Washington, jumping into the Facebook control room for a chilling look at their inaction in the face of fomenting violence in our own country. Connecting that particular dot requires some timeline fudging of the dual whistleblower-and-Zuckerberg story threads, but you understand why Sorkin went to the trouble. It’s an event representing the kind of behavior that Facebook probably enabled, both ideologically and logistically.Yet Sorkin also insists on containing that behavior in stodgy, old-fashioned terms. The January 6 riots are framed as particularly far beyond the pale in large part because they bring harm to police officers – which connects back to the movie’s opening sequence, where a drunk and racist woman livestreams her horrible comments to non-white police officers on Facebook. Won’t someone please think of the cops?! (It’s as if Sorkin can’t conceive of racism so blatant unless it’s been officially documented by the police.) This is how Sorkin knows the proper order has been threatened.View image in fullscreenJeremy Strong in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Leah Gallo/Sony Pictures/APWhen Frances quits her Facebook post and testifies in front of Congress, the movie implies with her moment of triumph that the reckoning is at hand, and that Zuckerberg has been, on some level, chastened and/or humiliated. The world has been pulled back from the brink. Meanwhile, the existence of even more damning cases against Facebook, like the idea that the companyenabled genocide in Myanmar, doesn’t get so much as a mention. One movie can’t be expected to cover the whole of the global internet, but that doesn’t stop The Social Reckoning from feeling awfully small.The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our ageRead moreA more subtle sign that Sorkin hasn’t oriented himself in the actual 2020s, and instead prefers a world that no longer exists: every cultural reference point he summons throughout the movie dates from around the middle of the 20h century. The reporter loves Show Boat. Later, he expresses his surprise and gratification that Frances makes reference to Frank Capra – then proceeds to recommend more of the director’s films, because she’s only seen two of them. A Zuckerberg handler makes reference to Gilligan’s Island to illustrate a point about the public’s gullibility. The most contemporary he gets, apart from the unavoidable current events, is name-checking Woodward and Bernstein. Has there ever been a movie that has somehow both depicted the Covid-19 pandemic and refused to acknowledge popular culture less than a half-century old?Doubtless he’d consider this a personal quirk; Sorkin loves musical theater and remembers classic-era television, and so shall his characters. What he’s unintentionally done is create a world nearly as insular and fantastical as the ones in early internet fantasies such as Hackers or Virtuosity, one where a Capra-esque triumph remains within arm’s reach of his plucky protagonist. Sorkin gets that the internet is a part of real life, not a mystical fad or a wholly internet world. He’s not raging against the machine, the way some of his detractors feared he might back in 2010. But his conception of real life itself feels stuck in a time that is, if not pre-internet, at very least pre-Trump. January 6 may have been a sobering event in that Facebook control room, but in this world, everyone was pardoned and the president who used social media to egg it was re-elected and further emboldened. Maybe, all these years later, those more alarmist takes on the internet via cinema weren’t so off-base after all. Compared with the rabbit holes of Eddington, the psychosis of Red Rooms, or even the mediated worlds of David Cronenberg’s The Shrouds, The Social Reckoning’s take on the internet movie doesn’t seem nearly paranoid, angry or scared enough. Sorkin may think he’s looking at the internet with clear eyes, but he’s wearing blinders.Explore more on these topicsDrama filmsAaron SorkinFacebookMikey MadisonJeremy StrongJeremy Allen WhiteSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Forever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with morals | Movies | The Guardian
description: Eamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition government
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Eamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition government
Content: One of the good guys … Eamon Ryan on the New York subway in Forever Is Now.Photograph: Soilsiú FilmsView image in fullscreenOne of the good guys … Eamon Ryan on the New York subway in Forever Is Now.Photograph: Soilsiú FilmsMoviesReviewForever Is Now review – political study of former Irish Green leader is like The Thick of It but with moralsEamon Ryan is shown to be principled, likable and hard working in a glowing portrait, filmed while serving in the country’s coalition governmentCath ClarkeTue 13 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis fly-on-the-wall documentary about theformer Irish Green party leader and cabinet minister Eamon Ryanreminded me of the political satire The Thick of It – but without the cynical gags and hapless self-serving politicians. Even after you factor in the skewing effect of it being a favourable portrait, showing him in the best possible light, Ryan comes across as one of the good guys: principled, likable and extremely hard working. The film follows his final 18 months serving in Ireland’s coalition government as minister for the environment and transport before stepping down in 2025.The title is something that Ryan’s 25-year-old son Tommy repeats over and over. “Forever … forever … forever.” Tommy is autistic and requires full-time care. When Ryan resigns from government, one of his reasons is to spend more time with Tommy. We see the pair of them at the allotment picking raspberries and walking the dog. But other than a quick glimpse of his wife, Victoria, the rest of Ryan’s family life is kept firmly behind closed doors.Instead, the cameras trail him on the road, talking to angry residents of an Irish town submerged by flood waters (again), and hustling at the UN general assembly in New York and two Cop conferences. At his side is formidable media adviser Edel Hackett (Malcolm Tucker with morals), who sifts through the daily torrent of online abuse, harassment and intimidation slung Ryan’s way.The film is lacking a little context: perhaps an interview or two with Ryan might have been helpful, giving some background to the Cop conferences and – for those unfamiliar with Irish politics – the ambitious climate laws he pushed through in office. Something on the general election wipeout of Greens in November 2024 would have been useful too. But no explanation is necessary watching Ryan’s crumpled crestfallen face in January 2025 as he packs up his ministerial office, watching Donald Trump’s inauguration on TV.Forever Is Now is in UK and Irish cinemas from 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGreen partyIrelandAutismEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champ | Movies | The Guardian
description: True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula
Content: Resident badass … Michelle Yeoh as Zhao Yanhong in It’s My Time.Photograph: Courtesy of Central City MediaView image in fullscreenResident badass … Michelle Yeoh as Zhao Yanhong in It’s My Time.Photograph: Courtesy of Central City MediaMoviesReviewIt’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champTrue story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formulaCath ClarkeTue 13 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprioeating raw bison liverto get into character, butMichelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cubeto prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship.Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.)Yeoh is enjoyably irascible as Zhao, who goes viral after thrashing a kid in her first competition. Her online fans call her “Grandma Zhao” and the film gently chips away at stereotypes of the older generation; fans assume Zhao is a cuddly elder, while younger cubers underestimate her skill and stamina. Yeoh brings intelligence to the role, but it’s odd that after making Zhao so testy and short-tempered, the film is all soft edges with a squishy centre. Next, can we expect a biopic of thesix-year-old Chinese girl who recently set a Rubik’s Cube world record, solving it in just over four seconds?It’s My Time is in UK cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsBiopicsPuzzle gamesSport filmsComedy filmsChinareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mag Mag review – giant female ghost loves people to death in Japanese comedy-horror  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sara Minami gives a wonderfully crazed performance in a twisted, fresh take on the genre as Yuriyan Retriever’s debut feature examines infatuation, bullying and beauty norms
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Sara Minami gives a wonderfully crazed performance in a twisted, fresh take on the genre as Yuriyan Retriever’s debut feature examines infatuation, bullying and beauty norms
Content: Bizarre … Sara Minami as Sanae and Oshiro Maeda as Hiroshi in Mag Mag.Photograph: Courtesy of Blue Finch Film ReleasingView image in fullscreenBizarre … Sara Minami as Sanae and Oshiro Maeda as Hiroshi in Mag Mag.Photograph: Courtesy of Blue Finch Film ReleasingMoviesReviewMag Mag review – giant female ghost loves people to death in Japanese comedy-horrorSara Minami gives a wonderfully crazed performance in a twisted, fresh take on the genre as Yuriyan Retriever’s debut feature examines infatuation, bullying and beauty normsLeslie FelperinTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in the 90s and 00s, Japanese horror (or “J-horror” if you want to save on syllables) wasmuch admired, reasonably widely distributed and sometimesremade in other languages. They never actually stopped making them in Japan, but the results don’t seem to get as much crossover exposure as they used to. That may be because we have quite enough horror getting made closer to home, especially since it’s so remunerative at the box office.Nevertheless, it’s good to see evidence that the genre keeps evolving in Japan just as it does everywhere else, and there is something tangibly fresh and kicky about this low-budget horror-comedy amalgam. Made bycomedian Yuriyan Retriever, an irrepressible character whose dadaist shtick got her onAmerica’s Got Talent twice, makes her directorial debut with this satirical ghost story which sends up male misogyny and women’s obsession with romance alike.Told in a series of interrelated chapters, the plot explores encounters with Mag Mag, a female ghost notable for her height (two metres), wild mane of hair, and generous proportions that go against Japan’s petite female beauty norms. When Mag Mag falls in love with a cute guy, he’s done for, because she will pursue him to the death – a passion that is finally consummated with fatal throttling and sucking out thelimerent object’seyes (a step beyond merely boiling the family bunny à la Fatal Attraction).Mag Mag’s backstory doesn’t get fully fleshed out until the last section, but Yuriyan rather implies she was a fat high school girl bullied into killing herself by mean classmates who therefore deserve persecution. (There’s a twist in store, however – one that really upends viewers’ assumptions about bullying victims.) Meanwhile, the obsessions of another young woman called Sanae (played by Sara Minami, delivering a truly crazed comic performance), who is also in love with one of Mag Mag’s victims, shows that women are just as capable of toxicity as men if they put their minds to it.There’s a bizarre sequence in which Sanae slathers her entire body in lubricant and forces her way through a sphincter-like orifice located where the mouth should be in a giant portrait of the guy that she is obsessed with, which is worthy of cult Japanese trash auteurTakashi Miikeat his most deranged. Somehow it’s not surprising to learn that Miike is one of the backers of Mag Mag, a sign that the older generation of Japanese horrormeisters are passing on the torch.Mag Mag is on digital platforms from 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsComedy filmsJapanAsia PacificComedyTakashi MiikereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The play that changed my life: ‘I was the badass queen in Titus Andronicus – we did it like A Nightmare on Elm Street’ | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effect
Author: Moira Buffini
Headline: Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effect
Content: Carnage … Flora Spencer-Longhurst (Lavinia) and William Houston (Titus) in Titus Andronicus at Shakespeare's Globe theatre, London, in 2014.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCarnage … Flora Spencer-Longhurst (Lavinia) and William Houston (Titus) in Titus Andronicus at Shakespeare's Globe theatre, London, in 2014.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe play that changed my lifeTheatreThe play that changed my life: ‘I was the badass queen in Titus Andronicus – we did it like A Nightmare on Elm Street’Shakespeare’s bloody revenge-fest is full of horror and grotesquerie but the camaraderie of performing it with a youth theatre had an upbeat effectMoira BuffiniTue 13 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTitus Andronicus has to be among William Shakespeare’s worst plays. In fact TS Eliot called it “one of the stupidest and most uninspired plays ever written”. Yet it holds a very special place in my heart. It’s a bloody revenge-fest in which each act of violence is more grotesque than the last. Titus Andronicus returns from war with “barbarous” Tamora, “Queen of the Goths”, as his prisoner. She stealthily proceeds to kill and destroy his family, and when he discovers this, he murders her sons and serves them up to her in a pie. The play ends with gudgeons of fake blood and a sea of carnage. In Shakespeare’s day it was a huge hit, a kind of slasher film of the 16th century.Plays are very powerful things and I have spent my life watching them and writing them. Some have been revelatory but none has affected me likeTitus Andronicus. It was the first play, outside of school, that I was ever in – so I suppose this is about the transformative power of youth theatre.My family were going through some difficult years and I had been “asked to leave” my small-town Catholic school (it’s still hard to say I was expelled). I was feeling pretty low. When I got into the National YouthTheatre, it felt like someone had offered me a lifeline, away from the circumstances I was in. I got to escape from north Wales for a few weeks and I went to London for the first time.View image in fullscreenUtterly ruthless … Estelle Kohler as Tamora, centre, with Piers Ibbotson and Richard McCabe in Titus Andronicus at the Pit, Barbican, London, in 1988.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianI found myself in a diverse company of young people from all over the UK. We didn’t understand a word of Titus Andronicus. We could hardly say it aloud. But our director was adamant that we could do it, so we flung ourselves in. I discovered the level of collaboration that happens when you’re rehearsing a play. The camaraderie wasn’t like anything I had experienced before. It was exhilarating. Being thrown in at the deep end made me unafraid of Shakespeare. It made me instinctively appreciate the way his language worked. More importantly, I began to have faith in who I was.To see or not to see? Every single Shakespeare play – ranked!Read moreI got cast as Queen Tamora. I learned her lines on the tube, saying them over and over. She was wronged, she was utterly ruthless and depraved. She was a mature woman, not a teenager like me, and she had badass lines. She was an absolutely transgressional woman. Being Tamora made me straighten my shoulders and stand strong.We put on our production in a school gym. In the performances, we went for the grotesquerie, full-throttle. I remember the faces of my fellow cast members, playing the shock and horror of the play’s murders as if it was A Nightmare on Elm Street. I’ve got no idea what the experience was like for our audience but by the time the production was finished, something in me had shifted. I saw a new direction in life. I got my act together, applied to study drama and I moved down to London. A bit of barbarous Tamora had rubbed off on me.Flarestorm by Moira Buffini is published by Faber on 22 October.Order your copy from guardianbookshop.com. title: ‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All Time | Music | The Guardian
description: Raised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndrome
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Raised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndrome
Content: ‘The universe rewards confidence’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyView image in fullscreen‘The universe rewards confidence’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyMusicInterview‘Girls aren’t supposed to be cocky’: Sophia Stel on the pressure of writing The Greatest Album Of All TimeTiffany LaiRaised as one of 11, the Vancouver artist (and model) is now signed by A24. She talks about her ultra-religious childhood and how – despite her album title – she still suffers from imposter syndromeTue 13 Oct 2026 06.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time Sophia Stel came to London, she slept outside in the freezing cold. The Vancouver songwriter had finished a live set last autumn, then gone out until 3am with her then crush, but when they returned to their Airbnb, they found that Stel’s manager had dead-bolted the door and fallen asleep. Stel plus crush looked for a hotel but ultimately had no choice but to kip on the doorstep. “We hadn’t spent that much time together and I got to see how she was in a stressful situation,” Stel says, smiling at the memory. “She kept her vibe up and tried to solve it – I knew I was so in love then.”A lot has changed in Stel’s life in the year since. She opened her business bank account as an artist, and that crush is now her girlfriend. “It’s a lot of change, but maybe because of my Sagittarius moon, I’m fine with it to an extent,” she says, only half-joking, when we meet at her publicist’s office in south London, the 27-year-old Stel in her uniform of vintage hoodie and Adidas trackies.Stel started gaining attention last summer when her swaggering, lonely-dancefloor banger I’ll Take It exploded on TikTok, then honed her sound – AutoTuned vocals merging with hazy electropop – over two EPs. She recorded the second, How to Win at Solitaire, in the basement of the Vancouver club where she worked, and it seemed to absorb a bittersweet afterparty energy through the walls. She soon signed with chic film production company A24’s record label, andLordeinvited her to support her live.So having ticked off so many achievements so quickly, why shouldn’t she call her debut LP The Greatest Album of all Time? The title comes from an interview in which Stel joked that, like everyone else, she wanted to make the greatest album of all time. “They made it the cover of the Instagram carousel and I was like, ‘I did not mean that,’” she says. “This is the type of pressure I’m trying to avoid!” So the title is mostly tongue-in-cheek but not entirely. “I think the universe rewards confidence, and sometimes as a girl, you’re not allowed to be as cocky. It’s nice to try and have a louder voice. It’s something I’m working on in my life.”Becoming a pop star has been a lesson in overcoming imposter syndrome. This past year, Stel has balanced performing with odd jobs painting houses and bartending. “I was so broke but I had never been around so many crazy wealthy people at the same time,” she says. “Sometimes I struggle with overextending myself financially because I want to feel rich … who doesn’t?”Her debut, almost all of it self-produced, tackles all of this with typically sly humour. On the skittering, bratty anthem Bitches Talk Shit, she protests: “’Cause you’re a rockstar you should have a lot of money / Course I am a pop star but I’m still very up and coming,” while the narcotised drawl of On My Dick reflects the whiplash experience of her meteoric year: “Scarlet told me no new friends / Cause all they want is dividends.”View image in fullscreen‘Being sceptical has helped me keep my sanity’ … Sophia Stel.Photograph: Mark HunterUnsurprisingly, Stel keeps her circle close. She lives with two of her younger brothers and her best friend in a Vancouver apartment, paying an enviable 650CA$ (£300) each. “They all come in and out of my room while I’m making music and I can tell if something’s fun because they’ll stick around for a while,” she smiles.For most of her life, Stel has lived with a lot of people. She grew up as one of 11 in an ultra-religious family, and describes her upbringing as “overstimulating” and “very extreme”. She found organised religion “really damaging” and has long since parted ways with it. “When you’re so indoctrinated growing up, you have to be conscious of what you believe in,” she says. “You learn a lot about listening to yourself and your body.”Strangely, that sounds like experience that could help her navigate her new career. “It has helped in industry decisions because if I’m told that things are one way, I’m sceptical,” she admits. “That’s proven to be really helpful in keeping my sanity.”View image in fullscreen‘One baby goat snapped in half and the other suffocated’ … the cover art for The Greatest Album of All Time.Photograph: Mikaela KautzkyStel also works as a model, despite hating being photographed. “Though I do love that it allows me to become financially stable,” she says. The brutal casting process contributed to the bluster in her lyrics. “I wanted to make an album that gave me the energy to get up and go to castings where I’m sure I’m not going to be selected, and still be confident.”Modelling for it-girl brands such as Gimaguas is in stark contrast to how Stel presents herself. For the cover of Greatest, she chose a poetic image of herself aged seven cradling a dead baby goat – a dark riff on the “greatest of all time” acronym – on the family farm. “I was sleeping in the barn with my best friend every night in the weeks leading up to the birth,” she says. When it came, “one of the babies was sideways and got snapped in half so the other one suffocated inside. That’s the one I’m holding.”And despite early acclaim for the record, Stel doesn’t put much stock in the opinion of others. “I had a park day with my brother last year where we smoked a joint and played soccer,” she says. “I was so happy and it felt very similar to playing my biggest show. That’s made me really conscious of what I do – I’m not going to chase a feeling if it’s going to feel pretty similar to a really good day doing anything else.”The Greatest Album of All Time is released via A24 Music on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled | Games | The Guardian
description: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull
Content: A woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiView image in fullscreenA woman on a mission … Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont's Curse.Photograph: KonamiGamesReviewCastlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilledEvil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, XboxThere are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dullHarper Jay MacIntyreTue 13 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed.Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull.To its benefit, Belmont’s Curse doesn’t pull any punches. Literally. The smallest minion can land a heavy blow and dodging even basic attacks, though occasionally counterintuitive, forces the player to intimately learn enemy habits. Every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled: bats burst into blood, demons burn to cinders. Every battle holds fresh twists and gimmicks.View image in fullscreenA significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges … Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.Photograph: KonamiExploration is less about remembering old, previously inaccessible routes then circling back, so much as mastering challenge rooms full of buzzsaws and blood pits. Learning how to juggle multiple tools at once becomes crucial, as some rooms start to resemble the notoriously tough platformer Super Meat Boy more than Symphony of the Night. Navigating these challenges requires acrobatics, air dashes and death-defying leaps. And while Castlevania veterans may expect something more subtle (secret-hunting and puzzle-solving is the classic stuff of the series), a significant portion of the maps is devoted to platforming challenges.As Rose progresses, she gains new magical attacks via tarot cards, and tools for reaching new areas. This is, however, an inconsistent game world. The castle library offers notebook-worthy puzzles, including a cathedral hidden within a cursed portrait that tasks you with playing music on a magic organ. After that, however, you might have to explore underground waterways packed with uninspired combat challenges. This may be the most virtually striking Castlevania since 2002’s Harmony of Dissonance and sometimes it’s also the most inventive and brain-teasing. In other moments, you’ll be bored to bloody tears.Belmont’s Curse improves considerably after an early twist forces Rose to grapple with the Belmont family legacy and her own anger. Once you’re out of the Parisian streets and into Dracula’s castle, there’s far more to love.The result is an earnest, likable game. There are undeniable shortcomings and moments of curse-worthy frustration, but every now and again, there is real cleverness on display, even if Belmont’s Curse can’t quite match contemporary peers such as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown or Hollow Knight: Silksong – the trendsetter now feels like something of a trend-chaser. For most Castlevania players, this will be more than enough. You have a whip, a castle, and a dark lord. Do you really need anything else?Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is released on 15 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesNintendo SwitchPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Our Bodies Have Been Bridges review – riveting portraits and the story of the first woman on Earth | Art | The Guardian
description: The three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communities
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: The three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communities
Content: Quiet and minimal … Laura Aguilar, Motion #50, 1999.Photograph: © Laura AguilarView image in fullscreenQuiet and minimal … Laura Aguilar, Motion #50, 1999.Photograph: © Laura AguilarArtReviewOur Bodies Have Been Bridges review – riveting portraits and the story of the first woman on EarthAutograph, LondonThe three-person headline show looking at South American feminism is displayed alongside Charan Singh: Your Tongue in My Mouth, an intimate study of Indian trans communitiesCharlotte JansenTue 13 Oct 2026 07.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 1990s, the late Chicana artist Laura Aguilar was living with depression. A friend took her on a road trip to New Mexico, where Aguilar made some nude self-portraits in the mystical landscapes. Those photographs evolved into a pivotal series shot in desert environments across the American south-west, Aguilar’s notable 1996 Nature Self-Portrait – considered an early work of intersectional feminist art, before the word had entered academic discourse.London gallery Autograph first worked on an exhibition of Aguilar’s in 1997, the year after she made Nature Self-Portrait, so this is something of a homecoming, a generation on. Aguilar’s contours, folds, and crevices sometimes disappear into the barren desert landscapes, assimilating the shapes of boulders or trees; at other times, her body is incongruous, soft flesh that can’t be held by the harsh, barren conditions. These images capture the paradox of a body that is both hypervisible and ignored.Several works from Nature Self-Portrait appear at the beginning of Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Autograph’s new three-person headline show. They’re so quiet and minimal, shot in black and white, they’d be easy to coast past – which is partly Aguilar’s point. Bodies like hers – large, queer, Chicana – had no visibility in culture at the time Aguilar made these works, while in real life her experiences were of an uncomfortable, scrutinised presence. Out here in the terrain of nowhere, Aguilar returns her body to the earth – a body wanting to just be a body, to not ache to fit in. A body with the same cracks, dents and curves as the land; hardy, wild and free. They’re photographs about rejection, but also embrace.View image in fullscreenRemembered scenes … Koyoltzintli, Mom curing me from the evil eye, c.1990 from Other Stories/Historias Bravas, 2011-2012.Photograph: © Koyoltzintli. Courtesy the artist.This is the beginning of three concurrent exhibitions at Autograph about rebellious bodies. In the first and largest, Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Aguilar’s story continues through two younger artists who also use their bodies as anchors, in pursuit of healing, truth and connection to ancestral female knowledge. In a diaristic, family album-style account of matriarchy and ritual, Other Stories/Historias Bravas, the artist Koyoltzintli re-enacts remembered scenes from her childhood in the Andean mountains of Ecuador.Her bare breasts are blessed by her aunt, for protection. In another picture, her mother braids her hair tenderly, the same way, the caption tells us, her grandmother had once done for her. Her mum takes her to sit among the iguanas at the local park, to cure her of her phobia of the reptiles. Routines of care passed down generations of women, through their bodies. Tangible, physical, felt knowledge and history is reflected in Koyoltzintli’s very direct, intimate approach to photography. In a group of works from the series Meda – indebted to Aguilar’s self-portraits – Koyoltzintli asked women to interact with the land as their ancestors might have, to trace a collective, imagined, silent story of the first woman on Earth. An alternative origin story.These works appear with Peruvian Tarrah Krajnak’s grainy, photocopied, archival images that focus on 1979 – the year the military regime ended in Peru, and also the year of the artist’s birth. The works explore the dissonance between women’s bodies portrayed in the country’s media and the private, personal experiences of living as a woman through that time and the years of armed conflict that followed. She takes images cribbed from newspapers and magazines published that year, and to query their veracity, photocopies, rephotographs, and interrupts them with her own image. The bodies here are agitated, unstable and unresolved.Upstairs, this dovetails seamlessly into Charan Singh’s Your Tongue in My Mouth. As the unforgettable title promises, Singh’s work is a joyful provocation, but also a serious meditation on desirability, sexuality and reciprocity – when certain bodies are seen by some as a burden, a threat.View image in fullscreenRiveting and regal … Charan Singh, Rasili, 2026.Photograph: © Charan SinghSingh’s lucid colour portraits of Hijra, Kothi and trans people combine a realist sensibility and theatricality – the subjects’ authenticity contrasts with choreographed poses; beautiful hand-painted backdrops behind them evoke a world of fantasy and escape. Riveting, regal portraits such as Umrao and Sonu have a timeless elegance: the subjects’ decision to wear traditional salwar kameez or anarkali-style dress, ornate brocade fabrics, their bodies adorned with henna and bindi, are intentional gestures that they also belong to a longer history in south Asia. These portraits are statements of dignity that claim their right to that place without words or apology.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe subtle tension between realism and artifice takes on a particular urgency against the backdrop of India’s deteriorating trans rights. In March 2026, legislative amendments to the country’s Transgender Persons Act 2019 rolled back protections for gender self-identification, raising profound questions about bodily autonomy, recognition and the right to define oneself. A timeline of transgender history and rights, displayed on a table at the centre of Singh’s exhibition, situates these intimate portraits within a longer struggle for visibility and legal recognition, grounding their gestures of self-fashioning and self-expression in a shifting and often hostile political reality.AtAutograph, Londonuntil 13 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtExhibitionsPhotographyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Georg Baselitz: The Heroes review – astonishing paintings take a savage swipe at history | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at
Content: Frankensteinian monsters … Georg Baselitz, 1. Kopf (1. Head), 1966.Photograph: Friedrich Rosenstiel, Köln. © Georg Baselitz 2026.View image in fullscreenFrankensteinian monsters … Georg Baselitz, 1. Kopf (1. Head), 1966.Photograph: Friedrich Rosenstiel, Köln. © Georg Baselitz 2026.Art and designReviewGeorg Baselitz: The Heroes review – astonishing paintings take a savage swipe at historyThaddaeus Ropac, LondonThe artist captures horror, disgust and guilt over Germany’s Nazi past. The colossal results are so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat atJonathan JonesTue 13 Oct 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the German painter Georg Baselitz died this year a chunk of Europe’s rapidly diminishing historical memory went with him. Baselitz was born in 1938, experienced Hitler’s Germany and the second world war as a young child, then found himself growing up in communist East Germany before escaping to the west and becoming an artist. His acidic, honest perceptions of the history he’d lived throughwill no longer be those of the living personI was lucky enough to encounter. But he has left us a gift: an exhibition in London he helped plan of his most astonishing history paintings, The Heroes.It’s a savage, merciless vision of modern history with feelings of horror, disgust and irreparable guilt hanging heavy in the poisoned air. But there’s a terrible joy too, the thrill of speaking the truth. You sense the liberation Baselitz must have felt when he set brush to canvas to start these paintings in 1965. Comparing the explosive rage and nihilism of his art to punk may be inadequate but the title of this series of colossal imaginary portraits is so scathingly ironic it’s like being spat at.View image in fullscreenMit Roter Fahne (With Red Flag), 1965.Photograph: Ed Gumuchian/Courtesy private collection. © Georg Baselitz 2026.Mit Rote Fahne – or With the Red Banner – depicts a massive, square-shouldered yet exhausted soldier holding a half-lowered flag that is a smear of red and black. A banner of blood, the redness congeals to form black scabs that suggest the shadow of the swastika. All around the soldier is a wasteland. Do we owe him compassion? No, he had none. The devastated world at his feet was destroyed by Germany’s heroes who fought in the second world war. When Baselitz painted these furious homages in the mid-1960s, these men were running West Germany’s banks and car companies.Another long-haired Hero, in a uniform with shorts, stands in a trashed, blood-stained landscape. This bland-faced character balances two crimson mittens, preparing apparently to let them go and to live on without these gory encumbrances, with clean hands.It’s as if Baselitz was walking around the increasingly affluent streets of West Germany, seeing healthy, optimistic faces and retching at how easily the crimes of the second world war could be shoved into the past. The Holocaust only ended 20 years ago, these paintings scream, when the armies advancing on Hitler’s Reich discovered the places where six million Jews were systematically murdered – how can we Germans hold our heads high and strut on?View image in fullscreenEin Moderner Maler (A Modern Painter), 1966.Photograph: Courtesy Berlinische Galerie - Museum of Modern Art, Photography and Architecture. © Georg Baselitz 2026.But if Germany is mired in shame, what about German art? Baselitz and his artistic peers Joseph Beuys and Anselm Kiefer, all of whom face German history head on, were sometimes accused by critics of glorifying it, or feasting on it, but there’s no hint of Teutonic grandeur here. In Ein Moderner Maler – A modern painter – Baselitz depicts an artist who can’t work because both hands are caught in man-traps. He sits defeated on the ground in military-looking clothes with armbands, as guilty and mad as all the other Heroes. He literally spills his guts in a parody of inner angst: a curl of intestines lies between his legs, while another section of bowel emerges from his side and becomes a spiralling pig’s tail. This is what the German artist’s romantic inner life has become. It’s OK to laugh. His hair is flattened on his head and he has a hint of a square moustache to remind you that Hitler, too, fancied himself an artist.Georg Baselitz – a life in picturesRead moreBaselitz reserves his deepest disgust for his own artistic mastery: painting has been smashed, it is no longer possible, say these brilliant paintings. Their uncoordinated, lumpen figures look like Frankensteinian monsters, made from bits and pieces of mud and flesh pathetically sewn together. One soldier, sitting under the trees, has a square head on top of a slumped, square body as blood drips on his head from two branches. He is a ghost inside his garments, there and not there.View image in fullscreenSchwarzgrundig (Black Grounded), 1966.Photograph: Mick Vincenz, Essen/MKM Museum Küppersmühle for Modern Art, Duisburg, Ströher Collection. © Georg Baselitz 2026.This way of depicting the human figure makes Baselitz unique. He has little in common with British postwar figurative artists such as Bacon and Freud for whom there is always a real, pulsing body they’re trying to record. Baselitz’s bodies are abstract, designed with irony and black humour, their sufferings absurd. Another Hero stands with his flies undone, grey spurts of semen emerging from his black trousers as he towers over a shattered landscape. His ecstatic expression tells us he’s turned on by it all while at his feet is a Disneyish duck, an emblem perhaps of the innocence he will feign in postwar life.What has happened to the art of memory? After all the artistic reckonings, the history books and Holocaust memorials, the far-right AfD is winning one election after another in Germany. For extremists of all hues it isn’t even necessary to deny the Holocaust – nowadays you can shrug it off, trivialise it, dismiss it as belonging to the distant past. And the Heroes walk again. Baselitz paints one of them waving, or is it saluting, in blood-soaked trousers with a ghostly shadow of a face. Around him in the European night white flecks fall slowly, like snow or ashes.At Thaddaeus Ropac Gallery, London, until 18 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designGermanyEuropeExhibitionsPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus  | Germany holidays | The Guardian
description: From ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn break
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn break
Content: Erfurt Cathedral in Thuringia.Photograph: Mo-Jo-Lo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErfurt Cathedral in Thuringia.Photograph: Mo-Jo-Lo/Getty ImagesGermany holidays‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by busFrom ancient forests to spas, medieval cities and the birthplace of Bauhaus, Thuringia packs a punch for a car-free autumn breakVeidehi GiteTue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germany’s Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaringmedieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa,the world’s largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries.Thuringia – often called the “green heart of Germany” – lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. It’s famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and I’m here for four days to explore using public transport.Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatz’s morning market, it’s just a short walk to one of the town’s other famous sights, the 120-metre-longKrämerbrücke– a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses.View image in fullscreenThe Krämerbrucke in Erfurt.Photograph: Sergey Dzyuba/AlamyErfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchants’ houses came partly fromwaid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) toPetersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root – Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in theAugustinian monastery(you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight).double quotation markWeimar, the birthplace of Bauhaus, and where Germany’s first democratic constitution was adopted, is full of historic sites and design gemsDinner is in a suitably historic setting;Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weißen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious).Next morning, I head toEgapark(a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses theGerman Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting.View image in fullscreenThe Bauhaus Museum in Weimar.Photograph: Imago/AlamyThe city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germany’s first democratic constitution was adopted, it’s full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit theBauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-Universität.The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to “cure, to relax, to refresh”.Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, theFriederiken Thermeis the town’s main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: atFriederikenschlösschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe thermal baths at Friederiken Therme in Bad Langensalza.Photograph: Imago/AlamyBut it’s the town’s gardens that really win me over. I wander Friederikenschlösschen’s restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden,Kofuku no Niwa(Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines.For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus toHainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germany’s largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. “Parts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,” says park director Rüdiger Biehl.Before hitting the trail, I stop at the park’s restaurant,Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch – roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold Köstritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, it’s mostly just the birds making noise – chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk.View image in fullscreenHainich national park.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamyTheBaumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. It’s a spectacular view, but the forest’s real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechstein’s bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season atTheaterplatz. It’s a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that I’ve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety – and all accessible with a few short bus rides.The trip was provided by theGerman National Tourist Board.Dorint Hotel am Domin Erfurthas doubles from £85. title: The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel
Content: Chicken broth needs to be barely simmered, andveryslowly, so don’t cluck it up by boiling it fast.Photograph: photovs/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenChicken broth needs to be barely simmered, andveryslowly, so don’t cluck it up by boiling it fast.Photograph: photovs/Getty Images/iStockphotoKitchen aideChefsThe secret to a non-cloudy chicken stockDon’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panelAnna BerrillTue 13 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy is my chicken stock always cloudy?Ryan, by emailFrom broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead. “It’s an underestimated kitchen job,” says Adam Byatt, chef/owner ofTrinity, in southwest London, and author ofTrinity: The Cookbook, which is published next week. “I love stock: it’s wholesome and fruitful, frugal and delicious.”Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author ofLozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.Lloyd Morse, chef and co-owner ofThe Palmerstonin Edinburgh, meanwhile, likes to simmer the bones first, “shoogling them occasionally”, to bring more of the scum to the surface: “You really need to skim the life out of it.” It’s only at this point that he adds the veg: “And keep skimming that top layer,” he says, adding that it’s important to be aware that “the more agitation or the hotter the pot gets, the cloudier the stock will be”.Essentially, “if nothing is ever actually boiled, Ryan’s stock should be nice and clear”, says Louis Lingwood, head chef atOsteria Vibratoin London, who cooks his chicken stock “on the lowest possible heat for a whole day”, before discarding the bones and leaving the stock to sit until all the fat rises to the top. Skim that off with a ladle, then reduce the stock very slowly.Lingwood has another trick up his sleeve to guarantee a clearer stock: get it in the freezer. “Defrost it through a sieve lined with muslin (or through a lined perforated tray), and the stock will be crystal clear.” Speaking of the freezer, freezing stock in ice-cube trays, then whacking them in a sealed container, is a welcome manoeuvre for those occasions when only small quantities of stock are required.Of course, Ryan could make his life a whole lot easier by simply cooking his stock in the oven, Morse says: “My top tip is to make it in an oven-safe dish, such as a Le Creuset [other brands are, of course, available], then pop it in the oven overnight to cook super slowly,” by which he means about 90C. “The indirect heat makes the clearest stock possible, plus, when you wake up, you’ll have a lovely smell in the kitchen.” Convenience food at its best.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Cook once, eat twice: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Roast chicken thighs with roasted squash, leeks and two punchy dressings
Author: Rukmini Iyer
Headline: Roast chicken thighs with roasted squash, leeks and two punchy dressings
Content: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeks.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeks.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.Cook once, eat twiceFoodCook once, eat twice: Rukmini Iyer’s miso chilli chicken recipeRoast chicken thighs with roast squash, leeks and two punchy dressingsRukmini IyerTue 13 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m delighted that it’s roasting tin season once again, and what better way to kick it off than with this chuck-it-in-the-oven sticky miso chilli chicken with squash and leeks? The sesame, miso, garlic and ginger marinade can go on the chicken ahead of time if you like (in which case, I’d include a squeeze of lime juice), but if you’re short on time, five minutes before cooking will do the trick. The vegetables cook under the chicken, in the manner of potatoes sitting under a rotisserie chicken, but with the added hit of flavour from the miso. Then, to make it really sing, there’s a punchy sesame, chilli and coriander dressing to finish.Miso chilli chicken with roast squash and leeksPrep15 minCook1 hr 10 minServes2,with leftovers30ml sesame oil60g miso paste– red or white, either works4garlic cloves, peeled and finely grated5cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely grated3 medium leeks, trimmed and cut into 2½cm-thick rounds1 medium butternut squash, peeled, halved, deseeded and cut into 4cm chunks1-1.2kgskin-on bone-in chicken thighsFor the dressing1tbsp soy sauce30ml sesame oilFinely grated zest and juice of 1 unwaxed lime2 spring onions, trimmed and finely chopped1 red chilli, finely sliced (pith and seeds removed if you want less heat)10g fresh coriander, roughly choppedSea salt, to tasteHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Mix the sesame oil, miso, garlic and ginger in a bowl, then use a heaped tablespoon of this mix to coat the leeks and squash in a large roasting tin. (The tin should be big enough that everything almost sits in one layer.)Slash each chicken thigh a couple of times with a sharp knife, then put them on top of the vegetables. Spread the remaining miso mix on top of each piece of chicken, then bake for one hour, until the chicken is well browned and cooked through, and the vegetables soft.When the tin has 10 minutes left in the oven, make the dressing. Whisk the soy sauce, sesame oil, lime juice and zest, spring onions, chilli and coriander in a bowl, taste and add a little sea salt or more soy sauce, if required.Drizzle the dressing all over the chicken and vegetables, and serve hot.Eat twiceIt’s never a bad idea to have half a tray of leftover roast chicken in the fridge, so even if cooking for two, I’d make the whole quantity and save the rest for epic next-day leftovers. My favourite thing to do is make a cracking peanut sauce-topped rice bowl: put Italian short-grain rice on to boil (half an hour), finely grate a carrot and a handful of fresh herbs (mint, coriander), then whisk 60g peanut butter (smooth or crunchy, cook’s choice), the zest and juice of one lime, 20ml soy sauce and a scant teaspoon of palm or dark brown sugar. Loosen with a tablespoon or so of water, until the mix is the texture of single cream, then taste and add a pinch more salt if needed – it should taste strong and punchy. (If your lime wasn’t particularly juicy, add more lime juice, too.) To serve, shred the leftover chicken (heat through with a tablespoon of water in a covered bowl for 40 seconds in the microwave), and reheat the leftover squash and leeks. Drain the rice well, dress with a tablespoon of oil, then divide between two bowls. Top with the chicken, the hot veg, and the carrot and herb mixture, then drizzle the peanut dressing all over the top. Finish with extra chopped peanuts and chilli, if you wish.Explore more on these topicsFoodCook once, eat twiceChickenMeatVegetablesAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content
